s: Welcome to the Loop, the commercial heart of Chicago, and one of the best places on earth to see how the modern city was invented.
The name comes from transportation.

In the late nineteenth century, cable car lines turned around in loops downtown, and in 1897 the elevated railroad tied its lines together in a ring of steel tracks above Wabash Avenue, Lake Street, Wells Street, and Van Buren Street.
That ring is still running over your head.
Strictly speaking, the Loop is the district inside it, but Chicagoans use the word for all of downtown.
Almost nothing you will see on this walk is older than 1871.
On the night of October eighth that year, a fire started in a barn on the West Side, near the property of Patrick and Catherine O'Leary.
The story that Mrs. O'Leary's cow kicked over a lantern is a legend, one a newspaper reporter later admitted he made up, and the city council formally cleared her in 1997.
But the fire was real.
Driven by a strong southwest wind across a city built largely of wood, it jumped the river and burned for more than a day.
It killed about three hundred people, left roughly a hundred thousand homeless, and destroyed the downtown almost completely.
What came next is the reason this tour exists.
Chicago rebuilt fast, and land in the center became fantastically valuable.
Architects and engineers, many of them young and drawn here by the rebuilding, faced a simple problem: how to stack more rentable offices on a small lot.
Masonry walls had to get thicker and thicker at the base the higher a building rose.
The answer was a skeleton of iron and then steel carrying the weight, with the outer walls hung on it like a skin.
Add the safety elevator, fireproofing, and plate glass, and you have the skyscraper.
William Le Baron Jenney's Home Insurance Building, finished in 1885 at LaSalle and Adams and demolished in 1931, is often called the first, though historians argue over the title.
The people who worked out the details are known as the Chicago School: Daniel Burnham and John Wellborn Root, William Holabird and Martin Roche, Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan.

Look for their signatures as you walk: steel frames expressed on the outside, wide three-part windows that came to be called Chicago windows, and, from Sullivan, ornament that seems to grow out of the building like a plant.
A generation later, a German émigré named Ludwig Mies van der Rohe arrived and made the steel frame itself into the art, in black steel and glass.
And in the 1960s and 1970s, the city added monumental public sculpture to its plazas by Picasso, Calder, Miró, and Chagall, all within a few blocks of each other.

We will start at the Willis Tower, on the west edge of the Loop, then visit the Board of Trade at the foot of LaSalle Street, and walk east and north through the heart of the Loop, finishing under the marquee of the Chicago Theatre.
Keep an ear out for the elevated trains, and keep looking up.
You're at the base of the Willis Tower, on Wacker Drive at Adams Street.
For most Chicagoans it will always be the Sears Tower.
When it was finished in 1973, it was the tallest building in the world, at a hundred and ten stories, and it held that title for almost twenty-five years.
It was built for Sears, Roebuck and Company, then the largest retailer on earth.
Richard Sears was a railroad station agent in Minnesota who started selling watches by mail in the 1880s.

He moved to Chicago and joined forces with a watchmaker named Alvah Roebuck, and their catalog grew into a book of more than a thousand pages that sold almost everything: clothes, tools, stoves, medicine, guns, even complete houses, shipped as kits by rail.
For farm families far from any town, the Sears catalog was the store.
In the Jim Crow South, Black customers could order from it without facing the humiliations of a white-owned store.
The man who turned Sears into a giant was Julius Rosenwald, whose name you'll hear again in Hyde Park and Bronzeville.
The tower was designed by Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, with the architect Bruce Graham and the engineer Fazlur Khan.
Look up and you'll see that it isn't one block but a bundle of nine square tubes, tied together.
The tubes stop at different heights, two at the fiftieth floor, two at the sixty-sixth, three at the ninetieth, and two go all the way to the top.
The setbacks were partly for the wind, and partly because Sears wanted big floors at the bottom for its own offices and smaller floors higher up to rent.
Sears moved its headquarters to the suburbs in the 1990s, and the building was renamed in 2009 for an insurance company.

On the hundred and third floor, the Skydeck has glass boxes that stick out from the side of the building, so you can stand with nothing but glass between you and the street, more than thirteen hundred feet below.
Inside the lobby on Wacker Drive, look for a large moving sculpture by Alexander Calder called Universe, with a sun, a pendulum, and spinning spirals.
It was unveiled the same day in 1974 as the Flamingo, which you'll see later on this walk.
You heard that the tower's engineer was Fazlur Khan.
He's one of the most important figures in the history of tall buildings, and his road to this corner was a long one.
Khan was born in 1929 in Dhaka, in what is now Bangladesh, the son of a mathematics teacher.

He studied engineering in Calcutta and Dhaka, and in 1952 he crossed the world on a Fulbright scholarship to the University of Illinois, where in three years he earned two master's degrees and a doctorate.
In 1955 he joined Skidmore, Owings and Merrill in Chicago, and apart from a short spell back home, he stayed for the rest of his life.
His gift was to see a skyscraper as a single problem in physics.
Above a certain height, the real enemy isn't the weight of the floors but the wind, pushing on one side of the building like a hand on a lever.
On the Michigan Avenue tour you'll hear how he answered it at the Hancock Center.
Here he took the same thinking further, binding several stiff tubes into one.
There's a story, told by people who worked with him, that the bundled tube was first explained with a handful of cigarettes, held upright in a fist and pushed down to different lengths.
Most versions give the cigarettes to the architect, Bruce Graham.
Whether it happened just that way, nobody can say, but it's a fair picture of the tower above you.
Khan never thought engineering was only engineering.
In 1971, when war broke out in what was then East Pakistan, he worked from Chicago to raise money and lobby Washington for the new country of Bangladesh.
Later he engineered the Hajj Terminal at the airport in Jeddah, in Saudi Arabia, a vast field of white fabric tents that shelters pilgrims on their way to Mecca.
A line of his is often quoted: the technical man must not be lost in his own technology; he must be able to appreciate life, and life is art, drama, music, and most importantly, people.
He died of a heart attack on a trip to Jeddah in 1982, at fifty-two.
He's buried in Graceland Cemetery on the North Side, near many of the architects you'll hear about today, and there's a sculpture in his honor here in the tower.
You heard how Sears grew from a watch business into the catalog that sold everything.

Before this tower, the company ran that empire from the West Side, from a complex of more than forty acres at Homan Avenue and Arthington Street that opened in 1906, with its own power plant and rail yards.
For most of the twentieth century, the catalog's orders were filled there, and the company's first retail store opened on the grounds in 1925.
The old Sears tower on that campus, fourteen stories tall, still stands, in a neighborhood now called Homan Square.
In 1924, Sears started a radio station to reach farm families and named it after itself: W L S, for World's Largest Store.
Its Saturday night program, the National Barn Dance, went on the air that April and became one of the most popular shows in the country, older than Nashville's Grand Ole Opry.

In the early 1930s, a young singer named Gene Autry had his own show on the station, made records for a label that Sears sold, and lent his name to a Gene Autry guitar in the catalog, all before Hollywood made him the singing cowboy.
The company's brand names outlived its catalog: Kenmore appliances, Craftsman tools, the DieHard battery.
In 1931, Sears went into car insurance, selling policies by mail, and borrowed the name of its tire brand, which had been chosen in a national contest in 1925.
The name was Allstate.
In the 1980s, it tried to become a financial supermarket as well, buying the brokerage Dean Witter and the real estate firm Coldwell Banker, and launching the Discover card.
Wall Street joked about socks and stocks.
Then the ground shifted under it.
Discount chains undersold Sears, and shoppers drifted to the malls and, later, online.
The big general catalog, more than a century old, was printed for the last time in 1993, and the West Side plant shut down the same year.
Sears merged with Kmart in 2005 and filed for bankruptcy in 2018, a long way down for the company that built the tallest building in the world.
Ground was broken here in August 1970, and the last beam went up in May 1973.
The frame took about seventy-six thousand tons of steel.
You heard that the tower held the world's height record for almost twenty-five years.
How it lost the title is a very Chicago grievance.

In 1996, the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat, the group of engineers and architects that keeps the official records, ruled that the Petronas Towers, going up in Kuala Lumpur, would be the tallest buildings in the world.
The Malaysian towers had decorative spires, and the council counted them as part of the architecture.
This tower had higher floors, a higher roof and far taller antennas, but antennas didn't count.
Chicagoans felt robbed, and the argument pushed the council to start keeping several kinds of height records instead of one.
These days, as it happens, the council has its headquarters in Chicago.
Then came Taipei 101 in 2004 and the Burj Khalifa in Dubai in 2010.
In 2014, New York's One World Trade Center took the title of tallest building in the country, with the help of a spire of its own.
Its roof is lower than this one.
The tower has had its adventures.
On Memorial Day in 1981, a young man named Dan Goodwin, dressed as Spider-Man, climbed the outside of the building with suction cups and hooks while firefighters spent hours trying to stop him.
He made it to the roof, was arrested, and was fined thirty-five dollars.
The name changed in 2009, and in 2015 the building was sold to the investment firm Blackstone, which spent hundreds of millions of dollars remaking its base.
The shops and restaurants that opened at the bottom in 2022 are called Catalog, a nod to the book that paid for all of this.
You are standing at the southern end of LaSalle Street, and the building closing off the end of the street is the Chicago Board of Trade.
LaSalle is Chicago's financial street, and this tower was placed to be the period at the end of its sentence.
The Board of Trade was founded in 1848 by merchants trying to bring order to the chaotic grain business.

Chicago sat between the farms of the Midwest and the markets of the East, and the Board created something new: standardized grades of grain, so that a bushel of number two wheat was interchangeable with any other.
Once grain was a standard commodity, people could trade promises to deliver it in the future.
That is the origin of the modern futures market, and for generations the price of the world's wheat, corn, and soybeans was set in shouting matches in trading pits inside buildings on this spot.
This building, the third Board of Trade on the site, opened in 1930.
It was designed by Holabird and Root, the next generation of the firms you will hear about all day, and it is one of the finest Art Deco skyscrapers in the country.

Look at the facade for carved sheaves of wheat, and at the hooded figures near the clock holding grain and corn, one of them a Native American figure holding corn, the other a Babylonian holding wheat, symbols of the two hemispheres of agriculture.
Now look all the way to the top.
That aluminum statue on the pyramid roof is Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain, by the sculptor John Storrs.
She is about thirty feet tall, and she has no face, only smooth, abstract planes.
The usual explanation is that Storrs reasoned no one on the ground would ever see her face from more than forty stories below, so he did not bother with one.
For decades she stood over the tallest building in Chicago.
The pits closed to open outcry trading in the 2010s as electronic trading took over, but the building is still a working office tower, and the Board of Trade is now part of CME Group.
The pits produced some of the most dramatic financial battles in American history.
Traders tried to corner the market, buying up so much of a commodity that anyone who had promised to deliver it would have to buy from them, at any price.
In 1897, a young speculator named Joseph Leiter, the son of one of Marshall Field's partners, tried to corner the world's wheat.

The meatpacker Philip Armour, who had sold wheat he didn't yet have, broke the corner by chartering icebreakers to smash a path through the frozen lakes and bring his grain from the north in the middle of winter.
Leiter lost millions.
The novelist Frank Norris turned stories like this into a novel called The Pit.
Traders in the pits communicated over the roar with a system of hand signals, palms facing in to buy, palms facing out to sell, and some of those signals are still taught today.
You heard that the Board invented standard grades of grain.
That idea came out of a machine.
In the 1850s, Chicago built huge steam-powered grain elevators along the river.
Grain arrived loose in railroad cars, rode belts of buckets up to the top of the elevator, poured into tall bins, and later slid down chutes into the holds of ships.
In a system like that, nobody could keep each farmer's sacks apart.
Grain from hundreds of farms ran together in the same bin, so it had to be sorted by grade, and the farmer got back not his own wheat but a receipt for so many bushels of a certain grade.
That receipt was the revolution.
A piece of paper could change hands far faster than grain could move, and merchants were soon trading contracts for grain that hadn't been harvested yet.

During the Civil War, with the Union army to feed, the trading boomed, and in 1865 the Board wrote formal rules for these futures contracts, including the deposit, called margin, that traders still put up today.
Not everyone thought it was honest.
Farm groups called it gambling.
And all over the country, storefront parlors called bucket shops let ordinary people bet on the Board's prices, which came in over the telegraph, without buying any grain at all.
The Board fought them for decades, insisting that its prices were its own property.
The case reached the Supreme Court, and in 1905 the Board won.
Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote the opinion, and he defended speculation itself.
Speculation of this kind by competent men, he wrote, is the self-adjustment of society to the probable.
That's still the idea behind every futures market in the world: that a crowd of people betting on tomorrow's price will find it faster than anyone else can.
Whether the price of bread should hang on that crowd is an argument that has never quite ended.
The Board had a younger rival a few blocks away, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, which started out in 1898 as a market for butter and eggs.
For decades it was the scrappier exchange, trading onions until Congress banned onion futures in 1958, a ban that's still the law, and then frozen pork bellies, the raw material of bacon.
The man who changed its fortunes came to America as a child refugee.
Leo Melamed was born in Bialystok, Poland, in 1932.
When war came, his family fled to Lithuania, where they got two of the transit visas that the Japanese diplomat Chiune Sugihara was writing for Jewish refugees, against his government's orders.
They crossed the Soviet Union on the Trans-Siberian Railway, sailed from Japan, and landed in Seattle in 1941.
In Chicago, as he tells the story, he was a law student who answered a newspaper ad from Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner and Beane, thinking it was a law firm.
It was a brokerage, and the job was running orders on the floor of the Merc.
By 1969 he was the exchange's chairman.
He saw that once the world gave up fixed exchange rates, which began when President Nixon cut the dollar's link to gold in 1971, the price of money itself would rise and fall like the price of wheat.
So why not trade it?
To win over the skeptics, he paid the University of Chicago economist Milton Friedman seven thousand five hundred dollars to write a paper on why the world needed a futures market in currencies.
The Merc opened one in May 1972.

The Board answered in April 1973 with an exchange for stock options, opened in what had been its members' smoking lounge, which traded nine hundred and eleven contracts on sixteen stocks on its first day.
That same spring, the economists Fischer Black and Myron Scholes published their formula for pricing options, in a University of Chicago journal.
Chicago had turned the trading pit from a market for crops into a market for risk.
In 2007, the younger exchange bought the older one.
The goddess on the roof was made by John Storrs, a Chicago-born sculptor who had studied in Paris with Auguste Rodin and spent much of his life in France.
His Ceres is pure Art Deco, a figure reduced to smooth planes and folds, cast in aluminum, a modern material for a statue in 1930.
Storrs stayed in France through the Second World War.
The German occupiers arrested and imprisoned him twice, and his daughter worked with the Resistance.
He died there in 1956.
The goddess appears inside too.
The 1930 building had a trading room several stories tall, and on its wall hung a mural of Ceres three stories high by the Chicago painter John Warner Norton.
When the room was remodeled in 1973, the mural came down and went into storage, and for nine years nobody saw it.
By the end of the 1970s, the Board needed more space, and it hired Helmut Jahn, then one of the rising stars of what was being called postmodern architecture.
Instead of ignoring the old tower, Jahn's addition, built onto the back of it in the early 1980s, echoes it: the same stepped shape and pyramid roof, translated into glass and metal.
If you walk around the building, look up and compare the two tops.
Inside the addition is an atrium twelve stories high, and one of its walls is the original limestone back wall of the 1930 tower, so the old building has become part of the new one's interior.
That's where Norton's mural came home.
Restored after its years in storage, it hangs in a steel frame high in the atrium, across from the stone of the building it was painted for.
LaSalle Street, stretching north from here, has been Chicago's money street for well over a century.
Look up the street at the block just in front of you, where two classical buildings with tall columns face each other.
On the left, on the west side, is the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.
On the right is the old home of the Continental Illinois bank, and its story is one of the great financial crises of the twentieth century.
In the early 1980s, Continental Illinois was the seventh largest bank in the country, and it had grown fast by lending aggressively, especially to oil and gas companies.
Many of those loans came from a small bank in a shopping center in Oklahoma City called Penn Square, which collapsed in 1982 when the oil boom went bust.
Continental's losses piled up.
In May 1984, rumors spread through markets overseas that the bank was failing, and big depositors around the world began pulling out their money by wire.
In about ten days, the bank lost close to a third of its funding.
Regulators faced a choice nobody had faced on this scale.
If Continental failed, hundreds of smaller banks that kept their money in it might fall too.
So the government stepped in.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation promised to protect every depositor, even those far above the insured limit, and that summer it put in a billion dollars and took over eighty percent of the company.
It was the biggest bank failure in American history until 2008.
That September, at a hearing in Congress, the comptroller of the currency admitted that regulators had no workable way to let one of the very largest banks fail.
A congressman from Connecticut, Stewart McKinney, put it bluntly.
We have a new kind of bank, he said.
It is called too big to fail.
The phrase has come back with every financial crisis since.
Walk a few steps north on LaSalle.
This red stone and brick fortress on the east side of the street is the Rookery, completed in 1888 by Burnham and Root.
It is one of the oldest high-rises still standing in Chicago, and one of its great interiors.
The name comes from the temporary city hall that stood here after the fire, a building that pigeons and crows found irresistible.
Locals called it the rookery, and Root, who had a sense of humor, carved stylized birds near the entrance.
Look for them around the arched doorway on LaSalle.
From the outside, the Rookery is a transitional building.
The street walls are heavy masonry carrying their own weight, but inside, the building is framed in iron.
Root designed it as a hollow square around a central light court, so that every office got daylight in an age of dim gas and early electric lamps.
The bottom two stories of the court were roofed with glass and iron, making a bright, two-story lobby.
If the building is open, step inside.
In 1905, the lobby was remodeled by Frank Lloyd Wright, who covered much of Root's ornate ironwork in white marble with incised gold patterns and added his own geometric light fixtures.
Look up at the spiral staircase that winds up the west side of the court, the oriel stair.
It is one of the most photographed spaces in the city.
Daniel Burnham kept his office here for a time.
He and Root were partners until 1891, when Root died suddenly of pneumonia at forty-one, just as the firm was planning the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893.
Burnham carried on alone and became the most powerful architect in America.
Chicago's ground made all of this harder.
Beneath the city lies soft, wet clay, and for many feet, nothing solid to build on.

Root's answer, first used a few years earlier, was the floating raft foundation: a mat of steel rails and concrete, laid in crisscrossing layers, that spread the weight of each column over a wide area, so the building floats on the clay like a raft.
Look closely at the Rookery's base and you'll see how wide and heavy it is.

Even so, many of Chicago's early skyscrapers settled several inches, some much more, and the problem wasn't solved until engineers began sinking caissons, deep shafts filled with concrete, down to bedrock about a hundred feet below the street.
John Wellborn Root was born in Georgia in 1850.

During the Civil War, his father made money in blockade running, slipping cotton past the Union navy to England, and after Atlanta fell in 1864, he sent his teenage son across the Atlantic to school near Liverpool.
Root came home to study engineering at New York University, and after the Great Fire, like so many young architects, he came to Chicago, where he met Daniel Burnham in a draftsman's office.
They were partners by 1873.
They worked because they were opposites.
Burnham was the salesman and organizer, the one who could walk into a boardroom and come out with a commission.
Root was the artist: a gifted pianist and organist, a writer and critic, quick, funny and charming.
Burnham handled the clients, and Root designed the buildings, this one included.
His family life was touched by loss.
His first wife died young, not long after their wedding.
His second wife, Dora Louise Monroe, was the sister of Harriet Monroe, the poet who later founded Poetry magazine here in Chicago, and who wrote the first biography of her brother-in-law.
In 1890, Burnham and Root were put in charge of the architecture of the coming World's Fair.
In January 1891, the leading architects of New York and Boston came to Chicago to begin planning it with them.
That same week, Root came down with pneumonia, and within days he was dead.
You heard that Burnham carried on alone.
People have wondered ever since what the fair, and American architecture, would have looked like if Root had lived.

He admired the bold, plain work being done in Chicago, and some historians believe he might have steered the fair away from the white classical style it finally took, the style that Burnham and the eastern architects chose and that shaped American public buildings for a generation.
Nobody can know.
What we have instead are the buildings he finished in his short career, and you're standing in front of one of the best.
The light court has been remade three times, and you can still read the layers.
Root's original court, in 1888, was a showpiece of ornamental iron, dark and intricate, under a roof of glass.
In 1905, the building's manager, Edward Waller, who had been one of Frank Lloyd Wright's early patrons, hired Wright to brighten it up, and you heard what he did with white marble and gold.
In 1931 came another remodeling, this time by William Drummond, who had once worked in Wright's studio in Oak Park.
He put in new elevators and added Art Deco touches, and to squeeze in more rentable space, he took out a pair of stairways and divided up part of the lobby.
Then came the dim years.

To stop the leaks and save on upkeep, the great glass roof over the court was covered with waterproofing and paint, and a room that Root had designed to be full of daylight was lit by electric bulbs for decades.
By the 1980s, the building was shabby and its future uncertain.
The restoration, finished in the early 1990s, brought the daylight back.
The architects, from a firm called McClier, chose to return the court to Wright's design of 1905 rather than Root's, and they protected the old glass roof by building a new skylight above it.
So when you look up, you're seeing an idea from 1888 through a renovation from 1905, under a rescue from the 1990s.
The Rookery is still a working office building, so be respectful of the people at work here.
The Frank Lloyd Wright Trust runs tours that start in the lobby, and they can take you into parts of the building that are otherwise closed to visitors.
In the late 1880s, Burnham and Root moved their offices to the top floor of the Rookery, and much of their early work on the 1893 World's Fair was done up there.
The fair is tied to the most famous story about Chicago's nickname.
Chicago had to beat New York, Washington and St. Louis for the right to hold the fair, and the fight was nasty.
The story goes that Charles Dana, the editor of the New York Sun, told his readers to pay no attention to the nonsensical claims of that windy city.
He meant not the weather but the city's boastful politicians and promoters, full of hot air.
It's a great story, repeated in countless guidebooks.
But nobody has ever found it in the Sun.
People who've combed through old newspapers found Chicago being called the windy city years earlier, in the 1870s, especially in Cincinnati, a rival for everything from pork packing to baseball.
In May 1876, the Cincinnati Enquirer ran the headline That Windy City over a story about a tornado that had struck Chicago.
Rival papers used the phrase both ways, for the gusts off the lake and for the hot air of Chicago's boosters.
The link to Dana doesn't show up in print until a Chicago Tribune article in 1933, decades after he died.
So the nickname may really be about the wind after all, at least partly.
And yet Chicago isn't especially windy.
By the weather records, several big American cities have higher average wind speeds, Boston among them.
What Chicago has is a lake that makes its own weather, and downtown streets that act like canyons.
Stand on a corner here in January, when the wind comes off the lake and funnels between the towers, and you'll understand why the name has never needed a better explanation.
Walk east along Adams Street to Dearborn Street and turn left.
On the west side of Dearborn, just north of Adams, is the Marquette Building, designed by Holabird and Roche and finished in 1895.
Step back across the street and look at the facade.
You can read the steel frame right through the brick and terra cotta: a grid of piers and spandrels, with wide windows filling each bay.
Those windows are the famous Chicago window, a large fixed pane of glass in the middle, flanked by two narrow sashes that open for ventilation.
In a time before air conditioning, this was the solution for light and air at once, and you will see it all over the Loop.

The building is named for Jacques Marquette, the French Jesuit missionary who, with the explorer Louis Jolliet, traveled through this area in 1673, and who camped near the Chicago River over the winter of 1674 and 1675.
Look at the bronze reliefs over the entrance, which show scenes of the expedition.
If the lobby is open, step inside and look up at the mosaic frieze that runs around the balcony.
It was made by the Tiffany studios, in glass and mother of pearl, and tells Marquette's story, with portraits of Marquette, Jolliet, and the Native people they met.
The lobby is one of the finest of its era, and the building is now headquarters to the MacArthur Foundation, which restored it.
Notice how the building is organized like a classical column.
There's a base, the two-story ground floor with its heavier stone, then a long, plain shaft of offices, and then a capital, the decorated cornice and top floors.
This three-part scheme became the standard formula for the American office building.
It was Louis Sullivan who explained it most famously, but you can see Holabird and Roche using it here in a businesslike way.
Their firm became one of the busiest in the Loop, and as Holabird and Root, it designed the Board of Trade.
Today the Marquette is the home of the MacArthur Foundation, best known for its genius grants, the large, no-strings-attached fellowships it gives every year to creative people in every field.
The bronze reliefs over the doors show the journey that made Marquette and Jolliet famous, so here's the journey.
In May 1673, the two men set out from the mission at Saint Ignace, at the top of Lake Michigan, with five French voyageurs in two birch bark canoes.
Jolliet was a fur trader born in Quebec, sent by the governor of New France to find out where the great river the Native people spoke of really went.
Marquette was a Jesuit priest who spoke several Native languages.
They paddled down Green Bay, up the Fox River, carried their canoes across to the Wisconsin River, and in the middle of June they floated out onto the Mississippi.
They went south for a month, past the muddy rush of the Missouri and the mouth of the Ohio, to a village of the Quapaw people near the mouth of the Arkansas River.
There they learned that the river ran to the Gulf of Mexico, not the Pacific, and that farther down were Spanish soldiers who might well arrest them.
They turned back, and on the way home, the Illinois people showed them the shortcut through Chicago.
Then the expedition's records nearly vanished.
In 1674, almost home, Jolliet's canoe overturned in the Lachine Rapids near Montreal.
He was barely rescued, but his companions drowned, among them a young Illinois boy who had been given to him, and his journal and maps went to the bottom.
He wrote his report from memory, and most of what we know comes from the account credited to Marquette.
Marquette had promised to return to the Illinois people, and he kept the promise though he was already ill, which is why he had to spend that winter camped by the river here.
He reached them in the spring, but heading north again along the lake, he died in May 1675, at thirty-seven, near what is now Ludington, Michigan, though the exact place is still argued over.
Two years later, according to the Jesuits, a party of Native converts found his grave, cleaned his bones, and carried them by canoe, in a box of birch bark, back to Saint Ignace.
You heard that the MacArthur Foundation makes its home here.
The man behind it, John D. MacArthur, was one of the richest men in America and one of the least showy.
He was the son of a traveling evangelist preacher.

He sold insurance, and in 1935, in the depths of the Depression, he bought a small, struggling Chicago company, Bankers Life and Casualty, and built it into a giant by selling inexpensive policies by mail.
He moved on into real estate, especially in Florida, where in his last years he ran his businesses from a table in the coffee shop of a hotel he owned in Palm Beach Shores.
His company bought this building in 1975.
When he died in 1978, most of his fortune went to the foundation he and his wife, Catherine, had set up in 1970, making it one of the largest private foundations in the country almost overnight.

The foundation moved in here, and in 2001 it began a long, careful restoration that included re-creating the building's cornice, the heavy crown along the roofline that had been stripped off decades before.
The foundation is best known for its fellowships, the so-called genius grants, which began in 1981.
You can't apply for one.
The nominators are anonymous, and the winners find out with a phone call out of the blue.
The award is now eight hundred thousand dollars, paid over five years, with no strings attached at all.
The foundation itself avoids the word genius.
The family had another famous name.

John's older brother Charles MacArthur was a Chicago newspaper reporter, and with his friend Ben Hecht he wrote The Front Page, a comedy set in the press room of the Chicago criminal courts, about reporters who'll do anything for a story.
It opened on Broadway in 1928, and Hollywood has remade it again and again, most famously as His Girl Friday.
Charles married the actress Helen Hayes.
Chicago's downtown street names are a short course in early American history.
Walk south from Washington Street, and you pass through the presidents almost in order: Madison, Monroe, Adams, Jackson, Van Buren, and then, past Ida B. Wells Drive, Harrison, Polk and Taylor.
The streets running north and south mostly honor the frontier.
Dearborn Street takes its name from Fort Dearborn, which was named for Henry Dearborn, Thomas Jefferson's secretary of war.
Clark Street is named for George Rogers Clark, who led the Revolutionary War campaign that won the Illinois country from the British.
LaSalle Street is named for the French explorer René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, who came through the Chicago portage in the 1680s on his way to claim the whole Mississippi valley for France.
Wells Street has the strangest story.
William Wells was captured as a boy in Kentucky by the Miami people, raised as one of them, and married a daughter of the Miami war chief Little Turtle.
He fought against the Americans and later for them, as a scout and interpreter.
In August 1812, he hurried to Fort Dearborn to help lead its garrison to safety, and he was killed in the attack on the evacuation.
According to survivors, the warriors who killed him ate his heart, to take in his courage.
For more than forty years, though, Wells Street wasn't Wells Street.
By 1870 it had become a strip of saloons and brothels, and the name seemed an insult to the hero, so the city renamed it Fifth Avenue.
It got its old name back in the 1910s.
Even the grid itself tells a story.
The streets of the original town were laid out in 1830 by the commissioners planning the Illinois and Michigan Canal, who were selling lots to pay for it.
Chicago began, in other words, as a real estate development, and it has been one ever since.
Cross Dearborn and walk into the open plaza across the street.
The black steel and glass towers surrounding you make up the Federal Center, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and completed in stages from the 1960s to the 1970s.
Mies had been director of the Bauhaus in Germany.
He left in 1937 as the Nazis made modern architecture impossible there and came to Chicago to head the architecture school at what became the Illinois Institute of Technology.
Here he spent three decades refining one idea: a building as a pure, rational frame.
Look at the thin steel I-beams running up the facades.
Structurally, they do almost nothing.
They are there to express the frame and give the walls rhythm.
"Less is more" is the phrase most associated with him.
The plaza is part of the design.
Notice that the paving grid lines up with the buildings, and the lobbies are walled in glass so the plaza seems to flow inside.
And then, in the middle of all that black and gray, there is the Flamingo: a fifty-foot sculpture of arches in bright vermilion steel by Alexander Calder.
Calder painted it a particular red that is now called Calder red, and it is the perfect foil to Mies's rigor.

The Flamingo was unveiled in October 1974 on the same day as Calder's moving sculpture inside the Sears Tower, and the city celebrated with a circus parade through the Loop, with Calder himself riding in a bandwagon.
Look south across Jackson Boulevard at the long, dark brown brick building.
That is the Monadnock, and it is our next stop.
One of the towers of the Federal Center is the Dirksen Federal Building, a federal courthouse.

In 1969, it was the scene of one of the most chaotic trials in American history, the trial of the Chicago Seven, the antiwar activists charged with conspiracy to incite riots during the 1968 Democratic convention.

The defendants, including Abbie Hoffman and Tom Hayden, mocked the court and wore judicial robes to the trial, and the judge, Julius Hoffman, no relation, sentenced them and their lawyers to prison for contempt.
One original defendant, the Black Panther leader Bobby Seale, demanded to represent himself, and the judge had him bound and gagged in the courtroom.
The convictions were later overturned on appeal.
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe was born plain Ludwig Mies, in 1886, in the old German city of Aachen, the son of a stonemason.
He never went to architecture school.
He learned to draw in his father's stone-carving shop and worked his way up in the offices of Berlin architects, including Peter Behrens, where Walter Gropius and Le Corbusier also worked for a time.
In the early 1920s, he remade his name.
Mies, in German, sounds like a slang word for lousy or miserable.
So he added his mother's family name, Rohe, with a Dutch-sounding van der in front, which sounded distinguished without claiming the von of the German nobility.
His most famous early building stood for less than a year.

For the 1929 world's fair in Barcelona, he designed the German Pavilion, a low building of marble, onyx, glass and chrome, with walls that seemed to slide past each other under a roof that seemed to float.
It was taken down after the fair and rebuilt on the same spot in the 1980s.
The steel and leather chair he designed for it, the Barcelona chair, is still made today.
In 1930 he became director of the Bauhaus, the famous design school, and in 1933, under pressure from the Nazis, he and the faculty closed it for good.
You heard that he came to Chicago a few years later.
He never became comfortable in English, and he let his buildings do most of his talking.
In Chicago he never lived in one of his glass boxes.

From the early 1940s until his death, he rented an apartment on East Pearson Street, a short walk from his famous towers on the lake, in a conventional building from 1916, hung with art by his old Bauhaus colleague Paul Klee.
He died in Chicago in 1969, before this plaza was finished.
One line is often credited to him, though nobody has traced where he first said it: God is in the details.
Look at the corners of these buildings, where steel meets glass, and decide for yourself.
You heard about the chaos in the courtroom here.

The trial ran for nearly five months, from September 1969 into February 1970, and the defendants were a cross-section of the antiwar movement: Tom Hayden and Rennie Davis, organizers from the student left; the pacifist David Dellinger; Abbie Hoffman and Jerry Rubin, founders of the Yippies, who treated politics as theater; and two academics, John Froines and Lee Weiner.
Their lawyers, William Kunstler and Leonard Weinglass, fought the judge at every turn.
The defense called a parade of famous witnesses to argue that the protests had stayed peaceful until the police attacked.
The poet Allen Ginsberg chanted on the witness stand.
The folk singer Judy Collins began to sing Where Have All the Flowers Gone, and Arlo Guthrie tried a song too, until the judge cut them off.
The novelist Norman Mailer and the comedian Dick Gregory testified.
The defense even called Mayor Daley, hoping to put him on trial instead, but most of its questions were ruled out of bounds.
Outside the courtroom, the city was in turmoil.
In December 1969, in the middle of the trial, Chicago police raided an apartment on the West Side before dawn and killed the Black Panther leader Fred Hampton, who was twenty-one.
The verdicts came in February 1970.
The jury acquitted all seven of conspiracy.
Froines and Weiner were cleared entirely, and the other five were convicted of crossing state lines to incite a riot and sentenced to five years.
Judge Hoffman had already handed out contempt sentences to every defendant and both lawyers, more than four years for Kunstler.
Then the case fell apart.
In 1972, a federal appeals court threw out the riot convictions, faulting the judge's open hostility to the defense, and the government decided not to try again.
The contempt charges were retried in 1973 before a different judge, who found four of the men guilty on a handful of counts and sent no one to jail.
The Flamingo's maker came from a family of sculptors.
Alexander Calder's grandfather made the giant statue of William Penn on top of Philadelphia's City Hall, and his father made the Swann Memorial Fountain a few blocks away.
Calder himself trained as a mechanical engineer, and you can see it in everything he built: the balance, the joints, the careful way the weight comes down to the ground.
In Paris in the late 1920s, he became famous for a circus.

He built it himself, in miniature, from wire, cloth, cork and string, with acrobats, a lion tamer and a sword swallower, and he performed it on the floor for audiences of artists and friends, working every figure by hand.
That's why Chicago welcomed him in 1974 with a circus parade.
His sculptures that moved got their name from Marcel Duchamp, who called them mobiles.
When Calder began making big sculptures that stood still, his friend Jean Arp suggested that those must be stabiles, and the name stuck.
The Flamingo is a stabile.
It was commissioned by the federal government, under a program that sets aside a small share of the cost of new federal buildings for art.

Calder worked out the design in a small model, and the full-size sculpture was cut and bolted together at Segre's Iron Works in Waterbury, Connecticut, which built many of his big stabiles in the 1960s and 1970s.
Walk underneath it.

Look at how the curving plates are stiffened with ribs and joined with bolts, more like a bridge than a statue, and at how lightly the whole thing seems to step on the plaza, landing on just a few narrow feet.
From each side it's a different creature.
Calder died in New York in 1976, two years after the Flamingo went up, and it remains one of his largest works in any public square.
You are now facing the Monadnock Building, which fills the block along Dearborn between Jackson and Van Buren.
It is really two buildings, and the difference between them tells the story of the skyscraper.
The northern half, designed by Burnham and Root and finished in 1891, is sixteen stories of load-bearing brick.
There is no steel frame carrying the outer walls.
To hold up that much masonry, the walls at the bottom are about six feet thick.
Walk along the sidewalk and look at how deep the window openings are at street level compared with the upper floors.
The owners asked for no ornament at all, and Root obliged with almost none.
Instead, look at how the walls gently curve outward at the top, like the neck of a vase, and how the corners are softly rounded at the base.
It is one of the most beautiful plain buildings ever made, and it was nearly the tallest that brick can reasonably go.
The southern half, finished in 1893 by Holabird and Roche, was built with a steel frame.
It is the same height, but its walls are thinner and its bays are lighter and more open.
Within two years, on the same block, the old way of building tall gave way to the new.
Inside, the Monadnock has kept much of its original character, including mosaic floors, a cantilevered staircase, and old storefronts along the ground-floor corridor.
It is still full of small offices and shops.
The name comes from Mount Monadnock in New Hampshire.
The building was financed by two brothers from Boston, Peter and Shepherd Brooks, who invested heavily in Chicago real estate and named several of their buildings after New England mountains.

Absentee investors from the East, like the Brookses, put up much of the money that rebuilt Chicago, and they often pushed their architects for plain, economical buildings with as much rentable space and as little decoration as possible.
Their manager in Chicago, Owen Aldis, has been called one of the unsung fathers of the Chicago School, because he insisted on buildings that were practical, light-filled, and easy to maintain.
You heard that the owners wanted no ornament.
Getting to that plain wall took years of argument.
Root's early sketches for this site, in the mid-1880s, dressed the building in an Egyptian style, with carved lotus flowers and flaring columns.
The Brooks brothers, writing from Boston, wouldn't have it.
Ornament, they believed, only collected dirt and cost money to repair.

The story goes that Root resisted at first, then came back one day and announced that the heavy lines of the Egyptian pyramids had caught his imagination, and that he would put the building up without a single ornament.
Many people see a trace of Egypt in it anyway.
That hollow flare at the top of the wall is close to the curved cornice that crowns an ancient Egyptian temple.
Brick had a hard limit, and this building found it.

When the walls carry the weight, every story added on top means thicker walls at the bottom, and here that thick base swallowed floor space on the most valuable floors, where shops paid the highest rents.
The weight was a problem too.
Under downtown Chicago lies soft, wet clay, and bedrock was too deep to reach with the methods of the day.
So the building stands on what engineers call a floating raft: a broad pad of concrete laced with iron rails and steel beams, spread out to share the load across the clay.
The engineers expected the building to settle about eight inches, and planned for it.
Over the years it sank about twenty.
Inside is another experiment.
The famous staircase is made with cast aluminum, at a time when aluminum was still a costly, almost precious metal, and it's often described as one of the first uses of aluminum in any building.
Root never saw the building finished.

He died in January 1891, while the walls were still rising, so in a way the Monadnock is his last word: the old way of building, pushed as far as it would go, and made beautiful by taking things away.
You heard that the building is named for a mountain in New Hampshire.
The name is much older than the building.

Monadnock comes from the Abenaki or a related Algonquian language of New England, and it's usually translated as something like the mountain that stands alone, though scholars argue over the exact meaning.
The mountain fits it.
It rises by itself above the rolling hills of southern New Hampshire, and it became a favorite of New England writers.
Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote a long poem about it, and Henry David Thoreau climbed it several times and camped on its bare rocky top.
Geologists borrowed the word too.
In their language, a monadnock is any isolated hill of hard rock left standing after the land around it has worn away.
The block you're facing was planned as four buildings in a row, each with its own entrance and its own mountain.
From north to south, they were the Monadnock, the Kearsarge, the Katahdin and the Wachusett: mountains in New Hampshire, Maine and Massachusetts, all with Native American names.
Burnham and Root's half held the first two, and the steel-framed half the other two.
Only the first name stuck, and the whole block has been the Monadnock for generations.
The Brooks brothers and their manager liked names like these.
Their earlier tower by Burnham and Root, the ten-story Montauk Block, built in 1882 a couple of blocks north of here, is often said to be the first building people called a skyscraper.
It was torn down in 1902.
Their Pontiac Building of 1891, by Holabird and Roche, still stands a few blocks south on Dearborn, named for the Odawa leader who led a war against the British in the 1760s.
And you've already seen their Marquette Building.
There's an irony in all of it.
By the time Boston money was naming Chicago towers in Native languages, the Potawatomi, who had lived here when the city began, had been pushed out of the region by treaty half a century before.
By the 1970s, the Monadnock looked like a building without a future.
The Loop was losing offices to new towers and to the suburbs, and old buildings all over downtown were coming down for parking garages and plazas.
Over the decades, owners had modernized the Monadnock the cheap way.
Its hallways had once been lined with marble, and with office walls of oak and textured glass that let daylight from the offices spill into the corridors.
Most of that glass and oak had been ripped out or covered over, along with much of the marble, and lowered ceilings hid the old plaster.

In 1979, the building was bought by William Donnell, who made a bet that sounded either visionary or foolish: that people would pay to work in a nineteenth-century office building if it really felt like one.
Instead of modernizing further, he set out to bring the Monadnock back to the way it looked in the 1890s, and to make that pay.
Working with the Chicago preservation architects Vinci Hamp, his team restored the building a floor at a time, through most of the 1980s.

They brought back the marble along the corridor walls, rebuilt the partitions of oak and glass, opened the hallways back up to their full height, and tucked the modern wiring and ductwork above lowered ceilings inside the offices, where nobody walking the halls would see it.
By one account, the work cost about a million dollars a floor.
In 1987, the National Trust for Historic Preservation named it one of the best restoration projects in the country, and the bet paid off.
The Monadnock has stayed popular with the kind of tenants it was built for: small firms that like an office behind an oak door, off a marble hallway, in a building with a story.
If the building is open, walk through the ground-floor corridor and look at the glass and the oak and the marble.
This is about as close as you can get, anywhere downtown, to the feeling of a Chicago office building when it was new.
Walk east to State Street and turn left, north, to the corner of State and Madison Street.
For many years this corner was said to be the busiest intersection in the world, and it is the zero point of Chicago's address grid.
Every address in the city is counted from here: north and south from Madison, east and west from State.
The white building on the southeast corner is the Sullivan Center, designed by Louis Sullivan for the Schlesinger and Mayer department store around 1899 and expanded by 1904.
For about a hundred years it was the Carson Pirie Scott store.
Look above the rounded corner entrance and along the first two floors.
That dense, swirling cast-iron ornament, painted a dark green, is Sullivan at his most inventive: leaves, vines, and geometric forms twisting into each other.
He wanted the ground floor to be rich and inviting at eye level, where shoppers would see it, like a picture frame around the display windows.
Now look higher.
The upper floors are almost the opposite: a simple white grid of terra cotta with wide Chicago windows.
Sullivan is famous for the phrase "form ever follows function," and this building shows what he meant.
A department store needs light and open floors, so the frame is expressed plainly, and the ornament is concentrated where people meet the building.
Sullivan's career collapsed after this building, and he died poor in a Chicago hotel room in 1924.
His former draftsman, Frank Lloyd Wright, always called him the master.
One block south, at State and Monroe, is the Palmer House, the hotel Potter Palmer built and rebuilt after the fire, now in its third building, from the 1920s.
Step into its lobby if you can and look up at the ceiling, painted with scenes from Greek mythology.
And look along State Street itself.
This was Chicago's great shopping street, lined with department stores: Marshall Field's, Carson Pirie Scott, Mandel Brothers, the Fair, and Sears.
A popular song from 1922 made it famous: "State Street, that great street."
In the 1970s, the city turned State Street into a pedestrian mall with buses only, and it nearly died.
The cars were let back in in 1996, and the street came back to life.
You heard that every address in the city counts from this corner.
Before 1909, that wasn't so.
Chicago had grown by swallowing its neighbors, and each town it annexed brought its own street names and its own house numbers, counted from its own starting points.
By the 1890s, the city had dozens of streets sharing the same names, and the same house number could mean very different distances in different parts of town.
Deliveries went astray, and visitors were hopelessly lost.
The fix came from a private citizen with no official job at all.
His name was Edward P. Brennan, and in 1901 he proposed a single system for the whole city.
Take State and Madison as the center.
Count every address outward from there.
Put eight hundred numbers to the mile, so that a hundred numbers make a standard block and the main streets fall every half mile, on round numbers.
Put even numbers on the north and west sides of every street, and odd numbers on the south and east.
And give every street a single name from one end to the other.
The city council adopted his plan in 1908.
The new numbers took effect across the city in 1909 and in the Loop in 1911, and hundreds of streets were renamed to get rid of the duplicates.
Brennan lived until 1942, and today honorary street signs here at State and Madison carry his name.
Here's how to use his gift.
Any Chicago address is also a map.
Wrigley Field is at ten sixty West Addison, and Addison Street is thirty-six hundred north.
So the ballpark is four and a half miles north of where you're standing, and a little more than a mile west.
Once you know the trick, you can work out where almost anything in the city is without looking at a map, which is exactly what Brennan had in mind.
You heard that Sullivan's career collapsed after this store.
First, here's how high he had climbed.
Louis Sullivan was born in Boston in 1856, the son of an Irish dancing master.

He spent a single year studying architecture at MIT, grew impatient with it, worked briefly for the architect Frank Furness in Philadelphia, and came to Chicago in 1873, to the boom after the fire, where he drafted for William Le Baron Jenney.
Then he spent a year at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, came back, and joined the office of Dankmar Adler, a gifted engineer and a master of acoustics.
As Adler and Sullivan, they became one of the most celebrated firms in America.
The turning point came at the World's Fair of 1893.

Sullivan designed the Transportation Building, one of the few big buildings at the fair that wasn't white: a long hall in reds and oranges and gold, with an enormous arched entrance called the Golden Door.
A French arts society awarded it medals.
But the fair's white classical palaces won over the public, and Sullivan never forgave them.
Decades later he wrote that the damage wrought by the World's Fair would last for half a century from its date, if not longer.
That same year, a financial panic dried up building across the country.
In 1895, Adler left the partnership for a job with an elevator company, and Sullivan, proud, prickly and drinking hard, drove away many of the clients who were left.
What he built in his last decades were small banks in small Midwestern towns, beginning with one in Owatonna, Minnesota, in 1908, which is still a bank.
People call them jewel boxes.

In his last years, living in a cheap hotel on the South Side, he wrote The Autobiography of an Idea, the story of his life told in the third person, and drew a set of plates called A System of Architectural Ornament.
He lived just long enough to see both books in print, and died in April 1924.
Beneath your feet is a hidden city, built in layers.
The deepest layer is about forty feet down.
Starting in 1899, a company with a franchise to lay telephone cables dug a network of tunnels under the Loop, far bigger than any telephone cable needed.
Soon it was running a narrow-gauge railroad through them, on tracks two feet apart, with little electric locomotives.

Its trains carried coal to the basements of office buildings and department stores, hauled away their ashes, and moved freight to and from the railroad stations, with branches running right into store basements along State Street.
At their peak, the tunnels ran for close to sixty miles.
Trucks finally beat them, the railroad shut down in 1959, and the tunnels were simply left behind.
They came back to life in April 1992.

The autumn before, a crew replacing the wooden pilings that protect a bridge on the Chicago River at Kinzie Street had driven a new piling too close to an old tunnel running under the riverbed, and cracked it.
An inspector found the leak and estimated a repair at about ten thousand dollars, but the job was still waiting on bids when, on April 13, the crack gave way.
River water poured into the tunnels and from there into basements all over the Loop.
One of the first signs was fish swimming in the basement of the Merchandise Mart.
Downtown was evacuated, the power was cut, and parts of the subway were closed for weeks.
Estimates of the total cost ran as high as two billion dollars, and Mayor Richard M. Daley forced out the acting transportation commissioner and fired other city officials.
The middle layer is the subway.

The State Street subway opened in October 1943, in the middle of the Second World War, and under this stretch of State its stations share one continuous platform more than half a mile long, often called the longest subway platform in the world.
And alongside it runs the Pedway, a network of walkways under and between downtown buildings.
It began in 1951 with a tunnel between two subway stations, and it now runs for about five miles.
In winter, some downtown workers barely come up at all.
Walk north on State Street to Washington Street.
On the southwest corner is a slender building that looks as though it was built decades later than it was.
This is the Reliance Building, and it was finished in 1895.
The ground floor was designed by John Root before his death, and the rest by Charles Atwood of Burnham's firm.
Look at how much of the facade is glass.
The steel frame is so light that the walls are mostly windows, with thin bands of white glazed terra cotta in between.
The projecting bays give every office windows on three sides.
When architects in the twentieth century went looking for the ancestor of the all-glass skyscraper, they often pointed here.
The white terra cotta had a practical purpose too.
Chicago in the 1890s was a city of coal smoke, and glazed terra cotta could be washed clean.
By the 1990s the building was badly run down.
It was restored and converted into a hotel, and you can see in the lobby some of the original elevator grilles and mosaic floors.
Across Washington Street, on the northeast corner, is the old Marshall Field's department store, a full block of granite built in stages in the early twentieth century by Burnham's firm.
Look for the great bronze clocks hanging over the corners of the building.
"Meet me under the clock" was how generations of Chicagoans arranged to meet downtown.
Marshall Field built the business on a simple idea: give customers what they want, take returns without argument, and treat shoppers like guests.
The store claims to have opened one of the first department store restaurants, the Walnut Room, and its chocolate mints, called Frango Mints, became a Chicago tradition.
Inside is a ceiling of glass mosaic made by the Tiffany studios, said to contain well over a million pieces.
In 2006, the store was renamed Macy's, and many Chicagoans still haven't forgiven it.
The Reliance went up in one of the strangest ways any skyscraper ever has: from the bottom, underneath people who were still at work upstairs.
The man behind it was William Ellery Hale, who had made a fortune building hydraulic elevators, the machines that made tall buildings practical in the first place.
In the late 1880s he owned an older building on this corner and wanted something much taller.
The trouble was the tenants on the upper floors, whose leases ran until 1894 and couldn't be broken.

So in 1890, Hale's builders propped up the top floors of the old building while they tore out the bottom and built a new base underneath it: the stone-faced ground floor and the basement that John Root designed.
Upstairs, people went on working.
When the last leases finally ran out in 1894, the old upper floors came down, and Charles Atwood's tower rose on Root's base.
Its steel frame went up in a matter of weeks.
Hale's son, George Ellery Hale, grew up to be one of the great astronomers of his age.
He built his first observatory at the family home on the South Side, then spent his life persuading rich men to pay for bigger and bigger telescopes.
You'll hear about one of those men at the Chicago Theatre, at the end of this tour.
Atwood's own story is a sad one.
He was one of the most gifted designers of his time, and the man behind some of the finest buildings at the 1893 fair.

But in December 1895, just after this tower was finished, he left Burnham's firm amid stories of illness and erratic behavior that have never been fully explained, and nine days later he was dead, at forty-six.
The building lost its crowning cornice in the 1940s and spent decades in decline.
In 1994 the city bought it to save it.
A new cornice of cast aluminum went up in place of the old one, and in 1999 the building opened as a hotel.
Marshall Field was a farm boy from Conway, Massachusetts, who came to Chicago in 1856, at twenty-one, to clerk in a dry goods house.
He was quiet, careful and famously thrifty, and he was very good at the one thing that mattered most in his business: knowing what customers would buy.
In 1865 he went into partnership with Potter Palmer and Levi Leiter.
Palmer soon left to build up State Street, and in 1881 Field bought out Leiter, and the store became Marshall Field and Company.
There's a famous story about where the store's motto came from.
Field was walking the floor one day and found a manager arguing with a woman over a complaint.
What are you doing, Field asked.
Settling a complaint, said the manager.
No, you're not, Field told him.
Give the lady what she wants.
Nobody can prove it happened, but the line became the store's slogan.
The man who did the most to turn that idea into a show was Harry Gordon Selfridge, who started at Field's as a stock boy in 1879 and rose to run the retail store.
He filled the windows with light, brought goods out where shoppers could touch them, opened a bargain basement, and is sometimes credited with the phrase the customer is always right.
In 1904, he left to buy a rival, Schlesinger and Mayer, in Sullivan's new building at State and Madison.
After about two months, he sold it to Carson Pirie Scott, which kept the store there until 2007.
Then Selfridge went to London, where in 1909 he opened the department store Selfridges on Oxford Street, and London had never seen anything like it.
He lived grandly and gambled heavily, lost control of the store in 1941, and died with little left.
Field died in 1906, the richest man in Chicago.
His store kept his name for a century, passing in 1982 to BATUS, the American arm of British American Tobacco, and then through a series of other owners before it became Macy's.
Not many department store clocks have made the cover of a national magazine.

In November 1945, just after the war, the Saturday Evening Post ran a cover by Norman Rockwell inspired by the Field's clocks: a repairman on a ladder beside the giant clock face, pocket watch in hand, setting the time.
It became one of the best-loved pictures of the store.
The mints have a stranger history than you might guess.
Frango Mints didn't start in Chicago at all.
They came from Frederick and Nelson, a department store in Seattle, which Marshall Field's bought in 1929.
Field's began making them here, in a candy kitchen on the thirteenth floor of the store across the street, and kept making them there for about seventy years.
Why Frango?
Nobody is quite sure.
A popular story says the candy was first called Franco, and that the name was quietly changed when Francisco Franco seized power in Spain.
It's a good story, but there's no solid evidence for it.
Since 2017, the mints have been made by Garrett, the Chicago popcorn company, and they still come in the familiar green box.
Christmas was the store's other great tradition.

Field's turned its State Street windows into elaborate holiday scenes, and generations of children were brought downtown to see them, then taken upstairs for lunch in the Walnut Room, beside the Great Tree, a towering decorated Christmas tree that has stood in the restaurant every holiday season since the early 1900s.
For many Chicago families, it was a ritual repeated every December.
When Macy's took over, it kept the windows, the tree and the mints.
It may be the main reason some Chicagoans have started to forgive it.

Step across the street and look up at the nearest clock, and you'll see why people chose it as a meeting place: you can see it from a block away, it always tells the time, and everybody knows exactly where it is.
Walk west on Washington Street to the large open plaza on your right.
This is Richard J. Daley Center Plaza, named for the mayor who ran Chicago from 1955 until his death in 1976.
The rust-colored tower behind it is the Daley Center, which holds courtrooms.
It is clad in Cor-Ten steel, designed to weather to this deep brown and then stop corroding.
And in front of it stands the Picasso.
Pablo Picasso designed it, but never came to Chicago.
He sent a model, and the fifty-foot sculpture was fabricated in Indiana from the same weathering steel as the building behind it.
It was unveiled in August 1967.
Picasso declined the fee he was offered and gave the design to the people of Chicago.
It has no title.
When it was unveiled, people argued about what it was.
A woman?
A baboon?
An Afghan hound?
Picasso never said, and Chicagoans have mostly settled on a woman's head, with long hair down the back.
Some people say it resembles the profile of a woman Picasso knew, but that is a guess.
Today it is beloved, and children use its sloping base as a slide.
Across Washington Street you can see a later sculpture, Joan Miró's tall figure, sometimes called Miss Chicago, standing in a small plaza beside the Brunswick Building.
Daley Plaza is also the city's front porch.
It hosts a Christkindlmarket in winter, a farmers market in summer, and many of Chicago's protests and celebrations.
Look at the building on the west side of the plaza, with tall columns, across Clark Street.
That's City Hall and the County Building, a single building completed in 1911, where the mayor and the city council meet.
On its roof is a garden of native prairie plants, planted in 2001 as an experiment to cool the building, and one of the first green roofs on a big American public building.
The Daley Center itself has a Hollywood claim to fame: in the 1980 comedy The Blues Brothers, the heroes crash their car through the lobby, chased by what seems like half the police in Illinois.
The idea came from the architects of the new Civic Center, as the Daley Center was first called.
They wanted a great sculpture for the plaza, and William Hartmann, a partner at Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, set out to get one from the most famous artist alive.
In 1963, he went to see Picasso at his home in the south of France, armed with photographs of Chicago and its buildings, and he made return visits.
Picasso, by then in his eighties, had never been to America and never would go.
But he agreed, and in 1965 he finished a model about forty-two inches tall, which you can now see at the Art Institute.
The money came from three Chicago charitable foundations: the Woods Charitable Fund, the Field Foundation of Illinois, and the Chauncey and Marion Deering McCormick Foundation.
The sculpture itself was built at the American Bridge plant of United States Steel in Gary, and trucked to Chicago in pieces.
On August 15, 1967, Mayor Daley pulled the cord that dropped the covering, and told the crowd that what is strange to us today will be familiar tomorrow.
Not everyone wanted to wait for tomorrow.
An alderman named John Hoellen proposed sending the thing back and putting up a statue of the Cubs star Ernie Banks instead.
Banks did eventually get his statue, outside Wrigley Field, in 2008.
Then came a twist that would have amused Picasso.
The Public Building Commission, which ran the Civic Center, had tried to copyright the design, so that it could control and sell the souvenirs.
But the model and early photographs had been shown in public without a copyright notice, and in 1970 a federal judge ruled that the design had fallen into the public domain.
You heard that Picasso gave his design to the people of Chicago.
A court made sure of it.
Anyone can put the Chicago Picasso on a T-shirt or a coffee mug, and over the years, just about everyone has.
Daley Plaza is the starting point of one of the best outdoor sculpture walks in America, and most of it is within a few minutes of where you're standing.
You heard about Miró's figure across Washington Street.
Its real title is simply Chicago.
It stands thirty-nine feet tall, made of concrete, steel, bronze and ceramic tile, and it was unveiled in 1981, when Miró was in his late eighties.

A block north, at Clark and Randolph, in front of the curved glass state office building designed by Helmut Jahn, stands Jean Dubuffet's Monument with Standing Beast, unveiled in 1984: a twenty-nine-foot tangle of white fiberglass outlined in black that you can walk right into.
Chicagoans nicknamed it Snoopy in a Blender.
The building behind it, long known as the Thompson Center, was bought by Google in 2022.

A few blocks south, at Dearborn and Monroe, is Marc Chagall's Four Seasons, a freestanding wall seventy feet long, fourteen feet high and ten feet wide, covered on all four sides in a mosaic of stone and glass in a great range of colors, with scenes of the seasons and of Chicago.
Chagall came to the city for its dedication in 1974.
A glass canopy was added in 1994 to protect it from the weather.
Chagall loved Chicago back.
A few years later he made the America Windows for the Art Institute, a row of deep blue stained glass celebrating American freedom and the arts, and dedicated them to the memory of Mayor Daley.
They were unveiled on May 15, 1977, which would have been Daley's seventy-fifth birthday.
Two more are worth the walk.
At Madison and Wells is Louise Nevelson's Dawn Shadows, from 1983, a thicket of black steel that looks different from every side.
And just across the river, at six hundred West Madison, Claes Oldenburg's Batcolumn, from 1977, is a lattice baseball bat a hundred feet tall, standing in front of a federal office building.
Oldenburg liked to take ordinary things and make them enormous, and in a city of tall columns, he gave Chicago a bat.
The tower behind the Picasso holds the courtrooms of Cook County, and in the early 1980s it was the scene of the biggest investigation of judicial corruption in American history.
For years, lawyers had known that some of the county's judges were for sale.
Cases could be fixed for a price, with the money passed through court clerks, police officers or lawyers who acted as bagmen.
In 1980, the FBI and the United States attorney's office began an undercover operation to prove it.
They called it Greylord, after the curled gray wigs worn by English judges.

The key undercover agent was a young prosecutor named Terrence Hake, who pretended to be a corrupt prosecutor and later a crooked defense lawyer, and spent years paying bribes while wearing a hidden recorder.
FBI agents posed as defendants in fake cases invented just for the investigation, so that there would be something to fix.
A judge from downstate Illinois, Brocton Lockwood, who was assigned to traffic court here, agreed to wear a wire as well.
And for the first time, the FBI won permission to plant a bug in a judge's chambers.
When the investigation became public in 1983, it was a sensation.
In all, ninety-two people were indicted, among them seventeen judges and forty-eight lawyers, along with police officers, deputy sheriffs and court clerks, and nearly all of them were convicted.
A later case was even darker: in 1994, a former judge named Thomas Maloney was sent to prison for taking bribes to fix murder trials.
Corruption didn't stop at the courthouse.
By the count of Dick Simpson, a former alderman who became a political scientist, more than thirty Chicago aldermen have been convicted of crimes since the 1970s.
The most famous is Ed Burke, who served on the city council for fifty-four years, longer than anyone in its history.
In December 2023, a federal jury convicted him of racketeering, bribery and attempted extortion, and in 2024 he was sentenced to two years in prison.
Chicagoans have a saying for all this, borrowed from an old alderman: Chicago ain't ready for reform.
Walk back east to State Street and turn left, north, to Lake Street.
Above you, the elevated trains rattle along the north side of the Loop.
And on the west side of State, just past Lake, is the sign that is almost a logo for the city: the vertical marquee of the Chicago Theatre.
The theatre opened in 1921, built by Balaban and Katz, the movie palace chain that turned going to the movies into an event.
It was designed by the brothers Cornelius and George Rapp.
Look at the facade above the marquee: a giant arch with a round stained-glass window, modeled on a French triumphal arch.
Inside is a grand lobby modeled on the Royal Chapel at Versailles, and an auditorium that seats about thirty-six hundred people.
Balaban and Katz were known for their showmanship and for what they called the comfort of the audience.
Their theatres were among the first in the country to be cooled in summer, with early air conditioning systems, which helped draw crowds in the heat.
By the 1980s, the theatre was in decline and threatened with demolition.
It was saved, restored, and reopened in 1986, and today it hosts concerts and comedy.
The marquee lit up overhead is a replica of the 1949 sign, and the six-story vertical sign spelling out Chicago is one of the most photographed spots in the city.
Look up at the elevated tracks.
They were built in the 1890s by a group of companies controlled by Charles Tyson Yerkes, a ruthless financier who ran much of Chicago's streetcar system and was famous for bribing aldermen.
He's said to have explained that the secret of success in his business was to buy up old junk, fix it up a little, and unload it on other fellows.
When Chicago finally turned against him, he moved to London and helped build the London Underground.
The ring of tracks he completed in 1897, the Union Loop, gave the downtown its name, and the trains still squeal around its tight corners every few minutes, more than a century later.
This is the end of the Loop tour.
If you keep walking north on State Street, you will reach the Chicago River in two blocks, where the Riverwalk tour begins.
You heard that Balaban and Katz turned the movies into an event.
They started on the West Side, in a family of Jewish immigrants who ran a small grocery.
The Balaban brothers went into the picture business when it was still nickelodeons, and they teamed up with a sharp young businessman named Sam Katz.
Their first big hit was the Central Park Theatre on Roosevelt Road, which opened in 1917 and is often called one of the first movie theatres anywhere with mechanical cooling.
Barney Balaban had worked for a cold storage company, and he knew how refrigeration worked.
Then came the Riviera, the Tivoli, and this theatre in 1921, each grander than the last.
They had a formula, and it worked.
Build next to the L or a streetcar line, so customers could ride to the door.
Make the building a palace, so that a factory worker could feel like a king for the price of a ticket.
Give a full show: a feature film, live stage acts and an orchestra.
And hire ushers in uniform, drilled like soldiers to be polite to every customer, whoever they were.
The music was part of the draw.
In the 1920s, the organist Jesse Crawford, known as the Poet of the Organ, played the theatre's mighty Wurlitzer and became a national star through records and radio.
The organ is still here.
In 1925, Balaban and Katz joined forces with Paramount, the Hollywood studio.
Sam Katz went to New York to run Paramount's theatres, and Barney Balaban later became president of Paramount Pictures, a job he held from 1936 to 1964.
The family that started in a West Side grocery ended up running one of the biggest studios in Hollywood.

And when the restored theatre reopened in September 1986, the star of the opening night gala was Frank Sinatra, singing on the stage where the Balabans' stage shows had once played between the pictures.
Charles Tyson Yerkes came to Chicago with a prison record.
He'd been a successful young financier in Philadelphia, handling the city's bonds, until the Chicago Fire of 1871 set off a panic in the markets.
Yerkes couldn't cover the city money he'd been using in his own speculations.
He was convicted and sentenced to two years and nine months in prison, and was pardoned after seven months.
In the early 1880s he moved to Chicago and set out to control its streetcars.
He took over the main lines on the North and West Sides, replaced the horses first with cable cars and then with electric trolleys, and ran them for profit above all else.
The cars were packed, and when riders complained, he's often quoted as saying that it's the strap-hangers who pay the dividends.
His great gamble came in 1897.
Yerkes got the state legislature to pass a law allowing Chicago to grant streetcar franchises for as long as fifty years, and then he asked the city council for exactly that.
