You heard that the Randolph Street end of this building honored the Grand Army of the Republic.
It's worth knowing just how powerful those old soldiers were.
The Grand Army was founded in April 1866 in Decatur, in central Illinois, by a former army surgeon named Benjamin Stephenson.
It began as a brotherhood of men who had fought for the Union, a way to remember the dead and look after widows and orphans.
It grew into something much bigger.
By 1890, it had more than four hundred thousand members, with posts in nearly every town in the North.
Those members voted, and they voted together.
The Grand Army became one of the most powerful lobbies in American history, and its great cause was pensions.
Congress kept widening the benefits for Union veterans and their families, until by the 1890s the pension bill was one of the largest items in the federal budget.
Politicians courted the old soldiers relentlessly, and the Grand Army helped elect five presidents who had been Union officers, from Grant to McKinley.
Grover Cleveland, who had paid a substitute to serve in his place during the war, vetoed hundreds of private pension bills, and many veterans never forgave him.
One of the Grand Army's leaders was an Illinois man, General John Logan.
In 1868, as its commander in chief, he issued an order setting aside the thirtieth of May for decorating the graves of the Union dead.
Decoration Day, as it was first called, became Memorial Day.
Here in Chicago, the state set aside the north end of this site for the veterans, and they gathered in the rooms beneath the second glass dome.
But even the Grand Army couldn't escape time.
As its members died, the rooms grew quiet, and after the Second World War the library took over the whole building.
The last member of the Grand Army, a former drummer boy named Albert Woolson, died in Minnesota in 1956, and the order died with him.
Since a restoration finished in 2022, the memorial rooms are open again, and you can stand where the veterans met.
You heard about the Tiffany dome above Preston Bradley Hall.
Here are a few more things to look for once you're inside.
Start with the words.
The mosaics around the arches and along the walls carry quotations about books and learning, and they aren't all in English.
The designers chose inscriptions in ten languages, ancient and modern, perhaps as a way of saying that a free public library belonged to all of human learning.
The names of great writers are worked into the decoration too.
Even if you can't read the scripts, see how many you can tell apart.
Then go to the other side of the building, to the old memorial hall on the Randolph Street side, and look up.
That dome is forty feet across, two feet wider than the famous Tiffany dome, and it's made of about sixty-two thousand pieces of glass.
A restoration completed in 2022 cleaned and repaired it piece by piece, and its colors glow again.
Many visitors never find it, which makes it one of the quiet pleasures of the city.
Back upstairs, the great hall carries the name of Preston Bradley, the pastor of the Peoples Church in Uptown, whose radio sermons reached millions of listeners for decades.
His broadcasts are even said to have inspired the long-running soap opera Guiding Light.
He served on the library's board for more than a quarter of a century, and the city honored him by putting his name on its most beautiful room.
Finally, think about the architects, Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge.
They were the heirs of Henry Hobson Richardson, the great Boston architect, and they took over his practice after his death in 1886.

In Chicago, Richardson designed the Glessner House on Prairie Avenue and the Marshall Field Wholesale Store, a massive stone warehouse in the Loop that many architects counted among his finest buildings, torn down in 1930.
His successors carried his firm into the next century, with the main quadrangle of Stanford University in California, the Art Institute down the avenue, and this library.
For more than twenty years, the person who ran Chicago's cultural life worked out of this building.
Her name was Lois Weisberg, and if you've ever seen a painted fiberglass cow standing on a sidewalk, in Chicago or anywhere else, you've seen a little of her influence.
Weisberg became the city's first commissioner of cultural affairs in 1989, under Mayor Richard M. Daley, and she held the job until 2011, one of the longest runs of anyone in his cabinet.
Before that, she had done a bit of everything.
In 1975, she helped found Friends of the Parks, a citizens' group that still fights for the city's parks and lakefront.
In 1983, she joined the staff of Mayor Harold Washington to run the city's special events.
Her ideas were cheerful and practical.
She turned a grassy, empty downtown block, known as Block 37, into Gallery 37, a summer program that paid teenagers to make art, her answer to kids hanging around the parks with nothing to do.
And in 1999, she helped persuade the mayor to fill the streets with Cows on Parade, hundreds of life-size fiberglass cows decorated by artists.
Some Chicagoans rolled their eyes, but the crowds loved them, the cows were auctioned for charity, and cities around the world copied the idea.
That same year, the writer Malcolm Gladwell profiled her in The New Yorker, under the title Six Degrees of Lois Weisberg.
His point was that she seemed to know everyone, in every walk of life, and that people like her, whom he called connectors, are how ideas and trends spread.
The profile became part of his best-selling book The Tipping Point.
Weisberg left the job in 2011 and died in 2016, at the age of ninety.
Some aldermen proposed renaming this building for her.
Whatever it's called, the free concerts, exhibitions, and festivals that pour out of it are her monument.
You're in Millennium Park, at the northwest corner of Grant Park, near Michigan Avenue and Washington Street.
Until the late 1990s, this was an ugly corner of the park, covered with railroad tracks and surface parking lots.
The city decked over the tracks and built a park on top of a parking garage.
It opened in 2004, years late and far over budget, but it became one of the most popular attractions in the Midwest.
The star is Cloud Gate, a sculpture by the British artist Anish Kapoor, which everyone calls the Bean.
It's made of more than a hundred and sixty stainless steel plates, welded together and polished so smooth that the seams are invisible.
Walk around it and under its arch, called the omphalos, or navel, and look at the reflections of the skyline and the people, warped and stretched.
To the north is the Jay Pritzker Pavilion, an outdoor concert stage designed by Frank Gehry, with its explosion of curling stainless steel.
Over the lawn stretches a trellis of steel pipes carrying the sound system, so the music sounds clear everywhere on the lawn.
Summer concerts here are free.
To the south is the Crown Fountain, by the Spanish artist Jaume Plensa: two glass block towers, fifty feet tall, facing each other across a shallow pool.
They show video portraits of about a thousand Chicagoans, who purse their lips, and then water spouts from their mouths, like the gargoyles of old fountains.
In summer, kids play in the water.
Millennium Park ended up costing several times its original budget, and private donors paid for much of it, which is why nearly every part of it carries a donor's name.

Look for the Lurie Garden, south of the Pritzker Pavilion, a garden of prairie plants and perennials, enclosed on two sides by a tall hedge meant to evoke Carl Sandburg's description of Chicago as the City of the Big Shoulders.

And east of the pavilion, look for the BP Bridge, a winding walkway designed by Frank Gehry and clad in stainless steel, which snakes over Columbus Drive toward Maggie Daley Park, a park full of playgrounds and climbing walls named for the wife of Mayor Richard M. Daley.
Under your feet, beneath the gardens and the garage, the Metra Electric trains still run into Millennium Station, along the same route the Illinois Central took along the lakefront in the 1850s.
When Cloud Gate was first unveiled in 2004, it wasn't finished.
The seams between its plates were still visible, and it was covered up again while workers spent months grinding and polishing them away.
Kapoor said he was inspired by liquid mercury.
He reportedly wasn't fond of the nickname "the Bean," but the name stuck before the sculpture was even complete.
You heard that Millennium Park came in late and over budget.
The story of how that happened explains a lot about the park around you.

When Mayor Richard M. Daley announced the plan in the late 1990s, it was a modest one: cover the railroad yards in this corner of Grant Park with a parking garage, put a park on the roof, and finish in time for the new millennium.
The city expected to spend about a hundred and fifty million dollars.
Construction began in October 1998.
Then the ambitions grew.
Frank Gehry was brought in to design a concert stage.
Anish Kapoor's sculpture, Jaume Plensa's fountain, a garden, an indoor theater for music and dance, and an indoor station for bicycle commuters were added.
Each addition made the park better and the bill bigger.
The park finally opened on July sixteenth, 2004, four years behind schedule, and the total came to roughly four hundred and seventy-five million dollars.
The city paid more than half, and private donors covered the rest, an enormous sum for a public park at the time.
The planners thanked those donors the way an old cathedral thanks its patrons, in stone.
Walk to the northwest corner of the park, at Michigan Avenue and Randolph Street, into Wrigley Square, and you'll find a curved row of tall limestone columns.
It's called the Millennium Monument, and it honors the people, companies, and foundations who paid for the park.
The columns have a history of their own.
They copy a semicircular colonnade, called a peristyle, that Edward Bennett, the designer of Buckingham Fountain, put on this spot in 1917.
The original was built of concrete, and the lake winters were hard on it.
In 1953, it was torn down to make room for an underground parking garage.
When Millennium Park was built, the peristyle came back in stone, a little smaller than before, to leave room for a ramp.
So the newest corner of Grant Park is also a careful copy of one of its oldest.
Anish Kapoor was born in Mumbai in 1954 and has spent most of his working life in London.

When Chicago chose his design for this plaza, he was already one of Britain's best known sculptors, the winner of the Turner Prize in 1991, famous for objects that seem to swallow light or bend the space around them.
Cloud Gate became the most famous of them all.
The numbers are simple to say and hard to picture.
The sculpture is thirty-three feet high, sixty-six feet long, and forty-two feet wide, and it weighs about a hundred and ten tons.
Every day, thousands of people put their hands on it, and every handprint shows.
So a crew wipes down the lower part by hand twice a day, and the whole sculpture gets a thorough scrubbing twice a year.
Being one of the most photographed objects in America has its complications.
In 2017, the National Rifle Association released a short, ominous promotional video that included a fleeting shot of the Bean.
Kapoor objected to his work being used to promote the group's message, and in June 2018 he sued for copyright infringement.
That December, the case was settled, and the image came out of the video.
The group said it had paid him nothing, and Kapoor declared victory anyway.
In August 2023, the city fenced off the plaza around the sculpture to replace the paving and make it easier for wheelchairs and strollers to reach.
For months, visitors could see the Bean only from a distance, through gaps in the construction barriers, and the work ran into 2024.
Before you leave, stand directly beneath the arch and look up into the hollow at its center.
Your reflection repeats, folding into itself again and again, and the skyline disappears.
That inner chamber, more than the view of the city, is where Kapoor's idea is clearest: a sculpture that is really about you, looking.

The concert stage north of the Bean is named for Jay Pritzker, and once you start looking for his family's name in Chicago, you see it everywhere: on the medical school at the University of Chicago, on the law school at Northwestern, on a military museum and library on Michigan Avenue, and, since 2019, in the governor's office in Springfield.
The family's story in America begins with Nicholas Pritzker, a Jewish immigrant from Kyiv, who arrived in Chicago in 1881.
The family started a law firm, and his grandsons, above all Jay, turned it into a base for deals.
They bought struggling companies, kept them, and fixed them, assembling a vast collection of businesses that made the family one of the richest in the country.
The best known of those businesses began in 1957, when Jay Pritzker bought a motel next to the Los Angeles airport.
It was called the Hyatt House, after one of the men who had built it, Hyatt von Dehn, and the Pritzkers kept the name.
Ten years later, they bought an unfinished hotel in Atlanta, designed by the architect John Portman around a soaring atrium with glass elevators.
It became the first Hyatt Regency, and atriums like it spread to hotels around the world.
Perhaps that's why Jay and his wife Cindy cared so much about architecture.
In 1979, they founded the Pritzker Architecture Prize, now often called the Nobel Prize of architecture.
Its first winner was Philip Johnson.
Frank Gehry won it in 1989, about a decade before he designed the pavilion, its steel trellis, and the winding bridge behind it.
Jay Pritzker died in 1999, five years before the pavilion that bears his name opened.
His relatives have stayed in public life.
His niece, Penny Pritzker, served as President Obama's secretary of commerce, and his nephew, J. B. Pritzker, was elected governor of Illinois in 2018.
You heard about the tall hedge around the Lurie Garden.
Step inside it, because this garden helped change the way public spaces are planted.
It sits entirely on a roof.
Beneath the soil is a parking garage, so every plant here grows in a layer of earth laid over concrete.

The garden covers about two and a half acres, and it was designed by a team that won a competition in 2000: the Seattle landscape firm Gustafson Guthrie Nichol; the theater designer Robert Israel, who shaped its concept and its lighting; and a Dutch nurseryman named Piet Oudolf, who chose the plants.
It was Oudolf's first commission in the United States.
A few years later, he planted the High Line in New York, and his style spread around the world.
That style is what you're looking at.

Instead of tidy beds of flowers that bloom, fade, and get pulled out, Oudolf plants drifts of tough perennials and grasses, many of them native to the Midwestern prairie, chosen to look good in every season.
In late spring, a river of purple salvia flows through the part of the garden called the Light Plate.
In summer, coneflowers and bee balm take over, humming with bees.
In fall, the grasses turn the color of wheat, and the seed heads are left standing into winter, for their shapes in the snow and for the birds that feed on them.
A boardwalk runs along a shallow channel of water called the Seam.
On a warm day, you can sit on the edge and dangle your feet in it.
At night, a long wall beside it is lit from below, and its glow reflects in the water.
The garden is named for Ann Lurie, a Chicago philanthropist, whose family's name you may also see on the children's hospital in Streeterville.
Before the city was built, much of the land around Chicago was tallgrass prairie, with grasses taller than a person.
This garden is a memory of it, growing on top of a parking garage.
Walk south along Michigan Avenue to the entrance of the Art Institute, guarded by two bronze lions.
The lions were sculpted by Edward Kemeys and installed in 1894.
The one on the south is said to be standing in an attitude of defiance, and the one on the north to be on the prowl.
When the city's teams win championships, the lions sometimes wear giant helmets or caps, and in December they wear wreaths.

The building was built for the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893, as a hall for a series of conferences held during the fair, including the World's Parliament of Religions, one of the first great meetings of the world's religious traditions.
After the fair, it became the Art Institute's home.
The Art Institute is one of the great art museums of the world.

Thanks partly to Bertha Palmer and other Chicago collectors, it has one of the finest collections of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings outside Paris, including Georges Seurat's huge painting, A Sunday on La Grande Jatte.

It also has two of the most famous American paintings: Grant Wood's American Gothic, which won a prize here in 1930, and Edward Hopper's Nighthawks, bought by the museum in 1942, the year it was painted.
Now look at the street sign at the corner of Adams Street and Michigan Avenue.
It says "Begin Historic Route 66."
This was the eastern starting point of the famous highway, which ran more than two thousand miles from Chicago to Santa Monica, California, and became a symbol of the open road.
If you go inside, look for two things that tell Chicago's own story.
One is the Thorne Miniature Rooms, sixty-eight tiny rooms built at a scale of one inch to one foot, showing interiors from European and American history in astonishing detail.
They were commissioned in the 1930s by Narcissa Niblack Thorne, whose husband was an heir to the Montgomery Ward fortune.
The other is the trading room of the old Chicago Stock Exchange, designed by Adler and Sullivan in 1894, with its stenciled walls and art glass.

When the Stock Exchange building on LaSalle Street was demolished in 1972, the photographer and preservationist Richard Nickel was killed when part of the building collapsed on him while he was trying to salvage its ornament.
The trading room was rebuilt inside the museum, and the building's great arched entrance now stands outside, on the museum's east side, facing Columbus Drive.
The museum has grown in stages, eastward over the railroad tracks behind it.
Its newest addition, the Modern Wing, designed by Renzo Piano, opened in 2009, with a footbridge across Monroe Street to Millennium Park.
And if the gallery with the big Seurat looks familiar, you may have seen it in the 1986 movie Ferris Bueller's Day Off, in which Ferris and his friends skip school and spend part of the day here.
The director, John Hughes, said the Art Institute had been a refuge for him when he was young.
You heard that the World's Parliament of Religions met in this building.
Its opening day, September eleventh, 1893, produced one of the most famous speeches ever given in Chicago.
The parliament grew out of a plan by a Chicago lawyer, Charles Bonney, to hold congresses of ideas alongside the world's fair, so that the fair would show off thought as well as machines.
A Presbyterian minister, John Henry Barrows, led the organizing committee.
For seventeen days, representatives of the world's faiths spoke in turn in a great hall in the new building, the Hall of Columbus, with room for about four thousand people.
Fullerton Hall, the museum's auditorium today, occupies roughly the spot where the speakers' platform stood.
On the first day, a thirty-year-old Hindu monk from Calcutta rose to speak.
His name was Swami Vivekananda, and he had come to America with little money and few connections.
He began with five words: Sisters and Brothers of America.
By most accounts, the audience rose and applauded for minutes before he could go on.
He spoke about tolerance, and against what he called sectarianism, bigotry, and its horrible descendant, fanaticism, which he hoped this gathering would help bring to an end.
He became the star of the parliament.
A New York newspaper called him the greatest figure there, and he spent the next few years lecturing across the United States and in Britain, founding the Vedanta Society in New York.
He died in India in 1902, at the age of thirty-nine.
India now celebrates his birthday as its National Youth Day, and many Indian visitors to Chicago come here to see where he spoke.
He wasn't the only speaker who left a mark.
A Buddhist reformer from Ceylon, Anagarika Dharmapala, made a strong impression.
And a Japanese Zen abbot named Soyen Shaku caught the attention of Paul Carus, a publisher in La Salle, Illinois.
Carus later brought Soyen Shaku's young student, D. T. Suzuki, to America, and Suzuki went on to do more than anyone to introduce Zen Buddhism to the West.
You heard that American Gothic won a prize here in 1930.
It almost didn't.
The painter, Grant Wood, was a quiet Iowa artist who had studied in Paris and then come home to paint the Midwest.

On a visit to the little town of Eldon, in southern Iowa, he noticed a small white farmhouse with a single pointed Gothic window in its upper gable, a fancy church-style flourish on a plain wooden house.
He sketched it and imagined the kind of people who might live there.
To paint them, he used people he knew.
The woman is his sister, Nan Wood Graham, who was about thirty.
The man is his dentist from Cedar Rapids, Byron McKeeby, who was sixty-two.
Neither of them farmed.
Look at how Wood repeated the shape of the pitchfork, in the stitching of the man's overalls and in the window behind the couple.
Wood entered the painting in the Art Institute's annual exhibition of American art.
One of the judges dismissed it as a comic valentine.
But a museum patron argued for it, and the jury gave it a bronze medal and a prize of three hundred dollars.
The museum bought it that year, and it has been here ever since.
Then came the reaction.
Newspapers reproduced it across the country, and many Iowans were offended, convinced that Wood was mocking farm people as grim and narrow, and dozens of them wrote to complain.
Nan was mortified that people took her for the wife of a man twice her age, and she said the couple were meant to be father and daughter.
Wood insisted he admired the people he painted.
In the hard years of the Depression that followed, the stern pair came to look less like a joke and more like a picture of endurance.
The painting has been copied and parodied more than almost any other American image.
It rarely travels, and its trip to Paris and London in 2016 and 2017 was its first outside the United States.
The house in Eldon still stands, and its visitor center lends out aprons and pitchforks, so you can pose in front of it.
In the spring of 1913, perhaps the most talked-about art exhibition in American history came to this building.
It's known as the Armory Show, after the National Guard armory in New York where it had opened that February.
It was America's first big look at modern European art: Cézanne, Van Gogh, and Gauguin, and younger painters like Picasso, Marcel Duchamp, and Henri Matisse.
In New York, crowds had laughed and argued in front of Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase, which one writer compared to an explosion in a shingle factory.
In Chicago, the reaction was harsher still.
Newspapers mocked the paintings, and there was even talk of a vice investigation.
Crowds came anyway, many of them to see what the fuss was about.
The angriest of all were the students at the Art Institute's own school, who had been trained in careful academic drawing and took Matisse's bright, flattened, distorted figures as an insult.
They nicknamed him Henry Hair Mattress.
On the show's last day, they staged a mock trial on the museum's south portico, with students playing the judges, and found the painter guilty.
Then they burned copies of three of his paintings, among them the famous Blue Nude.
Accounts differ about the climax.
Some say they burned an effigy of Matisse himself, and others say they were stopped before they could.
The school's officials had heard about the plan and forbidden it, but some of the teachers were cheering the students on.
History has been kind to Matisse and unkind to his judges.
Within a generation, the Art Institute was collecting modern art in earnest.
In 1953, it bought Matisse's great canvas Bathers by a River, which he considered one of the most important paintings of his career.
You can see it today in the Modern Wing, not far from the spot where the students put his work on trial.
You heard that Route 66 began at this corner.
Here's how it got its number, a story of politics, pride, and a good ear.
In 1925 and 1926, federal and state officials set out to number the country's main highways in one national system for the first time.
Roads running east and west would get even numbers, and the most important of them would end in zero.

A highway official from Tulsa, Oklahoma, named Cyrus Avery was the great champion of a long diagonal road from Chicago to Los Angeles that would run through his state, and he wanted it to be Route 60.
Kentucky objected.
Its governor was upset that no route ending in zero would cross his state, and he wanted the number 60 for a road through Kentucky.
The argument dragged on for months.
A compromise gave the Chicago road the number 62, but Avery didn't like it.
Then he and the chief highway engineer of Missouri noticed that the number 66 hadn't been assigned to anything.
In April 1926, they sent a telegram to Washington saying they preferred it.
Avery thought it would be easy to remember and pleasant to say.
The final plan was approved that November.
He was right about the sound.
In 1939, John Steinbeck called it the mother road in The Grapes of Wrath, the road that carried families fleeing the Dust Bowl west to California.
In 1946, the songwriter Bobby Troup turned it into a song, Get Your Kicks on Route 66, and Nat King Cole made it a hit, with its list of towns from Chicago to the coast.
The interstates replaced the old road, and it was officially decommissioned in 1985, but it has never been forgotten.
In 2026, it turned a hundred.
One more detail.
The Begin sign is on Adams Street, which carries traffic west, and the matching End sign is a block south on Jackson Boulevard, which carries traffic east.
And about a mile west on Jackson, across the river, Lou Mitchell's restaurant has been serving breakfast since 1923, and Route 66 travelers have long treated it as their first stop.
Walk south and east through the gardens to Buckingham Fountain, the centerpiece of Grant Park.
It was dedicated in 1927, a gift from Kate Buckingham, a wealthy art collector, in memory of her brother Clarence, who had been a director of the Art Institute.
The design was inspired by the Latona Fountain at the Palace of Versailles, but at roughly twice its size.
It's one of the largest fountains in the world.
The fountain is built of pink Georgia marble, in three tiers, like a wedding cake.
Look at the four pairs of bronze sea horses around the base.
They represent the four states that border Lake Michigan: Illinois, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Indiana.
The basin itself represents the lake.
From spring to fall, the fountain puts on a water show every hour, with the central jet shooting up to about a hundred and fifty feet.
At night, there's a light and music show.
Look back toward the city from here.
The view of the skyline from Buckingham Fountain is one of the most famous in Chicago, and you may recognize it from the opening credits of the television show Married with Children.
The fountain was designed by Edward Bennett, who had worked with Daniel Burnham on the Plan of Chicago, and its sea horses were made by a French sculptor, Marcel Loyau.
Kate Buckingham didn't just pay for the fountain.
She also set up a fund to pay for its upkeep, worried that the city might not take care of it.
Notice how the fountain fits into the plan of the park.

It sits on the line of the broad street that runs west from here into the Loop, and it's the centerpiece of a formal composition of gardens, terraces, and promenades in the French style, the kind of grand, ordered landscape that Burnham imagined for the whole lakefront.
You heard that Kate Buckingham gave this fountain in memory of her brother.
She was one of the most generous and least visible people in Chicago's history.
Her father, Ebenezer Buckingham, made the family fortune in grain elevators, the giant storehouses along the river that held the wheat and corn of the Midwest before it was shipped east.
The family spread into banking, steel, and real estate.
Kate never married.
She was devoted to her brother Clarence and her sister Lucy Maud, and as each of them died, she inherited the family wealth and gave much of it away.
Clarence had fallen in love with Japanese art at the world's fair of 1893, and he spent the rest of his life collecting Japanese woodblock prints.
His collection, some two and a half thousand prints, went to the Art Institute, where it's still counted among the finest outside Japan.
Kate had her own passion.
Over nearly two decades, she gave the museum more than four hundred ancient Chinese ritual bronzes, in memory of Lucy Maud, and they became the foundation of its collection of Asian art.
She had traveled often in Europe and admired its great public fountains, and she wanted Chicago to have one that could stand beside any of them.
When the fountain was finished, she didn't trust the city to keep it up.
So she gave three hundred thousand dollars more for its maintenance and made the Art Institute, rather than the park commissioners, the custodian of the fund.
Her estate later paid for one more monument, the statue of Alexander Hamilton that stands in Lincoln Park.
Notice whose names are on her gifts.
The fountain is named for her brother, and the bronzes were given in her sister's memory.
Her own name is easy to miss, and that seems to be how she wanted it.
Everything you see at Buckingham Fountain depends on something you can't see: a two-level pump house buried beneath the plaza.
The fountain holds about a million and a half gallons of water.

During the big shows, the pumps push about fourteen thousand gallons a minute through the jets, enough to drive the central column to its full height while the smaller jets and the sea horses' spouts play around it.
There are three main pumps, of different sizes, and some of the original equipment from 1927 kept running for decades.
For years, the computer that ran the shows wasn't even in Chicago.
By one account, the control system sat in Atlanta, Georgia, until a renovation in 1994 moved it into the pump house.
In 2013, the Park District replaced it with modern controls.
Water and stone don't get along in a Chicago winter.
Water seeps into the joints, freezes, and pries them apart, and by the early 1990s the fountain was leaking.
The 1994 renovation, which cost about two point eight million dollars, rebuilt the three smaller upper basins, and later projects have gone on repairing the marble, the plumbing, and the lights.
Every fall, the fountain is shut down for the winter, and it comes back to life in the spring, an event many Chicagoans treat as a sign that the cold is finally over.
While you're here, look at the sea horses with fresh eyes.
The French sculptor Marcel Loyau studied real sea horses in a scientific collection in Paris before he modeled them, and the figures won him a national prize at the Paris Salon of 1927.
Look for the fins, the ridged bodies, and the curled tails that he took such care to get right.
You heard about Montgomery Ward's lawsuits to keep the lakefront open.
There was an older fight over this shoreline, and it went all the way to the Supreme Court.
Its result still shapes how Americans treat their lakes, rivers, and coasts.
In the years after the Civil War, the Illinois Central Railroad was one of the most powerful companies in the state.
Its tracks already ran along the shore on a trestle, and it wanted much more: a harbor, docks, and room to grow.
In 1869, the Illinois legislature passed what became known as the Lake Front Act.
It handed the railroad more than a thousand acres of lake bottom off downtown, essentially the whole bed of the Chicago harbor, to fill and build on.
Charges of corruption hung over the vote from the start.
Public anger grew, and in 1873 the legislature repealed the act.
The railroad refused to accept it, arguing that a grant is a grant, and that the state couldn't take back what it had given.
It kept building along the shore while the lawsuits dragged on for years.
In December 1892, the Supreme Court decided the case, four votes to three.
Justice Stephen Field wrote for the majority.
The bed of the lake, he said, wasn't like an ordinary piece of land that the state could sell.

The state held it in trust for the people, so that they could fish, sail, and travel on the water, and a legislature could no more give that trust away to a private company than it could give away its power to govern.
The repeal stood.
For most of a century, the decision was a quiet precedent.
Then, in 1970, a law professor named Joseph Sax argued that it should be the foundation of a public trust doctrine to protect natural resources, and courts around the country took up the idea.
Lawyers in cases over beaches, rivers, and wetlands still cite the case of the Illinois Central and the Chicago lakefront.
So as you look out from the fountain toward the water, remember that part of what keeps it public is a ruling about this very shore.
Walk west from the fountain toward Michigan Avenue, through Congress Plaza, where two giant bronze horsemen guard the entrance to the park.
They're the Bowman and the Spearman, by the Croatian sculptor Ivan Meštrović, installed in 1928.
Look closely: the archer has no bow, and the spearman has no spear.
The sculptor left the weapons to your imagination.
Then walk south on Michigan Avenue to Balbo Drive.
The enormous hotel on the corner is the Hilton Chicago.
It opened in 1927 as the Stevens Hotel, and with about three thousand rooms, it was the largest hotel in the world.
It had its own hospital, a bowling alley, a theater, and a miniature golf course on the roof.
It was built by James Stevens and his son Ernest, whose family also ran an insurance company.
The Depression ruined them.
The hotel went bankrupt, and Ernest Stevens was charged with embezzlement, though his conviction was overturned.
His youngest son, John Paul Stevens, grew up to become a justice of the Supreme Court.
During the Second World War, the Army bought the hotel and used it as barracks for thousands of airmen in training, who did their drills in Grant Park.
After the war, it was bought by the hotelier Conrad Hilton.
In August 1968, this was the headquarters hotel of the Democratic National Convention.
The country was torn apart by the Vietnam War, and Martin Luther King Junior and Robert Kennedy had both been assassinated that spring.

Thousands of antiwar protesters came to Chicago, and Mayor Richard J. Daley was determined to keep order, with nearly twelve thousand police officers on duty and thousands of National Guard troops and federal soldiers standing by.
All week, the police and the protesters clashed in Lincoln Park and here in Grant Park.
On the night of August twenty-eighth, while the delegates were nominating Vice President Hubert Humphrey at the convention hall near the stockyards, marchers tried to leave Grant Park.
At this intersection, right in front of the hotel, the police charged into the crowd, clubbing protesters, reporters, and bystanders.
People were shoved through the plate glass windows of the hotel's bar.
Television cameras filmed it all under the bright lights at the hotel's entrance, and the footage was broadcast across the country that night, while the convention was still going on.
The protesters chanted, "The whole world is watching."

Inside the convention hall, Senator Abraham Ribicoff of Connecticut, speaking from the podium, condemned what he called Gestapo tactics on the streets of Chicago, while Daley shouted back at him from the floor.
An official investigation later described what happened here as a police riot.
Eight protest leaders were charged with conspiracy, and they became known as the Chicago Seven after one defendant's case was separated from the others.
Before you move on, look at the street sign.
Balbo Drive is named for Italo Balbo, an Italian aviator, who led a fleet of twenty-four seaplanes from Italy to Chicago in 1933, landing on the lake during the Century of Progress world's fair.
The city gave him a hero's welcome and renamed Seventh Street in his honor.
But Balbo was also one of the leaders of Mussolini's Fascist party, and there have long been calls to change the name.
In 2018, the city renamed the broad street that runs west from Buckingham Fountain, which had been Congress Parkway, for the journalist and anti-lynching crusader Ida B. Wells.
It was the first street in downtown Chicago named for a Black woman.
You heard that the Stevens family built this hotel and lost it, and that one of the family's sons became a Supreme Court justice.
His name was John Paul Stevens, and his long life ran through some of the great moments of the American century.
He was born in 1920, and he was seven when the hotel opened.
For a boy, it was a wonderland.
Famous guests passed through the lobby, and young John Paul met two of the most celebrated flyers of the age, Charles Lindbergh and Amelia Earhart.
Then the Depression came, and the family's world fell apart.
The hotel went into receivership, his father was tried and convicted, and although the conviction was thrown out, the fortune was gone.
At twelve, he went with his father to Wrigley Field for the third game of the 1932 World Series, between the Cubs and the Yankees.
In the fifth inning, Babe Ruth hit his famous home run, the one he supposedly called by pointing toward the bleachers first.
Baseball historians have argued for decades about whether Ruth really pointed.
Stevens, a lifelong Cubs fan, never had any doubt.
He said he saw it.
He joined the Navy on December sixth, 1941, the day before Pearl Harbor, and spent most of the war in Hawaii as an intelligence officer, studying the patterns of Japanese radio traffic.
He was on duty in 1943 when decoded messages allowed American fighter planes to intercept and shoot down the plane carrying Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, who had planned the attack on Pearl Harbor.
Stevens received a Bronze Star, but he later admitted to mixed feelings about a mission aimed at killing one particular man.
After the war, he became a Chicago lawyer and then a federal judge, and in 1975 he became President Gerald Ford's only appointment to the Supreme Court.
He served there for nearly thirty-five years, retired in 2010, and died in 2019, at the age of ninety-nine.
You heard about the night of August twenty-eighth, in front of this hotel.
Here's more of what happened that week, much of it within sight of where you're standing.
The protests began as theater.

On August twenty-third, a few days before the convention opened, the Yippies, a band of radical pranksters, presented their own candidate for president at the Civic Center downtown, the plaza with the Picasso.
The candidate was a pig, which they called Pigasus.
The police arrested the pig, along with Jerry Rubin, the folk singer Phil Ochs, and several others, who were released on bonds of twenty-five dollars each.
The Yippies were delighted.
The police were not amused.

This hotel was the convention's headquarters, and both leading candidates for the nomination had their campaigns here: Vice President Hubert Humphrey, and the antiwar senator Eugene McCarthy, whose young volunteers filled the hallways.
Across Michigan Avenue, protesters gathered in the park around the statue of General John Logan, on the little hill just south of here.
At one point, demonstrators climbed onto the bronze horse and tried to plant a Viet Cong flag on it, and the police waded into the crowd to pull them down.
The violence wasn't only outside.
On the convention floor, security men roughed up the CBS reporter Dan Rather as he tried to interview a delegate, on live television.
Walter Cronkite, anchoring from the booth, said, I think we've got a bunch of thugs here, Dan.
The week ended with one more scene in this building.

Early on the morning after the convention closed, police came up to the fifteenth floor, where McCarthy's staff had their offices and a makeshift first aid station, saying that objects had been thrown at officers from the windows.
They beat several of the young campaign workers.
That December, a report for a national commission on violence, prepared under a Chicago lawyer and businessman named Daniel Walker, called what had happened a police riot.
It also faulted protesters for provoking the police with taunts and thrown objects.
Four years later, Walker was elected governor of Illinois.
You heard about Balbo Drive.
About a mile south of here, in a grove of trees just east of Soldier Field, stands a stranger reminder of Italo Balbo: a real column from ancient Rome.
It was a gift from Benito Mussolini.
After Balbo's squadron of seaplanes landed on the lake in 1933, Mussolini had a column taken from Ostia, the old port of ancient Rome, and shipped to Chicago.
It's about two thousand years old, and it stands on a modern stone base, dedicated in 1934.
The inscription on the base, in Italian and English, says that Fascist Italy, by command of Benito Mussolini, presents the column to Chicago in honor of the flight.
Balbo's own story ended badly.
He fell out of favor in Rome, and he is said to have disliked Mussolini's alliance with Hitler and his anti-Jewish racial laws.
He was sent away to govern Libya, and in 1940, early in the Second World War, his plane was shot down over Tobruk by mistake, by Italian anti-aircraft gunners.
In English, his name lived on in an odd way: for years, any big formation of aircraft was called a balbo.
For decades, few people paid attention to the column.
That changed in 2017, after a deadly white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, set off a national argument about monuments.
Protesters gathered here to demand that the column come down and that Balbo Drive be renamed.
Many Italian American groups objected, saying the monument honored a great feat of flying and the pride of Italian immigrants in the 1930s, not fascism.
In 2018, the city gave Ida B. Wells a different street.
In 2020, it took down the statue of Christopher Columbus that had stood in Grant Park since the 1930s.
And in 2022, a city advisory committee recommended removing the Balbo monument.
The column is still there, weathered and worn, its future undecided.
If you walk to Soldier Field, stop and read the inscription, and decide for yourself what it says about the city that kept it.
Before you leave this corner, look again at the two bronze horsemen at the entrance to Congress Plaza.
Their maker, Ivan Meštrović, lived one of the most dramatic lives of any artist whose work stands in Chicago.
He was born in 1883 to a poor Croatian family and grew up in a village in the stony hills of Dalmatia, herding sheep and carving figures from wood and stone.
With help from patrons, he went to study at the academy in Vienna, and by his late twenties he was famous across Europe, hailed by many as the great sculptor of the South Slavs.
Chicago's horsemen came from the height of his career, and they were installed in 1928.
Walk around them.
The riders are Native American warriors, bare-chested, one drawing a bow that isn't there, the other poised to hurl a spear that isn't there either.
Notice the tension in the horses and in the riders' arms, as if the whole group is caught in the instant before the arrow flies.
Because your eye supplies what's missing, the action feels even more alive.
Then history caught up with him.
When the Axis powers broke up Yugoslavia in 1941, Croatia fell under a Fascist regime called the Ustaše.
Meštrović was arrested in Zagreb that November and held in prison for about three and a half months.
He was freed after appeals from the Catholic Church reached all the way to the Vatican, and he left the country, never to live there again.
After the war, he settled in the United States.
In 1947, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York gave him a one-man show, a rare honor for a living sculptor.
He taught at Syracuse University and then at the University of Notre Dame, in South Bend, Indiana, where he kept working until his death in 1962.
Much of his late work was religious, shaped by the war and by his months in prison.
So the horsemen at the park's gate are the work of a man who became an exile, made in his golden years, long before the world he knew came apart.
Walk back east along Balbo Drive, across Columbus Drive, to the big lawn south of Buckingham Fountain.
This is Hutchinson Field, the largest open lawn in Grant Park.
On the night of November fourth, 2008, a crowd of hundreds of thousands gathered here to hear Barack Obama speak, after he was elected the first Black president of the United States.
Obama had come to Chicago in 1985 as a young community organizer on the South Side, and it was here that he'd built his career, as a state senator and then as a United States senator from Illinois.
People who were in the crowd remember it as a night of joy, with strangers hugging and weeping.
Television cameras caught the civil rights leader Jesse Jackson in the crowd, tears running down his face.
"If there is anyone out there who still doubts that America is a place where all things are possible," Obama began, "tonight is your answer."
The contrast with August 1968, a few hundred yards away and forty years earlier, was lost on no one.
Grant Park has gathered huge crowds many times.
In October 1979, Pope John Paul II celebrated Mass here, before one of the largest crowds in the city's history.

And on November fourth, 2016, eight years to the day after Obama's victory speech, this field held the rally for the Chicago Cubs, who had just won the World Series for the first time in a hundred and eight years.
The city estimated that millions of people lined the parade route and filled the park.

Every summer, the field fills up again for Lollapalooza, a rock festival that began in 1991 as a traveling tour, founded by the singer Perry Farrell, and that has settled in Grant Park every summer since 2005, drawing more than a hundred thousand people a day.
And the city has offered free outdoor concerts in the park for generations.
The Grant Park Music Festival, which puts on free classical concerts all summer, now at the Pritzker Pavilion, began in 1935.
It was started by James Petrillo, the powerful head of Chicago's musicians' union, as a way to put musicians to work during the Depression.
You heard that the free summer concerts in Grant Park were started by James Petrillo.
For decades, he was one of the most feared men in American entertainment.
Petrillo was born in Chicago in 1892, the son of Italian immigrants.
He started out playing the trumpet, but his real gift was organizing.
In 1922, he became president of the Chicago Federation of Musicians, the local musicians' union, and he ran it with an iron hand for decades.
Radio stations, hotels, and theaters learned that if they crossed Petrillo, their musicians would walk out.
His Grant Park concerts began in 1935, in a bandshell that stood here on Hutchinson Field.

Its successor, the Petrillo Music Shell, stands to the north, near Columbus Drive and Jackson Boulevard, and in 1984 it became the first home of the Chicago Blues Festival, a year after the death of Muddy Waters.
In 1940, Petrillo became president of the national union, the American Federation of Musicians, and he took on the record companies.
Records and jukeboxes, he argued, were putting live musicians out of work, and the players who made the records got nothing when they were played again and again.
On August first, 1942, in the middle of the Second World War, he ordered union members to stop making records altogether.
There were no exceptions, not even for symphony orchestras or famous bandleaders.
Decca gave in in 1943, but the two biggest labels, Columbia and Victor, held out until November 1944, when they agreed to pay royalties into a union fund.
The strike changed popular music.
Singers didn't belong to the musicians' union, so the record companies kept recording them, backed by choirs of voices instead of instruments.
During the ban and after it, the singers who had been featured with the big bands became stars on their own, and the big bands began to fade.
Congress struck back in 1946 with a law aimed squarely at his tactics, which everyone called the anti-Petrillo act.
He led the national union until 1958, and he died in 1984, at the age of ninety-two.
On election night in 2008, the gates to this field opened in the early evening, and tens of thousands of people with tickets filed onto the grass.
Many more came without tickets and filled the park around them, watching on giant screens.
The city's estimate of the total crowd was about two hundred and forty thousand.
They waited for hours.
At ten o'clock Chicago time, as the polls closed on the West Coast, the television networks declared Barack Obama the winner, and the park erupted.
Oprah Winfrey was somewhere in that crowd, along with the Reverend Jesse Jackson.
About an hour later, Obama walked onto the stage with his wife, Michelle, and their two young daughters.
The speech he gave is remembered for the opening line you heard at this stop, and for its refrain, Yes we can.
But the passage many people remember best was about a single voter.
He told the crowd about Ann Nixon Cooper, a woman in Atlanta who was a hundred and six years old.
She had been born just a generation after slavery, he said, at a time when someone like her couldn't vote for two reasons: because she was a woman, and because of the color of her skin.

Then he walked through the century she had lived: the despair of the Dust Bowl and the Depression, the bombs falling on Pearl Harbor, the buses in Montgomery and the fire hoses in Birmingham, a man landing on the moon.
And this year, he said, she had touched her finger to a screen and cast her vote.
Between the memories came the refrain, and the crowd answered it each time: Yes we can.
Ann Nixon Cooper lived to see Obama take office.
She died the following year, at the age of one hundred and seven.
Four years later, when Obama won reelection, he celebrated indoors, at McCormick Place on the lakefront, a mile or so south of here.
Grant Park had its night only once.
Every summer for decades, this end of Grant Park smelled of barbecue smoke, fried dough, and cheesecake.
The reason was the Taste of Chicago, once billed as the biggest food festival in the world, and it began as a one-day party.
The idea came from a restaurateur, Arnie Morton, whose name you may know from the steakhouses he founded.
His son Peter, by the way, was one of the founders of the Hard Rock Cafe.
Arnie Morton persuaded Mayor Jane Byrne to close Michigan Avenue on the Fourth of July in 1980 and line it with booths from Chicago restaurants, each selling small portions of its specialties.
The organizers expected perhaps a hundred thousand people.
Estimates of the crowd that actually came ran as high as a quarter of a million.
The next year, the Taste moved here, to Grant Park, where there was room to grow, and it grew enormously.
At its height, it ran for a week or more around the Fourth of July and drew crowds estimated in the millions.

For many families from the city and the suburbs, it was the one time each year they ate their way across Chicago's neighborhoods without leaving downtown: ribs and Italian beef, pierogi and tamales, egg rolls and deep dish pizza, and giant turkey legs eaten off the bone while walking.
Restaurants came and went, but one booth was there from the start.
In 1980, Eli Schulman, who ran a steakhouse called Eli's The Place for Steak, brought his cheesecake to the first Taste.
It was such a hit that his family built a whole business around it, and Eli's Cheesecake now ships across the country from a bakery on the Northwest Side.
For decades, it was the last of the original vendors still taking part.
The festival has shrunk in recent years and moved around the calendar, but the idea that started here, a city tasting itself, has been borrowed by many other cities.
Walk south through the park, and through the tunnels or along the paths, to the Museum Campus.
This area was created in the late 1990s, when the city moved Lake Shore Drive to the west, so that the three museums here could be joined in one landscape.
The white marble Greek temple in front of you is the Field Museum of Natural History.
It was founded after the 1893 fair, to keep its natural history collections, and it was named for Marshall Field, Chicago's greatest merchant, who gave a million dollars to start it.
The museum moved into this building in 1921.
Field built the department store that bore his name on State Street into one of the great stores of the world, with the motto "Give the lady what she wants."
He was, at his death in 1906, one of the richest men in America.
The museum's most famous resident is Sue, the most complete Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton ever found, discovered in South Dakota in 1990 by a fossil hunter named Sue Hendrickson.
After a legal battle over who owned it, Sue was sold at auction in 1997 for more than eight million dollars, and the Field Museum bought her with the help of McDonald's and Disney.
The museum's collections also include Egyptian mummies, gems, and the famous man-eating lions of Tsavo.
The museum's first home was the Palace of Fine Arts, left over from the 1893 fair in Jackson Park, the building that is now the Museum of Science and Industry.
This building was designed by Daniel Burnham's firm and completed after his death.
Look at the porches at either end, where the roof is held up by sculpted women, in the manner of the Erechtheion, a temple on the Acropolis in Athens.
Marshall Field's nephew Stanley Field ran the museum for fifty-six years, and the great hall inside is named for him.
Today, the hall is dominated by the cast skeleton of a titanosaur, one of the largest dinosaurs ever found, and Sue has her own gallery upstairs.
The lions of Tsavo are worth a visit too.
In 1898, two lions without manes attacked the workers building a railway bridge over the Tsavo River in Kenya, killing many of them.
The engineer in charge, John Henry Patterson, finally shot them, and years later he sold their skins and skulls to the museum.
Patterson claimed the lions had killed a hundred and thirty-five people.
Scientists who have studied the lions' remains estimate a much smaller number, about thirty-five, but the legend of the man-eaters has never faded.
Now look south.
The stadium with the classical colonnades is Soldier Field, which opened in 1924 and was dedicated to the soldiers who had died in the First World War.
In 1927, more than a hundred thousand fans watched Gene Tunney beat Jack Dempsey here, in the famous boxing match of the long count.

In July 1966, Martin Luther King Junior led a rally here for the Chicago Freedom Movement, his campaign against segregated housing in the city, and then marched with the crowd to City Hall, where he taped a list of demands to the door.
Since 1971, Soldier Field has been the home of the Chicago Bears.
In 2003, a new stadium was built inside the old colonnades.
Many critics hated it, and said it looked as if a spaceship had landed on top of the old stadium.
A few years later, Soldier Field lost its status as a National Historic Landmark.
You heard that Sue was found in South Dakota in 1990 and sold at auction after a legal fight.
The fight was stranger than most people know.
The bones turned up on a summer day in August 1990.

A crew from a private fossil company, the Black Hills Institute, had a flat tire, and while most of the team drove into town to get it fixed, Sue Hendrickson went walking along a bluff and spotted bones weathering out of the rock.
They turned out to belong to the most complete Tyrannosaurus anyone had ever dug up.
The bluff was on a ranch owned by Maurice Williams, a member of the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe, and the institute paid him five thousand dollars.
The company's president, Peter Larson, believed they had bought the fossil.
Williams later said the money was only for permission to dig.
And there was a bigger complication.
Because the land lay inside a reservation, it was held in trust by the federal government, and the government had a say over what was taken from it.
In 1992, agents of the FBI, backed by the National Guard, raided the institute and took the skeleton away.
The courts eventually ruled that Sue belonged to Williams, with the federal government as trustee.
In the long federal investigation that followed, Larson was convicted on customs charges and sent to prison, a sentence many of his supporters thought far too harsh.
Williams decided to sell, and Sotheby's auctioned the skeleton in New York on October fourth, 1997.
There were nine bidders, and the bidding was over in about nine minutes.

The Field Museum won, with backing from McDonald's, Walt Disney World Resorts, and the California State University system, for a total of about eight point four million dollars, by far the most ever paid for a fossil at that time.
Upstairs in Sue's gallery, look for the real skull, displayed in a case of its own.
It's too heavy to sit on the mounted skeleton, so the skull on the body is a lightweight cast.
And nobody knows whether Sue was female or male.
The name honors the woman who found the bones.
When you walk into the great hall of the Field Museum, look for the two African elephants locked in battle.
They're the work of one of the most remarkable people ever to work here, Carl Akeley.
Akeley grew up on a farm in western New York and learned taxidermy at a natural history supply house in Rochester.
In those days, the craft mostly meant stuffing skins with straw and rags until they looked lumpy and sad, and he thought animals deserved better.
He came to Chicago in 1896 to work for the young Field Museum and developed a new method.
First he sculpted the animal's body in clay, muscle by muscle, from careful measurements and photographs.
Then he made a light, hollow form from the clay model and stretched the skin over it.
The results looked alive.
He and his wife, Delia, collected the elephants on an expedition to East Africa, and they went on display in 1909.
When the museum moved to this building, they came by train and took up their places in the great hall, where they have stood for more than a century.
Akeley's life was a string of adventures.
In Somaliland, by his own account, a leopard attacked him, and he killed it with his bare hands.
On Mount Kenya, a wild elephant nearly crushed him to death.
And he never stopped inventing.

When the museum's first home, the old exposition building in Jackson Park, began to crumble, he devised a gun for spraying cement onto its walls, an ancestor of the sprayed concrete used today in tunnels and swimming pools.
He also designed a motion picture camera light and quick enough to follow animals in the field, and the filmmaker Robert Flaherty used two of them to shoot Nanook of the North.
In 1909, Akeley moved on to the American Museum of Natural History in New York, and later he studied mountain gorillas in central Africa.
He persuaded King Albert of Belgium to protect them, and in 1925 the king created Albert National Park, the first national park in Africa.
Akeley died there the next year, of dysentery, on the slopes of Mount Mikeno, and he is buried in the park he helped create.
You heard about the famous fight here in 1927 between Gene Tunney and Jack Dempsey.
Here's what the crowd saw.
It was a rematch.
A year earlier, in Philadelphia, Tunney, a careful, clever boxer and a former Marine, had taken the heavyweight title from Dempsey, the most ferocious puncher of his time.
Everyone wanted to see Dempsey try to win it back.

The paid attendance here was reported as a hundred and four thousand, nine hundred and forty-three, and the gate came to more than two and a half million dollars, said to be the first time any event had taken in two million.
Millions more listened on the radio.
For six rounds, Tunney outboxed Dempsey.
Then, in the seventh, Dempsey caught him with a flurry of punches, and Tunney went down for the first time in his career.
Under a rule that was still new, a fighter who scored a knockdown had to go to the farthest neutral corner before the referee would start the count.
Dempsey, out of long habit, stood over his fallen opponent and then went to his own corner.
The referee, Dave Barry, refused to begin counting until Dempsey moved, and precious seconds passed before he did.
Tunney got up at the count of nine.
But by most estimates, he had been on the canvas for about fourteen seconds, well past the ten that would have ended the fight.
He kept away from Dempsey for the rest of the round, knocked him down in the eighth, and won the decision.
Dempsey's fans swore he had been robbed.
Tunney always insisted he could have gotten up sooner.
Dempsey never fought for the title again.
Tunney defended it once more and then retired as champion, married an heiress, and became a businessman who liked to lecture on Shakespeare.
His son, John Tunney, became a United States senator from California.
Nobody has ever settled the argument about those fourteen seconds, and that's why the fight still has a name of its own.
Before it became home to the Bears, Soldier Field was the city's great gathering place, built to hold crowds no other place in Chicago could.
It opened in 1924 with a plain name, Municipal Grant Park Stadium.
On November twenty-seventh, 1926, it was formally dedicated as Soldier Field at the annual football game between Army and Navy.
More than a hundred thousand people watched the service academies play to a twenty-one to twenty-one tie, in what was called one of the greatest games ever played.
Some of the biggest crowds came for events you might not expect.

In 1937, the city's high school football championship, the Prep Bowl, between Austin High School and Leo, a Catholic school, drew an estimated hundred and twenty thousand people, far more than the stadium had seats.
It's often cited as the largest crowd ever to watch a football game in the United States.

In October 1944, President Franklin Roosevelt, campaigning for a fourth term, spoke here in the evening to a crowd reported at a hundred and ten thousand, probably the largest he ever addressed in person.

On July twentieth, 1968, about a thousand athletes with intellectual disabilities, from twenty-six states and Canada, competed here in the first Special Olympics games, and Eunice Kennedy Shriver announced the new movement from the field.
A young Park District physical education teacher, Anne Burke, had helped organize the games, and she later became chief justice of the Illinois Supreme Court.
For the fiftieth anniversary, in 2018, a monument called the Eternal Flame of Hope was dedicated beside the stadium.
And on June seventeenth, 1994, Soldier Field opened the World Cup, the first ever played in the United States.
Oprah Winfrey hosted the opening ceremony, and in a staged moment, the singer Diana Ross was supposed to kick a penalty into a goal that would then split in two.
She missed, and the goal split in two anyway.
Germany, the defending champions, then beat Bolivia one to nothing.
Walk east along the lakefront past the Shedd Aquarium, an octagonal marble building that opened in 1930.
It was founded with a gift from John G. Shedd, who had worked his way up from stock boy to president of Marshall Field and Company.
In its early years, the aquarium brought in seawater by railroad tank car from the ocean.
At the end of the peninsula is the Adler Planetarium, a twelve-sided building with a copper dome, which opened in 1930.
It was the first planetarium in the Western Hemisphere, founded by Max Adler, an executive at Sears, Roebuck.
From here, you have one of the finest views of the Chicago skyline.
Look south at the long, green island stretching into the lake.
This is Northerly Island, the only one built of the chain of islands imagined in Burnham's plan.
In 1933 and 1934, it was part of the site of Chicago's second world's fair, the Century of Progress.
Later, it became a small airport, Meigs Field.
On the night of March thirtieth, 2003, Mayor Richard M. Daley, who wanted a park here, sent bulldozers to carve huge X's into the runway without warning.
Planes were stranded at the airport.
The city was fined, but the airport never reopened.
Today, Northerly Island is a nature park with an outdoor concert venue.

The Century of Progress fair, in 1933 and 1934, celebrated the hundredth anniversary of Chicago's founding as a town, and it was held right here, along the lakefront and on Northerly Island, in the depths of the Depression.
Its motto was "Science Finds, Industry Applies, Man Conforms."
The fair opened with a stunt that delighted the public.
Astronomers aimed telescopes at the star Arcturus, and its light, turned into electric current by photoelectric cells, switched on the fair's lights.
That starlight was believed to have left Arcturus about forty years earlier, around the time of Chicago's last great fair, in 1893.
The fair was a hit, and unlike most world's fairs, it paid back its investors.

Visitors came to see streamlined trains, model homes made of steel and glass, and a dancer named Sally Rand, who performed with nothing but two large ostrich feather fans and was arrested for it more than once.
Several of the fair's Homes of Tomorrow were later moved across the lake to Beverly Shores, Indiana, where you can still see them.
Max Adler, who founded the planetarium, had been a concert violinist before he became an executive at Sears.
He was the brother-in-law of Julius Rosenwald, who built Sears into a giant and founded the Museum of Science and Industry.
Families like theirs, rich from mail order, meatpacking, and retail, built almost every great cultural institution you've seen on this tour.
This is the end of the Grant Park tour.
You heard that the Shedd's first seawater came by railroad.
The numbers were remarkable.
In 1930, a fleet of twenty tank cars made eight round trips between Key West, Florida, and Chicago to bring in about a million gallons of ocean water, enough to fill the saltwater galleries.
The fish needed a ride too.

So the aquarium had its own railroad car built, a custom coach called the Nautilus, fitted with tanks and equipment to keep animals alive on the long journey, and a spur track ran right up to the building.
For nearly three decades, until 1959, the Nautilus went out on collecting trips and came back loaded with fish and other sea creatures for the galleries.
It was a rolling aquarium, and a sign of how hard it was, in those days, to keep ocean animals alive in the middle of a continent.
The Shedd's most famous resident arrived in 1933, the year the world's fair opened outside these doors.
He was an Australian lungfish, collected in Sydney.
Lungfish belong to an ancient family of fish that can breathe air, gulping it at the surface into a single lung, and they can live for a very long time.
This one was already an adult when he came.
The staff called him Granddad.

Granddad lived at the Shedd for eighty-four years, through the Depression, the war, and every renovation, spending most of his time lying quietly at the bottom of his tank and now and then rising for a breath.
The aquarium estimated that a hundred and four million people saw him.
In February 2017, after he stopped eating and his organs began to fail, the staff decided to put him to sleep.
At the time, he was believed to be in his mid-nineties, the oldest fish living in any public aquarium.
Five years later, scientists who studied his DNA concluded that he was probably even older, about a hundred and nine.
You heard that the Adler was a first for this side of the Atlantic.
Here's how it came to be, and why it was so new.

In the early 1920s, engineers at the Carl Zeiss company in Jena, Germany, invented a machine that could project the night sky onto the inside of a dome: thousands of stars, the planets in their wandering paths, the sun and the moon, all moving as they do in nature, at whatever speed you liked.
The first public planetarium opened at the Deutsches Museum in Munich, the great museum of science and technology.
In 1928, Max Adler traveled to Germany with an architect, Ernest Grunsfeld Junior, and they toured the Deutsches Museum with its founder, Oskar von Miller.
Adler came home determined to give Chicago a planetarium of its own.
He bought a Zeiss projector, the first to operate outside Europe, and paid for a building to house it.
The planetarium opened on May twelfth, 1930, his birthday.
Grunsfeld's design is a landmark of its era: a low, twelve-sided building of polished granite under its copper dome, with almost no windows, so that it looks more like a monument than a museum.
The first director, an astronomer named Philip Fox, wanted more than a sky show.
He persuaded Adler to buy a celebrated collection of antique scientific instruments assembled by a dealer in Amsterdam: astrolabes, sundials, globes, and telescopes, some of them centuries old.
It made the Adler a museum of the history of astronomy as well as a theater of the stars.

Look also for the Atwood Sphere, a hollow metal globe about seventeen feet across, first shown at the Chicago Academy of Sciences in 1913, with hundreds of tiny holes punched through it in the patterns of the stars.
On a guided tour, you can ride inside it while light pours through the holes and a sky of pinpoint stars turns around you.
It's the oldest working sky simulator in the world, a homemade planetarium from before the Zeiss machine existed.
The original projector was retired long ago, but the Adler's first sky shows started a planetarium boom in America.
Within a few years, cities from Philadelphia to New York to Los Angeles had their own.
You heard that Mayor Richard M. Daley sent bulldozers to tear up the runway here one night in 2003.
The airport they destroyed had been a Chicago institution for more than half a century.
It was named for Merrill Meigs, publisher of the Chicago Herald and Examiner, a Hearst newspaper, and the city's loudest champion of aviation in the 1930s and 1940s.
He argued that a great downtown deserved its own airport, and the island built for the world's fair seemed the perfect place.
The airport opened in 1948, and two years later it was named for him.
Meigs Field had a single runway, about a mile from the Loop, and it was beloved by business travelers, private pilots, and politicians, who could land within minutes of their offices.
It also became famous far beyond Chicago.

For years, Microsoft Flight Simulator, the most popular flying program for home computers, started its players at Meigs, so millions of people around the world took off from this runway on their screens without ever seeing Chicago.
Daley had long wanted to turn the island into a park, and the airport's defenders had fought him to a standstill for years.
Then, without warning to the pilots or the federal government, city crews cut giant X's into the runway in the middle of the night.
Daley said he was protecting downtown from a possible terrorist attack by air.
Many Chicagoans saw it as a mayor ending an argument his own way.

The Federal Aviation Administration fined the city thirty-three thousand dollars for closing the airport without the required notice, and in 2006 the city agreed to pay back a million dollars in federal airport money it had used on the demolition.
Congress later raised the penalty for closing an airport without notice, in a measure known as the Meigs Legacy Provision.
None of it brought the runway back.
Today, the island is a park of prairie, wetland, and lakeshore paths, with a concert stage at its north end.
Twice a year, the air above you becomes one of the great highways of North America.

Millions of songbirds, warblers, thrushes, sparrows, and many more, migrate between their breeding grounds in the north and their winter homes in the south, and many of them travel at night along the western shore of Lake Michigan.
The lake works like a guide rail.
Birds that would rather not cross open water follow the shoreline, and it funnels them right past downtown Chicago.
For a small bird finding its way by the stars, a brightly lit city is a trap.
Lit windows draw birds in and confuse them, and glass reflects trees and sky so convincingly that birds fly straight into it.
Few places show this more starkly than McCormick Place, the convention center just south of here on the lakefront, whose Lakeside Center has long walls of glass facing the lake.

For about forty years, scientists and volunteers connected with the Field Museum, among them a longtime bird collections manager named David Willard, have walked around that building on migration mornings, collecting the birds that died overnight.
Their specimens form one of the longest records of bird collisions anywhere.
On a normal morning, they might find anywhere from none to fifteen.
But after one night in October 2023, during an enormous wave of migration, volunteers picked up nearly a thousand dead birds.
Willard described a carpet of them along the windows.
The records had already shown what helps.
Researchers found that when fewer windows were lit, far fewer birds died, and Chicago's Lights Out program asks building owners downtown to dim their decorative lights during migration.
After the disaster of 2023, McCormick Place spent more than a million dollars covering the Lakeside Center's glass with a film that birds can see.
The next fall, volunteers counted fewer than twenty deaths there.
So if you're here at dawn in May or October, look and listen.
Northerly Island's restored prairie and wetlands have become a resting place for exhausted travelers, and the shrubs may be full of birds that have flown all night, with a long way still to go.
This tour starts at the southern edge of the Loop and heads south into a part of the city that has been reinvented more times than almost any other.
In the 1870s and 1880s, Prairie Avenue, about a mile and a half south of the Loop, was the most exclusive address in Chicago.

After the Great Fire, the families who ran the city's biggest businesses built mansions here: Marshall Field, the merchant; George Pullman, the sleeping car king; Philip Armour, the meatpacker; and John Glessner, the farm machinery maker.
It was close enough to the Loop for a carriage ride to the office, and far enough to feel like a world apart.
It didn't last.
The railroads that had made these men rich surrounded the neighborhood with tracks and yards, and smoke and noise drifted in.
Just to the west, a red-light district called the Levee grew up, with saloons, gambling halls, and brothels, protected by corrupt politicians.
By 1900, the wealthy were moving north to the Gold Coast, and most of the mansions of Prairie Avenue were eventually torn down for factories and warehouses.
Meanwhile, the blocks just south of the Loop filled with railroad stations, printing plants, and showrooms.

Six major passenger stations ringed the downtown, and the streets around Dearborn Station became the center of the printing industry, which produced the timetables, catalogs, maps, and magazines that the railroads carried across the country.
Along Michigan Avenue, a row of showrooms for the new automobile companies grew up, and in the 1950s, one of those buildings became the most important studio in the history of the blues.
By the 1970s, much of the South Loop was empty.
Since then, it has been rebuilt as a neighborhood of lofts, townhouses, and towers, and a handful of the old mansions have been saved as museums.
We'll start at the Auditorium Building on Michigan Avenue, walk west to the library and south through Printers Row, and then east to Prairie Avenue, ending at Chess Records.
You are on Michigan Avenue at Ida B. Wells Drive, which until 2018 was called Congress Parkway, in front of the massive granite and limestone building that fills the block to the west.
This is the Auditorium Building, completed in 1889 by Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan, and it was the project that made them famous.
It was a remarkable combination: a theater with about four thousand seats, a luxury hotel, and an office building, all wrapped in one heavy, rusticated exterior.
The idea came from a businessman named Ferdinand Peck, who wanted a great opera house for Chicago that ordinary people could afford, paid for by the hotel and the offices around it.
When it was finished, its tower was the tallest structure in the city, and the building was one of the largest in the country.
President Benjamin Harrison came to its dedication.
Adler was the engineer and the acoustical genius of the firm.
The theater's acoustics are still considered nearly perfect, and great musicians and singers performed here.
Sullivan designed the interior, with gold-leaf arches lined with hundreds of the newfangled electric light bulbs.
A young draftsman named Frank Lloyd Wright worked on the drawings.
The building is so heavy that it has sunk more than two feet into Chicago's soft clay over the years.
Look at the floor of the lobby, and you may notice it slopes.
The hotel and theater struggled in the Depression, and during the Second World War, the theater was used as a servicemen's center, with a bowling alley on the stage.
In 1947, the building was bought by Roosevelt University, a new college founded to be open to students of all races and backgrounds at a time when many universities were not.
The theater was restored and reopened in 1967.
It's worth seeing inside if you can.

Next door, at 410 South Michigan, is the Fine Arts Building, built in the 1880s as a showroom for the Studebaker carriage company, and later converted into studios for artists, musicians, and writers.
It still is, and its old elevators are still run by operators.
The building was so famous that it was used even before it was finished.
In June 1888, the Republican Party held its national convention in the half-built theater, and nominated Benjamin Harrison, who came back the next year, as president, to dedicate the building.
Walk around to the south side of the building, along Ida B. Wells Drive.
In the 1950s, when the street was widened to carry traffic from the new Eisenhower Expressway into the Loop, there was no room left for a sidewalk.
So the city cut the sidewalk right through the building, carving an arcade out of the old hotel's ground floor.
You walk under the Auditorium, beneath the rooms where guests once slept.
Ferdinand Peck was a rich man with an unusual idea about music.

The son of one of Chicago's pioneer merchants, he was a lawyer and a tireless civic booster, and he believed that a great city needed great music, and that it shouldn't belong only to people like him.
In the 1880s, grand opera in America meant boxes.

At the Metropolitan Opera House, which opened in New York in 1883, the best places in the hall were rings of private boxes, rented by the richest families in the city, who came as much to be seen as to listen.
Peck wanted the opposite: a hall where a clerk with a single ticket could see and hear as well as a millionaire.
He tried the idea out first.
