In 1885, he organized an opera festival in the huge exhibition hall that then stood on the lakefront, where the Art Institute is today, and Adler and Sullivan built a temporary theater inside it for crowds of several thousand.
The crowds came, and the sound was superb.
Peck had found his architects.
In December 1886, he incorporated the Chicago Auditorium Association and raised the money from the city's business leaders.
He wanted no boxes at all.
His investors insisted on some, so in the end there were a few dozen, pushed off to the sides, holding only a small share of the audience.
The rest of the house was a great sweep of individual seats, more of them than the Metropolitan had.
Opening night was December ninth, 1889.
Crowds lined the streets to watch the guests arrive.
The president and the vice president were in the audience, and the star of the evening was Adelina Patti, the most celebrated soprano of her day, who sang Home, Sweet Home.
For the next forty years, this was the musical heart of the city.

The orchestra that became the Chicago Symphony, founded in 1891 by the conductor Theodore Thomas, played here until it moved into its own hall up the avenue in 1904, and Chicago's opera companies made this stage their home until 1929, when they left for a new opera house on the river.
Under the sidewalk here, there's no solid rock for a long way down.
What there is, is clay: firm near the top, soft and wet below.
In the 1880s, Chicago's builders didn't try to reach bedrock.
They spread their buildings out on top of the clay, the way snowshoes spread your weight on snow, and trusted it to hold.
The Auditorium was the biggest test of that idea anyone had tried.
Dankmar Adler and the engineer Paul Mueller designed what's called a raft, a floating foundation of crisscrossed timbers and railroad beams, encased in concrete.
On top of it they stacked stone footings in stepped pyramids, to carry the thick outer walls.
Adler tested the ground before he trusted it.
He loaded trial footings with heavy bars of pig iron and measured how far they sank.
His biggest worry was the tower.

It would be much heavier than the rest of the building, and it would go up last, so its footings would sink later and deeper than the walls around them, and the building could crack where the two met.
So as the lower floors rose, he loaded the basement under the future tower with pig iron and bricks, about as heavy as the finished tower would be.
As the tower went up, workers took the extra weight away, a little at a time, so that the ground beneath had already done most of its settling.
It mostly worked.
The heavy outer walls have sunk more than the light interior, so floors inside tip and roll, but the building has stood for well over a century.
The theater was full of machinery too.
Under the stage were twenty-six hydraulic lifts that could raise and lower sections of the floor for scenery.
In the ceiling, great hinged panels could be lowered to close off the top two galleries, shrinking the hall for a smaller crowd.
And in hot weather, fans drew in outside air and pushed it over ice before it flowed into the hall, which made the Auditorium one of the first theaters anywhere that was both heated and cooled.
Louis Sullivan gets most of the credit for this building, but the man who made it stand up and sound right was his partner, Dankmar Adler.
Adler was born in 1844, in a small town in central Germany.
His mother died at his birth, and according to a family story, his father named him Dankmar, joining the German word for thanks to a Hebrew word meaning bitter.
His father, Liebman Adler, was a rabbi.
He brought the family to America when Dankmar was a boy, first to Detroit and then, in 1861, to Chicago, to lead the city's oldest Jewish congregation.
The son went to war.
He served in the Union army with an Illinois artillery battery, and he did engineering and mapping work in the campaigns around Chattanooga and Atlanta.
Afterward, he learned the building trade in Chicago drafting rooms, and after the fire of 1871, there was more work than anyone could handle.
What made his name was sound.
In 1879, he designed the Central Music Hall, at State and Randolph, and its acoustics were so admired that theater builders across the country began to seek his advice.
Even Carnegie Hall in New York, which opened in 1891, consulted him.
Around the time of the music hall, he hired a gifted, prickly young draftsman named Louis Sullivan, and within a few years he made him his partner.
Adler handled the engineering, the clients, and the money, and Sullivan the design.
If you can get inside the theater, look up.
Its great golden arches step outward from the stage, each one wider than the last, like the bell of a horn.
They carry the sound to the farthest seats, and they carry the lights as well: art, acoustics, and engineering in a single gesture.
Adler also cared about his profession.
When Illinois passed the first law in the country requiring architects to be licensed, in 1897, he served as president of the state board that examined them.
He died in 1900, at fifty-five, the half of the partnership that the public forgot and that architects never did.
Before you go, take a closer look at the doorway of the Fine Arts Building, just north of the Auditorium.
Carved over it are the words All Passes, Art Alone Endures.
The building went up in 1885 for the Studebaker brothers of South Bend, Indiana, who made wagons and carriages and needed a place in Chicago to assemble and sell them.
Their architect was Solon Spencer Beman, who was designing George Pullman's company town at about the same time.
In 1898, Beman remodeled it for a new life, taking off the top floor and adding three more, and filling it with studios for artists and musicians, and a theater.
For a few years before the First World War, these halls were the center of literary Chicago.
The Dial, a respected literary magazine, had its offices here, and in 1907 its editor, Francis Fisher Browne, opened a bookstore on the seventh floor, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright.
In 1912, Maurice Browne and Ellen Van Volkenburg started the Chicago Little Theatre in a tiny hall on the fourth floor, with just ninety-nine seats, staging serious modern plays for small audiences.
It's often credited with starting the little theater movement that spread across the country.
In 1914, a young woman named Margaret Anderson started a magazine in room nine seventeen and named it The Little Review, after the theater downstairs.
She published the boldest new writers she could find.
After the magazine moved to New York, it began printing James Joyce's novel Ulysses, chapter by chapter, and its editors were taken to court for obscenity.

The sculptor Lorado Taft had a studio here, and so did W. W. Denslow, the illustrator who drew the first pictures of Dorothy, the Scarecrow, and the Tin Woodman, for The Wonderful Wizard of Oz in 1900.
Step inside if the building is open, and climb the stairs.
The halls are lined with wooden doors and frosted glass, and behind them you may hear violins, pianos, and singers practicing, much as you would have a century ago.
Walk west on Ida B. Wells Drive to State Street.
The enormous red brick and granite building on the corner, with huge green metal ornaments on its roof, is the Harold Washington Library Center, Chicago's main public library, which opened in 1991.
Look up at the roof corners.
Those giant green figures are owls, the symbol of wisdom, perched among swirling leaves and seed pods.
The design, by the architects Hammond, Beeby, and Babka, was chosen in a public competition.

It deliberately echoes the heavy stone buildings of the nineteenth century around it, like the Auditorium and the Rookery, and it was controversial at the time for looking backward rather than forward.
Inside, on the top floor, there's a glass-roofed winter garden.
The library is named for Harold Washington, who in 1983 became Chicago's first Black mayor.
Chicago's politics had long been dominated by a powerful Democratic political machine, which had been led for over two decades by Richard J. Daley.
Washington, a congressman from the South Side, ran as a reformer, and he won with a coalition of Black, Latino, and white liberal voters, with an extraordinary turnout in Black neighborhoods.
His first years in office were consumed by what were called the Council Wars, as a majority of the city council, mostly white aldermen, blocked his agenda.
Washington won a second term in 1987, but he died of a heart attack at his desk in City Hall, months later.
He remains a beloved figure, and the library holds an exhibit about his life.
Washington's 1983 campaign was one of the most dramatic in the city's history.
In the Democratic primary, he beat both the sitting mayor, Jane Byrne, and Richard M. Daley, the son of the late mayor, who split the white vote between them.
In Chicago, winning the Democratic primary had always meant winning the election.
But this time, many white Democrats deserted their party for the Republican candidate, Bernard Epton, in a campaign full of open racial appeals.
Washington won by a narrow margin.

His slogan was "Chicago works together," and he set out to dismantle the patronage system that had kept the old machine in power, opening city jobs and contracts to people who had long been shut out of them.
When he died, in November 1987, thousands of people lined up for hours, in the cold, to file past his casket at City Hall.
Many Chicagoans still speak of him simply as Harold.
When the library opened, it was said to be the largest public library building in the world.
Take the escalators to the top floor to see the winter garden, under its glass roof.
Harold Washington was born on the South Side in 1922, and politics ran in the family.

His father, Roy, was a lawyer and a Methodist minister, and one of the first Black precinct captains for the Democratic Party, at a time when most Black Chicagoans still voted Republican, for the party of Lincoln.
In the Second World War, Harold served in a segregated engineering unit of the Army Air Forces, building airfields in the Pacific, and he came home a first sergeant.
Then he enrolled at a brand-new school, Roosevelt College, which soon moved into the Auditorium Building, a couple of blocks east of here.
Roosevelt had a remarkable beginning.
In 1945, the president of a downtown college was told by his board to count his students by race and religion.
He refused, telling them, the story goes, that we don't count that way, and he was forced out.
Many of the faculty and students followed him to start a new college, open to everyone, named for Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt.
Harold Washington was elected to lead its student council, and after graduating in 1949, he went on to law school at Northwestern.

When his father died, in 1953, Harold took over his precinct, in the Third Ward organization of Ralph Metcalfe, the Olympic sprinter who had won a gold medal running on the same relay team as Jesse Owens, in Berlin.
For years, Washington was a loyal soldier of the machine.
He went to the state legislature in Springfield in 1965, and he stayed for sixteen years.
There were stumbles.
In the early 1970s, he was convicted of failing to file his income tax returns for several years, and he spent about a month in jail.
But he was also growing more independent of the machine, and in 1977, after the death of the first Mayor Daley, he ran in the special election for mayor and finished far behind.
In 1980, he was elected to Congress.
Two years later, when Black Chicagoans began organizing to elect a mayor of their own, he was the man they wanted.
Harold Washington didn't simply decide to run for mayor.
He was drafted.
By 1982, many Black Chicagoans felt betrayed by Mayor Jane Byrne.
They had helped elect her in 1979, and they believed she had then sided with the old machine against them.
That summer, Jesse Jackson's Operation Push led a boycott of ChicagoFest, the mayor's big music festival on Navy Pier.
A journalist and radio commentator named Lu Palmer had already been calling for a Black candidate, with a slogan that spread all over the South Side: We shall see in eighty-three.
The candidate they wanted was the congressman from the South Side, and he set conditions.
He would run only if the movement put tens of thousands of new voters on the rolls and raised real money first.
So churches, community groups, and Black radio stations launched a registration drive aimed at the deadline for the fall election, with a rallying cry: Come Alive October Five.
Volunteers signed people up wherever they gathered, in churches, on street corners, and at bus stops, and the rolls swelled.
On November tenth, 1982, he announced his campaign.
His campaign, he told supporters, was about the plan, not the man.
After his upset in the primary, the general election, against the Republican Bernard Epton, turned ugly.
Epton's slogan was Epton, Before It's Too Late, and everyone understood what it meant.
On Palm Sunday, Washington and the former vice president Walter Mondale visited Saint Pascal's Church, on the Northwest Side.
They were met by a jeering crowd and had to be escorted out by the police, and the scene went out on television across the country.
On election day, April twelfth, 1983, nearly one point three million people voted.
Washington won by about forty-eight thousand.
Winning the election turned out to be the easy part.
At the new mayor's first city council meeting, in May 1983, twenty-nine of the fifty aldermen, nearly all of them white, took control of the council and its committees.
Their leader was Edward Vrdolyak, the chairman of the Cook County Democratic Party, a sharp-tongued lawyer from the Southeast Side.
Washington had twenty-one votes.
For three years, the two sides fought over almost everything.
The twenty-nine blocked the mayor's appointments to city boards and rewrote his budgets.
Washington vetoed their measures, and they never had the votes to override him.
Reporters started calling the city Beirut on the Lake, after the war-torn capital of Lebanon, and the fight got the name it still has, a play on the Star Wars movies: Council Wars.
The way out came through the courts.
Black and Latino voters had sued over the city's ward map, arguing that it had been drawn to weaken their votes, and a federal court agreed and ordered new boundaries.
In 1986, special elections were held in seven redrawn wards, all of them represented by members of the opposing bloc.
Washington's candidates won four.
The last two were decided in runoffs that spring, and one of the winners was Luis Gutiérrez, a young Puerto Rican activist who later served many years in Congress.
Now the council was split twenty-five to twenty-five, and the mayor cast the deciding vote.
In 1987, Washington won a second term, beating Jane Byrne in the primary and Vrdolyak, running on a third-party ticket, in the general election.
Then, just months after his second inauguration, he was gone.
The council chose his successor in an all-night meeting, while crowds outside chanted for Timothy Evans, the alderman most of Washington's followers wanted.
At about four in the morning on December second, 1987, it elected Eugene Sawyer instead, a quiet Black alderman, with most of his votes coming from the old opposition bloc.
Washington's coalition split apart, and in 1989, Richard M. Daley was elected mayor, the office his father had held for twenty-one years.
For fourteen years before this building opened, Chicago had no proper main library.

When the old one on Michigan Avenue was turned into the Cultural Center, in 1977, the central library moved into rented floors of an office building at four twenty-five North Michigan Avenue, and most of its books went into storage.
A plan to put the library into an empty department store on State Street was drawn up and dropped.
In July 1987, a few months before he died, Mayor Washington and the city council approved a design competition and the money to build.
Five teams of architects and builders made the final round, a citizens' jury chose the winner in June 1988, and the library opened in October 1991, named for the mayor who had set it in motion.
Now take a closer look at the walls.
The ornament on this building was meant to be read.
Look for the round medallions with the face of Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain and harvests, framed by ears of corn, for the farm country that made Chicago rich.
Look, too, for the faces of the cold north wind, figures the designers called Windy City men.

Much of the sculpture, including the owls on the roof, was the work of Raymond Kaskey, who also made Portlandia, the huge hammered copper goddess who kneels over the entrance of a city office building in Portland, Oregon.

Inside, in a niche off the main lobby, is a mosaic by the painter Jacob Lawrence called Events in the Life of Harold Washington, in tiles of blue, yellow, and green, ringed with words from the mayor's first inaugural address.
And on the ninth floor, the library's special collections keep Harold Washington's own papers: his speeches and the records of his years in office.
It's a fitting place for them, in the building he set in motion, a few blocks from the college where his political life began.
Walk south on State Street and then west to Dearborn Street, and walk south along Dearborn to Polk Street.
At the end of the street stands Dearborn Station, a brick building with a clock tower, built in 1885.
It's the oldest surviving passenger train station in Chicago.

For nearly a century, this was the Chicago terminal for the Santa Fe Railway, whose famous trains, like the Super Chief, carried movie stars, businessmen, and tourists between Chicago and Los Angeles.

Because Chicago was the meeting point of the eastern and western railroads, long-distance passengers almost always had to change stations here, which is part of the reason Chicago became such a hotel town.
The station closed in 1971, and the train shed behind it was torn down.
The head house now holds offices and shops.
The blocks along Dearborn and Plymouth Court, leading up to the station, are called Printers Row.
From the 1880s to the mid-twentieth century, this was one of the great printing centers of America.
Look at the tall, heavy brick loft buildings with big windows, built to let in light for typesetters and press operators, and with floors strong enough to hold heavy printing presses.
The railroads needed tickets, timetables, maps, and brochures, and the mail-order companies needed catalogs, and Chicago printed them.
The biggest of the printers was R. R. Donnelley and Sons, whose Lakeside Press building is just to the west, on Plymouth Court.
For generations, Donnelley printed telephone directories, catalogs, books, and magazines, including Time and Life.
By the 1970s, the printers had moved out.
Printers Row became one of the first places in Chicago where old industrial buildings were converted into loft apartments, and it's now a lively residential neighborhood.
Every June, the Printers Row Lit Fest fills the street with booksellers.
As you walk along Dearborn Street, look up at the buildings.
At number 431, the Manhattan Building, finished in 1891 and designed by William Le Baron Jenney, was one of the first buildings anywhere to reach sixteen stories, held up by an iron and steel frame.
At number 720, the Franklin Building, built in 1912 for a printing company, has a colorful tile mural over its entrance, showing printers at work, pulling the first impression from a press.
R. R. Donnelley's old Lakeside Press building, on Plymouth Court, was designed by Howard Van Doren Shaw.

The company later built an even bigger plant about a mile south, on Cermak Road, a Gothic fortress decorated with the marks of famous early printers, which is now one of the largest data centers in the world.
Since 1903, the company has given its friends a small book every Christmas, a series of firsthand accounts of American history called the Lakeside Classics.
It's one of the longest-running series in American publishing.
Here's the strange thing about the railroad capital of America: almost no train went through it.
Railroads from the East ended in Chicago, and railroads to the West began here, each at its own station.
A traveler going from New York to San Francisco had to get off one train, cross downtown, and board another.
There were six big passenger stations around the Loop: Union Station, the North Western Station, LaSalle Street, Grand Central, Central Station down by the lake, and Dearborn, right here.
If you came in from New York on the Twentieth Century Limited, you arrived at LaSalle Street.
If you were going on to Los Angeles on the Santa Fe, you left from here.
For more than a century, the business of getting people and their trunks from one station to the next belonged largely to one company, Parmelee.
Franklin Parmelee started it in the 1850s with horse-drawn omnibuses, and for generations, many railroads sold their through passengers a Parmelee transfer coupon along with the ticket.
Its coaches, and later its buses, were as much a part of the Chicago scene as the trains themselves.
Travelers grumbled, and just after the Second World War, a railroad executive named Robert Young turned their grumbling into full-page newspaper ads.
A hog, they said, can cross the country without changing trains, but you can't.
It was true.
Freight cars were handed from one railroad to the next all the time, while people had to haul their luggage across town.
The ad embarrassed the railroads into running a few sleeping cars that were switched from one company's train to another's, so that a passenger could stay in bed from coast to coast.
But most passengers kept changing stations to the end.
In 1971, Amtrak took over nearly all the country's passenger trains and gathered Chicago's long-distance routes into Union Station.
Dearborn saw its last long-distance trains that spring, and Central Station closed the next year.
Within a few years, Central Station and Grand Central, which had closed even earlier, had both been torn down.
Dearborn was luckier.
Its head house survived.
Of all the trains that left from this station, the most glamorous was the Santa Fe's Super Chief.
It started running in 1936, a train made up entirely of sleeping cars, pulled by the railroad's new diesel engines, and it cut the trip from Chicago to Los Angeles to under forty hours.
It cost extra to ride, and the people who could afford it were the people of Hollywood.
Movie stars traveled east and west on it so often that it became known as the Train of the Stars, and photographers waited at the stations to catch them stepping down.

Stars coming from New York usually arrived on the Twentieth Century Limited at LaSalle Street Station, a few blocks north, and crossed the Loop to board the Super Chief here, the eastern train behind them and the western one ahead.
The train's look was part of its fame.
Its diesel engines soon wore the Santa Fe's red and silver warbonnet colors, and the cars inside were decorated with designs drawn from the art of the Southwest.
The food came from the Fred Harvey company, which ran the dining cars on the Santa Fe and the restaurants in its stations, famous for their waitresses, the Harvey Girls.
In 1951, the train added the Turquoise Room, a small private dining room in the lounge car that passengers could reserve for a party of up to twelve.
The railroad advertised it as the only private dining room in the world on rails.
Airplanes ended its reign.
By the 1960s, the stars flew.

Amtrak kept the train running after 1971, from Union Station, and its descendant, the Southwest Chief, still leaves Chicago every afternoon for Los Angeles, across Kansas, Colorado, New Mexico, and Arizona, much as the Super Chief did.
Two of the great names in American printing grew up in Chicago, and both started small.
Richard Robert Donnelley came to Chicago from Hamilton, Ontario, in 1864, a young printer with large ambitions.
The Great Fire of 1871 wiped out his business, and he started over.
Under his son, Thomas, the company grew into one of the biggest printers in the country, and its name became a byword for quality.
Thomas Donnelley believed printing could be an art as well as an industry.

In the late 1920s, the company set out to show what American printing could do, with a project it called the Four American Books: Thoreau's Walden, Dana's Two Years Before the Mast, the tales of Edgar Allan Poe, and Herman Melville's Moby Dick.
The Moby Dick became the most famous.
The Lakeside Press published it in 1930, in three volumes and only a thousand copies, with hundreds of haunting black and white drawings by the artist Rockwell Kent.
It's often called one of the great American illustrated books, and collectors still prize it.
Rand McNally began in Chicago too.
In 1856, a printer named William Rand opened a shop in the city, and a couple of years later a young Irish immigrant, Andrew McNally, came to work for him.
For a time, the two of them ran the printing plant of the Chicago Tribune, but their future lay with the railroads that met in Chicago.
They did printing jobs for the lines and published a guide to their timetables, and in December 1872, the guide carried their first map.
Railroad maps led to atlases, and when Americans took to the road in automobiles, Rand McNally sold them road maps by the millions.
For much of the twentieth century, if you unfolded a map on a family road trip, there was a good chance it came from a Chicago company.
Why here?

Because the city sat at the center of everything a printer needed: paper arriving by rail, the biggest customers in the country in the railroads and the mail-order houses, and trains that could carry the finished work anywhere in America within days.
For the better part of a century, the clatter of presses was the sound of these streets, and the smell of ink hung over them day and night.
From Printers Row, walk about a mile south and east, or take a bus, to 18th Street and Prairie Avenue.
You are now in the Prairie Avenue Historic District, all that remains of Chicago's first millionaires' row.
On the west side of the block, along Indiana Avenue, look for a white wooden house with a columned porch.
That's the Clarke House, built around 1836, which makes it the oldest house in Chicago.
It was built for Henry Clarke, a merchant, when this was open prairie, far from the small town on the river.
The house has been moved twice.
In 1872, it was moved to the South Side, and in 1977, the city brought it back near its original site, lifting it over the elevated railroad tracks on the way.
Now walk to the corner of 18th Street and Prairie Avenue.
The rough granite house on the southwest corner, which looks like a fortress, is the Glessner House, completed in 1887.
It was designed by Henry Hobson Richardson, the great Boston architect, for John Glessner, a partner in a company that made farm machinery, which later became part of International Harvester.
Richardson turned the house inward.
Its street walls are heavy and nearly windowless, giving privacy from the noise and dirt of the city, while the rooms open onto a sunny private courtyard on the south side.
Prairie Avenue's other residents were shocked.
George Pullman, who lived across the street, is said to have complained that he didn't know what he'd done to have that thing staring him in the face every time he went out his door.
Richardson died before it was finished, at forty-seven.
In 1966, the house was going to be demolished, and a group of architects bought it to save it.
The organization they formed became the Chicago Architecture Center, which runs the river boat tours.
Glessner House is now a museum, with its original furniture and decorations.
The Clarke House has its own sad story.
Henry Clarke died in the cholera epidemic of 1849, and his widow, Caroline, kept the family afloat by selling off pieces of their land, as the city grew out to meet the house.
The Glessners raised two children here, and their daughter, Frances, became one of the most remarkable people ever to grow up on Prairie Avenue.
As Frances Glessner Lee, she became fascinated with how deaths were investigated, at a time when police and coroners often missed the evidence in front of them.

In the 1940s, she built a series of tiny, astonishingly detailed dollhouse rooms, each showing a real death scene, with every clue in place, down to the calendars on the walls and the food in the kitchens.
She called them the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, and they were used to train detectives.
They're still used for training today, and she's often called the mother of forensic science.
Henry Hobson Richardson was the most admired architect in America in the 1880s, and this house is the only building of his still standing in Chicago.
He was born in Louisiana in 1838, studied at Harvard, and then went to Paris, to the École des Beaux-Arts, only the second American to study architecture there.
His breakthrough was Trinity Church in Boston, finished in 1877, a great mass of stone with round arches and a heavy central tower.

The style he developed, rough stone, deep round arches, and a feeling of enormous weight, came to be called Richardsonian Romanesque, and for a generation it spread across the country, to courthouses, libraries, train stations, and city halls.
His greatest Chicago building was the Marshall Field Wholesale Store, a block-long warehouse in the Loop, as plain and powerful as a Roman aqueduct, long since torn down.
Louis Sullivan admired it enormously, and his design for the Auditorium, where this tour began, grew plainer and heavier after the wholesale store went up.
In the Auditorium's great stone walls, you can still see Richardson's influence.
Richardson worked at a furious pace in his last years, even as his health failed.
He was a huge man, and he suffered from a kidney disease that he knew was killing him.
He kept working anyway, and the Glessner House was among the last designs he completed.
His successors carried out his drawings after his death.
Now look closely at the walls.
The granite blocks are cut rough on their faces but laid with great precision, in bands of different heights.
The deep arched entrance seems carved out of solid rock.
The windows are few and deliberate.
There's almost no ornament at all, and yet the house has more presence than any of the fancier mansions that once surrounded it.
That was Richardson's gift: making a building seem as if it had always been there, and always would be.
Frances Glessner was nine years old when her family moved into this house, and she grew up inside its walls, taught by private tutors.
Her brother, George, went to Harvard.
Frances wanted to go to college too, and to study medicine, but her parents believed that college was no place for a girl.
In 1898, she married a lawyer named Blewett Lee, and they had three children, but the marriage failed, and they divorced in 1914.
The turn in her life came through her brother's Harvard classmate, George Burgess Magrath, who became the medical examiner in Boston.
Over many conversations, he told her how often deaths were misjudged, by coroners who were elected and had no medical training, and by investigators who didn't know what to look for.
She was fascinated, and when she came into the family fortune, she put it to work.
In the early 1930s, she endowed a department of legal medicine at Harvard, the first of its kind in the country, and gave it a library.
She did much more than write checks.

Starting in 1945, she ran week-long seminars in homicide investigation for experienced police detectives, and she planned every detail herself, down to the grand dinner at the Ritz-Carlton hotel in Boston that ended each week.
In the 1940s, the New Hampshire State Police, near the family's summer estate, made her an honorary captain, and she's often described as the first woman police captain in the country.
She died in 1962.

Her tiny death scenes are kept today at the medical examiner's office in Baltimore, and in 2017 and 2018 the Smithsonian displayed them in Washington, where crowds lined up to study them, trying to solve the cases.
The answers have never been published.
They're still used to train investigators, and the people who know the solutions keep them to themselves.
Look across Prairie Avenue from the Glessner House, and you'll see what the street's other residents thought a mansion should look like.
Directly across the avenue, on the southeast corner, is the Kimball House, finished in 1892 for William Wallace Kimball, whose company was one of the biggest makers of pianos and organs in America.
It's a French chateau in gray stone, with turrets and a steep slate roof, designed by Solon Spencer Beman, the architect of Pullman's company town.
It's everything the Glessner House isn't: open to the street, proud, and a little showy.
Next door to it stands another survivor, the Coleman House, from the 1880s.
In 1991, these two mansions became the headquarters of the United States Soccer Federation, and in 2023 they were sold, to be turned back into homes.
Walk south toward 19th Street.
On the west side is the Keith House, from about 1870, one of the oldest houses on the avenue.
A little farther, at nineteen nineteen, is the house of Marshall Field Junior, the merchant's son, where he was fatally shot in 1905, in circumstances you'll hear more about at the end of this tour.
It has been restored and divided into homes.
These few houses are almost all that's left.
In the 1880s, mansions lined the avenue for blocks, built by the men who ran the city's railroads, banks, and stores.
Within a generation, most of their families had moved to the North Side, and over the following decades, nearly all of the houses were torn down for warehouses, printing plants, and parking lots.

Stand here for a moment and try to fill in the gaps: carriages at the curb, lawns behind iron fences, and some of the richest people in America living side by side, a few blocks from the railroad yards that made their fortunes and would eventually drive them away.
The Clarke House has outlived almost everything around it, partly by moving out of the way.
Henry Clarke and his wife, Caroline, came to Chicago from the East in 1835, when the town had only a few thousand people.
They built far out on the prairie, in the Greek Revival style that was fashionable back East, with a columned portico like the front of a Greek temple.
Its frame is made of heavy timbers, joined in the old way, and it was solid enough to survive two long journeys across the city.
In 1872, the year after the Great Fire, a tailor named John Chrimes bought the house and had it moved about four miles south, to Wabash Avenue at 45th Street.
According to the city's history of the house, he feared another fire, and one of his children was sick and needed country air.
The columned portico came off for the move.
The family lived there for decades, and later the house became the rectory of Saint Paul Church of God in Christ.
By the 1970s, it was recognized as the oldest house in Chicago, and the city decided to bring it home.
The move, in December 1977, was harder than anyone had planned.
To get the house over the elevated train tracks, the movers had to jack it high in the air, and then a hard freeze set in.
The hydraulic equipment froze, and for about two weeks the oldest house in Chicago sat stranded beside the tracks, waiting for a thaw.

It finally came to rest here, near its original site, and was restored as a museum, furnished as a prosperous family's home might have been in the 1850s and 1860s, when Chicago was turning from a frontier town into a metropolis.
It's worth going inside if it's open.
The town of Chicago didn't become a city until 1837, so when you stand in these rooms, you're standing in a house that's older than the City of Chicago itself.
Walk east on 18th Street toward Calumet Avenue.

Somewhere along here, on the east side of Prairie Avenue at number 1729, stood the mansion of George Pullman, the man who built the Pullman Palace Car Company and made the railroad sleeping car a symbol of luxury.
Marshall Field lived down the block, at 1905.
Both houses are long gone.
Pullman had a special interest in this spot.
The tradition in Chicago was that this was near where the Battle of Fort Dearborn took place, on August fifteenth, 1812.

When the garrison and settlers evacuated the fort, heading south along the beach toward Fort Wayne, they were attacked by a large force of Potawatomi warriors, allied with the British in the War of 1812.
Most of the soldiers, and many women and children, were killed, and others were taken captive.
For more than a century, Chicagoans called it the Fort Dearborn Massacre.
In 1893, Pullman commissioned a bronze sculpture of the event and placed it near his house.
It showed a Potawatomi chief, Black Partridge, protecting a settler's wife from a tomahawk.
For many years, it stood in the lobby of the Chicago Historical Society.
Today, it's in storage, after Native American groups objected to its portrayal of the battle.
The small park on the corner of 18th and Calumet is called Battle of Fort Dearborn Park, dedicated in 2009.

Historians now describe the event from both sides: the Potawatomi were fighting to defend their land from the spreading American settlement that would soon push them out of the Chicago area entirely, through a treaty signed in 1833.
For many years, an old cottonwood tree stood near this corner, and Chicagoans said it was the very tree where the battle had been fought.
The so-called Massacre Tree died, and it was cut down in 1894.
Whether the battle really happened here, or somewhat farther north, near what's now Roosevelt Road, is still debated by historians.
Like many Chicago landmarks, this one rests partly on legend.
In the summer of 1812, Fort Dearborn was a lonely post at the far edge of American territory.

When war broke out with Britain that June, the British and their Native allies quickly captured the American fort on Mackinac Island, at the top of Lake Michigan, and General William Hull ordered Fort Dearborn abandoned.
The commander, Captain Nathan Heald, met with the Potawatomi leaders gathered around the fort and promised to hand over the fort's goods if they let the garrison leave in peace.
Then, afraid of what the goods might be used for, he had the extra guns and ammunition and the barrels of whiskey destroyed, dumped in the river and down a well.
To the Potawatomi, it looked like a promise broken.

On the morning of August fifteenth, the column marched out of the gate and turned south along the beach: about fifty-five soldiers, a dozen militiamen, nine women, and eighteen children, with a small escort of Miami warriors led by the scout William Wells.
About a mile and a half down the shore, where a ridge of sand dunes ran beside the beach, between four and five hundred Potawatomi warriors attacked.
The fight lasted perhaps a quarter of an hour.
The Miami escort rode away.
Twenty-six soldiers were killed, along with all twelve militiamen, two women, and twelve children, who had been riding in a wagon.
Heald, wounded, surrendered the survivors.
The captives were taken to villages across the region.
Some died, some were ransomed by traders over the following months, and some were held for a year or more.
The day after the battle, the warriors burned the fort.
For the Potawatomi, it was a victory in a war they hoped would halt the American advance into their country.
That hope died two years later, when Britain made peace with the United States and left its Native allies to face the Americans alone.
The figure in Pullman's sculpture is Black Partridge, a Potawatomi chief whose village stood on the Illinois River, near what's now Peoria.
He had been a friend of the Americans.
He wore a silver peace medal they had given him, as a token of that friendship.
In the days before the evacuation, according to the accounts of survivors, he came to the fort and handed the medal back to Captain Heald.
His young men were determined to fight, he said, he could not restrain them, and he would not wear a sign of peace while he was forced to act as an enemy.

During the battle, the story goes on, he saved Margaret Helm, a young officer's wife and the stepdaughter of the trader John Kinzie, by pulling her into the lake and holding her there, out of reach, until the fighting stopped.
That's the scene the sculpture shows.
It comes from the Kinzie family's account, and like much of that account, it can't be checked against any other source.
What happened next is rarely told.
In October 1812, Illinois militia marched north to punish the Potawatomi villages around Peoria Lake.
Black Partridge came home to find his village burned and, by one account, his daughter and grandchild dead.
The chief who had saved American lives then took up arms against the Americans himself, and he joined an attack on the new American fort at Peoria, which failed.
In 1815, with the war over, he signed a treaty of peace.

His name survives in Black Partridge Woods, a forest preserve southwest of the city, on the bluffs above the Des Plaines River, where spring-fed streams run through wooded ravines, on land his people once called home.
And the Potawatomi remember the battle not as a massacre but as a fight for their homeland, one they were about to lose.
Twenty-one years after the battle, the Potawatomi left Chicago for good, and they left by treaty.
In September 1833, thousands of Potawatomi, Ottawa, and Ojibwe people gathered around the little town for a treaty council with American commissioners.
For weeks, their camps spread across the prairie, and traders, land speculators, and whiskey sellers crowded in to profit.

The treaty they signed on September twenty-sixth gave up the last of their lands in northern Illinois and southern Wisconsin, about five million acres, in exchange for land west of the Mississippi and payments of money and goods.
Part of the money went to pay debts that traders claimed the tribes owed them.
Two years later, in August 1835, before they departed, some eight hundred warriors gathered for a last war dance.
Painted and carrying their weapons, they danced through the streets of the town, past the houses and stores of the people who had taken their land, while the settlers watched, uneasy.
A young lawyer named John Dean Caton, who later became chief justice of the Illinois Supreme Court, saw it and wrote about it years afterward.
Then they were gone, west to new lands in Missouri and Iowa, and later to Kansas.
Not everyone went.
Leopold Pokagon, a Potawatomi leader in southwestern Michigan who had become a Catholic, won the right for his band to stay.
Sixty years later, at the World's Fair of 1893, his son Simon Pokagon spoke to an enormous crowd on Chicago Day, about the city that had been built on his people's land.
The Potawatomi nations live on today, in Kansas, Oklahoma, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Indiana.

And Chicago is home to one of the largest urban Native American communities in the country, much of it brought here in the 1950s and 1960s by a federal program that encouraged families to move from reservations to cities.
Walk west on Cullerton Street to Michigan Avenue and look for the rough stone church on the west side of the avenue, near 20th Street.
This is Second Presbyterian Church, the church of many of the Prairie Avenue families.
The church was built in 1874, designed by James Renwick, the New York architect of Saint Patrick's Cathedral.
In 1900, a fire gutted the interior, and the congregation rebuilt it in the new Arts and Crafts style.
If it's open, step inside.

The result is one of the most beautiful church interiors in America: dark wood, painted murals of angels and saints by the artist Frederic Clay Bartlett, and a remarkable collection of stained glass windows, including several by the Tiffany studios.
The Arts and Crafts movement started in England in the nineteenth century, as a protest against mass production.
It emphasized handmade craftsmanship, natural materials, and simple, honest design.
Look at how the decoration in this church is inspired by plants and nature.
It's the same spirit you saw in the Prairie School houses of Frank Lloyd Wright.
As the wealthy families moved north, the church lost most of its members.
It survived through the years when the neighborhood around it was abandoned and industrial.
Today, with new residents moving in, it's growing again.
Look along this stretch of Michigan Avenue.
Many of the old buildings have huge plate glass windows on the ground floor.
That's because this was Motor Row.

In the early twentieth century, dozens of automobile companies, including Ford, Buick, and Cadillac, had their showrooms and dealerships along here, on what was then the main road south out of the city.
The murals in this church were painted by one of its own members, Frederic Clay Bartlett, who grew up nearby, the son of a wealthy hardware merchant.
His father's firm, Hibbard, Spencer, Bartlett, was one of the biggest hardware wholesalers in the country, and the brand name it created, True Value, still hangs over hardware stores across America.
Frederic studied painting in Germany and France and came home to work in the Arts and Crafts spirit, as much a decorator as a painter.
He was still in his twenties when fire gutted the church in 1900, and its rebuilding gave him the chance to paint on a grand scale.
If you're inside, notice how the painting, the woodwork, and the glass all seem to belong together.
That was the point.
In the Arts and Crafts way of thinking, a room was a single work of art.
He had a second career as a collector.
With his second wife, Helen Birch, he bought modern French paintings at a time when few Americans would: Cézanne, Van Gogh, Gauguin, Toulouse-Lautrec, and the young Picasso.
In 1924, they bought Georges Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte.
Helen died the next year, and in her memory, Frederic gave their collection to the Art Institute.
That's how one of the most famous paintings in the world came to Chicago, from a family that worshipped in this church.
Later in life, he married again and spent his winters in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, at a house called Bonnet House, which he painted and decorated with the same playful hand.
It's a museum now, too.

So if you ever stand in front of La Grande Jatte, with its crowds of tiny dots and its Sunday strollers by the river, remember the man who brought it to Chicago, and where he first learned to paint on a grand scale: on these walls, among the angels.
The Arts and Crafts movement came to Chicago in a rush around 1900, and it took a very Chicago turn.
In 1897, a group of artists, architects, and reformers founded the Chicago Arts and Crafts Society at Hull House, Jane Addams's settlement house on the Near West Side.
They believed that good design and honest handwork could improve the lives of the people who made things, as well as the people who bought them.
But unlike the English reformers who inspired them, they were willing to make peace with the machine.
Workshops sprang up all over the city.
The Kalo Shop, founded in 1900 by a woman named Clara Barck Welles, made hand-hammered silver, trained a generation of silversmiths, and kept working until 1970.
Northwest of the city, a terra cotta company began making Teco pottery, in soft, matte greens, with designs by some of Chicago's leading architects.
Bookbinders, weavers, and furniture makers set up shop in studios downtown.
Then, in March 1901, a young architect from Oak Park stood up at Hull House and made the case for the machine more boldly than anyone.
In a lecture called The Art and Craft of the Machine, Frank Lloyd Wright argued that the machine wasn't the enemy of beauty at all.
In the hands of an artist, it could make simple, beautiful things for everyone, not only for the few who could afford handmade ones.
That argument, between the handmade and the machine made, runs through everything you've seen on this tour.
This church's interior is the handmade ideal, every surface designed and crafted by hand.
A few blocks north, the presses of Printers Row turned out books and catalogs by the million.
And on Prairie Avenue, the richest families in Chicago filled their houses with handcrafted furniture paid for by reapers, sleeping cars, and canned meat, made by machines.
Chicago, being Chicago, wanted both.
The automobile came to Chicago early.
On Thanksgiving Day, 1895, the Chicago Times-Herald newspaper sponsored one of the first automobile races in America, from Jackson Park to Evanston and back, about fifty-four miles, through snow.
Only two cars finished.
The winner, Frank Duryea, took more than ten hours.
By the 1910s, this stretch of Michigan Avenue had become Motor Row, a long line of showrooms, garages, and parts dealers, selling dozens of makes, most of them long forgotten.
Why here?
Partly because of the Coliseum, a huge exhibition hall a few blocks northwest, at Wabash Avenue and 15th Street, where the Chicago Auto Show began in 1901.
Buyers who had seen the new models at the show could walk over and order one.
The Coliseum had other uses too.
Five Republican national conventions met there, including the one in 1912, when Theodore Roosevelt's supporters walked out.
That August, they came back to the same hall to launch their own party, the Progressives, nicknamed the Bull Moose.
The showroom buildings were designed to sell.

Their tall ground floors put the newest models on display to everyone passing by, and inside, freight elevators big enough to carry automobiles lifted them to the floors above, where they were stored and repaired.
Motor Row faded as the dealers followed their customers out to the neighborhoods and the suburbs, and many of its buildings became warehouses.
The city made it a landmark district in 2000, and today its old showrooms hold restaurants, offices, and event halls.
The auto show goes on, though.
It's held every winter at McCormick Place, a short walk southeast of here, and it's one of the biggest in the country.
Walk south on Michigan Avenue to number 2120, a narrow building with a blue awning.
This was the headquarters and studio of Chess Records from 1957 to 1967, and it's one of the holiest sites in American music.
Chess was founded by two brothers, Leonard and Phil Chess, Jewish immigrants from Poland who arrived in Chicago as children.
In the 1940s, they ran nightclubs on the South Side, and they saw the music Black migrants from the Mississippi Delta were bringing to Chicago's clubs.
They started a record label and began recording it.
The Chicago blues was electric: the Delta blues of the South, played on amplified guitars, with drums and harmonica, loud enough to cut through a crowded South Side bar.
Muddy Waters, who had come up from Mississippi in 1943, was its king, and Chess recorded him.
The label's roster became legendary: Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Little Walter, Bo Diddley, Etta James, and Chuck Berry, whose records for Chess helped invent rock and roll.
The great songwriter and bass player Willie Dixon wrote many of their songs and ran the sessions.
The music recorded at Chess went across the Atlantic and inspired a generation of British musicians.
In 1964, the Rolling Stones, who had named themselves after a Muddy Waters song, came here to record, and they called one of the songs they recorded 2120 South Michigan Avenue.
The building is now the home of Willie Dixon's Blues Heaven Foundation, founded by Dixon, who fought for years to recover royalties for blues musicians.
You can tour the old studio.
Chess had already helped launch rock and roll before it moved here.
In 1951, the label released a record called Rocket 88, recorded in Memphis by Sam Phillips and credited to Jackie Brenston and his Delta Cats, a band led by Ike Turner.
Many people call it the first rock and roll record.
A few years later, Etta James recorded At Last for a Chess label, and it became one of the most beloved songs of the century.
This stretch of the city has a much older and rougher history too.

Just a few blocks west, between about 18th and 22nd Streets, lay the Levee, Chicago's most notorious vice district, where hundreds of brothels and saloons operated openly in the early 1900s under the protection of the local aldermen.

The most famous was the Everleigh Club, run by two sisters, Ada and Minna Everleigh, which had gold-leafed pianos and rooms decorated in different themes, and was patronized by wealthy men from around the country.
When Marshall Field's son was shot in 1905 and died a few days later, the official story was that he had shot himself by accident at his home on Prairie Avenue.
But a rumor spread that the shooting had happened at the Everleigh Club.
There was never any proof, and it remains a legend.
The mayor shut the Everleigh Club down in 1911, and the Levee was closed soon after.
This is the end of the South Loop tour.
Nearby, at Cermak Road, is the Cermak-McCormick Place Green Line station, which will take you back downtown.
Willie Dixon was born in Vicksburg, Mississippi, in 1915.
As a boy he wrote poems, and he heard the blues everywhere around him, in juke joints, in work camps, and, after he was picked up for hoboing as a teenager, on a county prison farm.
He came to Chicago in 1936, a big, powerful young man, and his first career was boxing.
In 1937, he won the Illinois Golden Gloves title as a heavyweight novice.
Then music took over.
He learned the bass and sang with vocal groups around the city.
In 1941, when the draft came for him, he refused to serve, saying he would not fight for a country that treated Black people the way his did, and he spent months in jail for it.
After the war, he formed a group called the Big Three Trio.
Before long, he went to work for the Chess brothers as a bass player and became much more: producer, arranger, talent scout, and above all songwriter.
He wrote Hoochie Coochie Man and I Just Want to Make Love to You for Muddy Waters, My Babe for Little Walter, and Spoonful, Little Red Rooster, and Back Door Man for Howlin' Wolf.
Wang Dang Doodle became a hit for Koko Taylor.
People called him the poet laureate of the blues.
His songs traveled around the world, recorded by the Rolling Stones, Cream, the Doors, and Led Zeppelin.
But for years Dixon saw little of the money, because like many blues writers, he had signed away the publishing rights to his songs.
He spent much of his later life fighting to get them back.
He sued Led Zeppelin, arguing that their song Whole Lotta Love took its words from his song You Need Love, which Muddy Waters had recorded in 1962, and the case was settled out of court in 1987.
He started the Blues Heaven Foundation in 1982, to help other musicians collect what they were owed.
He died in 1992, and afterward his widow, Marie, moved the foundation into this building, the place where so many of his songs had been recorded.
In June 1964, five young Englishmen on their first American tour walked through this door to record.
For the Rolling Stones, it was a pilgrimage.
Mick Jagger and Keith Richards had renewed their boyhood friendship on a train platform in England, when Keith noticed that Mick was carrying a couple of Chess records.
Much of the music they loved had been recorded in this building and in the label's earlier studios.
In two days of sessions, they cut more than a dozen tracks, including a song called It's All Over Now, which became their first number one hit in Britain.
Then there's the story.
Keith Richards has told it many times.

When the band walked in, he said, there was Muddy Waters, the king of Chicago blues, up a ladder, painting the ceiling, because his records weren't selling and the Chess brothers had put him to work around the building.
It's a story about the way America treated its own great musicians, while young white Englishmen got rich playing their songs.
But almost nobody else who was there remembers it that way.
Marshall Chess, Leonard Chess's son, who was working at the label that summer, has said flatly that there's no truth in it, and he teases Keith about it as one of his fantasies.
The band's bass player, Bill Wyman, remembered something smaller: Muddy Waters helping to carry their amplifiers in from the car.
So it's a legend.
Maybe it grew out of that small kindness, or a workman on a ladder, or a memory blurred by time and by everything that came after.
What's documented is the music, and what happened next.

Young white fans who loved the Rolling Stones went looking for the records of the men the Stones had learned from, and in the late 1960s, Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, and other Chess artists found new audiences on college campuses and at rock festivals, far from the South Side bars where their music had been born.
Leonard and Phil Chess were born in Motal, a small Jewish town in what was then Poland and is now Belarus.
Their father emigrated to Chicago first, and the rest of the family followed in 1928, when Leonard was eleven.
The brothers grew up on the South Side and went into the bar business.
In the 1940s, Leonard ran a nightclub called the Macomba Lounge, at 39th Street and Cottage Grove Avenue, where he heard the music the Great Migration had brought north.
In 1947, he invested in a small record company called Aristocrat, started that spring by Charles and Evelyn Aron, because the musicians in his clubs had nowhere to record.
In 1948, it released Muddy Waters' I Can't Be Satisfied, which became Muddy's first hit.
By 1950, the brothers had bought out their partners, and they gave the label their own name.
They ran it like a family store.
Leonard handled the artists and the recording, and spent weeks on the road, driving through the South with records in the trunk, visiting disc jockeys and record shops.
Phil ran the office.
Over the years they added other labels, including Checker and Argo, and recorded jazz, gospel, and soul as well as the blues.
Their reputation is mixed.
Some of their artists remembered them as loyal friends who lent money and paid hospital bills.
Others felt cheated, and argued that the brothers had paid them in cars and cash advances instead of fair royalties.
Both things may be true.
In 1963, the brothers bought a radio station and renamed it WVON, the Voice of the Negro.
With its disc jockeys, the Good Guys, it became the most important Black radio station in the city, and it carried the news of the civil rights movement as well as the music.
Its call letters are still on the air in Chicago today.
In 1969, the brothers sold the company.
A few months later, in October, Leonard died of a heart attack, at fifty-two.
Phil lived until 2016.
The label's catalog has been sold and resold since then, but the records made here have never gone out of print.
Look south along Michigan Avenue to 22nd Street, now called Cermak Road.
On the corner, for a century, stood a big brick hotel called the Lexington, built in 1892 for visitors to the World's Fair.
In 1928, Al Capone moved his headquarters into the Lexington, taking over a suite of rooms, and he ran his empire from here until his conviction for tax evasion, in 1931.
How Capone got here starts a block west, at twenty-one twenty-six South Wabash, where Big Jim Colosimo ran the most famous restaurant in the Levee.
Colosimo had started out, by most accounts, sweeping streets, and he rose to become the boss of the district's brothels, with the protection of the First Ward's aldermen.
To help run his businesses, he brought in Johnny Torrio, a hard young man from Brooklyn who was said to be a relative of his wife's.
On May eleventh, 1920, Colosimo was shot dead in the entrance of his café.
No one was ever convicted.

Torrio, who took over, was widely suspected of arranging it, because Prohibition had begun that January, and Colosimo, it's said, had little interest in the bootlegging business that was about to make his successors rich.
Torrio's right-hand man was a young tough he had known back in Brooklyn, Al Capone.
In 1925, after Torrio was badly wounded in an ambush, he retired and handed the business to Capone.

The Lexington's strangest moment came on April twenty-first, 1986, when the television reporter Geraldo Rivera hosted a live two-hour special from its basement, promising to open Capone's secret vault.
Tens of millions of people watched.
The crew broke through the wall and found little more than dirt and an empty bottle or two.
The hotel was torn down in the 1990s.

So if you've spent the afternoon walking from the opera house to the blues, end it with this thought: the same few blocks also gave the country its most famous gangster, and one of its most famous empty rooms.
This tour walks north up Michigan Avenue, the stretch Chicagoans call the Magnificent Mile, and then east to the lake through Streeterville and down to Navy Pier.
A hundred years ago, there was no grand avenue here.
North of the river, Michigan Avenue was a quiet residential street called Pine Street, lined with houses and churches, and it ended at the river.
You crossed by ferry or a narrow swing bridge.
The 1909 Plan of Chicago, by Daniel Burnham and Edward Bennett, imagined a broad boulevard leaping the river and connecting the Loop to the north side.
The city followed the plan.
The Michigan Avenue bridge opened in 1920, the street was widened, and within a decade it was lined with new towers: the Wrigley Building, the Tribune Tower, hotels, athletic clubs, and offices.
The name Magnificent Mile came later, in 1947, from a real estate developer named Arthur Rubloff, who was trying to sell the street's future.
It worked.
Over the next half century, the avenue filled with department stores, hotels, and vertical shopping malls, and it became one of the great retail streets in the country.
East of the avenue lies Streeterville, which has one of the strangest origin stories of any neighborhood in America.
Much of it did not exist in 1880.
It was lake.
It was built out of landfill, some of it dumped deliberately, some of it rubble, and a man named Cap Streeter claimed that new land as his own country.
You'll hear his story near the lake.
Look for three things on this walk.
First, the survivors: two stone buildings that made it through the Great Fire of 1871.
Second, the Chicago engineering tradition, in the tapered black Hancock tower and in Mies van der Rohe's glass apartments by the lake, which changed how the world built tall residences.
And third, the names of companies that made fortunes here: Palmolive soap, Playboy magazine, Wrigley gum, and the department stores of State Street that followed their customers north.
We will start near the corner of Michigan Avenue and Grand Avenue, walk north to Oak Street, cut east to Lake Shore Drive, and then head south through Streeterville and along the lake to Navy Pier.
You are on Michigan Avenue a few blocks north of the river.
Look south and you can see the Wrigley Building and Tribune Tower framing the bridge, and north, the long canyon of shops and hotels that is the Magnificent Mile.
Look for the building at 505 North Michigan, on the east side of the street, with a gold-and-blue onion dome perched on its roof.
It is now a hotel, but it was built in 1929 as the Medinah Athletic Club, a private club for the Shriners, the fraternal order known for their red fez hats and their charity hospitals.

The Shriners took their imagery from an imagined Middle East, which explains the dome, and the carved reliefs on the facade, and the club's lavish interiors, which included a running track, a bowling alley, and a junior Olympic swimming pool on an upper floor, decorated with tiles in a Spanish style.
The champion swimmer and Tarzan actor Johnny Weissmuller is said to have trained in that pool, a story the hotel likes to tell.
The club opened just months before the stock market crash.
By the mid-1930s, it had failed.
The building has been a hotel ever since.

The dome had a practical idea behind it, too: the club's designers reportedly hoped it could serve as a mooring mast for dirigibles, which in the late 1920s many people believed would become a common way to travel.
The same dream was attached to the spire of the Empire State Building in New York.
No airship ever tied up at either one.
As you walk north, notice how the avenue is lined with planters and flowerbeds in the median and along the sidewalks.
They are replanted every season, with tulips in spring and kale and grasses in fall, and they are part of a deliberate effort, since the 1990s, to make the avenue feel like a garden.
The men who built the club with the onion dome belonged to one of the most colorful fraternities in America, and they took their fun seriously.

The Shriners began in New York in the early 1870s, when a doctor named Walter Fleming and an actor named William Florence decided that the Freemasons, the old and solemn fraternal order they both belonged to, needed a livelier branch.
According to the order's own story, Florence had been entertained by an Arab diplomat on his travels abroad and came home with the idea.
They dressed their new order in an invented Arabian costume: the red fez, leaders called potentates, and local chapters called temples, named for places in the Muslim world.
Only Masons could join.
The order spread fast, and its members became famous for their parades, their marching bands, and the little cars they drove in tight circles down the street.
Chicago's chapter took the name Medinah, after the holy city in Arabia.
In 1912, it built Medinah Temple, a couple of blocks northwest of here at Wabash Avenue and Ohio Street, with domes and horseshoe arches and an auditorium that held more than four thousand people.

For decades it was the home of the Shrine Circus, and from around 1970, the Chicago Symphony, under its music director Georg Solti, made many of its famous recordings in that big hall, which recording engineers preferred to the orchestra's own hall downtown.
The temple still stands.
After the Shriners sold it, it became a furniture store, and more recently a temporary casino.
By the 1920s, the Medinah Shriners wanted a clubhouse to match, and they hired Walter Ahlschlager, an architect who also designed grand movie palaces, to build this tower on the avenue.
It didn't last, as you've heard.
The Shriners have far outlived their club.
Their best-known work began in 1922, when they opened their first hospital for children, in Shreveport, Louisiana.

Today there are Shriners children's hospitals across North America, including one on Chicago's Northwest Side, and for most of their history they treated their young patients without charging their families anything at all.
Whether or not Johnny Weissmuller ever swam in the pool upstairs, he was very much a Chicago boy, and his story begins with a small fib.
He was born in 1904 in Freidorf, a village of German-speaking farmers in what was then Hungary and is now part of Romania.
His family brought him to America as a baby, lived for a while in the coal country of western Pennsylvania, and then settled in Chicago, where his father ran a tavern.
Johnny was a skinny, sickly boy, and as the story goes, a doctor told him that swimming would build up his strength.
He took to the water off the city's beaches, and by most accounts he left school young to go to work, as a bellhop among other jobs.
In 1920, he got a tryout with Bill Bachrach, the coach at the Illinois Athletic Club, on Michigan Avenue south of the river.
Bachrach saw at once what he had.
He rebuilt the young man's stroke, and in 1922 Weissmuller became the first person to swim a hundred meters in under a minute.
To swim for the United States, he needed to be an American.
So, by most accounts, he gave his birthplace as Windber, Pennsylvania, where his younger brother had been born, and the record books believed him for decades.
At the Paris Olympics in 1924, he won three gold medals, plus a bronze in water polo.
In Amsterdam in 1928, he won two more golds.
By most accounts, he never lost a race in his amateur career.
Then Hollywood called.
In 1932, he played Tarzan for the first time, and he went on to play him in a dozen films, with a jungle yell that became one of the most famous sounds in movie history.
He died in 1984 in Acapulco, Mexico, where he had spent his last years.
So whatever the hotel says about its pool, remember that the real story of how Tarzan learned to swim in Chicago is better.
When Arthur Rubloff gave this street its famous name, he wasn't describing it.
He was advertising it.
After the Second World War, North Michigan Avenue looked tired.
Hardly anything had been built since the Depression began, and many of the buildings along it were aging and shabby.
Rubloff was a real estate man who had founded his own company in 1930, at the very bottom of the Depression, and he made his living by imagining what a street could become.
In 1947, he unveiled a plan for the whole avenue, from the river to Oak Street, with drawings by the architects Holabird and Root.
It showed handsome new buildings, remodeled old ones, and a boulevard lined with fine shops, and he gave it a name that sounded like a promise: the Magnificent Mile.
It was part vision and part sales pitch, and Rubloff was a gifted salesman.
Much of the plan was never built.
But the name stuck, and the idea behind it, that this avenue could be the city's showroom, came true over the next forty years.

Little shops gave way to famous names from New York and Paris, and the department stores came one after another: Marshall Field's and Lord and Taylor in Water Tower Place, then Neiman Marcus, then Bloomingdale's in a new tower at the north end.
In the 1990s, some stores began selling experiences as much as goods, with showrooms built like theaters, and people came just to look.
Rubloff kept building, around the city and beyond it.

His company developed Evergreen Plaza, one of the early big shopping centers, just past the city's southwest edge, and, in the 1960s, Carl Sandburg Village, a cluster of apartment towers and townhouses built on cleared blocks of the Near North Side.
He died in 1986.
By then, the name he had invented to sell a street was on maps, banners, and guidebooks around the world.
In recent years, as shopping has moved online, some of the big stores have closed, and the avenue is reinventing itself again.
Rubloff would have understood.
A street, to him, was always a story you had to keep selling.
Walk north to Chicago Avenue.
In the middle of the modern shopping district, here is something that looks like a toy castle: the Chicago Water Tower, with its pale yellow limestone, its battlements, and its little turrets.
It was finished in 1869, designed by William W. Boyington.
Inside the tower was a tall iron standpipe running nearly the full height of the tower.
The pumps across the street pushed water up into it, which helped to steady the water pressure and smooth out the surges from the steam pumps.
The castle was just an elaborate cover for a pipe.
The pumping station across Michigan Avenue, in the matching stone, was the other half of the system.
It pulled clean water from a crib two miles out in Lake Michigan through a tunnel under the lake bed, an engineering project led by Ellis Chesbrough that was completed in 1867.
Out there, the water was supposed to be beyond the reach of the city's sewage, which was pouring into the lake from the river.
That was not the end of the problem, as the river tour tells, but it was a start.
Then, in October 1871, the Great Fire swept north across the river and through this neighborhood.
It burned almost everything.
The water tower and pumping station survived, scorched but standing, although the fire knocked out the pumps, which made firefighting even more hopeless.
After the fire, the tower became a symbol of the city's survival, and it has been treasured ever since.
The tower has had its critics.
Oscar Wilde, who visited Chicago in 1882, is often quoted as calling it a castellated monstrosity with pepper boxes stuck all over it.
But Chicagoans have repeatedly saved it from the wrecking ball, and today it holds a small gallery.
The pumping station across the street still pumps water for part of the city, and it also houses a theater.
Just north of the Water Tower, on the east side of the avenue, rises Water Tower Place, a gray marble tower that opened in 1975.
Its lower floors hold a shopping mall stacked eight stories high, around a glass-walled atrium with escalators, and above it are a hotel and condominiums.
It was one of the first vertical shopping malls in the country, and when it was finished it was the tallest reinforced concrete building in the world.
Its success helped pull the city's shopping center of gravity from State Street, in the Loop, north to Michigan Avenue, where it has stayed.
The man who designed this castle, William Boyington, was one of the busiest architects in early Chicago, and once you know his style, you can spot it around northern Illinois.

He was born in Massachusetts in 1818, trained as a carpenter, and learned architecture in New York before moving to Chicago in 1853, when the city was booming and almost any building was a good business.
Over a long career he designed hotels, churches, railroad stations, and the grand Board of Trade building of 1885 at the foot of LaSalle Street, long since replaced.
For the waterworks, he chose a style called castellated Gothic, with battlements and turrets borrowed from medieval castles.
He had used it before.
He designed the gates of Rosehill Cemetery, on the North Side, in that style, and before that, the state penitentiary at Joliet, a fortress of the same yellow stone that held prisoners until 2002.
If you've seen the opening scenes of The Blues Brothers, you've seen it.
The stone itself is a local story.
It's a hard, yellowish limestone quarried along the Des Plaines River southwest of the city, around Joliet and a town then called Athens, now Lemont.
In the years around the Civil War, it was a favorite building stone in Chicago, used for churches and fine houses all over town.
Most of them burned in 1871 or were torn down later, which is one more reason these two buildings are precious.
Now take a closer look.
The blocks are rough-faced, left with the marks of the quarry, so they catch light and shadow.
The tower rises in stages, each a little narrower than the one below, to a small lantern at the top, and its corners are guarded by little turrets, the ones Oscar Wilde made fun of.
Inside all that stone, as you've heard, there was only a pipe, about three feet wide and well over a hundred feet tall.
Boyington lived until 1898, long enough to see his castle become the city's favorite survivor.
In his later years he lived up the North Shore in Highland Park, where he served as mayor, and he's buried at Rosehill, behind the gates he designed.
Of all his buildings, though, this is the one Chicago would never let go.
In 1871, Chicago fought fires with steam engines, and the steam engines needed water from the city's mains.
That's why what happened here, in the small hours of Monday, October ninth, mattered so much.
The fire had started on Sunday evening on the West Side, near DeKoven Street, and around midnight it jumped the South Branch of the river and raced into downtown.
A strong, hot wind blew from the southwest, carrying burning boards and shingles over the rooftops, and some time after one in the morning, the fire crossed the main branch into the North Side.
The pumping station's roof was framed in wood.
Some time after three in the morning, burning debris carried on the wind landed on it.
The roof caught fire, and by about half past three it had fallen in on the engines below.
The pumps stopped.
All over the city, the hoses went dry, and from then on, there was little anyone could do but run.
And run they did.
Tens of thousands of people fled north, carrying what they could, through streets so jammed that wagons couldn't move.
Many ended up at the lakeshore, some standing in the water for hours with wet blankets over their heads while the fire roared behind them.
Others crowded into the old city cemetery at the south end of what's now Lincoln Park, sheltering among the graves.
The North Side burned all through Monday.
Block after block of wooden cottages, and the mansions of the rich, went down together, as far north as Fullerton Avenue.
Late that night, it finally began to rain, and by Tuesday morning the fire was dying out.
When people came back, there was almost nothing left in this part of the city.
But here at Chicago Avenue, scorched and blackened, the castle and its pumping station were still standing.
The engines were repaired, the water flowed again, and Chicagoans adopted the two buildings as proof that their city could survive anything.
About two miles straight out from here, under the lake, is the far end of one of the great engineering feats of the 1860s, and it started at a shaft near where you're standing.
Ellis Chesbrough's plan, drawn up in 1863, called for a tunnel only five feet across, lined with brick, running more than ten thousand feet through the clay beneath the lake bed.
Nothing quite like it had been tried.
Work began on the shore in 1864.
Crews sank a shaft near the lake and started digging east, by hand, with picks and shovels, by lamplight, hauling the clay back to the shaft in small cars.
Far out in the lake, the city built a crib: a huge, five-sided box of timbers, framed on shore, towed out into open water, and sunk in place by filling its compartments with stone.
A shaft went down through the middle of it, and a second crew began digging west, toward the shore, from the middle of the lake.
For most of that year, the two crews worked toward each other in the dark, guided only by surveyors' instruments and arithmetic.
In November 1866, they broke through.
When they did, the two halves of the tunnel were less than eight inches out of line.

Masons followed the diggers, lining the tunnel with two layers of brick, and on March twenty-fifth, 1867, clean water from far out in the lake began flowing through it into the pumps here and out to the city.
It was a sensation.
Engineers came to study it, and the crib became one of the sights of Chicago, a lonely little fortress on the horizon.
The first tunnel was soon overwhelmed by the growing city, and others followed, longer and deeper, as Chicago kept reaching farther into the lake.
Today the system delivers hundreds of millions of gallons a day.
But it all began with two crews of diggers, meeting in the middle, under the lake.
In February 1882, the most talked-about young man in the English-speaking world stepped off a train in Chicago.
Oscar Wilde was twenty-seven.
He had published one book of poems, and he was famous mostly for being famous: for his long hair, his velvet suits, his lilies and sunflowers, and his witty talk about beauty.
He had come to America on a lecture tour that would last most of the year, and Chicago was an early stop.
On February thirteenth, he spoke at Central Music Hall, downtown, on the decorative arts, telling his audience how Americans ought to furnish their homes and beautify their cities.
The newspapers had a wonderful time with him, mocking his clothes and quoting every phrase.
His famous insult to the Water Tower, the castle in front of you, came out of that visit.
But there's a second half to the story that's rarely told.
Wilde went inside the pumping station across the street, and he loved what he found there.
