Back in England the next year, in a lecture about his American travels, he described the great engines, the rise and fall of their rods and the turning of their wheels, as one of the most beautifully rhythmic things he had ever seen.
Think about that.
The man who mocked the castle praised the machinery inside the building next door, the very thing the city had wrapped in battlements because it assumed no one would want to look at it.
Wilde was saying, in his way, what a generation of Chicago architects would soon say in steel: that the useful thing, honestly shown, can be beautiful in itself.
His advice to Americans was to look to their own craftsmen and their own landscape for beauty, instead of copying Europe.
Chicago took that advice in its own way.

Within a few years of his visit, its architects were raising the plain, powerful office towers that made the city famous, on frames of iron and steel, with little borrowed ornament, while the little castle on Michigan Avenue kept its battlements and its pepper boxes, and the city came to love it anyway.
Continue north along Michigan Avenue.
On the west side, you will pass a gray stone Gothic church with a quiet, grassy courtyard.
This is Fourth Presbyterian Church, completed in 1914, designed by Ralph Adams Cram, the great American champion of Gothic church architecture.
Step into the courtyard if the gate is open.
It is one of the most peaceful places on the avenue, and the cloister walk around it is designed to feel like a college quad at Oxford.
Now turn around and look up at the giant across the street: the black, tapering tower crossed with huge diagonal braces.
This is the building long known as the John Hancock Center, finished in 1969.
Its official name is now simply its address, 875 North Michigan Avenue, but most people still call it the Hancock.
It was designed at Skidmore, Owings and Merrill by the architect Bruce Graham and the engineer Fazlur Khan, a Bangladeshi-born structural engineer who reshaped tall buildings.
Khan's insight was that a tall building could act like a hollow tube, with its outer walls carrying the wind loads.
The giant X braces on the outside tie the walls together, so the tube is stiff, and the tower used far less steel than a conventional design would have for a building of its height.
Khan went on to engineer the Sears Tower with the same team.
The Hancock was designed as a city in a tower, which was a new idea at the time.
The lower floors were stores and parking, then offices, and above that, apartments, with a pool and a grocery store for residents.
The taper is part of the logic: offices want big, deep floors, and apartments want smaller ones with windows, so the building narrows as it rises.
The observation deck near the top has one of the best views in the city, and on a clear day you can see across the lake to Indiana and Michigan.
The Hancock nearly didn't get built as planned.
Its original developer, Jerry Wolman, who also owned the Philadelphia Eagles football team, ran into financial trouble during construction, and he lost both the building and the team.
The John Hancock insurance company, which had lent the money, took over the project and finished it.
The building quickly became a symbol of Chicago, and its two tall antennas carry television and radio signals for much of the city.
Fourth Presbyterian Church had about the worst first day a congregation could have.
It was formed early in 1871, when two older Presbyterian churches on the North Side, North Presbyterian and Westminster, joined together.
On Sunday, October eighth, 1871, the new congregation dedicated its church.
Only a few hours after the evening service ended, the Great Fire swept into the North Side, and the church was destroyed.
By the church's own count, a hundred and twenty-five of its hundred and thirty member families lost their homes that night.
They regrouped, built a new church at Rush and Superior Streets, and dedicated it early in 1874.
The congregation grew along with the wealthy North Side neighborhoods around it.
In 1909, it called a new pastor, John Timothy Stone, an energetic preacher with big ambitions, and he persuaded his people to take a gamble.

Instead of building another church in the settled streets where most of them lived, they would move to Pine Street, a quiet residential street near the lake, right in the path of the grand boulevard that the Plan of Chicago promised.
The cornerstone was laid in September 1912, and the church opened two years later, well before the new bridge brought the traffic of the Loop up this street.
The gamble paid off.

Under Stone, Fourth Presbyterian became one of the largest Presbyterian congregations in the country, and in 1913 he was elected moderator of his church's General Assembly, the highest office it could give.
The church that had once stood on a sleepy street found itself in the middle of the busiest shopping district in the Midwest.
It has made that location part of its mission.
Today the church runs tutoring programs for children, services for people without homes, and concerts that are free to anyone who wanders in from the avenue.
If the doors are open, step into the sanctuary.
Look up at the stone arches and the painted wooden ceiling, and listen to the quiet.
The traffic outside is close enough to touch, and inside you can't hear it at all.
Under the Hancock, the ground is soft clay for a long way down before you reach solid rock.
A tower this heavy couldn't float on that clay the way the buildings of the 1880s did.
It needed legs that reached all the way to bedrock.
Those legs are called caissons.
Each one is a deep, round shaft drilled down through the clay and filled with concrete, so that it becomes a solid column standing on rock.
The tricky part is the clay itself, which is wet and soft and wants to squeeze back into the hole.
Builders keep it out with steel casings and careful timing, and if they hurry, the concrete may not fill the shaft completely.
At the Hancock, someone hurried.
In 1967, with the steel frame already rising, engineers noticed that part of the building was settling more than it should.
When they looked into it, they discovered voids in some of the caissons, weak spots where the concrete hadn't filled the shafts the way it was supposed to.
A building that was meant to stand on solid legs was standing, in places, on flawed ones.
Construction stopped.
For about four months, crews went back underground to redo five of the caissons, with the partly built tower waiting above them.
The delay helped push the developer, Jerry Wolman, out of the project, as you've heard, and the insurance company took over.
The repairs worked, and the tower was finished in 1969.

But the episode became a lesson that engineers still talk about: the hardest part of building a skyscraper is often the part no one ever sees, and a building that seems to defy the wind a thousand feet up depends, in the end, on what was done right, or wrong, in the dark under the street.
So as you look up at those great diagonal braces, spare a thought for the columns beneath your feet.
On Veterans Day, November eleventh, 1981, crowds gathered on these sidewalks to watch a man in a Spider-Man costume climb the outside of the Hancock.
His name was Dan Goodwin, a young man from Kennebunkport, Maine, and he wasn't only looking for attention.

On Memorial Day that year, he had climbed the Sears Tower, then the tallest building in the world, and ten days before this climb, his first try at the Hancock had ended almost as soon as it began, when his gear failed.
He said he climbed to make a point: if a fire broke out high in a skyscraper, firefighters had no good way to reach the people trapped above it, and cities ought to be doing something about that.
The Chicago Fire Department did not appreciate the point.
As Goodwin worked his way up the Hancock's black walls, the fire commissioner, William Blair, ordered his men to stop him.

Around the thirty-seventh floor, while Goodwin hung from a homemade hook on the steel, firefighters on a floor above turned a high-pressure hose on him, and others reached for him with long hooked poles.
For about two hours, they kept him from climbing any higher.
Then Mayor Jane Byrne stepped in.
She called off the fire department, and Goodwin went on climbing, all the way to the top.
The police arrested him afterward, and among the charges was performing an acrobatic act without safety equipment.
It was a very Chicago scene: a daredevil, a stubborn bureaucracy, a mayor who knew a crowd pleaser when she saw one, and a skyscraper as the stage.

Goodwin went on to climb other tall buildings and towers in North America, and he spent years campaigning for better ways to fight fires and rescue people in high-rises, which was the cause he had claimed from the start.
Look up at the walls and the great diagonal braces, and imagine clinging to them in a November wind, with a fire hose aimed at your head and thousands of people watching from the street below.
Here's a building to look for later on this walk.
A few blocks southeast of here, near the lake at Ontario Street, is a tall, pale concrete tower with giant X shapes running up its sides.
It's called the Onterie Center, and it was the last major work of Fazlur Khan, the Hancock's engineer.
The family resemblance is deliberate.
Khan's great insight, as you heard, was to treat a tall building as a stiff tube, with the outside walls resisting the wind.
At the Hancock, steel diagonals tie the walls together.
At the Onterie Center, the same idea is carried out in concrete.
Instead of steel braces, the X's are made by filling in window openings with solid concrete, in a pattern of giant diagonal lines, so that the wall itself becomes a braced tube.
It's often described as the first concrete high-rise anywhere to be braced this way.
It came out of the same office, Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, that produced the Hancock and the Sears Tower.
Khan didn't live to see it built.
He died in 1982, at fifty-two, and the tower was finished in 1986.
The Onterie Center is easy to overlook, an apartment building on a quiet side street, but engineers know it well.
In a city that loves to show off how its buildings stand up, it's a last, quiet signature from one of the most important engineers of the twentieth century.

While you're thinking about the Hancock's family, notice how many of the towers around Streeterville and the Gold Coast followed its other big idea, the city stacked in a single tower: shops and parking at the bottom, then offices or a hotel, then homes, with groceries, a pool, and a gym a short elevator ride away.
When the Hancock opened, that was a daring experiment, and people wondered whether anyone would really want to live that way.
In this part of Chicago, it turned out, a great many people did, and they still do.
Keep walking north.
At Walton Street, look at the building on the east side of the avenue, the elegant limestone tower with setbacks that step back as it rises.
This is the Palmolive Building, finished in 1929 by Holabird and Root, the same firm that designed the Board of Trade.
It was headquarters for the Colgate-Palmolive-Peet company, maker of the green Palmolive soap, made with palm and olive oils.
At the top, the company installed a powerful rotating searchlight called the Lindbergh Beacon, named for the aviator Charles Lindbergh, to guide planes into Chicago.
It swept across the city for decades, until new high-rise neighbors complained about the light in their windows.
In 1965, the building changed tenants in a way that made it famous all over again.
Playboy Enterprises, founded in Chicago by Hugh Hefner, who had launched Playboy magazine here in 1953 on a kitchen table, bought a long lease and moved in.
For years, giant letters on top of the tower spelled out PLAYBOY, lit up at night above the Gold Coast.
Playboy moved its headquarters in 1989, and the building is now condominiums.
Hefner's famous mansion, the original Playboy Mansion, was a few blocks away on North State Parkway.
Across Walton Street, at the very top of the Magnificent Mile, stands the Drake Hotel, which opened in 1920.
Its owners, the Drake brothers, had built it out on what was then the edge of the lake, and it became one of the city's grand hotels, where presidents and royalty stayed.
There is a popular story that Joe DiMaggio and Marilyn Monroe carved their initials into the bar of the hotel's Cape Cod Room.
That is a legend that has never been confirmed.
Just past the hotel is Oak Street Beach, where Lake Shore Drive curves around a wide beach right in the shadow of the towers.
The soap that paid for this tower was born in Milwaukee, and it became one of the best-selling soaps in the world largely through advertising.
At the end of the 1890s, the B. J. Johnson Soap Company of Milwaukee introduced a new bar made with palm and olive oils, colored green, and named for both: Palmolive.
Soap was a crowded business, and most bars looked and smelled about the same, so the company bet on advertising, on a scale few soap makers had tried.

Its ads told readers that palm and olive oils had been the beauty secrets of Cleopatra and ancient Egypt, and in the 1920s they promised that a woman who washed with Palmolive could keep that schoolgirl complexion, a slogan that ran for years.
The soap did so well that the company renamed itself after it.
In the mid-1920s, Palmolive merged with Peet Brothers, a soap maker from Kansas City, and in 1928 the combined company merged with Colgate, the old soap and toothpaste maker from the East.
The new giant was called Colgate-Palmolive-Peet, and its new tower here, finished the next year, was one of the most elegant office buildings in Chicago.
The soap business left another mark on American culture, and much of it was made in Chicago.
In the 1930s, soap companies sponsored daytime radio dramas aimed at women listening at home, and the shows came to be called soap operas.
Many of the earliest ones were written and broadcast here.

A former schoolteacher named Irna Phillips created one of the first, Painted Dreams, on a Chicago station in 1930, and she went on to create Guiding Light and As the World Turns, which ran for decades, first on radio and then on television.
She's often called the mother of the soap opera.
The company dropped Peet from its name in 1953, and today Colgate-Palmolive is based in New York.
But the green soap is still sold around the world, and the tower on Michigan Avenue still carries its name, almost a hundred years after a Milwaukee soap maker's advertising budget put it there.
When Playboy moved into this tower in 1965, the company was only twelve years old, and it had grown out of one young man's ordinary Chicago life.
Hugh Hefner was born in Chicago in 1926 and raised in a strict Methodist household on the Northwest Side.

He served in the Army at the end of the Second World War, studied psychology at the University of Illinois, and went to work writing promotional copy, including a job at Esquire, the men's magazine, which had been founded in Chicago.
When Esquire moved to New York and wouldn't give him a small raise to come along, he decided to start a magazine of his own.
He raised about eight thousand dollars, including a thousand from his mother, and put the first issue together in his apartment on the South Side.
It had no date on the cover, because he wasn't sure there would ever be a second one.
Its big attraction was a set of pictures of Marilyn Monroe, taken years earlier for a calendar, which he had bought for a few hundred dollars.
It went on sale in late 1953 and sold more than fifty thousand copies, enough to keep going.

The formula was a mix that no one had quite tried: pictures of women alongside serious fiction, long interviews, and articles telling young men how to dress, what to drink, and how to furnish an apartment.

Over the years the magazine published Ray Bradbury, Ian Fleming, and Vladimir Nabokov, and interviews with figures from Martin Luther King Junior to Jimmy Carter, who told the magazine in 1976 that he had committed adultery in his heart.
In 1960, the company opened its first Playboy Club, just around the corner on Walton Street, and the clubs soon spread across the country and overseas.
By the time Playboy's name went up over Walton Street on this tower, it was one of the most recognizable brands in the world, and it had been made in Chicago.
The Drake was built by a family of hotel men.
John B. Drake had run the Grand Pacific, one of the great hotels of the Loop, and his sons, John and Tracy, carried on the trade.
In 1910, they opened the Blackstone, at the south end of Michigan Avenue downtown, and ten years later they built this one, so that the avenue had a Drake hotel at each end.

They bought the land from the family of Potter Palmer, the merchant who had made the lakeshore north of here the most fashionable address in Chicago, and they hired the architects Marshall and Fox, who had designed the Blackstone.

Benjamin Marshall was a showman as much as an architect, and he gave the Drake the look of an Italian Renaissance palace: limestone outside, and inside, a sweep of stairs rising from the street to the Palm Court, the elegant lounge at the heart of the hotel, with a fountain at its center.
The hotel opened on New Year's Eve, 1920, with a grand party for Chicago society.
Building out here was a bet that the city would follow the new Michigan Avenue bridge north, and it did.
The guest book reads like a history of the century.
According to the hotel, Winston Churchill stayed here in 1929.
Queen Elizabeth the Second came in July 1959, during her tour for the opening of the Saint Lawrence Seaway, which turned Chicago into a port for oceangoing ships.
Princess Diana stayed in 1996, on her only visit to Chicago, the year before her death.
The hotel likes to say that both of them took afternoon tea in the Palm Court, and you can still do the same, among the palms, often to the sound of a harp.

In a city that tears down so much, the Drake has stayed remarkably itself for more than a century, a reminder of the age when the grandest thing a city could offer a traveler was a beautiful hotel by the lake.
Walk east on Walton or Chestnut Street to Lake Shore Drive, then turn south a block.
The two identical black steel and glass towers set at right angles to each other are 860 and 880 Lake Shore Drive, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and completed in 1951.
They look ordinary today, because so many buildings around the world copy them.
In 1951, they were revolutionary: glass boxes of apartments, floor-to-ceiling windows, the steel frame expressed on the outside.
Look closely at the facades.
The vertical steel I-beams you see were added purely for appearance.
The real structural steel had to be covered in concrete for fire protection, so Mies added these exposed beams to show the frame.
He was willing to be practical in order to be beautiful.
Now for the ground you are standing on.
In 1886, a man named George Wellington Streeter, who called himself Captain, ran his small boat aground on a sandbar a few hundred feet offshore, roughly near here.
The boat stayed, and Streeter encouraged contractors to dump fill around it.
Sand and debris piled up, and soon there were acres of new land.
Streeter declared that this land was not part of Illinois at all, since it had not existed when the state's boundaries were drawn.
He called it the District of Lake Michigan, and he sold lots to buyers.
For more than thirty years, Streeter fought the city, the police, and wealthy property owners who said the new land belonged to them, sometimes with lawsuits and sometimes with shotguns.
He was finally evicted for good in 1918, and he died in 1921.
He lost every case, but he won the name.
The neighborhood built on his landfill is still called Streeterville.
Look at the road in front of the towers, Lake Shore Drive.

It began in the 1880s as a pleasure drive along the lake, pushed by Potter Palmer, and over the next century it was extended north and south into an expressway along almost the entire lakefront, much of it on landfill, with parks and beaches on the lake side.
It's one of the great urban drives in the world, and in 1971 a Chicago folk-rock trio, Aliotta Haynes Jeremiah, wrote a song about driving it at night that became a local anthem.
The drive used to have a dangerous S-curve where it crossed the Chicago River, a notorious spot for crashes.
The curve was straightened in the 1980s.

Mies van der Rohe gets the credit for these towers, but they wouldn't exist without a young developer named Herbert Greenwald, who was willing to bet that ordinary buyers would want to live in a glass box.
Greenwald met Mies in 1946.
Mies was running the architecture school at the Illinois Institute of Technology on the South Side, and he had built very little in America.
Greenwald hired him to design an apartment building on the South Side lakefront, the Promontory, in Hyde Park, finished in 1949.
It had a concrete frame, a first step.
Then, with a partner, Robert Hall McCormick, Greenwald announced these two towers, cooperative apartments in steel and glass.
Mies treated them as a single composition.
Because the two towers are turned at right angles, they shift and overlap as you walk past, like a sculpture you can circle.
At the bottom, the glass walls of the lobbies are pulled back behind the columns, leaving a covered walk around each base, and a flat steel canopy joins the two.
Everything sits on a plain paved terrace, with nothing to distract from the grid.
When they were finished in 1951, they were among the first tall apartment buildings anywhere with walls almost entirely of glass, and architects came to study them from around the world.
Within a decade, their descendants were rising in cities everywhere.
Greenwald and Mies went on to build more together: the dark towers just to the north of these, finished in 1956, and Lafayette Park, a whole neighborhood of towers and townhouses in Detroit.
The partnership ended suddenly.
In February 1959, Greenwald was killed when the airliner he was on crashed into the East River in New York, on its approach to LaGuardia Airport.
He was in his forties.
Mies outlived him by ten years and kept working, but he had lost the developer who first proved that his kind of building could sell.
Cap Streeter told so many stories about himself that it's hard to say where the man ends and the legend begins.
So here's what's documented, and here's what he claimed.
He was born in Michigan, near Flint, probably in 1837, though some records give a later year.
By his own account, before he reached Chicago he had been a Civil War soldier, a circus showman, and a riverboat captain, and some of that may even be true.
He arrived in 1886 with his second wife, Maria, aboard a small steamboat called the Reutan.
In his telling, a storm drove it onto the sandbar.
What's certain is that he and Maria defended their sandbar like a frontier family defending a homestead.
The wealthy owners of the lakefront, among them the soap and lard millionaire Nathaniel Fairbank, sent lawyers, and Streeter filed lawsuits of his own.
When the police came, he met them armed.
In 1894, when the police came for him, Maria is said to have driven them off with a kettle of boiling water.
He was a businessman too.
In 1893, during the World's Fair, he refloated the Reutan and ran it as an excursion boat, carrying fairgoers down the lakeshore to Jackson Park.
And he kept selling lots in his district to buyers willing to gamble that a squatter's deed might someday be worth something.
In 1918, a judge ruled once and for all that the land was not his.
He died on January twenty-second, 1921, and even then the fight wasn't quite over, because his heirs and the people who had bought lots from him kept pressing claims for years.
Look for reminders as you walk.
A few blocks south and west of here, one of the neighborhood's streets is Fairbanks Court, named for the family of his old enemy.
The whole neighborhood, of course, is named for him.
The millionaire got a side street.
The squatter got the map.
Lake Michigan looks permanent from here, a calm blue line at the edge of the city.
But it rises and falls, sometimes over years and sometimes in minutes, and the drive in front of you has felt both.
Over the years, the lake's level goes up and down with the rain, snow, and evaporation across its whole enormous basin.
In October 1986, it reached the highest level on record.
In January 2013, it hit the lowest, more than six feet below that peak, and Chicago's beaches grew wide.
By 2020 it was back up near the record, and that January a winter storm drove waves over the lakefront path and onto Lake Shore Drive, tearing up the trail and closing parts of the road.
Over minutes, the lake can be even more dangerous.
On a Saturday morning, June twenty-sixth, 1954, a fast-moving line of storms crossed the southern end of the lake, and the sudden jump in air pressure set off a wave.
It came ashore along the North Side, from Wilmette down to North Avenue, as much as ten feet high, and it swept fishermen off the piers and breakwaters at Montrose Harbor and North Avenue.
By most counts, eight of them drowned.
At the time, it was called a seiche, the sloshing of water from one side of a basin to the other.
Scientists now call it a meteotsunami, a tsunami set off by the weather instead of an earthquake.
Now look at the edge of the water.
Between 1910 and 1931, Chicago armored much of its shore with big limestone blocks, laid in steps on top of wooden cribs and pilings.
Over the decades, the wood rotted, the stones slumped, and the waves chewed at the land behind them.

Since the late 1990s, the city, the Park District, and the Army Corps of Engineers have rebuilt more than nine miles of it, mostly in concrete, as broad steps where people sit in summer to watch the water.
They're built for the lake at its worst, because sooner or later, the lake comes back.
Walk south and west to Chicago Avenue, between Lake Shore Drive and Michigan Avenue.
The building with the broad flight of stairs, clad in cast aluminum panels, is the Museum of Contemporary Art, which opened here in 1996.
It was designed by the German architect Josef Paul Kleihues, on the site of an old National Guard armory, and it faces a sculpture garden that runs back toward the lake.

The museum was founded in 1967 by a group of collectors and critics who felt the Art Institute wasn't paying enough attention to the art of their own time, and its first home was a small former bakery on Ontario Street.
In 1969, the artist Christo wrapped that building entirely in tarpaulins and rope, one of the first of his famous wrappings.
The museum has a reputation for provocative exhibitions, and Chicago artists have long had a strong place in it.
Look around you at the hospitals and medical buildings that fill the blocks to the south.
This is the Chicago campus of Northwestern University, whose main campus is in the suburb of Evanston.
Here are its law and medical schools and a cluster of hospitals, including Northwestern Memorial and Lurie Children's.
It's one of the largest medical centers in the Midwest.
Not all of it has survived.

A few blocks south, on Superior Street, stood Prentice Women's Hospital, designed by Bertrand Goldberg, the architect of Marina City, and finished in 1975, with a four-lobed concrete tower that looked like a cloverleaf cantilevered over a glass base.
Architects around the world campaigned to save it, but the university won the fight and demolished it in 2014 to build a research tower.
It's become a famous case in the debate over when modern buildings deserve protection.

In the late 1960s, while New York's art world was busy with cool abstraction and Pop Art soup cans, a handful of young Chicago artists went in a completely different direction, and the city has been proud of them ever since.

Most of them had studied at the School of the Art Institute, and in 1966, six of them, Jim Falconer, Art Green, Gladys Nilsson, Jim Nutt, Suellen Rocca, and Karl Wirsum, put on a group show at the Hyde Park Art Center, on the South Side, with the encouragement of its exhibition director, Don Baum.
They called themselves the Hairy Who, a joke name, and instead of serious catalogs they printed comic books.
Their work was loud, funny, crude, and obsessive: bright flat colors, cartoon figures with twisted bodies, puns, and painstaking detail.
They borrowed from comics, tattoos, advertising, and the work of self-taught outsider artists they admired, and some of them painted on the back of sheets of plastic, like old sign painters.
Plenty of critics in New York didn't know what to make of them.
Chicago loved them.
They showed together for only a few years, in Chicago, San Francisco, New York, and Washington, and broke up in 1969.

But other young artists showing at Hyde Park worked in the same spirit, among them Roger Brown and Ed Paschke, and a critic, Franz Schulze, gave the whole loose movement a name that stuck: the Chicago Imagists.
Several of them went on to long careers.
Jim Nutt and Gladys Nilsson, who married young, became two of the most admired painters to come out of the city.
This museum collects their work, and in 2018 the Art Institute gave the Hairy Who a big retrospective.
If the galleries are open, look for them.
It's some of the most Chicago art there is: a little rude, very funny, and made with a craftsman's care.
The museum's reputation for provocation was earned early, and two of its most famous moments came from artists who worked with the strangest materials of all: a human body and a whole house.

In April 1975, in the museum's first home on Ontario Street, a young California artist named Chris Burden lay down on the gallery floor beneath a large sheet of glass, propped at an angle against the wall, with a clock hanging nearby.
He had set himself a rule and shared it with almost no one: he would stay there until someone interfered.
Visitors came and went.
The museum closed for the night, and then for a second night, and Burden stayed where he was, without food or water.
After about forty-five hours, a member of the museum's staff set a container of water down within his reach.
Burden got up at once, and the piece, which he called Doomed, was over.
Who, it asked, decides when art ends?
Three years later, the museum bought the townhouse next door to expand into, and before the builders arrived, it handed the old house to Gordon Matta-Clark.

The son of the Chilean painter Roberto Matta, he had trained as an architect and made his name cutting buildings open: he sawed a house in New Jersey in half, and carved a great cone through two old buildings in Paris.
Here, he cut huge circles through the townhouse's walls and floors, so that visitors, led through by the museum's guards, could look up, down, and across through a spiral of openings.
He called it Circus, or The Caribbean Orange.
It was open for about two and a half weeks, and then the house was rebuilt into galleries.
That summer, Matta-Clark died of cancer, at thirty-five.

At the very same time, in the museum's own galleries next door, a show was running that would look prophetic: the first solo museum exhibition in the United States for a Mexican painter then far less famous than she is today, Frida Kahlo.
The towers of hospitals and laboratories around you began with a gift from a widow.
Montgomery Ward, the mail-order merchant, died in 1913.
His widow, Elizabeth Ward, wanted a memorial to him, and beginning in 1923 she gave Northwestern University a series of gifts that added up to more than eight million dollars.

Northwestern had decided to bring its professional schools together on a new campus near downtown, here on the young landfill of Streeterville, and Mrs. Ward's money built the centerpiece: the Montgomery Ward Memorial Building, a Gothic tower for the medical and dental schools.
The architect was James Gamble Rogers, who designed many of the Gothic buildings at Yale.
He gave Northwestern a campus stretched upward instead of outward, in limestone, with pointed windows and carved trim.
Alongside it, a gift from Rachel Mayer in memory of her husband, the Chicago lawyer Levy Mayer, built a home for the law school, and a third building, Wieboldt Hall, housed the business school.
They opened in 1926 and 1927, and you can still see them along Chicago Avenue.
Hospitals gathered around the medical school.
Two older ones, Passavant and Wesley Memorial, combined in the 1970s to form Northwestern Memorial Hospital.
In 2012, Children's Memorial Hospital moved here from its longtime home in Lincoln Park and took a new name, Lurie Children's.
Not every building has been kept.

When the university moved to tear down Prentice Women's Hospital, the city's landmarks commission met in 2012, voted to give it preliminary landmark protection, and then, in the same meeting, voted to take that protection away, clearing the way for the wrecking ball.
Preservationists never forgot it.
All of this rose on land that a century and a half ago was open water.
The doctors and students hurrying along these sidewalks are standing, just as you are, on Cap Streeter's lake.
Walk east to the lakefront and south to Ohio Street Beach, a small, curving sandy beach tucked between the high-rises and Navy Pier.
It's a favorite place for open-water swimmers and triathletes, who train along the buoys in the summer.
Look out at the lake.
On a clear day, you can see a few small round structures standing in the water, a couple of miles offshore.
These are the water cribs: intake structures where Chicago draws its drinking water from deep in Lake Michigan, through tunnels under the lake bed.
The first one, built in the 1860s, supplied the Water Tower and pumping station on Michigan Avenue.
The cribs were once staffed by keepers who lived on them, sometimes for weeks at a time, and kept them free of ice.
Just to the north of the beach, on a peninsula of landfill, is the Jardine Water Purification Plant, which opened in the 1960s.
It's one of the largest water treatment plants in the world, and it filters drinking water for millions of people in Chicago and its suburbs.

The land on top of the plant is a park called Milton Lee Olive Park, named for an eighteen-year-old soldier from Chicago, Private First Class Milton Olive, who in 1965, in Vietnam, threw himself on a grenade to save the men around him.
He was awarded the Medal of Honor, the first given to a Black soldier in the Vietnam War.
The lake is Chicago's great natural resource.
It provides the city's water, moderates its weather, and gives it its lakefront, twenty-six miles of mostly public parks and beaches, protected since the days of Montgomery Ward.
The cribs on the horizon look peaceful from the beach, but building them was dangerous work, and the worst disaster in their history happened on a January day in 1909.
As the city grew, it kept pushing its intakes farther out, to reach water beyond the pollution near the shore.
Every new intake needed a tunnel, and the tunnels were dug the old way, by crews of men working beneath the lake bed in shifts around the clock.
To save the long trips back and forth by boat, the contractors housed many of the workers out on the water.
In the winter of 1909, crews were digging a tunnel to bring fresh water to the growing South Side.
About a mile out from 71st Street, on a temporary crib, stood a wooden barracks where a hundred or so men ate and slept, above the shaft that led down to their tunnel.
On January twentieth, fire broke out in that building, and it raced through the dry timber.
The men had almost nowhere to go.
Some were trapped inside, and others ended up in the freezing lake.
A fire tug and other boats hurried out from shore, and their crews pulled survivors from the water, but by the end of the day about sixty men were dead, and some counts run higher.
No one ever settled how it started.
One newspaper blamed an explosion of dynamite in the shaft below.
A rumor blamed a worker who had sprinkled gasoline around the bunks to kill bedbugs.

Photographs taken in the days afterward, now in the collection of the Chicago History Museum, show relatives of the victims stepping off a streetcar, and men picking through the charred wreck during the inquest.
The tunnel was finished, and the new intake went into service.
But when you look out at those little towers on the water, remember the men who dug the tunnels beneath them, and what it cost to bring the lake into the city's taps.
In the summer of 1967, beaches like this one were covered with dead fish.
They were alewives, small silvery fish about the length of your hand, at home in the Atlantic Ocean.
They had found their way into the upper Great Lakes through the canals built for ships, and in Lake Michigan they found a paradise.
The lake's big native predator, the lake trout, had been nearly wiped out in the 1940s and 1950s by another invader, the sea lamprey, a parasite that latches onto fish and feeds on their blood.
With almost nothing to eat them, the alewives multiplied into the billions.
Alewives are fragile, and they die off in great numbers when conditions in the water change.
Every year, some washed up on the beaches.
In 1967, they died by the billions, and all along the southern shore of the lake, the beaches were buried in rotting fish.
Chicago sent crews with tractors and trucks to scrape them up, swimmers stayed away, and people still remember the smell.
The cure came from Michigan.
A state fisheries chief named Howard Tanner had a bold idea: bring in a predator from the Pacific.
In the spring of 1966, Michigan released hundreds of thousands of young coho salmon into rivers that flow into the lake, and the next year, Chinook salmon.
The salmon fattened on alewives and grew big, and over the following years, the alewives were brought under control, and a whole new sport fishery was born.
In summer, charter boats leave Chicago's harbors every morning to fish for salmon.
It's an artificial balance, kept going by stocking, and newer invaders have changed the lake again.

Zebra and quagga mussels, which arrived in the ballast water of ships, have filtered the water so clear that in places you can see the bottom many feet down, and they've starved the tiny creatures at the bottom of the food chain.
Lake Michigan looks like wilderness from this beach, but it's one of the most rearranged bodies of water on earth.
The park beside you carries the name of a young man from Chicago who lived only eighteen years.
Milton Lee Olive the third was born in the city in November 1946.

He joined the Army as a teenager and volunteered to be a paratrooper, and by the fall of 1965 he was a private first class with the hundred and seventy-third Airborne Brigade, one of the first American combat units sent to Vietnam.
On October twenty-second, 1965, his platoon was moving through the jungle near Phu Cuong, pursuing enemy soldiers, when a grenade landed in the middle of a small group of men.
Olive grabbed it, pulled it against his body, and fell on it.
He was killed, and the men around him survived.
The next April, at a ceremony at the White House, President Lyndon Johnson presented the Medal of Honor to Olive's father and stepmother, with Mayor Richard J. Daley among the guests.

In his remarks, the president read aloud from a letter that Olive's father had written to him, a grieving father's plea that his son's sacrifice might help bring Americans of every race and faith together in goodwill.
Then the president promised that the nation would never forget Milton Lee Olive the third.
It was the spring of 1966.
The civil rights movement was at its height.
Martin Luther King Junior had moved into an apartment on Chicago's West Side that winter, and that summer he would lead marches for open housing through white neighborhoods of the city.
A young Black man from the city had given his life for the men beside him, and his father had answered with a plea for brotherhood.
Chicago kept the president's promise in its own way.

Besides this park, his name is on Olive-Harvey College, one of the City Colleges, on the far South Side, which honors him together with Carmel Harvey, another young Chicagoan who received the Medal of Honor for giving his life in Vietnam.
On a summer afternoon, with families on the lawn and the skyline behind them, it's worth remembering whose name this place carries.
Walk south along Lake Shore Drive to Grand Avenue, then east to the long pier reaching out into the lake.
This is Navy Pier.
It opened in 1916 as Municipal Pier, part of Burnham's plan, and it stretches more than half a mile out into Lake Michigan.
It was built for lake shipping and passenger steamers, with warehouses on the pier and a recreation area at the end.
Look at the two towers at the far end and the domed auditorium, the Grand Ballroom, which are original.
The pier was renamed in 1927 to honor the Navy veterans of the First World War.
During the Second World War, it really did become a Navy base, a training center for thousands of sailors and aviation mechanics.

Out on the lake, the Navy converted two old paddle-wheel passenger steamers into aircraft carriers, the USS Wolverine and the USS Sable, and young pilots practiced landing on them, safely far from enemy submarines.
One of those pilots was a young George H. W. Bush.
Many planes went into the lake during training, and some have since been recovered and restored.
After the war, the University of Illinois opened a branch campus on the pier for returning veterans, nicknamed Harvard on the Rocks, until 1965.
The pier was redeveloped and reopened in 1995 as a public attraction, with a giant Ferris wheel.

That's fitting, because the very first Ferris wheel was built in Chicago, by the engineer George Washington Gale Ferris Junior, for the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893, as Chicago's answer to the Eiffel Tower.
Today's wheel was put up in 2016.
Ride it for one of the best views back toward the skyline you've just walked through.
Today, Navy Pier is one of the most visited attractions in the Midwest.
Along its length are a children's museum, the Chicago Shakespeare Theater, restaurants, and boat docks where you can catch an architecture tour or a cruise.
On summer nights there are fireworks over the lake.
Walk out to the very end, past the old Grand Ballroom, where the pier opens up to the lake, for a sense of how far out into the water it reaches.
This is the end of the Michigan Avenue and Streeterville tour.
In the warmer months, water taxis run from the pier to the river and to the Museum Campus.
The pier you're walking on was built to solve a very practical problem.
By the early 1900s, the Chicago River was choked.
Lake steamers carrying freight and passengers had to work their way up the narrow river to docks downtown, waiting for bridges to swing open, while the open bridges held up traffic in the streets.
The Plan of Chicago called for big piers out in the lake instead, where ships could dock in open water, and the city built one of them here.

Its architect, Charles Sumner Frost, had designed railroad terminals, and he gave the pier the logic of a station: long sheds for freight and passengers, ships tying up alongside, and two levels so that cargo could move on one and people on another.
Streetcars ran out along it.
At the far end, he put the things that would draw crowds: a domed hall for concerts and dances, places to eat, and open promenades over the water.
It opened in July 1916, and within two years it was pressed into service for war.
During the First World War, it held barracks for servicemen and even a jail for men who had dodged the draft.
Afterward it became a favorite summer escape, where Chicagoans came out by streetcar to catch the lake breeze, dance, and board excursion boats.
But it never became the shipping hub the planners imagined.
Freight moved to trucks and railroads, and the passenger steamers faded away.
After its years as a naval training station and a college campus, the pier sat half empty for decades.
It hosted trade shows and festivals, among them ChicagoFest, the giant music festival of the late 1970s and early 1980s, while the city argued about what to do with it.
The answer came in the 1990s, when a new public authority took it over and rebuilt it, and the pier that was built for freight became a place built for fun.
If you ever fly out of O'Hare Airport, look for an old Navy fighter plane on display in Terminal Two, a stubby Grumman Wildcat.
It's painted to honor the man the airport is named for.
But the plane itself came out of the lake, off this pier.
During the Second World War, as you heard, Navy pilots learned to land on two converted lake steamers out on Lake Michigan.
Not all of them made it, and well over a hundred planes ended up on the lake bottom, where the cold, fresh water preserved many of them remarkably well.
This Wildcat went down during training in the 1940s and lay on the lake bed for almost fifty years, until it was raised in 1992 and restored for the airport.
The man it honors, Edward O'Hare, known as Butch, grew up in St. Louis and graduated from the Naval Academy in Annapolis.
On February twentieth, 1942, flying from the carrier Lexington in the South Pacific, he found himself nearly alone between his ship and a formation of Japanese bombers.
In a few minutes of furious flying, he shot down or damaged several of them and broke up the attack.
He became the Navy's first ace of the war and received the Medal of Honor.
In November 1943, he disappeared during a night battle near the Gilbert Islands, at twenty-nine.
In 1949, Chicago renamed its new airport, Orchard Field, in his honor.
His father's story is darker.

Edward O'Hare senior, known as Easy Eddie, was a lawyer from St. Louis who ran dog tracks in partnership with Al Capone's organization, and he quietly helped federal agents build the tax case that sent Capone to prison.
In November 1939, a week before Capone was released, Easy Eddie was shot to death in his car.
A popular story says he turned informer to give his son a clean name and a place at Annapolis.
It's a moving story, but whether that was really his reason, no one can say for sure.
What is certain is that father and son both ended up as part of Chicago's story, one in the history of its gangsters, the other on its busiest airport.
Look up at the big wheel.
It's the second Ferris wheel to stand on Navy Pier, and the story of the two of them says a lot about how this place has changed.
The first one went up in 1995, when the pier reopened.
It was about a hundred and fifty feet tall, and it was said to be modeled on the original Ferris wheel from the World's Fair of 1893, which you can hear about on the Hyde Park tour.
For twenty years it turned here, and it became one of the most familiar sights on the lakefront, lit up at night against the dark water.
By the time the pier turned a hundred, in 2016, its managers wanted something bigger.
They took the old wheel down and sold it, and it was set up again in Branson, Missouri, for a new crowd of riders.
In its place went the Centennial Wheel, which opened in May 2016.

It's about a hundred and ninety-six feet tall, nearly fifty feet taller than the old one, and its forty-two gondolas are enclosed and climate controlled, with seats, so the wheel can keep turning through a Chicago winter.

From the top, you can see the whole route you've just walked: the Hancock and the Palmolive tower, the beaches and the high-rises of Streeterville, and to the south, the Loop, Grant Park, and the Museum Campus.
Out on the water, you may spot the cribs, and on the clearest days, the smokestacks of the Indiana shore, far across the bottom of the lake.
This tour explores the Gold Coast, the few blocks between Michigan Avenue and Lincoln Park that have been Chicago's richest neighborhood for more than a century.
It did not start that way.
After the Great Fire of 1871, the fashionable address in Chicago was Prairie Avenue, on the South Side, where the families of George Pullman, Marshall Field, and Philip Armour lived.
The land along the lake north of the river was swampy, sandy, and mostly empty.
The man who changed that was Potter Palmer.
He had made a fortune in dry goods, in a store that later became Marshall Field's, and then in real estate, transforming State Street into the city's main shopping street.
In the 1880s, he bought up the marshy land along the lake north of Oak Street, filled it, and built himself and his wife Bertha a turreted stone castle on the new Lake Shore Drive.
Where the Palmers went, society followed.
The value of the land around them soared, and Palmer made a second fortune selling it.
The Gold Coast that grew up here is a mix of styles.

You will see Romanesque mansions with heavy stone arches, French chateaux, Georgian Revival townhouses, and, sitting quietly among them, a house designed by Louis Sullivan and a young Frank Lloyd Wright that pointed toward a completely different future.
From the 1920s on, many mansions were torn down for elegant apartment towers, so the neighborhood is a layer cake of the Gilded Age and the twentieth century.

The Gold Coast has had its colorful side too: gangsters shooting it out in the street in the 1920s, anarchists and hoboes giving speeches in the park, celebrities in the Pump Room, and Hugh Hefner's first Playboy Mansion.
We will start at Holy Name Cathedral, south of the neighborhood proper, and walk north, ending at the edge of Lincoln Park.
You are at the corner of State Street and Superior Street, in front of Holy Name Cathedral, the seat of the Roman Catholic archbishop of Chicago.
The Gothic Revival church was designed by Patrick Keely and dedicated in 1875, after an earlier church was lost in the fire.
Chicago has one of the largest Catholic populations in the country, built from waves of Irish, German, Polish, Italian, and Mexican immigrants.
For much of the twentieth century, the city's politics and its parishes were tightly woven together, and Chicagoans still often answer the question of where they grew up by naming their parish.
In October 1926, this corner was the site of one of the most notorious killings of the Prohibition era.
Hymie Weiss, a leader of the North Side Gang and an enemy of Al Capone, was gunned down as he crossed State Street toward his headquarters above a flower shop, which stood across the street.
The gunmen fired from a window of a rooming house nearby.
Some of the bullets struck the front of the cathedral, and for years afterward, people pointed to marks on the cornerstone.
The church has since been renovated, but the story is part of the city's lore.
Look up at the cathedral's ceiling if you go inside.
Hanging high above the altar are several red hats, called galeros, which belonged to cardinals of Chicago.
By tradition, a cardinal's hat is hung from the ceiling of his cathedral after his death, and it stays there until it decays and falls, which is said to symbolize the passing of earthly glory.
Weiss wasn't the first gang leader to die on this corner.
His boss, Dean O'Banion, ran the North Side Gang from a flower shop across the street, Schofield's, where he arranged the elaborate floral tributes for gangland funerals.
In November 1924, three men came into the shop, one shook his hand and held on, and the others shot him.
The killing, widely blamed on Capone's organization, started the war in which Weiss and so many others died.
Gangsters went to mass here, too.
Holy Name has seen a great deal of Chicago's history, from the funerals of mayors to a visit from Pope John Paul the Second in 1979.
For more than twenty years, the man who led this cathedral did everything on a grand scale.
George Mundelein, a New Yorker of German descent, arrived as archbishop of Chicago in 1916, when he was only forty-three.
His welcome nearly killed him.
That February, the city's leading men gave him a banquet at the University Club downtown, with the governor of Illinois among the guests.
A cook in the club's kitchen, an anarchist named Jean Crones, had laced the soup with arsenic, and more than a hundred diners fell violently ill.
The new archbishop came through it unharmed.
The cook slipped away, and by most accounts he was never caught.
Mundelein went on to build as no Chicago churchman had before.
He built a great seminary, Saint Mary of the Lake, on farmland north of the city, in a village that soon renamed itself Mundelein in his honor.

In 1924 the pope made him a cardinal, and two years later he brought the International Eucharistic Congress to Chicago, the first time that great Catholic gathering had been held in the United States.
For several days in June 1926, the city was full of pilgrims.
Huge crowds filled Soldier Field for Mass, and on the last day, a crowd estimated in the hundreds of thousands, by some counts close to a million, traveled out to his new seminary.
He was outspoken, too.
He was a strong supporter of Franklin Roosevelt and the New Deal, and in 1937, speaking to his priests, he called Adolf Hitler an Austrian paperhanger, and a poor one at that.
The German government protested to the Vatican, and the Vatican stood by its cardinal.
He died in 1939.
A great deal of the Catholic Chicago you can still see, from the seminary's lakeside campus to churches and schools across the city and suburbs, was built in his time.
If Mundelein was the builder, Joseph Bernardin was the peacemaker, and the way he spent his last years here moved people far beyond his own church.
He was born in Columbia, South Carolina, in 1928, the son of Italian immigrants.
He became archbishop of Chicago in 1982 and a cardinal the following year.

He was known as a patient consensus builder, and he argued for what he called a consistent ethic of life, linking the church's opposition to abortion with opposition to the death penalty, to nuclear war, and to poverty.
Then, in November 1993, a former seminarian named Steven Cook filed a lawsuit accusing Bernardin of abusing him years before.
The cardinal denied it, calmly and in public, and within a few months Cook withdrew the claim, saying he could no longer trust memories that had surfaced under hypnosis.
What happened next is the part people remember.
At the end of 1994, Bernardin went to see his accuser.
Cook was dying of AIDS.
They met at a seminary outside Philadelphia, and Bernardin brought a Bible and a chalice.
He told Cook he forgave him, and the two men celebrated Mass together.
In 1995, Bernardin learned that he had pancreatic cancer.
He spent much of the time he had left visiting other people with cancer, and he wrote a short book about facing death, The Gift of Peace.
He finished it two weeks before he died, on November fourteenth, 1996.
His funeral was held here, in the cathedral he had led for fourteen years.

People of many faiths, and of none, mourned him, and the story of the cardinal and his accuser at the same altar is still told as one of the most remarkable acts of forgiveness in modern American religious life.
If the doors are open, step inside and look up.
The nave is covered by a vast wooden ceiling, made of thousands of carved and fitted pieces, some seventy feet above the floor.
It has had a hard time lately.
On February twelfth, 2008, a piece of it, a chunk of wood weighing about ten pounds, broke loose and fell all the way to the floor.
Engineers went up to inspect the ceiling, piece by piece, and found more than four thousand pieces that were loose or missing.
The cathedral closed for emergency repairs.

Crews restored the thirty-two columns that hold up the ceiling of the nave, and engineers added thirty-four steel tie rods, thirty of them hidden above the ceiling, to bind the old roof trusses and the ceiling together.
Later that year, the cathedral reopened.
Then, early on the morning of February fourth, 2009, fire broke out in the attic, in the dark space between that wooden ceiling and the roof.
Investigators traced it to a faulty system meant to melt ice along the roofline.
Firefighters stopped the fire before it could bring the ceiling down, but the roof was badly damaged, and the water used to fight the fire soaked the sanctuary.
Holy Name closed again, and it reopened that August.
So the ceiling above you has been taken apart, tied together, burned over, and soaked, and it's still there.
Look for the long rows of columns that carry it, and then look high above the altar for the red hats of Chicago's cardinals, which you heard about outside.
It's a reminder that a church this old is never really finished.
Every generation of Chicagoans who worship here inherits it, and has to keep it standing for the next.
Walk north on State Street and west on Walton Street to Washington Square Park.
The small square, laid out in the 1840s, is one of the oldest parks in the city.
On its north side stands the Newberry Library, a dark granite building in Spanish Romanesque style, completed in 1893 and designed by Henry Ives Cobb.

It was founded with money left by Walter Loomis Newberry, an early Chicago banker and land speculator, and it is a free, independent research library, with famous collections of maps, Native American history, and genealogy.
The park in front of it had a very different reputation.
For much of the twentieth century, it was known as Bughouse Square, bughouse being slang for an insane asylum.
From roughly the 1910s to the 1960s, it was the city's great outdoor free speech forum, where orators stood on soapboxes and argued with the crowd on any subject.
Socialists, anarchists, members of the radical union called the Industrial Workers of the World, religious preachers, poets, and cranks of all kinds spoke here.
The writer and activist Lucy Parsons, widow of one of the men executed after the Haymarket affair, spoke in this park.
Crowds came to heckle as much as to listen, and the heckling was part of the show.
The Newberry Library brings the tradition back each summer with the Bughouse Square Debates, where speakers once again climb onto soapboxes in the park.
The Newberry is a library for researchers, but anyone over high school age can get a reader's card and use it.

Its collections include one of the great libraries of maps in the country, the business archives of the Pullman Company and the Illinois Central Railroad, a huge collection on Native American history gathered by the collector Edward Ayer, and rare books and manuscripts going back to the Middle Ages.
It also has one of the largest genealogy collections in the country, and many visitors come to trace their families.
Just off the square, in a narrow alley called Tooker Place, was the Dill Pickle Club, a bohemian nightclub and forum that flourished from the late 1910s into the early 1930s.
Its door was painted with a sign telling visitors to step high, stoop low, and leave their dignity outside.
Writers like Carl Sandburg and Sherwood Anderson, the lawyer Clarence Darrow, radicals, poets, and curious society people all crowded in for lectures, debates, plays, and jazz.
One of the regulars was Ben Reitman, a doctor who treated the poor and was known as the King of the Hobos, and who was the manager and lover of the anarchist Emma Goldman.
The library in front of you exists because of a will, two short lives, and a long wait.
Walter Loomis Newberry came west from Connecticut and settled in Chicago in 1833, when it was still a muddy frontier town of a few hundred people.
He bought land on the North Side while it was cheap, and as the city grew over it, he became one of the richest men in Chicago, with interests in banking and railroads as well as real estate.
In 1868, on a voyage to France to join his wife and daughters, he died at sea.
There's an old Chicago story, told for generations and impossible to prove, that his body came home preserved in a cask of rum, and that he was buried at Graceland Cemetery still inside it.
His will provided for his family, but it had an unusual condition.
If his two daughters died without children of their own, his estate was to found a free public library on the North Side.
Both daughters died young, in 1874 and 1876.
After his widow died in 1885, the trustees set to work, and on July first, 1887, the Newberry Library was founded, with an estate worth more than two million dollars.
The trustees hired as librarian William Frederick Poole, who had built the Chicago Public Library from scratch after the Great Fire.

Since the city already had a public library for borrowing books, the Newberry became something else: a free library where anyone with a serious question could come and read, but where the books never leave the building.
That's still how it works.

You can't take anything home, but with a reader's card, the collections are yours to use, more than a century after a banker's daughters died without heirs and left their father's fortune to the city.
You can't see them from the park, but some extraordinary things are kept inside that granite building.
The Newberry's most requested treasure is a modest-looking handwritten book from around 1700.
It holds the oldest known copy of the Popol Vuh, the sacred story of the K'iche' Maya people of Guatemala.
A Dominican priest named Francisco Ximénez wrote it out in the K'iche' language, with a Spanish translation running beside it.

Without his copy, the story might have been lost: how the gods tried to make people from mud, and then from wood, before they succeeded with maize, and how a pair of hero twins outwitted the lords of the underworld in a deadly ball game.
It came to Chicago with Edward Ayer, a businessman who made his fortune in lumber and spent much of it collecting books and documents about the Native peoples of the Americas.
He began giving his collection to the Newberry in 1911.
The vaults also hold the only copy in Chicago of Shakespeare's First Folio, the collected plays published in 1623, seven years after his death.
About half of his plays had never been printed before it, so without this book we might have lost Macbeth, The Tempest, and Twelfth Night.
The Newberry's copy has notes scribbled in its margins by earlier owners.

And there are Chicago treasures here too: the drawings of Oswald Cooper, a Chicago lettering artist, for Cooper Black, the soft, chunky typeface of the 1920s that later turned up on countless record covers and storefront signs, and the archives of Mister Kelly's, the Rush Street nightclub you'll hear about at the next stop.
The library shows some of its treasures in free exhibitions, and it has put a great deal of its collection online, including every page of the Popol Vuh.
Of all the speakers who climbed onto soapboxes in this park, few had a life as dramatic as Lucy Parsons.
Even her beginnings are uncertain.
She was born around 1851, in Texas or perhaps Virginia, and historians believe she was very likely born into slavery, though she herself spoke instead of Mexican and Native American ancestry.

In Texas in the early 1870s, she married Albert Parsons, a former Confederate soldier who had become a Radical Republican, and the couple, facing hostility over their marriage across the color line, moved to Chicago.
Here they became leaders of the anarchist labor movement, organizing workers and campaigning for the eight-hour day.
After the Haymarket bombing in 1886, Albert was among the men convicted and hanged.
Lucy spent the rest of her life defending his memory and attacking the system that had killed him.
She traveled the country speaking and writing, and the police broke up her meetings and arrested her again and again.
A Chicago police official is said to have called her more dangerous than a thousand rioters.
In June 1905, she was one of the few women among the delegates who gathered in Chicago to found the Industrial Workers of the World, the radical union whose members later spoke in this very park.
She kept speaking into old age, and for years she was one of the best-known voices at Bughouse Square.
She died on March seventh, 1942, in a fire at her home.
Afterward, the authorities came and took away her library of books and her personal papers, and they were never returned.

Her life was, in a way, the whole story of this park: the conviction that ordinary people had the right to stand up in public and say what they believed, however unpopular, and the long effort of the powerful to make them stop.
Walk north on Dearborn or State Parkway to Goethe Street.
At the corner of State Parkway and Goethe stands a hotel that was long known as the Ambassador East.

It was the home of the Pump Room, a restaurant named for the famous Pump Room in the English spa town of Bath, which opened in 1938 and became the place where celebrities stopped on their journeys between New York and Los Angeles.
Trains between the coasts changed in Chicago, and stars often spent a night here between trains.
The most coveted seat was called Booth One, where Humphrey Bogart, Lauren Bacall, Judy Garland, and many other stars posed for photographs.
Now walk a few steps north to number 1340 North State Parkway, the large red brick and limestone mansion on the east side of the street.
This was the original Playboy Mansion.
Hugh Hefner, who was born in Chicago and started Playboy magazine in 1953, bought it in 1959.
He lived here and threw famous parties, with a pool, a bowling alley, and a brass plate on the door with a Latin motto that roughly translated as: if you don't swing, don't ring.
Playboy was a Chicago company, and for years it was one of the most visible in the city, with its giant sign on the Palmolive Building and its Playboy Clubs.

Hefner moved to Los Angeles in the 1970s, and the mansion was later donated to the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, which used it as a dormitory before it was sold and turned into condominiums.
Look along this stretch of State Parkway, and you'll see some of the grandest townhouses in the city.
A few blocks east of here, along Rush Street and Division Street, is the Gold Coast's nightlife district, a strip of bars, steakhouses, and clubs that has been busy since the 1950s.
In those years Rush Street was a famous entertainment strip, with jazz clubs and supper clubs where rising performers played.
One of them, Mister Kelly's, gave early stages to comedians and singers who went on to become stars, including a young Barbra Streisand.
Today the area around Rush and Oak Streets is full of steakhouses and hotel bars, and its triangle of outdoor patios is a people-watching spot on summer evenings.
The Pump Room was the creation of Ernie Byfield, a Chicago hotel man with a gift for theater.
It opened on October first, 1938, in the Ambassador East, and from the start it was as much a show as a restaurant.
Byfield loved fire.

Waiters carried dishes to the tables in flames or set them alight right beside you, and the Pump Room is often credited with helping start the craze for flaming food that swept American restaurants after the Second World War.
Byfield is said to have joked that the whole effect was like Halloween in hell.
The real show was in the corner: Booth One, a cream-colored leather booth where the most famous guest in the house was seated, in full view of everyone else.
For years, a headwaiter named Arturo Petterino decided who got it, steering the stars into the corner and everyone else to tables where they could watch them.
Byfield died in 1950, but the Pump Room carried on for decades.
What finally dimmed it wasn't the food.
It was the jet plane.
Once stars could fly from coast to coast in an afternoon, they no longer had to spend a night in Chicago between trains, and the parade of celebrities thinned out.
The Pump Room lived on through new owners and makeovers.
After the hotel changed hands and was renamed, a restaurant called Booth One took its place for a couple of years, from 2017 until 2019.

Today you have to imagine it: the clink of glasses, the flash of a photographer's bulb, the waiter crossing the room with dinner on fire, and every head turning toward the corner to see who had been given Booth One.
Mister Kelly's opened on Rush Street in November 1953, at first as a restaurant, and within a year it had a stage.
It was run by two brothers, George and Oscar Marienthal, who also ran the London House, a jazz supper club downtown, and later a theater called the Happy Medium.
The name came from the club's first manager, Pat Kelly, with the Mister added, the story goes, for a touch of class.
The room was small and intimate, and the brothers had a knack for booking performers just before the rest of the country discovered them.
Barbra Streisand you've heard about.
Sarah Vaughan recorded a live album there in 1957.
Ella Fitzgerald sang there.
Comedians from Lenny Bruce to Richard Pryor worked out their acts in front of its audiences, and a young Maya Angelou, long before she was famous as a writer, sang calypso there.
In the last week of 1969, Dizzy Gillespie played the room.
In 1956, the brothers even put their clubs on television, in a music show broadcast in color on Chicago's NBC station, a rare thing at the time.
Oscar Marienthal died in 1963 and George in 1972, and Mister Kelly's closed in 1975, the same year as the London House.
Tastes had changed, and the great age of the supper club was over.
But the club's memory is in good hands.

Its records, photographs, and contracts are at the Newberry Library, which you just passed, and in 2024 the library mounted an exhibition about the club, its owners, and the performers who got their start on its little stage.
For a few years in the 1950s and 1960s, if you wanted to see who was going to be famous next, a narrow room off Rush Street was the place to be.
The house at thirteen forty North State Parkway is older and more respectable than its reputation.
It was built in 1899 for a surgeon, Dr. George Isham, and designed by James Gamble Rogers, the architect who later gave Northwestern its Gothic campus near the lake and gave Yale much of its look.
In 1959, the year he bought the house, Hugh Hefner also went on television.

His show, Playboy's Penthouse, was taped in a Chicago studio and set in a make-believe bachelor apartment, where guests drifted around with drinks in their hands while musicians and comedians performed as if at a party.
It went on the air in October 1959 and ran in syndication for two seasons.
The guest list on the first night included Nat King Cole, Ella Fitzgerald, the comedian Lenny Bruce, the songwriter Cy Coleman, and the novelist Rona Jaffe.
What made the show unusual was that Black and white guests mingled as equals, sitting together, talking, and laughing, at a party broadcast on American television in 1959.
Hefner said later that because of it, no stations in the Deep South would carry the show.
For the musicians, it was a rare chance to be seen at ease, talking with the host and the other guests, instead of performing one number and leaving the stage.
Some of the episodes survive, and they're a remarkable record of jazz and comedy at the end of the 1950s.
A decade later, Hefner revived the idea in Los Angeles with a new show, Playboy After Dark.
By then he was spending more and more of his time in California, and in the 1970s he moved there for good.
But the formula, the magazine, the clubs, and the television party, had all been worked out here in Chicago, many of them behind the doors of this house.
Walk east to Astor Street, a quiet, tree-lined street named after the fur baron John Jacob Astor, as if to borrow some New York money for Chicago.
It is one of the best preserved streets of mansions in the city.
Walk to number 1365 North Astor.
The house on the corner of Schiller Street looks deceptively simple compared to its neighbors: a cube of thin Roman brick on a stone base, with a balcony in the middle of the front.
This is the Charnley-Persky House, built in the early 1890s for James Charnley, a lumber businessman, by the firm of Adler and Sullivan.
The young draftsman who worked on it was Frank Lloyd Wright, then in his twenties, who would later claim a large share of the credit for it.

Whoever deserves it, historians often point to this house as an early sign of what would become modern American architecture: clean, horizontal lines, unbroken surfaces, ornament limited to a few rich places like the balcony.
Compare it to the heavy, picturesque Romanesque and Queen Anne mansions around it, built at the same time.
The house is now the headquarters of the Society of Architectural Historians, which offers tours.
As you walk along Astor Street, look for a few other gems.
At 1444 North Astor is an Art Deco townhouse, called the Russell House, designed by Holabird and Root in 1929.
And look for the Patterson-McCormick Mansion at 20 East Burton Place, a huge palazzo of brick and terra cotta by Stanford White of New York, built for a family that controlled the Chicago Tribune.
James Charnley and Louis Sullivan were friends as well as client and architect, and around 1890 they did something together that tells you a lot about the house in front of you.
They bought neighboring lots on the Mississippi Gulf Coast, at Ocean Springs, and built vacation cottages side by side among the pines and live oaks above the water.
Sullivan's firm designed both, and like this house, they're usually seen as collaborations between Sullivan and his young draftsman, Frank Lloyd Wright.
They were simple wooden houses with broad porches for the southern heat, a long way from the castles and chateaux the rich were building elsewhere.
Sullivan loved his place there, and for years he escaped to it in the winter.
For a man who spent his working life in Chicago's noise and smoke, it was a kind of paradise, and he wrote about it fondly long afterward.
In 2005, Hurricane Katrina struck the coast.
Sullivan's cottage was destroyed, and the Charnleys' was badly damaged.
It was painstakingly restored, in work finished in 2013, and you can visit it today.
The Chicago house had its own rescue.
In 1995, a philanthropist named Seymour Persky bought it and gave it to the Society of Architectural Historians for its headquarters.
That's why it carries two names: Charnley for the family that built it, and Persky for the man who made sure the public could go inside.

When you look at the house, then, think of it as one of a family: a city house and two cottages by the sea, all designed in the same few years by the same two restless young minds, one of them about to become the most famous architect in America.
Walk a couple of blocks north to Burton Place and look at the big palazzo of brick and terra cotta on the corner.

It was built in the early 1890s by Stanford White, the star New York architect, for Elinor Medill Patterson, a daughter of Joseph Medill, the great editor of the Chicago Tribune, and her husband, Robert Patterson, who worked at the Tribune and later ran it.
The Medill newspaper money produced two remarkable grandchildren, and they both grew up in the Pattersons' world.
Their son, Joseph Medill Patterson, helped run the Tribune and then, in 1919, started a new kind of paper in New York, a tabloid full of photographs, crime, and scandal, called the Daily News.
Within a few years it had the largest circulation of any newspaper in America.
Their daughter, Eleanor, known as Cissy, was even more colorful.

After an unhappy marriage to a Polish count, she went to work for William Randolph Hearst's newspapers in Washington, bought them, and merged them into the Washington Times-Herald, making her one of the first women to run a major American daily.
Their cousin, Robert McCormick, ran the Tribune itself, as you may have heard on the river tour.
After Robert Patterson died in 1910, the house was sold to Cyrus McCormick Junior, the head of International Harvester and son of the inventor of the reaper.
It stayed in the family's wider circle, since Elinor's sister had married into the McCormick clan.
In 1927, the society architect David Adler added a wing at the back that roughly doubled the size of the house, and in 1978 it was divided into condominiums.
For a few decades, though, this one house was home to the family behind three of the best-known newspapers in the country.
Across State Parkway from the Patterson-McCormick mansion, on the corner of Burton Place, is a house that makes a perfect companion to the Charnley House.
It was built in 1902 for Albert and Elsa Madlener, and designed by the architect Richard Schmidt, working with his gifted designer, Hugh Garden.
Schmidt had worked with Louis Sullivan early in his career, and you can see the influence.
Like the Charnley House, it's essentially a cube, of brick on a stone base, calm and almost severe beside the turrets and gables of its neighbors.
And like the Charnley House, it saves its richness for a few chosen places.
Look at the doorway, framed in intricate ornament, and at the way the windows are grouped and set into the wall.
It's a building on the hinge between two ideas.

It still has the formal symmetry of an old-fashioned mansion, but its plain walls and flat horizontal lines point toward the Prairie School houses that Wright and his circle were beginning to build in Oak Park and on the South Side.
The house became a Chicago landmark in 1973.
For decades it has been the home of the Graham Foundation, founded in 1956 with money left by Ernest Graham, who ran Daniel Burnham's firm after Burnham's death.
His firm, Graham, Anderson, Probst and White, designed the Wrigley Building, Union Station, and the Merchandise Mart.
The foundation gives grants to architects and writers on architecture, and it holds exhibitions in the house that you can usually visit for free.

So in a few blocks, you can see the whole argument of the Gold Coast: the mansions that dressed up as European palaces, and these two quiet boxes that asked what an American house should look like instead.
Walk east to Lake Shore Drive, and look at the apartment towers between Banks Street and Schiller Street.
This is the site of the house that created the Gold Coast: the Palmer castle, at 1350 North Lake Shore Drive.
Potter Palmer built it in the early 1880s.
It was a fantasy of a castle in brown stone, with turrets and an eighty-foot tower, and supposedly no outside doorknobs, so that no one could enter unless a servant opened the door from inside.
The Palmers held court here for decades.
Bertha Honoré Palmer was as formidable as her husband.
In 1893 she was president of the Board of Lady Managers of the World's Columbian Exposition, responsible for the Woman's Building.
She was also an early and passionate collector of French Impressionist paintings, buying works by Monet, Renoir, and Degas when they were still controversial.
Many of the paintings she collected are now at the Art Institute of Chicago, and they're one of the reasons its Impressionist collection is among the best in the world.
Potter Palmer is also remembered for the Palmer House hotel downtown.
The first one opened shortly before the Great Fire and burned less than two weeks later.
He rebuilt immediately, promising a fireproof hotel, and the Palmer House still stands on State Street.
The hotel's kitchen is often credited with inventing the chocolate brownie for the 1893 fair, which Bertha is said to have requested as a portable dessert for fairgoers.
That's a story the hotel tells, and it's a good one.
The castle itself was torn down in 1950 and replaced with these apartment buildings, which is a pattern repeated up and down the drive.
