The Palmers' castle was designed by two young architects in their twenties, Henry Ives Cobb and Charles Sumner Frost, and both names turn up elsewhere on these walks.
Cobb went on to design the Newberry Library and the first buildings of the University of Chicago.
Frost went on to design Navy Pier.
The castle took from 1882 to 1885 to build and cost at least a million dollars, at a time when a comfortable family house cost a few thousand.
Inside, it was a stage set for entertaining, with grand reception rooms where Bertha Palmer received Chicago society and a parade of famous visitors.
Her family was well connected.
Her sister Ida had married Frederick Dent Grant, a son of President Ulysses Grant.
During the World's Fair of 1893, the Palmers entertained royalty.
The Infanta Eulalia of Spain, an aunt of the young Spanish king, came to see the fair, and the Palmers gave a grand party in her honor.
The princess, the story goes, had been heard to sniff that she would not be received by an innkeeper's wife, a jab at the Palmer House hotel.
Chicago took the insult personally, and the gossip outlived the visit by many years.
After the Palmers were gone, the castle became too big and too costly for anyone to want.
It passed through other hands, sat empty for years, and came down, as you heard, in 1950.
What survives of it is mostly paper: photographs, floor plans, and descriptions in old society pages.

But stand here and imagine it, a dark stone fortress on the lakefront, with lamps burning in its windows and carriages lining up along the drive, and you'll understand how one house could pull a whole neighborhood toward it.
When the World's Fair opened in 1893, Bertha Palmer, as you heard, was at the head of the women who ran its Woman's Building, and she meant to make that building a statement.
The building itself was designed by a young architect named Sophia Hayden, the first woman to graduate in architecture from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Inside were exhibits of women's work from around the world.

At the dedication ceremonies for the fair, the autumn before it opened, Bertha Palmer gave a speech with a line that was widely quoted: even more important than the discovery of Columbus, she said, was the fact that the government had just discovered woman.
For the building's great hall, she wanted murals, and she persuaded Mary Cassatt, the American painter who lived in France and showed with the Impressionists, to paint one.
Cassatt's mural, called Modern Woman, was enormous, nearly sixty feet long and more than twelve feet high, and it hung high on the wall.
Its center showed young women in modern dress picking fruit from the tree of knowledge.
The side panels showed girls chasing fame and women making music and dancing.
Facing it, at the other end of the hall, was a companion mural, Primitive Woman, by another American painter, Mary MacMonnies.
The reviews were mixed.
After the fair, the Woman's Building came down like most of the others, and the mural was taken away.
It was last recorded in 1912, and then it simply vanished.
No one knows whether it was destroyed or is rolled up in some forgotten storeroom.
The only color image of it is a reproduction printed in a book about the fair.
In 2026, the Art Institute told its story in a major Cassatt exhibition.
It remains one of the great lost artworks of Chicago, commissioned by the woman who lived on this spot.
Potter Palmer died in 1902 and left his fortune to Bertha.
There's a story that when his lawyer warned that she might marry again, Palmer replied that if she did, her second husband would need the money.
Whether he really said it or not, she never remarried, and she proved perfectly able to manage what he left her.
In 1910, when she was about sixty, she went to look at a sleepy town on the west coast of Florida called Sarasota.
She had seen it advertised, the story goes, in a Chicago newspaper.
She liked it so much that she began buying land, and within a few years she owned more than eighty thousand acres in and around the town.
She ran it like a business.

On one stretch she started a cattle ranch called Meadowsweet Pastures, and she brought new methods to Florida ranching, fencing her herds in and dipping the cattle in vats to kill the ticks that spread disease.
She experimented with crops, built roads, and sold land to settlers, and her name drew other wealthy northerners to the area.
For herself, she made a winter estate on the bay at Osprey Point, with gardens that are still preserved as part of a historic site.
She died in 1918.

Years later, much of her ranch land became Myakka River State Park, one of the oldest and largest state parks in Florida, where alligators bask along the river and the old Florida landscape she knew is still protected.
Sarasota remembers her as one of the founders of the modern city.

The woman who made a Chicago castle the center of society ended her life as one of the largest landowners on the Gulf Coast of Florida, and in many ways she was the more remarkable businessperson of the two Palmers.
Walk north along Lake Shore Drive to number 1524, a limestone mansion with a columned facade facing the lake.
It's one of the very few mansions left on this stretch of the drive, which was once lined with them.
It was built in 1917 for Eleanor Robinson Countiss, the daughter of a wealthy Chicago family, and designed by Howard Van Doren Shaw, one of the favorite architects of Chicago's rich.
Shaw modeled it on the Petit Trianon, the small palace built for Marie Antoinette at Versailles.
Since the 1950s, the house has held one of the strangest museums in Chicago: the International Museum of Surgical Science, founded by the International College of Surgeons.

Inside the elegant rooms are four floors of the history of medicine: ancient skulls with holes drilled in them by prehistoric surgeons, sets of amputation saws, early X-ray machines, an iron lung, and paintings and sculptures of famous moments in medicine.
Some of it is grisly.
All of it is fascinating, and you can see the mansion's original paneling, staircases, and fireplaces as you go.
Look up and down Lake Shore Drive at the high-rise apartments that replaced the mansions.
By the 1920s, the rich were already moving into luxury apartment buildings, which were easier to run than a house full of servants, and the drive filled with cooperatives.
Many of the most famous, like the ones at 1500 and 999 Lake Shore Drive, have apartments of a dozen rooms or more on a single floor, with views straight out over the lake.
The museum in this mansion grew out of one Chicago surgeon's very big idea.
Max Thorek was born in Hungary in 1880 and came to Chicago with his family in 1897, as a teenager without much money.
He was determined to become a doctor, and according to the museum's own telling, he learned to play the drums so that he could join the university band and help pay his way.
He earned his medical degree in 1904, and a few years later, with another young doctor, Solomon Greenspahn, he founded the American Hospital on the North Side.
It later took his name, and today it's Thorek Memorial Hospital.
He was a surgeon with ambitions far beyond his own operating room.

He wrote textbooks and a lively autobiography, A Surgeon's World, and in 1935 he founded the International College of Surgeons, in Geneva, Switzerland, to bring surgeons from many countries together at a time when the world was drifting toward war.
The college made its headquarters here in Chicago, in a mansion on this same stretch of Lake Shore Drive.
The college began collecting: old surgical instruments, paintings, books, and manuscripts, meant at first for a hall of fame honoring surgery's heroes.
Members and friends sent objects from around the world, and on September ninth, 1954, the collection opened to the public as this museum.
One of the first exhibits was the Hall of Immortals, a gallery of twelve large stone statues of great figures from the history of medicine.
Thorek died in 1960.

He left behind a hospital, a worldwide society of surgeons, and this odd and wonderful museum, which still surprises nearly everyone who walks through its elegant front door expecting just another old mansion.
Howard Van Doren Shaw, who designed this mansion, was the architect Chicago's rich families called when they wanted a house that looked like old money.
He was born in Chicago in 1869, studied at Yale and then studied architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and opened his own practice in the 1890s.
Most of his work was houses: great country houses in Lake Forest and along the North Shore, and city houses like this one, in English, Italian, and French styles, always beautifully built.
His own house was more personal.
In 1897 he built Ragdale, a rambling Arts and Crafts summer home in Lake Forest.
It stayed in his family, and since the 1970s it has been a retreat where writers and artists come to work.
In Lake Forest he also designed Market Square, finished in 1916, a little town center of shops and offices arranged around a green, built with a developer named Arthur Aldis.
It's often described as one of the first planned shopping centers in America, and it still looks like a village square from an English novel.

You may have met his work elsewhere on these walks: the old Lakeside Press building for the printer R. R. Donnelley, in the South Loop, and the parish buildings around the courtyard of Fourth Presbyterian Church on Michigan Avenue.
He died in 1926, still in his fifties.

His daughter, Sylvia Shaw Judson, became a sculptor, and one of her pieces, a small bronze of a girl holding up two bowls, became famous decades later as the Bird Girl, the statue on the cover of the bestselling book Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil.
Talent, it seems, ran in the family, and it ran from grand houses to a little girl in a Savannah cemetery.
Among the strangest things in the museum are the skulls with holes cut in them.
They're evidence of the oldest surgery we know of, and the story they tell is more hopeful than you might expect.
The operation is called trepanation: cutting, scraping, or drilling an opening through the skull of a living person.
People were doing it thousands of years before anyone wrote anything down.

Skulls with these openings have been found at Stone Age burial sites across Europe and in many other parts of the world, and some of the most remarkable come from ancient Peru, where surgeons of the Inca and earlier peoples performed the operation often.
How do we know the patients lived?
Bone heals.
When someone survived for months or years after the operation, the edges of the opening grew smooth and rounded with new bone.
Studies of skulls from Peru suggest that by Inca times, a large majority of patients survived.
Over the centuries, the surgeons seem to have learned which cuts were safest.
Why did they do it?
Some patients had head wounds, perhaps from clubs or sling stones, and opening the skull may have relieved pressure or removed broken bone.
Others may have been treated for headaches, seizures, or illnesses of the mind, or for reasons we can only guess at, such as letting out an evil spirit.
The idea never completely disappeared.

Surgeons in Europe were still opening skulls to treat head injuries in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and modern neurosurgeons do it too, with far better tools, for some of the same reasons.
So as you look at those skulls, think of the patients who walked away from those operations, thousands of years before anesthesia or antiseptics, and lived long enough for their bones to heal.
Walk north and west to the corner of North Avenue and State Parkway.
The large red brick mansion surrounded by a lawn, with a remarkable roof crowded with chimneys, is the Archbishop's Residence, built around 1880.
Count the chimneys if you can.
There are said to be nineteen of them.
It was built when this area was at the very northern edge of the city, next to a cemetery that was later moved to create Lincoln Park.
The Queen Anne style residence was the home of Chicago's Catholic archbishops for more than a century, and visiting dignitaries stayed here, including Pope John Paul the Second, in 1979.

The Gold Coast you have just walked was built by the wealth of a single generation of Chicagoans, the merchants, meatpackers, railroad men, and real estate speculators who rebuilt the city after the fire.
Their mansions show what they wanted to be seen as: European aristocrats.
The houses designed by Sullivan, Wright, and Mies just a few blocks away show the other side of the city: a place that wanted to invent something new.
Look north, across North Avenue.
That's Lincoln Park, the city's largest park, and the Lincoln Park tour starts just across the street, at the Chicago History Museum.
This is the end of the Gold Coast tour.
The man who built this house was Patrick Feehan, Chicago's first archbishop.
He was born in Ireland, in County Tipperary, in 1829, and came to America as a young priest in the early 1850s to serve in Saint Louis.
He spent fifteen years as bishop of Nashville, and in 1880, when the pope raised Chicago to an archdiocese, Feehan was chosen to lead it.
His Chicago was a city of immigrants, and his great challenge was keeping them together in one church.
Germans, Poles, Bohemians, Italians, Lithuanians, and others each wanted priests who spoke their language and churches built in the style of home.

Feehan generally let them have them, allowing what were called national parishes, so that a Polish family and an Irish family living on the same street might belong to different parishes, a few blocks apart.
Under him, the number of parishes and Catholic schools in the archdiocese grew enormously.
In 1885, he built this residence, on what was then the quiet northern edge of the settled city, beside the old cemetery that was becoming Lincoln Park.
Before that, the bishops of Chicago had lived in a house a few blocks west, at LaSalle Street and North Avenue.
He died in 1902.
Every archbishop of Chicago after him lived in this house, with its nineteen chimneys, for well over a century, until one of them decided not to.
In the fall of 2014, a new archbishop arrived in Chicago, Blase Cupich, and he made an announcement that surprised a lot of people: he would not live in this mansion.
He moved instead into the rectory at Holy Name Cathedral, where you started this tour, living alongside the parish priests.
He was following the example of Pope Francis, who after his election the year before had chosen to live in a Vatican guesthouse instead of the grand papal apartments.
The residence stayed in use for official events and to house important guests, but in 2019 the archdiocese said it was considering selling it.

Like many dioceses, the church in Chicago has been closing and merging parishes as congregations shrink, and the cost of keeping up a mansion of this size, with all those chimneys, is hard to justify.

Whatever becomes of it, the house tells a story about how the church once saw itself in this city: a powerful institution, with a palace for its leader on the most fashionable edge of town, grand enough for a pope to stay in.
The choice to leave it tells a story too, about a church trying to look less like a power and more like a neighbor.
Stand on the sidewalk and look at it for a moment.
Few buildings in Chicago carry as much history so quietly, and few have outlived the world they were built for so completely.
Those nineteen chimneys weren't only decoration.
When this house was built, fireplaces were still part of how a big house was heated and how its rooms were judged.
Even in homes with furnaces, every important room had a fireplace of its own, and every fireplace needed its own flue to carry the smoke up and out.
A grand house meant many fires, and many fires meant many chimneys.
Keeping them going was hard work.
Servants carried coal and wood up from the basement, tended the fires, and hauled the ashes back down, all winter long.
As steam and hot water heating spread in the following decades, the forest of chimneys on houses like this one began to look old-fashioned.
The architects of the 1880s turned the necessity into ornament.
In the Queen Anne style, chimneys were made tall and decorative, often grouped in clusters and built of patterned brick, and they helped give a house its lively, irregular skyline.
Look at the roof as a whole: steep slopes meeting at different angles, gables and dormers popping out, very little quite symmetrical.
That restless outline was the point.
A Queen Anne house was meant to look as if it had grown over time, like an old English manor added to by generations.
Now think back to the Charnley House and the Madlener House, built only a few years later.
Their outlines are calm and boxlike, with no parade of chimneys and gables.
In less than twenty years, the most adventurous architects in Chicago had moved from a skyline of chimneys and gables to the plain, clean block.
You can see both ideas on this one short walk.
This short tour explores Old Town, a small neighborhood of narrow streets and old cottages just west of Lincoln Park, around the crossing of North Avenue and Wells Street.
In the 1850s and 1860s, this was the northern edge of Chicago, and it was settled largely by German immigrants.
Many of them were truck farmers who grew vegetables for the city's markets, and the area was nicknamed the Cabbage Patch.
The heart of the community was a German Catholic parish, Saint Michael's, which still towers over the neighborhood.
In October 1871, the Great Fire burned all the way up here.
Nearly everything was lost, except for the shell of Saint Michael's Church.
The residents rebuilt quickly, many of them in small, modest cottages on narrow lots, and a lot of those cottages are still here, which gives the neighborhood its intimate, village-like scale.
The neighborhood went through hard times in the early twentieth century, and then in the 1950s and 1960s, it was rediscovered.
Artists, writers, and young people moved into the cheap old houses.
Wells Street became a strip of coffee houses, folk clubs, bars, and head shops, Chicago's answer to Greenwich Village and Haight-Ashbury.
The name Old Town itself was popularized by an art fair, the Old Town Art Fair, which started in 1950 and is still held every June.
Two institutions that came out of that era are world famous: the Second City comedy theater, which opened in 1959, and the Old Town School of Folk Music, which opened in 1957.
We'll visit the first and pass where the second began.
We will start at the Moody Church, at Clark Street and North Avenue, walk west to Wells Street, wind through the Old Town Triangle, and finish at Saint Michael's and the Buddhist temple beside it.
You're at the corner of Clark Street and North Avenue, beside a massive brick church with arched windows and a broad, tiled roof, in a style inspired by the early churches of Byzantium and Italy.
This is the Moody Church, completed in 1925.
Its sanctuary seats close to four thousand people, which made it one of the largest Protestant churches in America.
It's named for Dwight L. Moody, one of the most famous preachers of the nineteenth century.
Moody came to Chicago from Massachusetts in 1856, at nineteen, to sell shoes.
He was a born salesman, and he soon turned his talents to religion, gathering poor children from the streets of the North Side into a Sunday school that grew into a church.
After the Great Fire destroyed it, he rebuilt, and then he and the gospel singer Ira Sankey went on preaching tours of Britain and America that drew enormous crowds.
He was, in a sense, the first modern mass evangelist.
In 1886, Moody founded a school to train ordinary men and women as missionaries and Bible teachers.
It became the Moody Bible Institute, which is still in the Near North Side, and which started one of the first Christian radio stations in the country in the 1920s.
The church that bears his name has been here since 1925.
Chicago's history is full of businessmen like Moody who brought the same energy to religion and reform that others brought to grain and steel.
As you walk west along North Avenue, you're entering the old German North Side.
You heard that Moody toured with the gospel singer Ira Sankey.
The two met in 1870, at a convention of the Young Men's Christian Association in Indianapolis.
Sankey was a big, genial man from western Pennsylvania who worked in the federal tax office back home in New Castle.
As the story is usually told, the singing at an early morning prayer meeting was dragging, and someone asked Sankey to start a hymn.
Afterward Moody came over, asked him a few questions, and told him he would have to give up his job and come to Chicago, because he had been looking for him for eight years.
Sankey took about six months to make up his mind.
His gift was making a simple song carry.
He sang solos at a small reed organ, slowly and clearly, so that every word reached the back of a hall holding thousands.
Moody preached, and Sankey sang the message home.
The most famous story about him comes from Scotland, in 1874.
On a train to Edinburgh, Sankey found a poem in a newspaper about a shepherd who leaves his ninety-nine sheep to search for the one that strayed, and he clipped it out.
A day or two later, at a meeting in Edinburgh, Moody preached on the Good Shepherd and turned to Sankey for a closing song.
Sankey had nothing ready, so he set the clipping on his organ, struck a chord, and made up the tune as he sang.
That's the story Sankey told, and The Ninety and Nine became one of the best-loved gospel songs of the age.
But an account published in 1876 says the tune was written beforehand.
Students of hymns point out that the first printed version uses only three chords, which is just what you'd expect from a melody invented on the spot.
Their songbooks sold by the hundreds of thousands.
Sankey gave his royalties away, in later years to the schools Moody founded in Massachusetts.
He spent his last years blind, and he died at his home in Brooklyn in 1908.
In the years after Moody's death, the title of America's most famous evangelist passed to a man Chicago had first cheered as a ballplayer.
Billy Sunday grew up poor in Iowa.
His father, a Union soldier, died in the Civil War when Billy was a baby, and the boy spent part of his childhood in orphans' homes.
He was fast, fast enough that in 1883 the Chicago White Stockings, the team that later became the Cubs, signed him as an outfielder.
He was never much of a hitter, but crowds loved to watch him run.

One night in 1886, as he told it, he was sitting on a curb on Van Buren Street with some teammates after an evening of drinking, when a band from the Pacific Garden Mission came by, playing hymns his mother used to sing.
He followed it inside, and soon he was converted.
He played a few more seasons, but in 1891 he gave up baseball for a job with the Young Men's Christian Association in Chicago, at a fraction of the pay.
He learned the revival business as an advance man for a traveling preacher, and then struck out on his own.
From the early 1900s through the First World War, Sunday preached to enormous crowds in temporary wooden tabernacles with sawdust spread on the floors.
When he called sinners forward, they walked down the sawdust aisles, and hitting the sawdust trail became an American expression for getting saved.
His preaching was pure theater.
He leapt onto chairs and slid across the platform like a runner stealing second.
He was one of the loudest voices for Prohibition, and his sermon against liquor, known simply as Booze, was famous.
Chicago never quite surrendered to him.
In 1922, the songwriter Fred Fisher published Chicago, That Toddlin' Town, which calls it the town that Billy Sunday could not shut down.
Sunday died in Chicago in November 1935.
He is buried in Forest Home Cemetery, in the western suburb of Forest Park, not far from the monument to the anarchists of the Haymarket affair.
Moody had little formal schooling, and his grammar was famously rough, but he started schools wherever he went.
In 1879, in his hometown of Northfield, Massachusetts, he opened a seminary for girls, and two years later, across the Connecticut River, a school for boys called Mount Hermon.
They were meant for young people of modest means.
In 1971 the two merged into one school, Northfield Mount Hermon, which is still there.
The Chicago school had a founder of its own, and it wasn't only Moody.
Her name was Emma Dryer.
She was a teacher who came to Chicago around the time of the Great Fire, and in 1873 Moody's church hired her to run its Bible work, training women to visit families in the poorest parts of the city.
For years she urged Moody to open a real training school, and in 1883 she started a gathering for Bible study and prayer called the May Institute.
Moody kept putting it off.

Then, early in 1886, he told a meeting in Chicago that the city needed what he called gap-men: ordinary men and women, trained in the Bible, to stand in the gap between the ministers and the masses who never went to church.
The institute counts its founding from that year, and early in 1887 the Chicago Evangelization Society was formally organized to do the work.
After Moody died, it took his name.
For a long time, Dryer was a footnote in the official story.
Today the school's own archives credit her as the person who did the most to bring it about, and in 2019 the institute announced new tributes to her on its campus.
The schools shared one idea with the man himself: that faith was something you did, not just something you believed.
Moody's students learned to preach on street corners, visit tenements and lead singing, and many of them went out as missionaries all over the world.
The institute still trains them, about a mile south of here.
Before you walk west, look south down Clark Street, across North Avenue.
On the right-hand side, a short block away, stands a grand clubhouse in the style of the Renaissance.
It is the Germania Club building, and it has one of the most unusual origin stories in Chicago.
In the spring of 1865, Abraham Lincoln's body came through Chicago on its way home to Springfield, and it lay in state at the courthouse downtown while tens of thousands of people filed past.
A group of German Americans, many of them veterans of the Union Army, formed a men's chorus to sing for the occasion.
The chorus became a club, and the club became one of the centers of German life in the city.
In the late 1880s it built this clubhouse, designed by the firm of Addison and Fiedler, where members gathered for concerts, dinners, dances and long evenings of song.
Chicago was one of the most German cities in America then.
The North Side had German newspapers, German theaters, German gymnastic societies and German beer gardens, and on many blocks you heard more German than English.
Then came the First World War.
When the United States declared war on Germany in 1917, anything German became suspect.
Across the country, schools dropped German classes, sauerkraut was renamed liberty cabbage, and families changed their names to sound less foreign.
The Germania Club changed its name too.
It became the Lincoln Club, reaching back to its own beginnings for a name nobody could call unpatriotic.
A few years after the war, it quietly took its old name back.
But the old German world never fully recovered.

The war, and then Prohibition, which closed the beer gardens and the breweries, broke up much of the public life that had held it together, and the families slowly moved on to other neighborhoods and suburbs.
The building was named a city landmark in 2011, a reminder of the men who sang for Lincoln.
You are on Wells Street, just north of North Avenue.
The theater at 1616 North Wells, with its ornate stone facade, is the home of the Second City, the most influential comedy theater in America.
It opened in December 1959, a few blocks north on Wells Street, and moved here in 1967.
It was founded by Bernard Sahlins, Howard Alk, and Paul Sills.
The name was a joke, borrowed from a snide series of magazine articles by the New Yorker writer A. J. Liebling, who had called Chicago the Second City.

Its roots go back a few years earlier to a group called the Compass Players, founded by students and former students around the University of Chicago, which pioneered a new kind of theater built on improvisation.
Many of the improvisation games came from Viola Spolin, a teacher who happened to be Paul Sills's mother.
Look at the stone facade with its carved figures.
It was salvaged from an older building downtown, the Chicago Garrick Theater, designed by Adler and Sullivan, which was demolished in 1961.
Some of its ornament was reused here.

The list of performers who came through the Second City is astonishing: Alan Arkin, Joan Rivers, John Belushi, Bill Murray, Gilda Radner, Dan Aykroyd, John Candy, Mike Myers, Tina Fey, Amy Poehler, Stephen Colbert, Steve Carell, and many more.
When Saturday Night Live started in 1975, a large part of its early cast came from Second City.
Next door is Piper's Alley, a passage named for Henry Piper, who ran a bakery here in the late nineteenth century.
In the 1960s it was a hippie bazaar, and today it holds the theater's training center and other stages.
Second City is only part of Chicago's comedy story.
In 1981, a producer named Charna Halpern founded a theater that became known as iO, and she was soon joined by a brilliant, eccentric improviser named Del Close.
Together they developed long-form improvisation, in which a team spins a whole evening out of a single audience suggestion.
Close taught many of the comedians who went on to Saturday Night Live and beyond.
Today Chicago has dozens of improv theaters and training centers, and thousands of students take classes every year, hoping to follow the same path.
You heard that the Second City's improvisation games came from Paul Sills's mother, Viola Spolin.
Her own teacher was a remarkable woman named Neva Boyd, who ran a training school for recreation workers at Hull House, the settlement house on the Near West Side.
Spolin began studying with her in 1924.
Boyd believed that play was serious business.

Games, folk dances and storytelling, she taught, could build confidence and cooperation, and help the children of immigrants from a dozen countries, who might not share a language, learn to get along.
In 1939, Spolin went to work for the Works Progress Administration, the New Deal jobs program, teaching drama in Chicago's neighborhoods.
Many of her students were immigrants and their children, and she found that scripts got in the way.
So she invented games instead.
Each one gave the players a simple problem to solve.
In one, two players face each other, and one follows the other's every move, like a reflection in a mirror.
In another, the players speak only in made-up gibberish, so they have to get their meaning across with their bodies and voices.
In another, they have to show the audience where they are, a kitchen or a bus stop, without ever saying it.
While the players worked, she called out instructions from the side, the way a coach shouts from the sidelines, and she called it side-coaching.
The point was to get the actors out of their heads and into the moment.
After the war she moved to California, and her son carried her games to the University of Chicago.
When the Compass Players started in Hyde Park in 1955, she came back to help train the first company.
In 1963 she gathered more than two hundred of her games and exercises into a book, Improvisation for the Theater, dedicated in part to Neva Boyd.
It is still in print, and it's used everywhere from acting schools to classrooms to business training.
In July 1955, Paul Sills and a producer named David Shepherd opened a new kind of theater in the back room of a bar near the University of Chicago, on 55th Street in Hyde Park.
The building is gone.
A fire station stands on the spot today, at 55th Street and University Avenue.
Shepherd, a New Yorker with family money and radical ideas, wanted a theater for ordinary people, as quick and cheap as a newspaper.
So the Compass Players didn't perform written plays.
They worked from scenarios, a page or so of plot, and made up the dialogue every night.
When the scenarios ran short, they took suggestions from the audience and improvised short scenes on the spot, using Viola Spolin's games.
The actors were extraordinary.
Elaine May, a brilliant, sharp-tongued young woman who sat in on university classes without enrolling, was in the first company.
Mike Nichols, who had left the university, joined soon after.
Shelley Berman, later famous for his one-sided telephone calls, was there, and so was Barbara Harris, who went on to star on Broadway and in the movies.
Nichols and May discovered that together they were magic.

Their two-person scenes, a smothering mother on the phone with her scientist son, a pair of nervous teenagers parked on a date, became the core of an act that made them stars in New York within a couple of years.
In 1960 they opened on Broadway in An Evening with Mike Nichols and Elaine May.
Later, Nichols became one of the great directors of stage and screen, and May a writer and director herself.
The Compass in Chicago didn't last.
It moved from one spot to another and folded after about two years.
But its ideas didn't fold.
The scenario, the audience suggestion, the games and the trust between players all went north to Wells Street, where Sills and his partners built the Second City on them.
Nearly every improv theater in the world can trace its family tree back to that back room on 55th Street.
In 1973, the Second City opened a theater in Toronto, and a few years later its company there made a television show.
Second City Television, known by its initials, S C T V, imagined the programming of a tiny, cheap TV station in a made-up town called Melonville.
Each episode flipped through the channel's whole schedule: the news, soap operas, talk shows, commercials and late-night horror movies.
The actors played both the station's staff and the stars of its shows, and they wrote most of the material themselves.
The cast was a dream team: John Candy, Joe Flaherty, Eugene Levy, Andrea Martin, Catherine O'Hara, Harold Ramis and Dave Thomas, later joined by Rick Moranis and Martin Short.
Several of them had worked the stage here on Wells Street.
Ramis was the show's first head writer, before he left for Hollywood, where he co-wrote Animal House, Caddyshack and Ghostbusters.
Some of its characters became cult favorites.
Flaherty played Count Floyd, the host of a horror-movie show who tried hard to be scary and never once was.
Andrea Martin played Edith Prickley, the station manager, in loud leopard print.
Levy and Candy played the Schmenge brothers, a pair of mournful polka musicians.
And then there were Bob and Doug McKenzie, two dim brothers in wool caps who sat in front of a map of Canada, drinking beer and talking about nothing at all.
They were born when the show moved to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which wanted two extra minutes of distinctly Canadian content in each episode.
Moranis and Thomas, half in protest, improvised the most Canadian thing they could imagine.
The bit became a hit record and a movie.
Starting in 1981, an American network ran the show in a longer, late-night version, and it won Emmy Awards for its writing.
Its alumni are still everywhere.
Decades later, Eugene Levy and Catherine O'Hara were still playing off each other, as the parents on the comedy Schitt's Creek.
Walk back to North Avenue and west toward Orleans Street.
In the 1960s and 1970s, Wells Street behind you and the blocks around here were crowded with folk music clubs, coffee houses, and bars.
One of the most important places was the Earl of Old Town, a bar and folk club on Wells Street, across from the Second City.
It was where Steve Goodman, who wrote the song City of New Orleans, and his friend John Prine, a mailman from the western suburbs, played their early sets.
Prine had been writing songs in his head while walking his mail route.
Right about here, at 333 West North Avenue, the Old Town School of Folk Music opened in December 1957.
It was founded by Win Stracke, a folk singer, and Frank Hamilton, a guitar teacher.
The school's idea was that anyone could learn to play, in group classes, by ear, and that folk music belonged to everyone.
It grew into one of the largest community music schools in the country, and it has since moved to bigger buildings in the Lincoln Square neighborhood, but it began here.

Back toward Wells, at 219 West North Avenue, is the Old Town Ale House, a bar that has been open since 1958, famous as a hangout for writers, reporters, and actors, including the film critic Roger Ebert.
Its walls are covered with paintings by its late owner, many of them caricatures of politicians.
Today, Wells Street is more upscale, with restaurants and boutiques, but the old storefronts are still there, and the street remains lively at night.
Steve Goodman was a lifelong, long-suffering Cubs fan.
He wrote a song called A Dying Cub Fan's Last Request, and in 1984, he wrote Go, Cubs, Go, which is still played at Wrigley Field after every Cubs win.
He died of leukemia that fall, just days before the Cubs clinched their first championship of any kind in almost forty years, and some of his ashes were said to have been scattered at Wrigley Field.
John Prine went on to become one of the most admired songwriters in America, and he played Chicago for the rest of his life.
Old Town had jazz, too.
A few blocks south, on Wells Street, was a club called the Plugged Nickel, where Miles Davis and his great quintet played a famous run of shows in December 1965.
The recordings, released years later, are considered some of the finest live jazz ever captured.
John Prine was born in 1946 and grew up in Maywood, just west of the city.

His parents came from Muhlenberg County, in the coal country of western Kentucky, and years later he wrote a song, Paradise, about the little town there that his family knew, and the coal company that strip-mined it away.
He served in the Army, much of it in West Germany, and then went back to delivering mail.
Around 1970, at an open-mic night at a folk club called the Fifth Peg, on Armitage Avenue, he grumbled that the singers weren't very good, and somebody dared him to do better.
He got up and played three of his own songs, and the room went quiet.
That's how he told it, anyway.
On another night in 1970, Roger Ebert, the film critic of the Sun-Times, wandered into the Fifth Peg.
As the story goes, he had walked out of a bad movie and stopped in for a beer.
He heard Prine and wrote a rave, published on October ninth, 1970, under the headline Singing Mailman Who Delivers a Powerful Message in a Few Words.
It was the first review Prine ever got.
His friend Steve Goodman did the rest.
In 1971, Goodman dragged Kris Kristofferson, then one of the hottest songwriters in the country, to hear Prine sing.
Kristofferson joked that Prine was so good they'd have to break his thumbs, and he invited both young men to open for him at the Bitter End, a folk club in New York.
The next morning, Jerry Wexler of Atlantic Records offered Prine a contract.
His first album came out that year, with Sam Stone, Angel from Montgomery, Hello in There and Paradise.
For the next half century he was the songwriter other songwriters admired most, from Bob Dylan to Bonnie Raitt.
He died on April seventh, 2020, of complications from Covid, in the first weeks of the pandemic.
Steve Goodman learned he had leukemia when he was barely into his twenties, and he lived the rest of his life at full speed, as if he knew his time was short.
He wrote his most famous song after a train ride.

He and his wife took the Illinois Central Railroad's daytime train, the City of New Orleans, downstate to Mattoon, Illinois, to visit her family, and Goodman sat by the window and wrote down what went by: freight yards and farm towns, junkyards of rusting cars, old men playing cards in the club car.
The song became a farewell to the passenger train itself, which was disappearing all over America in those years.
The famous story is how Arlo Guthrie came to record it.
Goodman spotted Guthrie at a Chicago bar, the Quiet Knight, and asked to play him a song.
Guthrie grudgingly agreed, so the story goes, on one condition: if Goodman bought him a beer, Guthrie would listen for as long as it took to drink it.
Goodman played City of New Orleans, and Guthrie loved it.
His recording became a top-twenty hit in 1972.
In 1984, Willie Nelson made it the title song of an album, and the next year it won the Grammy for best country song.
Goodman had died a few months before, so the award came too late for him to accept it.
His friendship with John Prine produced another classic.
Goodman wrote You Never Even Call Me by My Name, the song that calls itself the perfect country and western song, with Prine's help, and David Allan Coe made it a hit.
Prine, the story goes, refused to take a songwriting credit, and Goodman thanked him with a jukebox.
The train still runs.
Amtrak's City of New Orleans now leaves Chicago in the evening and rolls into New Orleans the next afternoon.
The Old Town School began in a living room in Oak Park.
In the mid-1950s, a young guitarist from Los Angeles named Frank Hamilton was giving guitar lessons in the home of Dawn Greening, a folk music lover there.
One of his students was Win Stracke, and Stracke saw that Hamilton's way of teaching could be the basis of a whole school.
Stracke was a big-voiced singer and actor who had worked in Chicago radio and early television, until the blacklist of the McCarthy years caught up with him.
He was dropped from a television soap opera for his politics, and Studs' Place, the show he did with his friend Studs Terkel, was canceled.
The two liked to call themselves the Chicago Two.
The school opened on December first, 1957, and the great bluesman Big Bill Broonzy played on opening night.
He was already ill, and he died the next summer.

Stracke wanted every class to end with what he called the Second Half, a jam session where students of every level played and sang together, so that beginners learned by joining in with players better than they were.
It made the place feel less like a school than a club, and people came back for years.
Among the teenagers who took lessons in the early days was Jim McGuinn, who later, as Roger McGuinn, led the Byrds.
Hamilton moved on after a few years and for a time played with the Weavers, the folk group whose hits had helped launch the revival.
Stracke stayed on as the school's first director, as the folk boom filled its classrooms.

In 1968 the school moved to Armitage Avenue, and since 1998 its main home has been a former public library on Lincoln Avenue, an Art Deco building that it renovated, with a concert hall where you can still hear folk, blues and music from all over the world.
Stracke died in 1991, but the Second Half lives on.
Walk north to Eugenie Street and look for a short street called Crilly Court, running north between Eugenie Street and Saint Paul Avenue.
It was developed in the mid-1880s by Daniel Crilly, a builder who wanted to create a little enclave of rowhouses and flats in the middle of the block.
On one side are brick rowhouses, and on the other, flats with balconies.
Look for the names carved over doorways; Crilly named some of the buildings after his children.
This part of Old Town is known as the Old Town Triangle, a district bounded by North Avenue, Clark Street, and the diagonal of Lincoln Avenue.

Wander the narrow streets around here, such as Menomonee, Wisconsin, and Orleans, and you'll see a remarkable variety of houses: small wooden worker's cottages built in the years after the fire, brick Italianate rowhouses, and large Victorian homes.
Some cottages sit below the level of the sidewalk.
That's because, in the decades after they were built, the city raised the streets to put in sewers, and some houses were never jacked up to match.
At 1710 North Crilly Court, the house where Henry Gerber lived in 1924 is a city landmark.
He founded the Society for Human Rights, the earliest documented gay rights organization in the United States, and it was shut down by police within months.
Look for the small, tucked-away gardens and alleys, which make this one of the most charming places to wander in Chicago.
In the 1960s, the Triangle was one of the first neighborhoods in Chicago to fight back against urban renewal, which had leveled large parts of the nearby Near North Side.
Residents organized and won protection for the old houses, and the area is now a city landmark district.
Henry Gerber was a German immigrant and a veteran of the American army of occupation in Germany after the First World War, where he'd seen a gay rights movement taking shape.
He came back to Chicago determined to start one here.
The state of Illinois gave his society a charter in December 1924.
Within months, police raided his home, arrested him, and seized his papers.
He lost his job at the post office and his savings, but he never stopped writing and arguing for gay rights.
His house was made a city landmark in 2001, and in 2015, it was named a National Historic Landmark.

After the fire of 1871, Chicago's business leaders and newspapers were determined that the city would never burn like that again, and they pushed for fire limits: a line inside which no new wooden buildings would be allowed.
Many of them wanted the line drawn at the city limits, which would have banned wood everywhere.
On the North Side, that sounded like a sentence of exile.
Many of the people here were German and Irish working families who had owned small frame houses and lost them in the fire.
They could afford to rebuild in wood.
Brick was out of reach.
A ban would turn owners into renters, or push them out beyond the city line.
So in January 1872, when the city council took up the question, the North Siders marched on it.
Their homemade banners, misspelled in a newcomer's English, said No Fire Limits on the North Side, and Leave a House for the Laborer.
Accounts differ on how rough things got when they reached the council chamber.
The council gave way.
The fire limits it passed that year left much of the North Side outside the line, and families here rebuilt in wood, quickly, often on the same lots.
Many of the wooden cottages around the Triangle date from the years right after the fire.
The victory didn't last.
On July fourteenth, 1874, a second big fire burned more than eight hundred buildings just south of downtown.
This time the insurance companies took charge.
Their national board demanded bigger water mains, a reorganized fire department, and a ban on wooden buildings everywhere in the city.
When the council dragged its feet, the board told its members to cancel their Chicago policies.
A city nobody would insure couldn't do business, and the council extended the fire limits to the city line.
The builders of cheap frame houses simply moved outside the city, to the towns that Chicago swallowed in the great annexation of 1889.
That's one reason so many wooden cottages stand in neighborhoods that were once beyond the city limits.
About a ten-minute walk south of here, across North Avenue, on a short street called Burton Place, is one of the most enchanting buildings in Chicago.
It's known as the Carl Street Studios, because Burton Place was called Carl Street when the building was made over.
The name changed in the 1930s.
In 1927, an artist named Sol Kogen bought an old mansion there and asked his friend Edgar Miller to help turn it into studios and apartments for artists.
Miller was a young artist who had come to Chicago from Idaho to study at the Art Institute.

The two had very little money, so they built with whatever they could salvage from buildings being torn down around the city: common bricks, oak doors and beams, sheets of marble, wrought iron, copper washtubs, even old plumbing pipes.
During the Depression, Kogen bought tiles by the truckload.
Miller did almost everything by hand.
He carved doors and beams, made stained glass, laid mosaics, painted murals and modeled sculpture, and he filled the place with animals, figures and patterns.
The courtyard and the front are a riot of tile, carved wood and brick laid in odd designs.
Inside, the apartments climb through rooms on different levels, with built-in benches, little balconies, winding stairs and windows of jewel-colored glass.
It looks like a fairy tale crossed with Art Deco.
The partners went their separate ways around 1935, but Kogen and others remade more houses on the street in the same spirit, and today Burton Place is listed as a historic district.
Miller lived until 1993 and kept working for decades, but for years he was nearly forgotten.
A book, Edgar Miller and the Handmade Home, and a group devoted to his legacy have brought his work back into view.
If you take the Little Italy tour, you'll meet more of it: a parade of stone animals he made for a public housing project.
The studios are private homes, so admire them from the sidewalk.
Here's how to read the old houses as you wander the Triangle.
Start with the lot.

Chicago's builders laid out most house lots twenty-five feet wide and about a hundred and twenty-five feet deep, so the classic worker's cottage is narrow and long, with its gable end facing the street.
That steep triangle of roof over the front is the signature of the type.
Next, count the stories.
Most cottages are one story or one and a half, the half being an attic room tucked under the roof, often lit by a small window in the gable.
Many sit on a raised basement, with a few steps up to the front door.
Owners often rented out the lower level, or put a second little house at the back of the lot, and the rent helped pay the mortgage.
Look at the door.
On many cottages it's set off to one side, opening into a narrow hall, with two windows beside it.
Then look up at the eaves.
Many have brackets, scrolls and a bit of molding, Italianate trim that came ready-made from planing mills.
In the decades after the Civil War, Chicago was the biggest lumber market in the world, and doors, windows and trim arrived by the carload.
How did they go up so fast?
With the balloon frame: a skeleton of light, machine-sawn studs nailed together, instead of heavy timbers joined by skilled carpenters.
Chicago likes to claim it invented the method in the 1830s.
Whether or not that's true, it was perfect for a city in a hurry.
Finally, look for the signs of later lives.
A brick front added to a wooden house.
A porch that came and went.
A dormer squeezed into the roof for another bedroom.
And the careful restorations of the last sixty years or so, since the artists and young families who saved this neighborhood started fixing up houses nobody else wanted.
Some of those modest cottages now sell for well over a million dollars.
Walk west to Cleveland Avenue and Eugenie Street.
In front of you stands Saint Michael's Church, with its tall brick bell tower topped with a green copper spire.
The church was built by German immigrants and completed in 1869.
It was one of the largest churches in the city.
Two years later, the Great Fire roared through, and Saint Michael's burned.
But its thick brick walls survived, and the parishioners, many of whom had lost everything, rebuilt the church inside those same walls.
It reopened in 1873.
The bell tower was raised to its current height afterward.
There is a well-known saying here that you're a true Old Towner only if you were born within the sound of Saint Michael's bells.
That's an echo of the old London saying about the bells of Saint Mary-le-Bow and Cockneys.
Step inside if it's open.
The interior is a feast of German Baroque decoration: carved altars, stained glass made in Munich, murals, and statues.
For generations, masses here were said in German.
The parish is run by the Redemptorist order, which has served here since the 1860s.
The neighborhood around it has changed many times over, from German farmers to artists and hippies and now affluent families, but Saint Michael's is still the anchor of Old Town.
The fire of 1871 burned north for more than a day, through Old Town and into what's now Lincoln Park.
It finally died out near Fullerton Avenue, about a mile north of here, when it ran out of buildings to burn and a light rain began to fall.
Thousands of people fled into the cemetery that then occupied the south end of Lincoln Park, and some waded into the lake to escape the heat.
The burned district stretched about four miles from south to north.
The parish began with a gift from a brewer.
Michael Diversey was a German immigrant who, with his partner William Lill, ran one of the leading breweries in early Chicago.

By the early 1850s, German families were pouring onto the cheap land around North Avenue, then the edge of the city, and the Catholics among them wanted a church of their own, where the sermons and the hymns would be in German.
In 1852, Diversey gave them a plot of land near North Avenue, and they put up a small wooden church.
It was dedicated on October seventeenth, 1852, with forty-three families, and it cost about seven hundred and fifty dollars, bell included.
It was named for Saint Michael the Archangel, and, as the story is told, as a quiet thank you to the man who gave the land.
The parish grew with astonishing speed.

Within a few years the frame church was far too small, and in 1860 the parish was handed to the Redemptorists, an order of priests founded in Italy in the 1700s and known for preaching missions, revivals that could last a week or more.
The first Redemptorist pastor said his first Mass here in February 1860.
The great brick church followed within the decade.
By the end of the century, Saint Michael's was one of the biggest German parishes in the city, with its own schools, choirs, mutual aid societies and clubs for every age.
A child could be baptized, schooled, married and buried without ever leaving the parish, and many were.
Diversey's name lives on, though most people who say it have no idea who he was.
Diversey Parkway, a mile and a half north of here, is named for him.
So the next time you hear a Chicagoan say Diversey, you'll know there's a brewer behind it, and behind him, the church in front of you.
In March 1855, Chicago elected a mayor from the Know-Nothing movement, a party that wanted to limit the power of immigrants and Catholics.
The new mayor, Levi Boone, a doctor and a relative of the frontiersman Daniel Boone, barred immigrants from city jobs.
Then he went after their drinking.

His council raised the price of a liquor license sixfold, from fifty dollars to three hundred, and cut its term from a year to three months, and the city began enforcing an old law that closed taverns on Sundays.
For the Germans of the North Side, a Sunday afternoon in a beer garden with the family was a cherished custom, and they saw the new rules as aimed squarely at them and at the Irish.
Many saloonkeepers defied the law, and the city arrested them.
On April twenty-first, 1855, a test case came to trial at the courthouse downtown, and a crowd of supporters marched south from the North Side to fill the square outside.
The mayor had the Clark Street bridge swung open to cut off the rest of the marchers on the north bank of the river.
When the bridge swung back and the crowd surged across, the police were waiting, and shooting broke out.
Boone called out the militia, and the fight was over quickly.
At least one man was dead, and some sixty people had been arrested.
The Know-Nothings won the street fight and lost the war.
The next March, German and Irish voters turned out in force and threw them out of office, and the fifty-dollar license came back.
Historians date the start of hard-fought party politics in Chicago's city elections to that riot.
It was the first of many battles in Chicago over beer, from Sunday closing laws to Prohibition, and the North Side Germans won most of them.
So the next time you order a beer in Chicago on a Sunday afternoon, you might lift it to the North Siders who marched to the river in 1855.
The fire that gutted Saint Michael's kept moving north, and almost nothing in its path survived.

One famous exception stands about half a mile north of here, at twenty-one twenty-one North Hudson Avenue: a small wooden cottage with Italianate trim, built in 1869 for a police officer named Richard Bellinger.
It was designed by William W. Boyington, the architect of the Water Tower on Michigan Avenue, one of the other famous survivors of the fire.
On the second day of the fire, as the flames came up from the south, Bellinger decided to fight.
He tore up the wooden sidewalk in front of the house and pulled down the wooden fence, so the fire would have nothing to creep along.
He raked away the dry leaves.
Then he soaked the roof and walls.
The pumps at the waterworks had stopped hours before, and the water soon ran out.
And here's where the legend begins.
When the water was gone, the story goes, Bellinger went down to his cellar, brought up his barrels of cider, and used them to soak the roof and put out every spark that landed on it.
The cottage that cider saved has been a Chicago favorite ever since.
Did it happen?
It's a wonderful story, and it has been told for more than a century and a half.
But in 1915, according to old newspaper reports, Mrs. Bellinger herself dismissed the cider story.
Whatever saved the house, whether water, cider, hard work or a lucky shift in the wind, it's one of the very few buildings in the burned district that came through the fire.
Neighbors have been arguing about the cider for generations, a little like the arguments over Mrs. O'Leary's cow.
If you walk up Hudson Avenue, you can stand on the sidewalk and decide for yourself.
It's a private home, so admire it from there.
Walk a block north to Menomonee Street.
At number 435, behind a garden, is a low building with a sweeping, Japanese-style roof.
This is the Midwest Buddhist Temple, built in 1971.
Its story begins in the Second World War.

In 1942, after Pearl Harbor, the federal government forced about a hundred and twenty thousand people of Japanese ancestry, most of them American citizens, out of their homes on the West Coast and into incarceration camps in the interior.
Starting in 1943, the government began releasing some of them on the condition that they resettle away from the coast.
Chicago, with its jobs and its distance from the Pacific, became the biggest destination.
By the end of the war, about twenty thousand Japanese Americans had moved here.
Many of them settled on the Near North Side, around Clark Street and Division Street, and later in Lakeview and Uptown.
In 1944, a group of them founded a Buddhist congregation in Chicago, which eventually built this temple here in Old Town.
Its members also helped revive the neighborhood in the 1960s and 1970s.
The temple's best-known event is the Ginza Holiday, a Japanese cultural festival held each summer, with food, taiko drumming, martial arts, and traditional crafts.
It's a small, quiet reminder of a chapter of Chicago's history that's often forgotten.
This is the end of the Old Town tour.
Lincoln Park is a few blocks to the east, where the next tour begins.
The temple's founder was a minister named Gyodo Kono.
Like the families he served, he was sent to an incarceration camp during the war, at Rohwer, in the swampy Delta country of southeastern Arkansas.
After his release he came to Chicago, and on July tenth, 1944, he founded what was then called the Midwest Buddhist Church.
Its first service was held not in Old Town but on the South Side, at a community hall on South Parkway, the boulevard now called Martin Luther King Drive.
The congregation grew as the resettlers put down roots, and in time it moved to the North Side, where many of its members lived.
Kono could have gone home.
According to the temple's own history, he was asked to return to Japan to take charge of a temple there, but he chose to stay with his congregation in Chicago.
In 1964 he began the campaign for a permanent home, and this building, designed by the architect Hideaki Arao, was dedicated on November sixth, 1971, twenty-seven years after the founding.
The congregation called it its Temple of Enlightenment.
Kono served the temple until his death in 1975.
Look at the building again.

Its low, horizontal lines and wide roof echo the temples of Japan, but it's built of modern materials for a modern American congregation, and the garden in front makes a quiet buffer between the street and the hall.
Inside, as in most temples of this tradition, the altar holds a golden image of Amida Buddha, standing and leaning slightly forward, as if already stepping toward anyone who calls his name.
Around it are candles, flowers and incense, and on special occasions the altar holds offerings of fruit and rice cakes.
If the temple is open, step in quietly.
Visitors are welcome at services, and nobody will expect you to know what to do.
You heard that Chicago became the biggest destination for Japanese Americans leaving the camps.
That was no accident.
The War Relocation Authority, the federal agency that ran the camps, opened its very first field office here, in the Loop, on January fourth, 1943.
It was run by Elmer Shirrell, who had been the first director of the Tule Lake camp in California.
To leave a camp, a prisoner had to pass a security review and usually needed a job or a sponsor waiting on the outside.
The first to come were mostly young, single and American-born, the children of immigrants, and many arrived with little more than a suitcase and an address.
Churches and volunteer groups opened hostels to tide them over, among them the Church of the Brethren and the American Friends Service Committee, the relief agency of the Quakers.
Wartime Chicago had plenty of work, in factories, offices, hotels and private homes.
Housing was harder.
Many landlords wouldn't rent to them, and many newcomers found rooms in old boardinghouses and cheap flats near the corner of Clark and Division.
Officials urged them to spread out and blend in, but people also needed one another, and the community built its own institutions.
In 1946, resettlers and the government set up the Chicago Resettlers Committee, to help newcomers find homes, jobs and their footing.
In 1954 it became the Japanese American Service Committee, which still serves the community today and keeps an archive of its history.
The old neighborhood around Clark and Division didn't survive.
In the 1960s, much of it was cleared for the Sandburg Village high-rises, and the families and shops moved north along Clark Street.
Many of the young people who arrived with a suitcase in 1943 lived the rest of their lives here.
Some of their grandchildren still come to this temple.
If you come to a Sunday service here, parts of it may feel surprisingly familiar.
In many temples of this tradition there are rows of seats facing the altar, a service book, hymns called gathas sung to piano or organ, and a Sunday school for the children, called Dharma school.
The tradition is Jodo Shinshu, or True Pure Land Buddhism, founded in Japan in the thirteenth century by a monk named Shinran.
Its teaching is simple at its heart.
You can't reach enlightenment by your own efforts, however hard you try.
Instead you entrust yourself to the boundless compassion of Amida Buddha.
The central practice is the Nembutsu, saying Namu Amida Butsu, not to earn anything, but in gratitude.
It was the faith of most of the Japanese immigrants who came to Hawaii and the West Coast.
In America, the temples took on some of the forms of Protestant churches, partly to fit in and partly to hold on to their American-born children.
The war turned that into a matter of survival.
In 1944, at a meeting held inside the Topaz camp in Utah, the national body of Jodo Shinshu temples renamed itself the Buddhist Churches of America.
The word churches was chosen to sound less foreign.
The organization also made English its official language and loosened its formal ties to the head temple in Japan.
That same year, this congregation was founded as the Midwest Buddhist Church.
Many of these congregations, this one included, have since gone back to calling themselves temples.
Each summer, the temple also holds Obon, a festival for remembering those who have died, with Bon Odori, circle dances that anyone can join.
The steps are simple, the drums are loud, and nobody minds if you get them wrong.
This tour explores Lincoln Park, the park, and then a corner of the neighborhood named after it.
Lincoln Park is the largest park in Chicago, stretching about seven miles along the lakefront, much of it on landfill.
Its southern end, where we start, has a strange history.
In the 1840s, the city set aside land here for the City Cemetery, at what was then the edge of town.

By the 1850s and 1860s, residents worried that burials so close to Lake Michigan were contaminating the water supply, and a doctor named John Rauch campaigned to move the cemetery and turn the land into a park.
In 1864, the city established a park here, first called Lake Park, and after President Lincoln's assassination in 1865, it was renamed in his honor.
Over the next decades, the graves were moved to new cemeteries farther from the city, such as Graceland and Rosehill.
But not all of them were moved, as you'll hear.
The park grew into one of Chicago's great public gardens, with a free zoo, a conservatory, ponds, beaches, statues, and a harbor.
Its landscape was shaped by many designers over more than a century.
West of the park, the neighborhood of Lincoln Park grew up as a mix of German, Irish, and later Puerto Rican and other communities.
In the 1920s, its streets saw some of the most notorious events of the gangster era.
Since the 1960s and 1970s, it has become one of the most affluent neighborhoods in the city, home to DePaul University and to blocks of beautiful Victorian houses.

We'll start at the Chicago History Museum, walk north through the park past the zoo and the conservatory, and then west into the neighborhood, past the site of the St. Valentine's Day Massacre and a park dedicated to the Wizard of Oz, ending at the Biograph Theater on Lincoln Avenue.
You are at the southern end of Lincoln Park, near Clark Street and North Avenue, beside the Chicago History Museum.

The museum, founded in 1856 as the Chicago Historical Society, is the city's memory: its collections include Lincoln's deathbed, artifacts from the Great Fire, and the history of the city's neighborhoods.
It is well worth visiting.
Now walk a little north and east, behind the museum.
In the grass, you'll find a heavy, dark stone tomb, surrounded by a fence.
This is the Couch tomb, built in 1858 for the family of Ira Couch, who ran the Tremont House, one of the city's grand early hotels.
It's the last obvious trace of the City Cemetery that once covered this whole area.
When the city removed the graves to create the park, the Couch family went to court to keep their tomb here.
Moving it would have been difficult and expensive, and the tomb stayed.
It's said that Ira Couch and several members of his family are still inside.
Removing the other graves was a long and imperfect process.
Thousands of graves, particularly those of poor people buried in unmarked plots, were never properly moved.
Construction projects in the park over the years have turned up human remains, and researchers believe many people still lie under the lawns.
As you walk through the south end of Lincoln Park, keep in mind that you may be walking over a cemetery.
Close by in the park, near the museum, is one of the finest statues in America: Abraham Lincoln: The Man, often called the Standing Lincoln, by the sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens, unveiled in 1887.
Lincoln stands in front of a chair, as if he has just risen to speak.
His head is bowed, deep in thought, and his left hand holds his lapel.
Saint-Gaudens spent years on it, and he worked from a life mask and casts of Lincoln's hands made in 1860.
Many people who had known Lincoln said it was the best likeness ever made.
Look at the curving stone bench, or exedra, around it.
That was designed by the architect Stanford White, Saint-Gaudens's frequent partner.
Lincoln had deep ties to Chicago.
He was nominated for president in 1860 at the Republican convention here, held in a temporary hall called the Wigwam, at Lake and Market Streets downtown.
Chicago in 1860 was a Republican, railroad, and grain town, and the nomination of a lawyer from Illinois was a victory for the Midwest.
The statue was paid for by a gift from Eli Bates, a lumberman who left money for it in his will.
Copies of the Standing Lincoln stand in London and Mexico City.
As you walk north through the park toward the zoo, look for another president: Ulysses S. Grant, on horseback, high on top of a massive stone arch overlooking the lagoon.
The monument was dedicated in 1891, and a huge crowd turned out to see it.
Grant had close ties to Illinois.
He was working in his family's leather goods store in Galena, in the northwest corner of the state, when the Civil War began, and he joined an Illinois regiment.
Grant Park, downtown, is named for him too.

In the fall of 1863, in the middle of the Civil War, two Chicago women, Mary Livermore and Jane Hoge, organized a great fair to raise money for the Sanitary Commission, the volunteer organization that sent food, medicine and nurses to Union soldiers.
It was the first of the big sanitary fairs that spread across the North, and people donated all kinds of things to be sold.
President Lincoln sent the most valuable gift of all: his own handwritten final draft of the Emancipation Proclamation.
Thomas Bryan, a Chicago lawyer and the president of the fair, bought it for three thousand dollars and gave it to the Soldiers' Home, a refuge in Chicago for disabled veterans.
Printed facsimiles of the document were sold to raise still more money.
The draft ended up in the care of the Chicago Historical Society, which displayed it in a big frame on the wall of its reception room.
The Society's building, near Dearborn and Ontario Streets, was supposed to be safe from fire.
It wasn't.

When the Great Fire swept across the North Side in October 1871, the building burned, and almost the whole collection was lost: books, letters, maps, the records of Chicago's early years, and Lincoln's proclamation with them.
The Society started over.
In the 1890s it built a fortress of rough granite on the same corner, and in 1932 it moved here, to the edge of the park, into the building that's now the museum.
The official copy in Washington, written out by a clerk, signed and sealed, survives.
Lincoln's draft of the earlier, preliminary proclamation, which he gave to a similar fair in Albany, survives in the New York State Library.
But the final draft in his own hand, the one he gave to Chicago, is gone.
Augustus Saint-Gaudens was born in Dublin in 1848, to a French shoemaker and an Irish mother, and he came to New York as a baby.
At thirteen he was apprenticed to a cameo cutter, carving tiny portraits in shell and stone, and at night he studied drawing.
In his twenties he trained in Paris and worked in Rome.
His big break was a statue of Admiral David Farragut, unveiled in Madison Square in New York in 1881, on a base designed by his friend Stanford White.
It was hailed as a new kind of American monument, a hero who looked like a real man, braced as if on a rolling deck.
The Standing Lincoln, six years later, made him the leading sculptor in the country.

He went on to create the Shaw Memorial in Boston, honoring the Black soldiers of the Fifty-fourth Massachusetts Regiment and their colonel, Robert Gould Shaw, a relief he labored over for some fourteen years.
Then came the gilded General Sherman, riding behind a winged Victory at the corner of Central Park.
And for his friend Theodore Roosevelt, he designed a twenty-dollar gold coin, first struck in 1907, which many collectors consider the most beautiful American coin ever made.
Other artists gathered around him at his summer home in Cornish, New Hampshire, where an art colony grew up.
The house and studios are now a national park.
He died in 1907, and Chicago has a second Lincoln by him that he never saw in place.
It's a seated figure in Grant Park, officially called Abraham Lincoln, the Head of State.
It was cast in 1908, shown in New York and at the San Francisco world's fair of 1915, and finally unveiled in Grant Park in 1926, after years of arguments over where it should go.
Stanford White designed its setting too, though he didn't live to see it either.
If you're in Grant Park, look for the family resemblance between the two Lincolns.
A short walk north of the museum, near Clark Street, a big granite boulder sits in the grass with a bronze plaque.
It marks the grave, somewhere nearby, of a man named David Kennison.
The plaque says he was the last survivor of the Boston Tea Party, and that he died in Chicago in 1852, at the age of a hundred and fifteen.
Kennison was a celebrity in his last years.
He told how, as a young man, he had helped dump British tea into Boston Harbor in 1773, and then fought in the Revolution, and he spoke of service in later wars too.
Chicagoans loved him.
In a raw young city with almost no history of its own, here was a living link to the founding of the country, and when he died, by most accounts, the city turned out to honor him.
He was buried in the City Cemetery, which then covered this ground.
In 1903, half a century later, patriotic groups placed this boulder in his memory, and for most of the next century his story was repeated in guidebooks and newspapers.
The trouble is that it doesn't hold up.
As early as 1914, a speaker in Oak Park was publicly doubting it.
Historians who have since gone through the records believe Kennison was born around 1764.
That would have made him about nine years old at the Tea Party, and about eighty-five, not a hundred and fifteen, when he died.
The Encyclopedia of Chicago now says plainly that he falsely claimed to be the Tea Party's last survivor.
So what is the boulder really?
It's a monument to a story that Chicago wanted to believe, and to the cemetery that still lies under the park.
Nobody knows exactly where in these lawns Kennison's body is.
The plaque only says that he lies near this spot, and that part, at least, is probably true.
The man in the tomb, Ira Couch, made his fortune in hotels.
In the 1830s he and his brother James took over a hotel at the corner of Lake and Dearborn Streets, named the Tremont House, and they rebuilt it more than once as the town grew.

The grandest version, designed by John Van Osdel, Chicago's first professional architect, was a five-story brick hotel with two hundred and sixty rooms, so big for a muddy prairie town that skeptics called it Couch's Folly.
It turned out to be no folly at all.
The Tremont became the place to stay in Chicago, and the place to be seen.
Politicians made it their headquarters, and Abraham Lincoln stayed there on his visits to the city.
Its most famous moment came in July 1858.
Senator Stephen Douglas opened his campaign for reelection with a speech from the hotel's balcony to a huge crowd in the street, with his Republican challenger, Lincoln, in the audience.
The next evening, Lincoln answered him from the same balcony.
Those two speeches were the curtain-raiser for the Lincoln-Douglas debates that summer and fall, which made Lincoln a national figure and set him on the road to the White House.
Ira Couch didn't live to see any of it.
He died in 1857, and his family built this tomb the next year.
The hotel he built burned in the fire of 1871.
His estate put up yet another Tremont House on the same corner, also designed by Van Osdel, and it stood until 1937.
So the heavy stone box in the grass is the last trace of two lost Chicago landmarks: the cemetery that became this park, and the hotel where Lincoln began the campaign that made him president.
Walk north through the park to the entrance of the Lincoln Park Zoo.
It's one of the oldest zoos in North America, and one of the very few major zoos that's still free to visit.
It began in 1868 with a gift of a pair of swans from the commissioners of Central Park in New York.
Animals were added over time, some donated, some bought.
Through the late nineteenth century, it was a typical Victorian menagerie of cages and pens.
Today, it's a modern zoo focused on conservation, and its exhibits for great apes are among its most famous.
Look for a few of the older buildings, such as the red brick Lion House, built in 1912, with decorative animal heads and a grand hall inside.
It was designed by Dwight Perkins, an architect of the Prairie School, a movement of Chicago architects led by Frank Lloyd Wright that celebrated the flat, wide landscape of the Midwest.
Next to the zoo is a working farm exhibit, the Farm-in-the-Zoo, which lets city kids see cows, pigs, and chickens.
And on the south side of the zoo is the old Café Brauer, a Prairie School restaurant building from 1908, built when this was a German-American part of town.
The zoo is also known for its gorilla breeding program and for its role in research on endangered species.
Admission is free because the zoo is owned by the Chicago Park District and supported by a private society, and Chicagoans fiercely protect that tradition.
The zoo has had some famous residents.
The most beloved was Bushman, a gorilla who arrived as a baby in 1930 and grew into a giant of more than five hundred pounds.
Crowds lined up to see him, and when he died in 1951, he was mounted and put on display at the Field Museum, where he still is.
In the 1940s and 1950s, the zoo's director, Marlin Perkins, hosted one of the first nature programs on television, Zoo Parade, broadcast from here, before he went on to host Wild Kingdom.
And there's a story every Chicago child used to hear.
In 1943, an elephant named Judy was supposed to be moved by truck from the Brookfield Zoo, in the western suburbs, to Lincoln Park.
Judy refused to get into the truck.
So her keepers walked her, all night, about eighteen miles through the city streets, and she arrived at Lincoln Park the next morning.
For three decades, one man shaped this zoo more than anyone else.
Lester Fisher came here in 1947 as its veterinarian, became director in 1962, and ran the zoo until he retired in 1992.
Fisher's passion was the great apes, and under him Lincoln Park became famous for them.
The zoo built up the largest gorilla population in North America, and in 1976 it opened a great ape house, later named for him, where visitors could watch whole families of gorillas and chimpanzees.
By 2004 the zoo had celebrated forty-five gorilla births since 1970, at a time when many zoos had trouble getting apes to breed at all.
That success depended on a change in thinking.
The old zoos had kept animals alone, as specimens to be looked at.
Fisher and his staff learned that gorillas, like people, need family life: a silverback leader, several females, young ones to learn from their elders.
Animals raised that way grew up knowing how to be parents themselves.
In 2004 the zoo replaced the Fisher building with the Regenstein Center for African Apes, which cost some twenty-six million dollars, the most expensive project in the zoo's history at the time.
