It gives western lowland gorillas and chimpanzees large indoor and outdoor spaces, with climbing structures, grass and room to get away from the crowds and from each other.

The zoo's scientists study how apes think and behave, and they help plan breeding for endangered species at zoos across the continent, so that small populations scattered in many cities can stay healthy over generations.
So when you look into the eyes of a gorilla here, you're seeing the latest in a long line of Lincoln Park apes, stretching back through Dr. Fisher's families to the most famous one of all, Bushman.
Bushman was the zoo's biggest star for twenty years, and in the fall of 1950, near the end of his life, he gave Chicago one more story.
One day that autumn, Bushman found his way out of his cage and roamed the zoo's primate house.
A full-grown gorilla of more than five hundred pounds was loose in a public building, and the news made the front page of the Tribune.
Keepers cleared the area and tried to coax him back.
One of them, a keeper named Eddie Robinson, tried to lead him toward his cage and was bitten, badly enough to need four stitches at Columbus Hospital.
Then came the part of the story that everybody remembers.
The zoo's director at the time, Marlin Perkins, knew something about Bushman: the great gorilla was terrified of snakes.
So, the story goes, a keeper brought out a small, harmless garter snake.
Bushman took one look, turned around, and hurried back into his cage.
Accounts of the afternoon differ.
A newspaper on the other side of the world reported that keepers used other animals from the zoo's exhibits to drive him back.
But the version that stuck, the one Chicago kids heard for decades, is the one with the garter snake: a five-hundred-pound giant sent home by a creature you could hold in one hand.
Bushman was already old for a captive gorilla, and his health was failing.
Crowds came to see him in his final months, and when he died, the city mourned him like a celebrity.
The snake became part of his legend, a reminder that even a king has something he's afraid of.
At the south end of the zoo, look for a pond ringed with tall grasses, a boardwalk around its edge, and, on one bank, a curving pavilion of pale wood.
This is the Nature Boardwalk, which opened in 2010.
It used to be the zoo's South Pond, a shallow, hard-edged artificial pool filled with city tap water, and murky for much of the summer.
The zoo and the Chicago architect Jeanne Gang's firm, Studio Gang, rebuilt it as a natural wetland.
They deepened the pond so the water would hold more oxygen, softened the shoreline, and planted native prairie and marsh plants, so the water could clean itself and support life.
Today it holds fish, turtles and frogs, along with dragonflies and the birds that hunt them.
The pond matters more than its size suggests.
Chicago sits on one of the great migration routes of North America, and every spring and fall, millions of songbirds follow the lakeshore.
To a tired warbler flying over miles of concrete, the green strip of Lincoln Park is a lifesaver, and a pond full of insects and cover is a place to rest and refuel.
Bird watchers come here with binoculars at dawn in May.
The pavilion is made of prefabricated wooden planks, bent into arcs and joined end to end.
Its ribbed, rounded shape was inspired by the shell of a tortoise, and there are no columns inside.
It's officially the Peoples Gas Education Pavilion, and it has become one of the most photographed spots in the park, especially at sunset, with the skyline behind it.
Walk the boardwalk slowly, and look down.
On a warm day you'll often see turtles lined up on a log, sunning themselves within sight of the Gold Coast.
Walk north through the zoo or along Stockton Drive to Fullerton Parkway.
On your right, just south of Fullerton, look for a small, almost hidden garden behind stone walls.
This is the Alfred Caldwell Lily Pool, one of the hidden treasures of Chicago.
It was designed by Alfred Caldwell in the late 1930s and built by the Works Progress Administration, the New Deal program that put unemployed workers to work on public projects.
Caldwell was a disciple of Jens Jensen, the Danish-born landscape architect who created the Prairie style of landscape design.

The idea was to recreate the natural landscape of the Midwest: a pond fed by a waterfall over layered limestone, like a river cutting through rock, surrounded by native plants and a stone pavilion with low, flat roofs.
Caldwell was so committed to the project that he is said to have sold his house to help pay for plants.
The garden was carefully restored in 2002.
Just north is the Lincoln Park Conservatory, a Victorian glass house built in the early 1890s.
It was designed by Joseph Lyman Silsbee, an architect who was Frank Lloyd Wright's first employer when Wright came to Chicago.
Inside are a palm house, a fernery, an orchid house, and a show house with seasonal displays.
Admission is free.

In front of the conservatory are formal gardens, and on the south end, a bronze fountain from the 1880s with storks and fish, the Bates Fountain, by Augustus Saint-Gaudens and his assistant Frederick MacMonnies.

Just north of here, across Fullerton Parkway, is the Peggy Notebaert Nature Museum, run by the Chicago Academy of Sciences, which was founded in 1857 and is one of the oldest scientific institutions in the Midwest.
Its building opened in 1999, and its most popular room is a butterfly haven, a greenhouse where hundreds of butterflies fly freely around visitors.
Beside it is North Pond, a small lagoon with a restaurant in an old Arts and Crafts warming shelter that ice skaters once used.
The man behind the Lily Pool lived a long and stubborn life.

Alfred Caldwell was born in St. Louis in 1903 and came to Chicago young, where he went to work for Jens Jensen and absorbed his belief that a landscape should feel like the land itself: prairie, woods, stone and water.
When the Depression hit, Caldwell became superintendent of parks in Dubuque, Iowa, and there he built Eagle Point Park, with low stone shelters stepping along the bluffs high above the Mississippi.
It was a New Deal project, and in 1936 it won a national award for design.
During the presidential campaign that year, Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt came to see it.
Back in Chicago he made the Lily Pool, and then Promontory Point on the South Side lakefront, which you'll hear about on the Hyde Park tour.
Then came a surprising turn.
Caldwell joined Mies van der Rohe at the Illinois Institute of Technology, where he taught for many years and shaped the landscape of Mies's campus.
The prairie romantic and the master of steel and glass made an unlikely pair, but they understood each other: both believed in order, simplicity and nature.
When the school dismissed Mies as its campus architect in 1960, Caldwell resigned in protest.
He also designed the landscape for Lafayette Park in Detroit, a housing development that Mies designed with the Chicago developer Herbert Greenwald.
Its towers and townhouses stand in a gentle park of trees and lawns, and in 2015 it was named a National Historic Landmark.
Caldwell was a poet, too, and a fierce teacher who could talk for hours about architecture, democracy and nature.
He died in 1998, at ninety-five.
Sit for a moment by the waterfall in the Lily Pool, and you're sitting inside the idea he spent his life defending.
The Chicago Academy of Sciences, which runs the nature museum just north of here, had a remarkable young founder named Robert Kennicott.
He grew up on his family's farm, called The Grove, in what's now Glenview, a sickly boy who was taught mostly at home and spent his days studying snakes, birds and small animals.
In his early twenties he helped found the Academy.

In 1859 he headed north for the Smithsonian Institution, and for about three years he traveled by canoe and dog sled through the wilderness of the Hudson's Bay Company and along the Yukon, collecting specimens and making friends with fur traders and native peoples.

In 1865 the Western Union company hired him to lead the scientists on one of the most ambitious projects of the age: a telegraph line from America to Europe the long way around, through British Columbia, Russian America and Siberia.
Kennicott took command of the expedition's scientific corps.
But in May 1866, at about thirty, he died near the trading post of Nulato on the Yukon River.
His friend William Healey Dall took over his work.
The telegraph line was never finished.
A cable was laid across the Atlantic in 1866, and the company gave up the following year.
But the timing of the expedition was extraordinary.
In 1867 the United States bought Russian America from Russia, and what Kennicott and his colleagues had learned about its rivers, wildlife and people helped Americans understand what they had bought.
Today we call it Alaska.
His name is on the map there: the Kennicott Glacier and the Kennicott River.
A copper town nearby took the name, misspelled as Kennecott, and so did the giant copper company that grew from its mines.
Back in Chicago, the Academy's collections, including much of his work, burned in the fire of 1871.
Step inside the conservatory.
It's free, and on a winter day, coming in from the cold into the warm, wet air is one of the great small pleasures of Chicago.
The glass house was built in stages between 1890 and 1895, replacing a small greenhouse from the 1870s.
Start in the Palm House, which opened in 1892, and look for the giant fiddle-leaf rubber tree, with its big, leathery, violin-shaped leaves.
It was planted in 1891, while the room was still being built, and it now rises about fifty feet, nearly to the top of the glass.
The Fern Room, which opened in 1895, is the most magical.
A still pool sits among ferns, mosses and low, spreading plants, and the whole room feels like a forest from the age of the dinosaurs.
Look for the sago palm, which isn't a palm at all.
It's a cycad, from a family of plants far older than flowers, which grew alongside the dinosaurs.

In the Orchid House, look for the hundreds of orchids, along with bromeliads, the relatives of the pineapple that store water in the cups of their leaves, and a few carnivorous plants that trap insects for food.
And the show house changes with the seasons, from a spring flower show to a holiday display in winter.
As you walk through, look up at the structure too: the slender iron ribs and thousands of panes of glass, curving overhead.
Victorian conservatories like this one were a kind of time machine and travel agency in one, a way for city people to see the plants of the tropics without leaving home.
When you step back outside, notice the formal garden, laid out with bright beds of flowers, a deliberate contrast to the wild, natural look of the Lily Pool next door.
Walk west on Fullerton and then south on Clark Street to the 2100 block.
On the east side of the street, near 2122 North Clark, there is a small lawn next to a senior housing building.
There is no marker here.
But this is where one of the most notorious crimes in American history took place.
On the morning of February 14th, 1929, seven men were waiting in a garage here, belonging to a trucking company called the S.M.C. Cartage Company.
Most of them were members of the North Side Gang led by George "Bugs" Moran, the rival of Al Capone.
A car pulled up, and several men got out, two of them dressed as police officers.
The gang members, apparently believing it was a routine police raid, lined up against the wall.
They were machine-gunned to death.
Moran himself was not there.
He was running late, and when he saw what looked like a police car, he stayed away.
The massacre was widely blamed on Capone, who was in Florida at the time.
No one was ever convicted.
But it was a turning point.
Public outrage at the violence helped turn the federal government against Capone, and he was convicted of tax evasion in 1931.
The garage was torn down in 1967.
The bricks from the wall where the men were shot were bought by a Canadian businessman, who displayed them for years, and some of them are now in the Mob Museum in Las Vegas.
When the police arrived, one of the victims, Frank Gusenberg, was still alive, with more than a dozen bullets in him.
A detective asked him who had shot him.
"Nobody shot me," he said.
He died a few hours later, keeping the gangster's code of silence to the end.
The massacre left investigators with an awkward question.
Two of the killers had worn police uniforms.
Were they real police?
In 1929, with Chicago's police so entangled with the gangs, nobody could rule it out.

To find out, investigators turned to Calvin Goddard, a doctor and former army officer who had made himself an expert in a new science, forensic ballistics: identifying which gun fired a bullet from the tiny scratches its barrel leaves behind.
Goddard examined the bullets and shell casings from the garage and showed that they had come from two Thompson submachine guns, and that they didn't match the guns carried by Chicago police.
Then the case broke open in another state.
On December fourteenth, 1929, a police officer named Charles Skelly was shot dead on a street in St. Joseph, Michigan.
Deputies searched a house near town rented by the gunman, who turned out to be Fred Burke, a killer for hire with ties to Capone's outfit.
They found an arsenal, including two Thompson guns.
Goddard test-fired them and matched them to the bullets from the garage on Clark Street.
Burke was eventually caught, but he was never tried for the massacre.
Michigan convicted him of killing Skelly, and he died in a Michigan prison.
The two guns are still kept by the sheriff's office in Berrien County, Michigan.
The case had a lasting result.
In its wake, Northwestern University opened the Scientific Crime Detection Laboratory, with Goddard as its director, often described as the first independent crime laboratory in the United States.
Its work in ballistics, fingerprints and lie detection helped turn detective work into a science.
Every television crime show with a lab in it owes something to the morning of February fourteenth, 1929.
George Moran wasn't really named George Moran.
He was born Adelard Cunin in St. Paul, Minnesota, in 1893, ran away from home as a teenager, and took a new name.
In Chicago he joined the North Side gang of Dean O'Banion and Hymie Weiss, and after both of them were killed, he ran what was left of it.
His nickname, Bugs, was slang for crazy, and people said it fit his temper.
After the massacre, reporters asked him who had done it.
Only Capone kills like that, he's said to have answered.
Capone, in Florida, supposedly shot back that the only man who kills like that is Bugs Moran.
Moran survived the massacre, but his gang didn't.
He had lost his best gunmen in a single morning, and over the next few years Capone's organization took over most of the North Side rackets.
Moran stayed in Chicago for a while, then drifted out of the big time into smaller schemes.
He never went straight.
In 1946 he was arrested for his part in a bank robbery in the small town of Ansonia, Ohio, and he spent the next ten years in the Ohio Penitentiary.
When he was released in 1956, he was arrested again, for an earlier bank robbery, and sentenced to ten more years.
He didn't serve them.
He died of lung cancer at the federal penitentiary in Leavenworth, Kansas, on February twenty-fifth, 1957, and he was buried in the paupers' section of the prison cemetery.
So the man who missed his own massacre because he was running late outlived nearly all of his enemies, including Capone, who died in 1947.
But the last boss of the North Side gang ended up broke, forgotten and buried in a prison yard, a long way from Clark Street.
Who were the seven men?
Frank Gusenberg and his brother Peter were among the gang's toughest gunmen.
Albert Kachellek, who went by the name James Clark, was another.
Adam Heyer looked after the gang's business affairs.
Albert Weinshank managed some of the businesses it used as fronts.
John May was an auto mechanic who did work for the gang, and by many accounts his German shepherd was tied up in the garage that morning and was found howling among the bodies.
And Reinhardt Schwimmer was a former optician and gambler who liked to hang around gangsters for the excitement.
That morning, it cost him his life.
Why did the killers move before Moran arrived?
One theory points to Weinshank.
He was about Moran's size and build, and he dressed much like him.
If lookouts across the street were watching for the boss, they may have seen Weinshank go in and given the signal.
And who were the killers?
Nobody was ever convicted, and the theories have multiplied for almost a century.
Most historians blame Capone's organization, with outside gunmen brought in so that nobody in Chicago would recognize them, and with Fred Burke, whose guns matched the bullets, among them.
Capone's own gunman Jack McGurn was charged, but he had an alibi: he said he had spent the morning in a hotel with his girlfriend, Louise Rolfe, whom the newspapers promptly named the Blonde Alibi.
The charges against him went nowhere.
Others have pointed at Detroit's Purple Gang, or at real policemen settling a score.
Capone himself was at his estate on Palm Island, near Miami, with a perfect alibi, which some people thought was the most suspicious thing of all.
Walk west on Dickens Avenue, through blocks of handsome Victorian rowhouses and graystones, to Oz Park, at Dickens and Larrabee Street.
Look for the statues: the Tin Man, the Cowardly Lion, the Scarecrow, and Dorothy with Toto, by the sculptor John Kearney.
There's also a children's playground called Dorothy's Playlot and an Emerald Garden.
The park is named for the land of Oz because Lyman Frank Baum wrote The Wonderful Wizard of Oz in Chicago.
Baum was a restless man.

He had been an actor, a playwright, a chicken breeder, a store owner, and a newspaper editor in South Dakota before he moved to Chicago in 1891, where he worked as a reporter and a traveling salesman for a china company.
He told stories to his four sons and their friends, and he started writing them down.
He lived in a house on Humboldt Boulevard, on the Northwest Side, while he wrote his most famous book.
The Wonderful Wizard of Oz was published in Chicago in 1900, with illustrations by a Chicago artist, William Wallace Denslow.
It was an immediate hit.
A musical version opened in Chicago in 1902 and then ran on Broadway, and Baum wrote thirteen more Oz books before his death in 1919.
People have long speculated that the Emerald City was inspired by the White City of the 1893 World's Fair, which Baum could have seen when he lived here.
It's an appealing idea, but Baum never said so, and it remains a theory.
Oz Park was created in the 1970s as part of an urban renewal plan for the neighborhood, and the statues were added starting in 1995.
It's a favorite of neighborhood families.
Before Oz made him famous, Baum's big idea was the store window.
In the 1890s, the great department stores were learning to sell with spectacle, and the window on the street was their stage.
Baum saw that the men who dressed those windows had no magazine of their own, so he started one.
The first issue of The Show Window appeared on November first, 1897.
It was a monthly of about sixty pages, full of photographs and advice, and Baum thought of it as an art journal.
He wrote about how to use electric lights, mirrors, revolving stands and moving figures to stop people in their tracks.

In 1898 he founded the National Association of Window Trimmers, which quickly grew to a couple of hundred members, and in 1900 he gathered his advice into a handbook, The Art of Decorating Dry Goods Windows and Interiors.
That October, with Oz on its way, he gave up the editorship.
Now think about the book he was writing at the same time.
In the original story, the Emerald City isn't really green at all.
Everyone who enters has to wear green-tinted spectacles, locked on by the Guardian of the Gates, and the spectacles make everything look green.
And the great Wizard turns out to be an ordinary man from Omaha, working his illusions from behind a screen.
A city whose dazzle comes from the way you look at it, run by a showman who hides the machinery: you don't have to be a literary critic to see a window dresser's imagination at work.
Baum never spelled out the connection, and no one can say for sure how much his day job shaped Oz.
But the next time you stop in front of a holiday window downtown, you might think of him.
The pictures that made Oz came from William Wallace Denslow, a newspaper artist and poster designer who had worked his way through print shops and newsrooms around the country.
He and Baum first teamed up on a book of nonsense verse, Father Goose, His Book, which was a best seller in 1899.
For The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Denslow did far more than illustrate.

He shared the book's copyright with Baum, and his drawings set the look of Oz for a generation: the Scarecrow's floppy, painted face, the Tin Woodman's funnel hat, the Lion's shaggy mane and Dorothy herself, a sturdy little girl in a checked dress.
The book was printed with color on nearly every page, an expensive gamble at the time.
Look closely at his work and you'll often find his signature, a little seahorse.
Success broke up the partnership.
After the stage version of Oz became a hit in 1902, the two men quarreled, partly over money, and they never worked together again.
Baum went on writing Oz books with a new illustrator, John R. Neill.
Denslow took his share and bought a small island in Bermuda in 1904.
He then proclaimed himself its king, under the title King Denslow the First, Monarch of Denslow Islands and Protector of Coral Reefs.
It's a wonderful title, but the reign didn't last.
He lost money on later stage ventures, drank heavily, sold the island, and died in obscurity in 1915.
His Oz is still the one many readers picture first, more than a century after he drew it.
Not bad for a newspaper artist who once crowned himself king of a rock in the Atlantic.
Before Hollywood, there was a Chicago musical.

The Wizard of Oz opened at the Grand Opera House on Clark Street in June 1902, with a script by Baum himself, and it was turned into a lavish spectacle by the director Julian Mitchell, with chorus girls, comic songs and elaborate stage effects.
It had more vaudeville than Kansas.
A lot of the story changed.
Dorothy's little dog Toto was replaced by a cow named Imogene.
New characters and songs were added, and the plot wandered wherever the jokes took it.
Baum's young readers may have been puzzled, but audiences loved it.
The stars were a vaudeville team, David Montgomery as the Tin Woodman and Fred Stone as the Scarecrow.
Stone's loose-limbed, rubbery dancing, as if his legs really were stuffed with straw, stole the show and made him a star.
The production moved to Broadway in January 1903, toured the country for years, and made a great deal of money, which is part of why Baum and Denslow fell out.
Almost four decades later came the movie.
Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer's Wizard of Oz of 1939 kept Dorothy's dog and dropped the cow.
It added the song Over the Rainbow, cast Judy Garland as Dorothy, and turned Kansas into sepia and Oz into blazing color.
It made one change that every fan knows: in the book, Dorothy's magic shoes are silver.
The studio made them ruby red, to show off its new color film.
One pair of those ruby slippers was stolen from a museum in Minnesota in 2005 and recovered by federal agents in 2018, which shows that people still want to go to Oz, whatever it takes.
Baum didn't live to see the film.
But the playground here, with its Emerald Garden, is a fair tribute to the show he first put on in Chicago.
Walk northwest on Clark Street and then west up Lincoln Avenue to number 2433, the Biograph Theater, with its old-fashioned marquee.

On the hot night of July 22nd, 1934, the bank robber John Dillinger, at the time the most wanted man in America and the FBI's Public Enemy Number One, came here to see a gangster movie, Manhattan Melodrama, starring Clark Gable.
He was with two women.
One of them, Ana Cumpanas, who used the name Anna Sage, was a Romanian immigrant facing deportation.
She had made a deal with the FBI, promising to point out Dillinger in exchange for help with her case.
She told agents she would be wearing an orange skirt, and the newspapers turned her into the Lady in Red.
When Dillinger walked out of the theater, FBI agents were waiting.
He was shot in the alley next to the theater and died there.
Crowds gathered, and some people dipped handkerchiefs in his blood as souvenirs.
Sage was deported anyway.
The Biograph was a movie theater for decades after that, and later it was converted into a live theater for plays.
Lincoln Avenue continues northwest from here, through a neighborhood of bars, restaurants, and Victorian houses.
Just to the south is DePaul University, one of the largest Catholic universities in the country, founded in 1898 by the Vincentian Fathers.
The man who led the ambush, the FBI agent Melvin Purvis, stood near the entrance and gave the signal to his men by lighting a cigar.
Seventy-five years later, in 2009, the scene was filmed here again, for the movie Public Enemies, with Johnny Depp as Dillinger, and the theater's facade was dressed up to look as it did in 1934.
This is the end of the Lincoln Park tour.
The Fullerton station on the Red, Brown, and Purple Lines, a few blocks west along Fullerton Avenue, will take you back downtown.
John Dillinger spent almost nine years in prison in Indiana for a botched holdup of a grocer in the farm town of Mooresville.

When he was paroled in 1933, he formed a gang and began robbing banks across the Midwest with a speed and style that made him a folk hero to some Depression-era Americans, who had little love for banks.
In January 1934 he was captured in Tucson, Arizona, and sent to the jail in Crown Point, Indiana, which was said to be escape-proof.
On March third, 1934, he walked out, using a wooden pistol that he claimed to have whittled himself, and drove off in the sheriff's own car.
He drove it across the state line into Illinois, and that was a mistake.
Taking a stolen car across a state line was a federal crime, and it brought the federal Bureau of Investigation into the hunt.
In April, federal agents surrounded a lodge in the north woods of Wisconsin called Little Bohemia, where the gang was hiding.
The raid was a fiasco.
Agents opened fire on a car of innocent men leaving the lodge, killing one of them, while Dillinger and his men slipped out the back.
Baby Face Nelson, one of the gang, killed an agent nearby.
Back in Chicago, Dillinger had a plastic surgeon work on his face and tried to burn off his fingerprints with acid.
He grew a mustache, dyed his hair, called himself Jimmy Lawrence, and started dating a waitress named Polly Hamilton.
On June twenty-second, his thirty-first birthday, the government declared him Public Enemy Number One.
He seemed to think he could hide in plain sight.
He went out on the town, and on a hot Sunday night in July, he went to the movies here, with Polly Hamilton on one arm and Anna Sage on the other.
Exactly a month after his birthday, he was dead in the alley next door.
The agent who lit the cigar was Melvin Purvis, a small, dapper lawyer from South Carolina who had joined the Bureau in 1927 and was running its Chicago office by his late twenties.
He was one of J. Edgar Hoover's favorites, until he became too famous.
The Dillinger hunt nearly ruined him.
After the disaster at Little Bohemia, there were calls for his firing, and Hoover sent another agent, Samuel Cowley, to take charge of the case.
But when the tip came from Anna Sage, it was Purvis who led the stakeout here, standing near the box office in the heat for nearly two hours while the movie played.
After the shooting, Purvis became a national hero.
Three months later, in October 1934, agents under his command killed another public enemy, Pretty Boy Floyd, on a farm in Ohio.
His face was in every newspaper, and that was the problem.
Hoover wanted the credit to go to the Bureau, and to himself.
Purvis found himself assigned to dull cases and watched closely, and in July 1935 he resigned.
He didn't fade away.
He made a deal with the company that made Post Toasties cereal, and kids could send in box tops to join the Junior G-Men, with badges and secret codes, under his name.
He served in the army in the Second World War and later went home to South Carolina.
In 1960, Purvis died of a gunshot wound from his own pistol, at home.
It was ruled a suicide, though some in his family believed it was an accident.
Hoover, who had long since written him out of the Bureau's official version of the Dillinger story, is said to have sent no condolences.
He was fifty-six, and the night of the cigar outside the Biograph had followed him all his life.
Almost as soon as the shots were fired, people began to say the dead man wasn't Dillinger.
The doubters had their reasons, or thought they did.
The face on the morgue slab had been altered by surgery.
Some said the dead man looked shorter and heavier than Dillinger, and that details in the autopsy didn't match.
In 1970, a writer published a book arguing that the Bureau had shot a small-time crook who resembled Dillinger, and covered up its mistake.
The idea has never quite gone away.
The government says, and most historians agree, that the man in the alley was Dillinger.
His fingerprints, damaged by the acid but not destroyed, were matched at the morgue, and his family identified him.
He was buried in Crown Hill Cemetery in Indianapolis, and his father had the grave reinforced with concrete and iron, to keep souvenir hunters from digging him up.
In 2019, relatives of his got a state permit to exhume the body for a television documentary, saying they wanted to settle the question.
The cemetery objected, and so did other members of the family.
The television network dropped out of the project, and in December 2019 a judge ruled that under Indiana law the cemetery's consent was required.
The grave stayed closed, and the cemetery's lawyers called the whole thing a decades-old conspiracy theory.
The alley has its own legends.
Ghost-tour guides tell of people who have felt a sudden chill there on summer nights, or glimpsed a figure running toward the street and falling.
Those are stories, of course.
But stand in the alley for a moment, and you can see why a city that loves its gangsters likes to believe John Dillinger never quite left.
DePaul University, just south of here, has a famous basketball story.
In 1942, a tall, awkward young man from Joliet named George Mikan enrolled.
He stood about six feet ten, wore thick glasses, and was so clumsy that another school had reportedly told him he'd never make a basketball player.
DePaul had a new coach that year, Ray Meyer, who was still in his twenties, and he saw something in Mikan.
He put him through drills of every kind: jumping rope, shadowboxing and footwork, and endless hook shots close to the basket, first with one hand, then the other, over and over.
Coaches all over the world still use that exercise, and they still call it the Mikan drill.
It worked.
Mikan became the most dominant player in the country.
He was so good at swatting shots away just above the rim that college basketball banned goaltending, a rule that's often credited, at least in part, to him.

In 1945 he led DePaul to the championship of the National Invitation Tournament in New York, then one of the most important tournaments in the sport, and in one game there he scored fifty-three points, as many as the whole other team.
As a professional, Mikan led the Minneapolis Lakers to five championships, and in 1950 the Associated Press named him the greatest basketball player of the first half of the century.
The big man, as a position, began with him.
Ray Meyer stayed at DePaul for forty-two seasons and won more than seven hundred games.
Today the university's teams play in a big arena near McCormick Place, but the old gym culture of Lincoln Park, and the drill, are where it started.
If you see kids practicing hook shots on a neighborhood court, you're watching George Mikan's lessons, eighty years on.
This tour explores Lakeview, a big North Side neighborhood that includes Wrigleyville, around the ballpark, and Northalsted, the heart of Chicago's gay community.
For most of the nineteenth century, this was not Chicago at all.
It was a separate township, Lake View, a mix of farms, lakeside resorts, and summer homes.
The land was low and sandy, and it became famous for celery, which German and Luxembourger farmers grew here and shipped downtown.
In 1854 a hotel called the Lake View House opened near the lake, giving the area its name.
Lake View was incorporated as a city in 1887 and then annexed by Chicago in 1889, part of a huge expansion that year which more than doubled the city's size.
Once the elevated train arrived, at the turn of the twentieth century, the farms disappeared under blocks of two-flats, three-flats, and courtyard apartment buildings.
The neighborhood filled with German, Swedish, and Irish families, and later with young people of every kind.
In 1914, a businessman named Charles Weeghman built a ballpark on the site of a former seminary at Clark and Addison Streets.
Two years later, the Chicago Cubs moved in.
The ballpark, later named Wrigley Field, gave its name to the surrounding blocks, now called Wrigleyville.
Starting in the 1970s, gay men and lesbians moved into the neighborhood around Halsted Street, and it became one of the most visible gay neighborhoods in the country.

We will start on Halsted Street, walk north to Wrigley Field, pass a tiny street that looks like London and an old movie palace, and end in Graceland Cemetery, where many of the people you've heard about on other tours are buried.
You are on Halsted Street near Belmont Avenue.
Look at the tall decorative pylons lining the sidewalk, ringed in rainbow colors.
They were installed by the city in the late 1990s, making this one of the first officially recognized gay neighborhoods in the United States.
The district is called Northalsted, and some people still call it by its older nickname, Boystown.
Look at the pylons more closely.
Many carry bronze plaques honoring lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender figures from history.
This is the Legacy Walk, an outdoor museum dedicated in 2012.

As you walk north on Halsted, you'll find plaques for people like Jane Addams, the Chicago social reformer who founded Hull House, the playwright Lorraine Hansberry, the mathematician Alan Turing, and Bayard Rustin, the organizer of the 1963 March on Washington.
Chicago has a long LGBTQ history.
The first gay rights organization in the United States that we know of was the Society for Human Rights, founded in Chicago in 1924 by Henry Gerber, a German immigrant and Army veteran.
It was shut down by police within months.
Gerber's house, on Crilly Court in Old Town, is now a city landmark.
The Chicago Pride Parade, one of the largest in the country, is held each June and runs through these streets.

Chicago's first Pride march was held in June 1970, a year after the Stonewall uprising in New York, when a small group of marchers walked from Washington Square Park, Bughouse Square, to the Civic Center downtown.
The parade moved to this neighborhood in the 1970s as the community grew here.
A few blocks north, at Halsted and Waveland, is the Center on Halsted, a large LGBTQ community center that opened in 2007, with a gym, a theater, and services for young people and seniors.
In 1961, Illinois became the first state in the country to stop treating sex between consenting adults of the same sex as a crime.
It happened quietly.
Lawyers rewriting the state's entire criminal code left the old sodomy law out, the legislature passed the new code, and the governor signed it that summer.
Hardly anyone remarked on it at the time.
The police didn't change their habits.
Gay bars were raided for years afterward, on charges like public indecency or keeping a disorderly house.
The most notorious raid came in the early hours of April twenty-fifth, 1964, at a bar called the Fun Lounge, just outside the city limits near O'Hare.
Cook County sheriff's deputies arrested more than a hundred people, and the newspapers printed many of their names, their addresses, and even where they worked.
People lost their jobs, and some lost their families.
The raid helped push Chicago's gay men and lesbians to organize.
In 1965 they founded a group called Mattachine Midwest, borrowing the name of an older homophile society on the West Coast.
It published a newsletter, spoke up when the police raided bars, and helped people who had been arrested.

Its legal adviser was Pearl Hart, a lawyer who had spent decades defending clients other lawyers wouldn't touch, from immigrants facing deportation to gay men caught in raids, and who stood by the group until her death in 1975.
Today, Chicago's library and archive of gay and lesbian history carries two names, Gerber Hart.
One is Henry Gerber, whose house you can see in Old Town.
The other is Pearl Hart.
Change at City Hall came slowly.
An ordinance banning discrimination based on sexual orientation was voted down by the City Council in 1986.
Mayor Harold Washington had backed it.
After his death, under Mayor Eugene Sawyer, it finally passed, in December 1988, by twenty-eight votes to seventeen.
In 2013, Illinois lawmakers voted to let same-sex couples marry, and by the middle of 2014, couples could marry anywhere in the state.
In 1981, doctors in New York and California began reporting rare cancers and pneumonias in young gay men.
Within a year or two, the same illnesses were turning up in Chicago.
The disease was named AIDS, and for most of the next fifteen years there was no effective treatment.
In this neighborhood, as in gay neighborhoods across the country, a generation of young men sickened and died, often within months of being diagnosed.
Much of the early response came from the community itself.
Back in 1974, a few medical students and volunteers had started a small clinic offering cheap testing for sexually transmitted infections to gay men.
It was soon named for Howard Brown, a former top health official of New York City who had come out publicly as gay a little over a year before he died.
When the epidemic arrived, Howard Brown was already there and already trusted.

It became one of the city's front lines, caring for the sick and taking part in some of the earliest research on the disease, and it's now one of the largest health centers of its kind in the country.
Others chose protest.
In April 1990, the activist group Act Up brought a national demonstration to Chicago.
One of its targets was the county's public hospital, which, the protesters charged, had no beds for women in its AIDS ward.
Many of the demonstrators were arrested.
To see how the city remembers those years, walk east to the lake, just south of Belmont Harbor.
From the 1960s into the 1990s, the stepped limestone blocks along the shore there, known as the Belmont Rocks, were a favorite gathering place for gay men, a place to sunbathe, swim, and be seen.
That spot is now the AIDS Garden Chicago.
Its centerpiece, installed in 2019, is a thirty-foot sculpture called Self-Portrait, by the artist Keith Haring, who died of AIDS in 1990 at the age of thirty-one.
It's the city's first public monument to the epidemic.
Among the people honored on these pylons is Jane Addams, the founder of Hull House, whose public life is told on the West Loop tour.
She's here because of a part of her life that her early biographers mostly left out: her forty-year partnership with a woman named Mary Rozet Smith.
Mary Rozet Smith came from a wealthy Chicago family, and she began volunteering at Hull House soon after it opened in 1889.
She was about eight years younger than Addams, and much less public.
She became one of the settlement's most generous supporters, helping to pay for its buildings and programs, and she became the center of Addams's private life.
By most accounts, Addams's earlier closest friend, Ellen Gates Starr, who had founded Hull House with her, drifted to the edge of that life as Mary moved to the middle of it.
The two women traveled together, and one surviving letter shows them asking a hotel for a double bed rather than two singles.
In 1904 they bought a summer house together on the coast of Maine, near Bar Harbor.
When they were apart, Addams wrote to Smith constantly, and she referred to their partnership as a marriage.
Many of their letters are gone, because Addams burned them.
What should we call them?
Historians still argue over the words.
Neither woman used the terms we would use today, and both guarded their privacy.
What isn't in doubt is that for four decades, each was the other's closest companion, and the people around them understood them as a couple.
Mary Rozet Smith died of pneumonia in February 1934.
Addams, whose own health had been failing for years, died fifteen months later, in May 1935.
Walk north on Halsted and then west on Addison Street to Wrigley Field, at Clark and Addison.
Look up at the red marquee at the main entrance.
It's one of the most famous signs in American sports.
The ballpark opened in 1914 as Weeghman Park, built for the Chicago Whales of the Federal League, a short-lived rival major league.
When that league folded, Weeghman bought the Cubs and moved them here in 1916.
The chewing gum magnate William Wrigley Junior, whose building you saw on the river, took control of the team, and the ballpark was renamed Wrigley Field in 1926.
It's the second-oldest ballpark in the major leagues, after Boston's Fenway Park.
The ivy on the outfield walls was planted in 1937 by a young Bill Veeck, who later became a famous team owner himself.
The center field scoreboard, built the same year, is still operated by hand: people inside slide the numbers into place.
And for decades, Wrigley Field had no lights.
The Cubs played only day games at home until 1988, when lights were finally installed after years of neighborhood opposition.
The Cubs won back-to-back World Series championships in 1907 and 1908.
Then they didn't win again for a hundred and eight years.
Fans blamed many things, including a curse.
In 1945, the story goes, a tavern owner named William Sianis was ejected from a World Series game with his pet goat, and he declared that the Cubs would never win again.
That's the Curse of the Billy Goat, a legend that Chicagoans half believed for decades.
In November 2016, the Cubs finally won the World Series, in Cleveland, in extra innings of the seventh game.
Back home, the victory parade and rally drew what the city estimated as millions of people.
Look across Waveland and Sheffield Avenues behind the outfield walls.
The bleachers on the roofs of those apartment buildings are the famous rooftop seats, where fans have been watching games for free, and later for a price, for generations.
And one more legend: in the 1932 World Series here against the Yankees, Babe Ruth is said to have pointed to the center field bleachers before hitting a home run to that very spot.
Whether he really called his shot is still argued about.
For half a century, Wrigley Field was also home to Chicago's football team.

The Bears played here from 1921 to 1970, and they got their name because their founder, George Halas, figured that football players were bigger than baseball players, so if the baseball team were the Cubs, his team should be the Bears.
After a game, look up at the flagpole above the center field scoreboard.
If the Cubs won, a white flag with a blue W flies over the ballpark, and the crowd sings Go, Cubs, Go, written by the folk singer Steve Goodman.
If they lost, a blue flag with a white L goes up instead.
Charles Weeghman made his fortune feeding the Loop's office workers.
Starting in 1901, he opened a chain of quick-service lunchrooms downtown, where a clerk could grab a sandwich and coffee and be back at a desk in minutes.
By 1914 he was a millionaire, and he wanted a ball club.
The established leagues weren't selling, so Weeghman joined an upstart.
The Federal League declared itself a third major league in 1914 and began luring players away from the other two.
Weeghman leased this block, where a Lutheran seminary had stood, and hired Zachary Taylor Davis, the architect who had designed Comiskey Park for the White Sox four years earlier.

Work began on March fourth, 1914, and the first game was played on April twenty-third, about seven weeks later, in a single-deck grandstand of steel and concrete that held about fourteen thousand people.
The team was known that first season as the Chi-Feds, and then as the Whales, and in 1915 the Whales won the Federal League pennant.
But the league was losing money.
It had sued the older leagues under the antitrust laws, in the courtroom of a federal judge named Kenesaw Mountain Landis, who let the case sit while the two sides negotiated.
After the 1915 season they made peace.
The Federal League disappeared, and as part of the deal, Weeghman was allowed to buy the Cubs, from Charles Phelps Taft, the half-brother of former President William Howard Taft.
Weeghman's luck soon ran out.
His lunchrooms faltered, and within a few years control of the club had passed to one of his partners, William Wrigley Junior.
The ballpark kept growing, and an upper deck went on in the late 1920s.
In 1941 the club added the round clock on top of the scoreboard, with dots in place of numbers.
In all the years since, no batted ball has ever hit that scoreboard.
The golfer Sam Snead is said to have hit it in 1951, with a golf ball he drove from home plate, but golf balls don't count.
The first night game in the major leagues was played in Cincinnati in 1935, and other ballparks soon followed.
Philip Wrigley, who ran the Cubs after his father's death, held out.
By the usual account, he finally bought the equipment to light this field in 1941, and the day after Pearl Harbor he gave it all to the war effort.
He never bought lights again.
Day baseball became part of what it meant to be a Cubs fan: games after school, sunburns in the bleachers, and office workers with mysterious afternoon appointments.
The darkness produced one of the ballpark's greatest moments.
On September twenty-eighth, 1938, the Cubs and the Pittsburgh Pirates were fighting for the pennant, tied in the ninth inning, with dusk falling so fast that the game was about to be called.
With two strikes on him, the Cubs' catcher and manager, Gabby Hartnett, hit a home run that many in the crowd could barely see.
The papers called it the Homer in the Gloamin'.
It put the Cubs in first place, and they clinched the pennant a few days later.
In 1981, the Wrigley family sold the team to the Tribune Company, which owned the television station that carried the games, and the new owners wanted lights.
Many neighbors were furious.
They feared crowds, traffic, and noise on summer nights, and one group picked a name whose initials spelled the team's: Citizens United for Baseball in Sunshine.
Lawmakers in Springfield and at City Hall passed rules that effectively barred night games here.
Then baseball's commissioner warned that if the Cubs ever reached the postseason, their home games might have to be played somewhere else.
In 1988, the city gave way.
The first night game was set for August eighth, 1988, a date full of eights.
It was rained out after three and a half innings, and the first official night game at Wrigley Field was played the following evening.
Even now, the city limits how many night games can be played here.
Cubs fans blamed a billy goat, as you heard.
But over the decades, they collected omens the way other fans collect autographs.
In 1969, the Cubs had one of their best teams in memory, with four future Hall of Famers: Ernie Banks, Ron Santo, Billy Williams, and the pitcher Fergie Jenkins.
In mid-August they led their division by nine games.
Then, on September ninth, during a game at Shea Stadium in New York, a black cat appeared from under the stands, circled Ron Santo as he waited on deck, and stared toward the Cubs' dugout.
The Cubs lost that game.
The next day the New York Mets passed them in the standings, and the Mets went on to win the World Series.
In 1984, the Cubs needed to win just one of three games in San Diego to reach the World Series.
They lost all three.
In the last one, a ground ball rolled through the legs of the first baseman, Leon Durham, and a story grew up that a teammate had spilled a sports drink on his glove in the dugout.
In 2003, the Cubs were five outs from the World Series, leading the Florida Marlins three to nothing here at Wrigley in the sixth game of the playoffs.
A foul ball drifted toward the seats down the left field line.
As the left fielder, Moisés Alou, leaped for it, several fans reached up too, and one of them, a young man named Steve Bartman, deflected it.
The Marlins scored eight runs that inning and won again the next night.
Bartman had to be escorted from the ballpark for his own safety, and he has avoided the public eye ever since.
A restaurant group bought the ball at auction for more than a hundred thousand dollars, and in 2004 it was blown up in a televised ceremony.
When the Cubs finally won in 2016, the team gave Steve Bartman a World Series ring.
Fans still argue over whether there was ever a curse at all, or just a great deal of bad baseball.
Long before most fans saw this ballpark, they heard it.
In the 1930s, a young announcer at W H O, a radio station in Des Moines, Iowa, broadcast Cubs games without leaving his studio.
A telegraph operator at the ballpark sent the bare facts, a strike, a fly ball to center, and the announcer turned them into lively play-by-play.
His name was Ronald Reagan.
Reagan loved to tell about a day in 1934 when the wire went dead in the ninth inning of a tie game, with Dizzy Dean pitching for the Cardinals.
Rather than admit it, he had the batter foul off pitch after pitch for several minutes, until the line came back.
Usually, in his telling, the batter was the Cubs' shortstop, Billy Jurges, though other versions name someone else.
It's the kind of story that got better every time he told it.
In 1937, Reagan persuaded the station to send him to the Cubs' spring training on Catalina Island, off California, which the Wrigley family owned.
While he was out west, he took a screen test at Warner Brothers, and the studio signed him.
Half a century later, near the end of the 1988 season, he came back to Wrigley Field as president, threw out the first pitch, and called part of the game from the broadcast booth.
His host in the booth that day was Harry Caray, the voice many fans remember best.
Caray had called games for the Cardinals and the White Sox, and at Comiskey Park he liked to sing along with Take Me Out to the Ball Game during the seventh-inning stretch.
As Caray told it, the Sox owner, Bill Veeck, the same man who had planted the ivy here, secretly switched on the public address microphone one day in 1976, and a tradition was born.
Caray brought it here when he joined the Cubs in 1982, and with games on WGN, carried by cable across the country, he helped make the Cubs a national team.
Since his death in 1998, guest singers, from movie stars to astronauts, have led the crowd.
Walk north on Seminary Avenue, just west of the ballpark, to Grace Street, and then turn east onto a short street called Alta Vista Terrace, running between Byron and Grace.
It feels like you've walked into another city.
This one block contains about forty narrow rowhouses, built in the early 1900s by the real estate developer Samuel Eberly Gross.
Gross was one of Chicago's most successful developers, famous for selling small, affordable houses to working people on installment plans.
Here he tried something different, modeled on the terraces of London.
Look closely at the facades.
Each house is different, with its own style of windows, cornice, and doorway.
But each one has a twin: the house diagonally across the street has the same design, mirrored.
Walk the length of the block and see if you can match the pairs.
In 1971, Alta Vista Terrace became the first historic district designated by the city of Chicago.
It's one of the most charming surprises in the city, just steps from the noise of Wrigleyville.
Samuel Gross had another, stranger claim to fame.
He had written a play, and when the French playwright Edmond Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac became an international hit, Gross went to court in Chicago, claiming that Rostand had stolen his plot.
In 1902, an American judge agreed with him.
It's one of the odder footnotes in the history of the theater, and Rostand's play, of course, is still performed around the world.
Alta Vista Terrace was a showpiece.
Samuel Eberly Gross made his real fortune with something much plainer: small houses sold on credit to people who had never owned property.
Gross worked on a grand scale.
He would buy a whole tract of farmland at the edge of the city, lay out streets, plant trees, put up dozens or hundreds of similar cottages, and give the development an appealing name.
Then he advertised as no one in Chicago had before.
His ads ran in the city's foreign-language newspapers as well as the English ones, and his big color posters showed neat cottages with gardens and families out front.
One of the best known was titled The Workingman's Reward.
The pitch was simple.
A family could move in after a small down payment and pay by the month, in amounts not much higher than rent.
Instead of enriching a landlord, the payments bought a home of their own.
For immigrants from countries where only the gentry owned land, that was a powerful promise.
Gross wasn't the only developer selling houses this way, but he was the biggest.

By one count he laid out more than twenty subdivisions and built some ten thousand houses, from neighborhoods near the stockyards to a whole suburb west of the city, which he named after himself: Grossdale.
In 1905 its residents renamed it Brookfield.
Buying on installments had a hard edge.
Under many contracts of the time, a family that fell behind could lose the house and everything it had paid in.
And Gross's empire ended abruptly.
In 1904, with several new projects barely begun, he sold off his holdings and left Chicago.
The houses stayed, and many of his cottages are still lived in today, more than a century later.
When the first families moved onto Alta Vista Terrace, Lake View had been part of Chicago for only about a dozen years.
Its annexation, in 1889, was part of the largest expansion in the city's history, and the deciding issue was water.
Lake View had grown fast in the 1880s.
It became a city of its own in 1887, and it ran its own waterworks, drawing from the lake.
But it was also pouring its sewage into the lake, and by local accounts its water was fouled again and again, with outbreaks of typhoid and cholera.
A small city couldn't afford the pumping stations, sewers, and fire and police protection that Chicago could provide, and more and more residents decided they'd be better off inside the big city.
On June twenty-ninth, 1889, voters in Lake View, in Hyde Park to the south, and in several other towns and townships went to the polls to decide whether to join Chicago.
Supporters promised better services and the prestige of a great city.
Opponents warned about Chicago's taxes, its politicians, and its saloons.
Some of the most determined opposition came from temperance voters in dry districts, who feared that once they were part of Chicago, the saloons would follow.
Annexation carried.

In one day, Chicago grew by about a hundred and twenty-five square miles, and the census the next year showed that it had passed Philadelphia to become the second-largest city in the country, with more than a million people.
The vote didn't clean up the water by itself.
That same year, the state created the Sanitary District, which went on to build the canal that reversed the river, the story told on the river tour.
As for Lake View, the city vanished from the map, but its name never did.
The neighborhood still uses it, run together into a single word.
The street signs around the ballpark read like a puzzle, with a Civil War battle, a Connecticut railroad builder, a lake storm, and one real mystery.
Start with Belmont Avenue, a few blocks south.
It's named for the Battle of Belmont, fought on November seventh, 1861, when Union troops attacked a Confederate camp at Belmont, Missouri, on the Mississippi River.

It was a small, confused fight that ended with the Union soldiers hurrying back to their riverboats, and it would be long forgotten if not for their commander, a little-known brigadier general named Ulysses Grant.
It was his first battle of the war.

Sheffield Avenue, which runs behind the right field bleachers, honors Joseph Sheffield, a Connecticut businessman who helped build the railroad from Chicago west to Rock Island, on the Mississippi, and who bought land on Chicago's North Side.
Back east, Yale named its school of science for him after he gave it a fortune.
Waveland Avenue, behind the left field bleachers, takes its name, according to the usual story, from the lake waves that once washed over this low, sandy ground in storms.
Then there's Addison Street, which runs past the main entrance.
It's usually said to honor Thomas Addison, a London doctor who first described the disorder of the adrenal glands now called Addison's disease.
But nobody has found a convincing reason why a Chicago street would be named for him, and he seems never to have had anything to do with the city.

Finally, Irving Park Road, which leads to the cemetery, comes from a suburb laid out after the Civil War and named, by most accounts, for the writer Washington Irving, the author of The Legend of Sleepy Hollow.
So as you walk toward Graceland, you're heading, in a manner of speaking, for the Headless Horseman.
Walk west on Grace Street to Southport Avenue and turn south to number 3733.
The small theater with the glowing vertical sign is the Music Box, opened in 1929, just as talking pictures were replacing silent films.
Like the Ramova in Bridgeport and many neighborhood movie houses of its day, the Music Box was built as an atmospheric theater.
Step inside and look up: the auditorium is designed like an Italian courtyard at night, with a dark blue ceiling where small lights twinkle like stars and projected clouds drift slowly overhead.
There are only about seven hundred and fifty seats, which made it a small, intimate neighborhood theater rather than a palace.
By the 1970s, most neighborhood theaters in Chicago had closed or been chopped up into multiplexes.
The Music Box survived as a revival house, and since 1983 it has been one of the leading independent cinemas in the country, showing classic films, foreign films, documentaries, and cult favorites.
Some screenings are accompanied by an organist playing the theater's organ, and its sing-along screening of The Sound of Music and its holiday double features have become neighborhood traditions.

Southport Avenue, around the theater, is a typical Chicago neighborhood shopping street, lined with brick two- and three-story buildings with shops below and apartments above, all within walking distance of the Brown Line.
When Lakeview was booming in the 1910s and 1920s, streets like this were where people did all their shopping, and they've come back to life in the last thirty years.
The kind of theater in front of you was the invention of one man, the architect John Eberson.
Born in what was then Austria-Hungary, he came to America around the turn of the twentieth century and designed theaters across the South and the Midwest.
His Majestic Theatre in Houston, opened in 1923, was the first of what he called atmospheric theaters.
Instead of a dome dripping with plaster and chandeliers, the auditorium was made to feel like the open air.
The side walls became the facades of an imaginary Mediterranean town, and overhead was a smooth plaster sky.
Part of the appeal was cost.
A traditional movie palace needed acres of ornate plasterwork.
An atmospheric got most of its magic from paint, lighting, and the audience's imagination, so it could be built faster and cheaper.
In the late 1920s, atmospherics went up all over the country.
Eberson himself designed several in Chicago, including the Avalon on the South Side, which survives as the New Regal, and the vast Paradise on the West Side, torn down in the 1950s.
The Music Box was a small cousin, designed by the Chicago architects Edward Steinborn and Louis Simon, and it was a careful business proposition.
The theater is tucked inside a larger building, with stores along the street and apartments upstairs, so their rents could help carry it.
The auditorium itself cost about a hundred and ten thousand dollars.
It opened on August twenty-second, 1929.
About two months later, the stock market crashed, and the great boom in theater building soon came to an end.
When you go in, look at the side walls before you look up.
They're designed to suggest the walls of old buildings around an Italian courtyard, so the dark ceiling above reads as the sky.
Nearly a century later, the trick still works.
The Music Box opened at a turning point in movie history.
In 1927, Warner Brothers released The Jazz Singer, with a few minutes of synchronized songs and speech, and audiences were thrilled.
Within two years, theaters across the country were scrambling to install sound equipment, and the studios had all but stopped making silent films.
The Music Box was built for the new era.
Its first feature, according to theater historians, was a talking picture called Mother's Boy, starring the popular tenor Morton Downey.
Yet the building also had chambers for organ pipes, a sign of how fast things were changing.
Just a few years earlier, every movie house needed live music to accompany silent pictures, from a lone organist in a small theater to a full orchestra in a palace.
Sound put thousands of theater musicians out of work.
The Music Box's organ chambers stood empty for more than half a century, until 1984, when a custom electronic organ was installed, with its speakers hidden where the pipes would have gone.
Today the theater is a guardian of film itself.

Its projection booth is one of the few left that can still run the big seventy-millimeter prints made for epics like Lawrence of Arabia and 2001: A Space Odyssey, and the theater holds a festival of them every year.
The people behind the Music Box have also shaped what the rest of the country sees.
In 2007, the company that runs the theater started a distribution business, Music Box Films, which brings foreign and independent movies to American screens.
One of its early hits was the original Swedish film of The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, in 2010.
So a neighborhood movie house on Southport Avenue helped decide what was playing in art houses from coast to coast.
About a mile and a quarter west of here, around Irving Park Road and Western Avenue, stood one of the first real movie studios in America.
Its founder, William Selig, had been a stage magician and the manager of a traveling minstrel show before he got hold of a motion picture camera in the 1890s and began making short films in Chicago.
In 1907, Selig built a proper studio, filling the block bounded by Irving Park, Western, Byron, and Claremont, with a glass-roofed stage to catch the daylight and a backlot for outdoor scenes.
The Selig Polyscope Company turned out westerns, comedies, and adventure pictures by the hundreds, and it gave a young cowboy named Tom Mix his start in the movies.
Mix went on to become the biggest western star of the silent era.
Selig's most notorious production came in 1909.
Former President Theodore Roosevelt had just left for an African safari, and the whole country wanted to see it.
Selig couldn't get a camera to Africa, so he staged the hunt himself.
He hired a vaudeville actor who looked something like Roosevelt, bought an aging lion for a few hundred dollars, dressed a set as the jungle, and filmed the hunt.
Hunting Big Game in Africa was a hit.
Newspapers of the day reported that it had been shot right here in Chicago, and plenty of moviegoers, it's said, thought they were watching the real thing.
Selig also saw that Chicago's gray winters were a problem for an industry that depended on sunlight.
In 1909 he sent a crew to Los Angeles, and his company is often credited with building the first permanent movie studio there.
Over the next decade the whole industry followed the sun west.
Selig's Chicago studio didn't survive the 1910s, and Essanay, the city's other big studio, which you can visit on the Uptown tour, didn't last much longer.
One building from Selig's lot still stands, on Claremont Avenue at Byron Street.
Walk north to Irving Park Road and east to Clark Street, to the gates of Graceland Cemetery.
Founded in 1860, Graceland is often called the cemetery of architects, and it's the resting place of many of the people who built Chicago.

It was designed as a peaceful landscape, by landscape architects including Ossian Cole Simonds, who believed a cemetery should feel like a natural park, with native trees and shrubs, open lawns, and winding drives.
It's a beautiful place to walk.
The cemetery office near the gate often has maps showing where the famous graves are.
Just inside, look for Eternal Silence, a hooded, robed figure by Lorado Taft, made in 1909 for the grave of Dexter Graves, an early hotel owner.
The bronze has turned green with age, except for the face, which is dark in the shadow of the hood.
There's a legend that if you look into its eyes, you'll see a vision of your own death, and another that it can't be photographed.
Visitors photograph it every day.
And look for the grave of Jack Johnson, the first Black heavyweight boxing champion of the world, who won the title in 1908.
Johnson was a flamboyant figure who refused to play the humble role white America expected of him.
He opened a nightclub in Chicago, the Café de Champion, and married white women, which outraged many white Americans.
In 1913, he was convicted under the Mann Act, a law against transporting women across state lines for immoral purposes, in a case widely seen as racially motivated.
He fled the country and later served time in prison.
In 2018, he was granted a posthumous presidential pardon.
Somewhere in these grounds is also George Pullman, the railroad sleeping-car magnate whose company town and the bitter strike of 1894 made him one of the most hated men in America.
When he died in 1897, his family feared his body might be dug up and desecrated.
He was buried at night in a pit lined with concrete and steel rails, under tons of cement.
The Pullman tour tells his story.
Baseball is here too.
Near the main drive, look for the grave of William Hulbert, who founded baseball's National League in 1876 and ran the Chicago team that became the Cubs.
His headstone is a giant stone baseball, carved with the names of the league's original cities.
And Ernie Banks, Mr. Cub, the Hall of Fame shortstop who played nineteen seasons at Wrigley Field and was famous for saying, "Let's play two," was buried here in 2015.
Look also for the little girl in the glass box: a lifelike marble statue of a child, sitting on a chair, sealed in a glass case.
She's known as Inez Clarke, and the legend says she died young in 1880, and that on stormy nights she vanishes from her box.
Historians who have dug into the records have found that even her name may be a mistake, but the statue is one of the most visited graves in the cemetery.
Graceland belongs to a movement that changed how Americans buried their dead.
In the early 1800s, most city dead went into crowded churchyards or bleak public burying grounds.

Then, in 1831, Boston's leading families opened Mount Auburn Cemetery, outside the city in Cambridge, as a landscaped garden with winding paths, ponds, and trees, where the living could stroll and remember.
It was such a success that cities across the country copied it, and for a generation these garden cemeteries served as America's first great public parks.
Chicago's own city cemetery, on the lakefront where Lincoln Park is now, was low, wet, and much too close to the city's drinking water.
In 1860, a lawyer and businessman named Thomas Bryan bought land out here, then well beyond the city limits, and founded Graceland.
Bryan was a devoted gardener, and a few years later he was the man who bought Lincoln's own draft of the Emancipation Proclamation at the city's great Sanitary Fair.
The first plan of the grounds was drawn by Swain Nelson, a Swedish-born gardener.
Then William Le Baron Jenney, the engineer who later designed the Home Insurance Building downtown, was hired to drain the marshy ground and dig the little lake to the north, Lake Willowmere.
The person who shaped Graceland most was Bryan's nephew, Bryan Lathrop, who led the cemetery for decades.
Lathrop wanted the grounds to read as one continuous landscape, not a city of little fenced family yards.

In the 1870s, on the advice of the landscape architect Horace Cleveland, the cemetery even turned the gravel paths between the graves into lawn, and owners were steered away from walling off their lots with fences, hedges, and stone curbs.
That's why Graceland feels so different from older burial grounds.
Here the monuments stand in a landscape, instead of the landscape squeezing in between the monuments.
Much of the landscape around you is the work of Ossian Cole Simonds, one of the most influential American landscape designers most people have never heard of.
Simonds grew up on a farm in Michigan and studied engineering and architecture at the University of Michigan, where one of his teachers was William Le Baron Jenney.
In 1878, Jenney brought him here to help with the drainage.
Simonds stayed for more than half a century, as the cemetery's superintendent until 1897 and as its consulting landscape gardener until his death in 1931.
From Bryan Lathrop he learned the English style of naturalistic landscape design, with its sweeping lawns and irregular groves.
But Simonds gave it a Midwestern accent.

Instead of exotic imports, he favored the trees and shrubs that grew wild in the region, like oaks, hawthorns, and dogwoods, and he planted them in thick masses along the edges, the way they grow at the margin of a woodland.
The centers he left open, so you look down long, sunlit lawns framed by trees.
As you walk, notice how the drives curve so that each bend opens a new view, and how the plantings screen out the busy streets beyond the walls.
Simonds became one of the founders of the American Society of Landscape Architects, in 1899, though he always preferred to call himself a landscape gardener.
He designed parks, campuses, and estates across the Midwest, and he worked for years on the northern extension of Lincoln Park.

In 1915 the writer Wilhelm Miller named him, along with Jens Jensen and Walter Burley Griffin, as a creator of what Miller called the prairie style of landscape gardening, the outdoor cousin of Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie School houses.
In 1920 Simonds put his ideas into a book, Landscape Gardening.
Its advice comes down to this: study nature, and learn from it.
William Hulbert's stone baseball marks the grave of the man who turned the game into a business.
Hulbert was a Chicago coal dealer and a backer of the White Stockings, a professional team founded in 1870.
The Great Fire of 1871 burned their ballpark, and the club sat out the next two seasons.

By 1875 Hulbert was running the team, and he secretly signed four stars of the champion Boston club, including the pitcher Albert Spalding, plus a young infielder from Philadelphia named Adrian Anson.
That broke the rules of the existing league, so Hulbert organized a new one.
In February 1876, he and other club owners met at a hotel in New York and founded the National League.
Unlike the old league, it was run by the owners, not the players, and a few years later it adopted the reserve clause, which bound a player to his team for as long as the team wanted him.
Chicago won the new league's first championship.
Spalding pitched and managed, and in 1876 he and his brother opened a sporting goods store in Chicago.
It grew into one of the biggest sporting goods companies in the world, and for a century it supplied the league's official baseball.
When Hulbert died in 1882, Spalding took over the club.
The team's great star was Anson, known as Cap, a big first baseman who led Chicago to five pennants in the 1880s and became, by most counts, the first player to reach three thousand hits.

He also made a public show of refusing to play against Black players, and historians count him among the men most responsible for the color line that kept Black players out of the major leagues until 1947.
The team went through several nicknames.
Early in the twentieth century, sportswriters started calling the young squad the Cubs, and the name stuck.
Jack Johnson won the heavyweight championship in Australia, the day after Christmas in 1908, and much of white America immediately went looking for someone to take it back from him.
Newspapers called the search a hunt for a Great White Hope.
The man they settled on was Jim Jeffries, the retired former champion, who had never lost a fight.
Jeffries came out of retirement, he said, to prove that a white man was better than a Black man.
They met in Reno, Nevada, on July fourth, 1910, in an outdoor ring built for the occasion, before a crowd of nearly twenty thousand.
Johnson toyed with Jeffries, smiling and talking as he fought, and in the fifteenth round, after Jeffries had been knocked down for the first time in his career, his corner stopped the fight.
That night, as Black Americans celebrated, white mobs attacked them in cities across the country, and a number of people were killed.
Even the film of the fight became a battleground.
Many cities banned it, and two years later Congress banned the shipping of prizefight films across state lines altogether, a ban that lasted until 1940.
After his conviction, Johnson fled to Europe.
In 1915 he lost his title to Jess Willard, in an open-air fight in Havana that went twenty-six rounds.
In 1920 he surrendered and served his sentence at the federal penitentiary in Leavenworth, Kansas, where, the story goes, he worked out an improved wrench that he later patented.
He spent his last years boxing in exhibitions, giving talks, and telling his own story to anyone who would listen.
In June 1946 he was driving fast through North Carolina when his car crashed, and he died soon afterward.
By the usual account, he had just stormed out of a roadside diner that refused to serve him because he was Black.
He was sixty-eight years old.
Walk north along the cemetery's drives toward Lake Willowmere, the small lake in the northern part of the grounds.
On a small island in the lake, under a plain boulder, is Daniel Burnham, the architect of the World's Fair and the Plan of Chicago.
John Wellborn Root, his partner, who died so young, is buried here too, not far away.
Look also for the Getty Tomb, designed in 1890 by Louis Sullivan for the family of a lumber merchant, Henry Getty.
Its intricate bronze gates and the lacy stone ornament on its upper half, contrasted with the plain stone below, make it one of Sullivan's masterpieces.
Architects come from around the world to see it.
Sullivan himself is buried in Graceland, under a rough stone put up by his admirers, with a bronze portrait medallion.
He died poor in 1924, and the monument was paid for by friends and colleagues.
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe is here too, under a simple, polished black granite slab, as minimal as one of his buildings.
So are the merchants and industrialists whose names you've heard on other tours.
Potter and Bertha Palmer lie in twin sarcophagi under a Greek temple of columns.
Marshall Field's grave has a seated, veiled figure called Memory, by Daniel Chester French, who sculpted the statue in the Lincoln Memorial.
Philip Armour, the meatpacker, is here, and Allan Pinkerton, the founder of the famous detective agency, who guarded Abraham Lincoln on his way to his first inauguration.
Wandering Graceland, you can trace the whole story of Chicago's rise in its gravestones.
In the Pinkerton family plot lies Kate Warne, whom Pinkerton hired in 1856 as the first female detective in the United States.
She helped him protect Lincoln on his secret journey through Baltimore to Washington in 1861, when the agency uncovered a plot to kill him on the way.
This is the end of the Lakeview tour.
The Sheridan station on the Red Line, a few blocks east of the cemetery's main gate on Irving Park Road, will take you back downtown.
Allan Pinkerton came to America on the run.
Born in Glasgow in 1819, he trained as a cooper, a barrel maker, and as a young man he joined the Chartists, a movement demanding the vote for working men.
In 1842, with the authorities after him, he married and sailed for America.
He settled in Dundee, Illinois, on the Fox River northwest of Chicago, and opened a cooperage.
One day in 1847, looking for wood for barrel staves on an island in the river, he stumbled on a camp of counterfeiters.
He helped the sheriff round them up, and before long he was a deputy sheriff himself.
In 1849 he became Chicago's first full-time police detective, and around 1850 he went into business for himself.
His agency's emblem was a wide-open eye over the words We Never Sleep, and it's often said that's where the phrase private eye comes from.
Pinkerton was a fierce abolitionist.

In March 1859, when John Brown passed through Chicago with a group of people he had freed from slavery in Missouri, Pinkerton sheltered them, gave Brown five hundred dollars, and got them onto a train to Detroit, on the road to Canada.
That fall, Brown led his raid on Harpers Ferry.

During the Civil War, Pinkerton ran intelligence for General George McClellan, under the name Major E. J. Allen, and his reports badly overestimated the size of the Confederate army, which helped make the cautious general even more cautious.
After the war, his agency chased train robbers and outlaws across the country.
His sons built it into one of the biggest private police forces in the country, hired by companies to guard property and break strikes.
In 1892, a gun battle between Pinkerton guards and striking steelworkers at Homestead, Pennsylvania, left men dead on both sides.
Pinkerton didn't live to see it.
He died in 1884, and the story goes that he slipped on a sidewalk, bit his tongue, and died of the infection that followed.
Louis Sullivan designed only three tombs in his career, and two of them are here.
Seeing them side by side is one of the best ways to understand what he was after.
The first is the Ryerson tomb, built in the late 1880s for Martin Ryerson, a lumber merchant who had died in 1887.
His son, also named Martin, was one of Sullivan's patrons, and later one of the great benefactors of the Art Institute and the University of Chicago.
Sullivan made the tomb of polished dark granite, combining two ancient Egyptian forms, a low, flat-topped tomb and a pyramid.
It's heavy, dark, and severe.
The second is the Getty tomb, from 1890, which you heard about at this stop.
Henry Getty built it for his wife, Carrie.
