Frank Lloyd Wright, who was working in Sullivan's office then, later wrote that outside of music he could think of no finer requiem.
The third is in Saint Louis.
The Wainwright tomb, from 1892, was built for the wife of Ellis Wainwright, a brewer, whose office tower in Saint Louis Sullivan had just designed.
It's a stone cube topped by a dome, plainer than the Getty tomb and lighter than the Ryerson.
All three show Sullivan working on the problem that occupied him all his life: how to make an architecture of his own time that didn't simply copy the past.
Even when he borrowed ancient forms, he stripped them down and then gave them ornament of his own, drawn from plants and geometry.

A few steps from Sullivan's own grave, look for the small marker of Richard Nickel, the photographer who spent his life documenting and trying to save Sullivan's buildings, and who died in 1972 inside one of them, the Stock Exchange, as it was being torn down.
Graceland rewards wandering, and its old monuments speak a language of their own.
Once you know a few words of it, you can read the stones as you walk.
An obelisk, the tall, tapering shaft borrowed from ancient Egypt, stood for eternity, and it was hugely fashionable among wealthy Victorians.
A column broken off partway up marks a life cut short.
An urn draped with cloth is a sign of mourning, the veil between the living and the dead.
A torch turned upside down means a life put out.
A lamb usually marks the grave of a child.
And if you see a gravestone carved to look like a tree stump, it may belong to a member of the Woodmen of the World, a fraternal insurance society that provided tree-stump markers to its members.
Then look for a few of Graceland's stranger monuments.
Peter Schoenhofen ran one of Chicago's big breweries, makers of Edelweiss beer, and his family's tomb, designed by the architect Richard Schmidt, is a small stone pyramid.
Guarding its door are a sphinx on one side and a Christian angel on the other, as if the family wanted to cover every possibility.
On the grave of Victor Lawson, who published the Chicago Daily News for nearly half a century, stands a towering knight gripping a sword.
It's called the Crusader, and it's by Lorado Taft, the sculptor of Eternal Silence.
The words carved below come from an old book of scripture: Above all things, truth beareth away the victory.
It's a fitting motto for a newspaperman.
And look for the grave of Fazlur Khan, the structural engineer behind the Hancock Center and the Sears Tower.
The architects who shaped the skyline are here, and so is one of the engineers who made it stand up.
This tour explores two neighborhoods on the Far North Side, about six miles north of the Loop: Uptown, along Broadway and Lawrence Avenue, and Andersonville, along Clark Street.
A century ago, Uptown was one of the great entertainment districts in America.
The elevated line reached here in 1900, and in the 1910s and 1920s, the neighborhood boomed.
Developers built apartment hotels, ballrooms, nightclubs, and movie palaces, aimed at the young, single office workers who were pouring into Chicago and wanted to live near the lake and the trains.
On a Saturday night in the 1920s, tens of thousands of people came to Uptown to dance at the Aragon, see a movie at the Uptown Theatre, or listen to jazz at the Green Mill.
Uptown was also, briefly, part of the movie business, because before Hollywood took over, Chicago was one of the centers of American film, and one of its biggest studios was here.
After the Depression and the Second World War, Uptown declined.

Its big apartments were divided into small units, and it became a landing place for newcomers with little money: white migrants from Appalachia in the 1950s, Native Americans relocated from reservations by a federal program, and later refugees from Southeast Asia, Ethiopia, and many other places.
For decades, it was one of the most diverse neighborhoods in the country, and also one of the poorest, with a large population in single-room hotels.
In recent decades, much of it has gentrified.
Andersonville, just to the west, has a different story.
It grew up as a Swedish community in the late nineteenth century.
Swedes came to Chicago in large numbers, and by 1900, Chicago had one of the largest Swedish populations of any city in the world.
Swedish shops, bakeries, delis, and churches lined Clark Street.

Many Swedes have since moved away, but the neighborhood has kept its Swedish flavor, and since the 1980s, it has also become one of the centers of Chicago's lesbian and gay community, known for its independent businesses.
We'll start at the corner of Broadway and Lawrence, in the heart of old Uptown, walk north and west through Argyle Street, then to Andersonville on Clark Street, and end at the lake in Edgewater.
You're at the corner of Broadway and Lawrence Avenue.
On the northwest corner, look for the green neon sign of the Green Mill Cocktail Lounge, one of the oldest and most famous jazz clubs in the country.
It opened in 1907 as a roadhouse, and around 1910 it was renamed the Green Mill, after the Moulin Rouge, the red mill, in Paris, complete with a green windmill on the roof.
In the 1920s, during Prohibition, a part owner was Jack McGurn, known as Machine Gun Jack, one of Al Capone's top gunmen.
There's a well-known story about the comedian and singer Joe E. Lewis, who performed here.
In 1927, he decided to leave for a rival club.
Shortly afterwards, he was attacked, and his throat was cut.
He survived, learned to speak and sing again, and went on to a long career.
The story was later made into a film starring Frank Sinatra.
Inside, there's a booth said to have been Capone's favorite, with a view of both doors, and there are stories of trap doors and tunnels under the bar.
Those are legends, but the club's dark wood, velvet booths, and statues haven't changed much since the 1930s.
The Green Mill is also where the poetry slam was born.
In 1986, a construction worker and poet named Marc Smith started a Sunday night competition here, where poets performed their work and the audience judged them.
Poetry slams have since spread all over the world.
Now look across Broadway at the huge, ornate building with the tall vertical sign.
This is the Uptown Theatre, opened in 1925 by Balaban and Katz, the same company that built the Chicago Theatre downtown, and designed by the same architects, the Rapp brothers.
With more than four thousand seats, it was one of the largest movie palaces in the country, with a lobby that rises several stories, like a Spanish cathedral.
It closed in 1981, and efforts to restore it have dragged on for years.
Jack McGurn, the Green Mill's gangster part owner, was the chief suspect in planning the Saint Valentine's Day Massacre in 1929, though he was never convicted.
Seven years later, almost to the day, on February 15th, 1936, he was shot dead in a bowling alley on Milwaukee Avenue.
Today, the Green Mill is still a working jazz club, open late every night, and it's one of the best places in Chicago to hear live music.
Before you leave the corner, walk a block south on Broadway to Leland Avenue, and look at the Uptown Broadway Building, built in 1926.
Its facade is covered with colorful glazed terra cotta in an extravagant Spanish style, with twisting columns, shields, and carved figures.
It's one of the most exuberant terra cotta buildings in a city full of them, and a reminder of how much money flowed into Uptown in the 1920s.
The Green Mill began as a place for mourners.

In 1907, when this part of the North Side was still thinly built up, a roadhouse here served drinks and food to people coming back from funerals at Graceland and Saint Boniface, the two big cemeteries a short ride away.
It was known as Pop Morse's Roadhouse.
In 1910, a businessman named Tom Chamales bought it and turned it into a pleasure garden, the Green Mill Gardens, with a big sunken garden for outdoor dancing and entertainment.
As the elevated trains brought crowds to Uptown, it became one of the busiest nightspots on the North Side.
Over the years the gardens disappeared, and the Green Mill shrank to the snug cocktail lounge you see today.
Then came the long slide.
Uptown sank into poverty after the Second World War, and the Green Mill sank with it.

A man named Steve Brend, who had started working there in 1938, bought it in 1960 and kept it going through the lean years, when the neighborhood was better known for its flophouses than its nightlife.
In 1986, a young bar owner named Dave Jemilo bought the club.
Instead of gutting the old room, he cleaned it up and restored it, and he made it a serious jazz room again.
That bet paid off.
The Green Mill became one of the places where Chicago's jazz musicians grew up.
The pianist and singer Patricia Barber has held down Monday nights here for years, and the singer Kurt Elling was a regular here early in his career.
The best reason to come is simple.
Late at night, with the lights low and a band playing, the Green Mill is about as close as you can get to stepping into the city's past while it's still going on around you.
On a Sunday night at the Green Mill, you can still see the show where it all started.
Marc Smith found most poetry readings deadly.
Poets mumbled into their manuscripts, and audiences sat in polite silence.
In late 1984 he started a Monday night open mic at a bar called the Get Me High Lounge, and he began experimenting with ways to wake things up.
The idea that stuck was competition, scored like a boxing match or an Olympic event.
In 1986 the show moved here, as the Uptown Poetry Slam, at about the time Dave Jemilo bought the place, and it has been here ever since.
The format was simple and deliberately rowdy.
Poets got a few minutes each, and the audience was encouraged to react out loud, with cheers, groans, and snapping fingers.
In the version of the slam that spread to other cities, judges picked at random from the crowd hold up scores from zero to ten, and the poet with the highest total wins.
Nobody was supposed to take the scores too seriously.
As slam poets like to say, the points are not the point; the point is the poetry.
From Chicago, slams spread to other cities, and by the early 1990s there was a national championship.

They helped turn spoken word into an art form of its own, they gave a stage to poets who had never been near a university writing program, and they carried poetry into high schools, where youth slams now draw crowds of teenagers who would never have sat through a traditional reading.
Smith, for his part, kept hosting the Sunday show for decades, still insisting that a poem should be performed, not just recited, and that the audience has a right to talk back.
Across Broadway, the Uptown Theatre was the biggest of all the palaces Balaban and Katz built, and it's often described as the largest freestanding theater in North America.
Freestanding is the key word.
Downtown, many movie palaces were squeezed into office buildings, with the auditorium tucked behind a narrow entrance.
Out here, where land was cheaper, the Rapp brothers could make the whole thing one monumental building, taking up a big piece of a city block.
The plan was a procession.
From the street you passed under the tall sign into the outer lobby, then into that cathedral of a grand lobby, and up broad staircases toward balconies that seemed to hang in midair.
The style is a lavish Spanish Baroque, with plaster ornament on nearly every surface.
Even waiting was part of the show.
The crowd for the next screening could fill those lobbies and feel like guests in a palace, not customers in a line.
The last show here was a concert by the J. Geils Band, in 1981.
Then the doors closed, and the building sat dark for decades, its plaster and paint suffering from neglect.
Preservationists campaigned for years to save it, and the building survived, which in a city that has lost most of its movie palaces is a small miracle.
In 2008, after a foreclosure, the Chicago concert promoters Jam Productions bought the Uptown for about three million dollars.
In 2018 the city announced a plan to restore it, at a cost then estimated at seventy-five million dollars, and the estimates have kept climbing since, well past a hundred million.
Restoring a building like this means recasting ornament by hand, rebuilding systems that are a century old, and bringing it all up to modern codes.
For now, the best you can do is stand on Broadway, look up at the facade and the sign, and imagine the crowds lining up on a Saturday night in 1925.
Walk east on Lawrence Avenue to number 1106, the Aragon Ballroom, with its tall, Spanish-style facade.
The Aragon opened in 1926, built by two Greek immigrant brothers, Andrew and William Karzas, who also owned the Trianon Ballroom on the South Side.
The interior was designed to look like the courtyard of a Spanish palace, with balconies, arches, tiled roofs, and a ceiling painted like a night sky, with twinkling stars and drifting clouds.
It was meant to feel like dancing outdoors.
In the age of the big bands, from the 1920s to the 1950s, the Aragon was one of the most famous ballrooms in America.
The great dance orchestras played here, and their performances were broadcast live on the radio across the country.
The Karzas brothers enforced strict rules of conduct to make the ballroom respectable: no improper dancing, and an atmosphere that made it safe for young women to come.
As big band dancing faded, the Aragon was used for many things, including roller skating, boxing, and wrestling.
Since the 1960s, it has been a concert venue, especially for rock, and it was known for a while by the nickname the Aragon Brawlroom, for its rowdy crowds.
Many of the biggest names in rock have played here, along with generations of Chicago's own bands.

As you walk along Broadway and Lawrence, look for other remnants of the old entertainment district, including the Riviera Theatre, at Broadway and Racine, which opened in 1917, and the big apartment hotels, built for single people, with small apartments and shared lobbies and dining rooms.
Andrew and William Karzas made their first fortune in the early movie business, running nickelodeons and then movie theaters.
In the early 1920s they saw a bigger opportunity in dancing.
Young people were pouring into the city to work in offices, stores, and factories, and dance halls were booming.
But many of the halls had bad reputations, for liquor, fights, and worse, and reformers campaigned against them.
The Karzas brothers built palaces instead, and they sold respectability as much as music.
The first was the Trianon, designed by the Rapp brothers, which opened in December 1922 at 62nd Street and Cottage Grove Avenue, in Woodlawn on the South Side.
Its decorations were borrowed from the palace of Versailles, its owners advertised it as the most beautiful ballroom in the world, and it could hold about three thousand dancers.
By one account, the band had to play a waltz every third number.
The Aragon followed in 1926, on the North Side, so the brothers had the city covered from both ends.
They ran their ballrooms like a well-mannered business.
Bands were chosen for sweet, danceable music rather than hot jazz, and the Trianon, according to some histories, booked only white bands.
Admission was kept cheap enough for a stenographer or a shop clerk.
The Trianon even had its own radio station, which helped spread its name across the Midwest.
The Trianon is long gone, torn down in 1967 to make room for low-income housing.
The Aragon has lasted far longer.
In the summer of 2026 it celebrated its hundredth birthday, still drawing crowds, though the music would have startled the Karzas brothers.
For years, millions of Americans who never set foot in Chicago knew this ballroom's name.
Starting in the late 1920s, the radio station WGN broadcast an hour of music from the Aragon almost every night, to listeners across the United States and Canada.
A family in Kansas or Ontario could roll back the rug and dance to the same band that was playing here.
No bandleader was more closely tied to the Aragon than Wayne King, known as the Waltz King.
He played the saxophone and led a smooth, sweet orchestra that specialized in waltzes, and his theme song, The Waltz You Saved for Me, became one of the most familiar melodies on the air.

His orchestra played the Aragon from 1927 into the middle of the 1930s, and in those years King was among the most popular bandleaders in the country, with a radio show of his own sponsored by a cosmetics company.
After the Second World War, Americans stayed home with their television sets, and the great ballrooms emptied one by one.
Fittingly, when the Aragon's ballroom era ended, Wayne King was booked to play the last dances, in February 1964.
In the late 1960s, the Aragon spent a couple of years as a nightclub called the Cheetah, before the rock concerts took over.
If you go to a show here, look up.
The make-believe Spanish night that the dancers saw is still overhead, so the crowd at a heavy metal concert is standing where couples once waltzed to Wayne King.
The room is also notorious among concertgoers for its echo.
It was built for saxophones and violins, not stacks of amplifiers, and bands have been wrestling with its sound for half a century.
Look at the big brick and terra cotta buildings along Lawrence Avenue and Sheridan Road.
Many of them went up in the 1920s as apartment hotels, a kind of housing that Uptown specialized in.
An apartment hotel was halfway between a hotel and a home.
Tenants rented by the week or the month, often furnished, in units of one or two rooms.
A bed might fold up into a closet during the day to turn the bedroom into a living room.

There might be a tiny kitchenette or no kitchen at all, because downstairs were the services of a hotel: a front desk, maid service, a dining room or coffee shop, and sometimes a ballroom or a swimming pool in the grander buildings.
The customers were the young office workers who were pouring into Chicago in the 1920s: secretaries, clerks, salesmen, and teachers, many of them living on their own for the first time.
They wanted to be near the lake, the elevated trains, and the nightlife, and they didn't want to cook or keep house.
Uptown gave them all of it.
The Depression and the war changed everything.

Apartments were cut into smaller and smaller units, and by the 1960s many of these buildings had become rooming houses, with shared bathrooms down the hall, renting cheaply by the week to people with nowhere else to go: migrants from the South, old men living on pensions, and later, people released from the state mental hospitals as they emptied out.
Since the 1990s, many of those buildings have been renovated into market-rate apartments, and the fight over what that means for poor residents has been one of Uptown's longest political battles.
One of the biggest, the Lawrence House, a short walk east of the Aragon, shows both sides of the story.
For decades it rented cheap rooms to people with few other choices.
In the 2010s it was renovated into stylish apartments, and most of its old tenants had to find homes elsewhere.
Walk north on Broadway to Argyle Street, and turn east.
This short stretch of Argyle, between Broadway and Sheridan Road, is the heart of what's sometimes called Little Saigon, or Asia on Argyle.
After the end of the Vietnam War in 1975, hundreds of thousands of refugees left Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, many of them by boat.
Many of them came to the United States, and some were resettled in Chicago, often in Uptown, where rents were cheap.
Ethnic Chinese from Vietnam, who had faced persecution there, were a large part of this group.
They opened restaurants, groceries, bakeries, jewelry stores, and travel agencies along Argyle Street, turning it into one of the most important Southeast Asian commercial streets in the Midwest.
There had been plans, in the 1970s, by Chinese American business leaders, to develop this area as a second Chinatown.
The arrival of the refugees gave the street its character.
Today, Argyle Street is famous for its Vietnamese restaurants, especially its bowls of pho, the beef noodle soup, and banh mi sandwiches.
In the late 2010s, the street was redesigned as a shared street, without curbs, so that pedestrians, cyclists, and cars mix, and it hosts night markets in summer.

The Uptown neighborhood around it has also been home to refugees and immigrants from Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia, Bosnia, and many other places, as well as a large Native American community, and it's one of the most diverse parts of the city.

In the 1950s and 1960s, Uptown was home to so many poor white migrants from the mountains of Kentucky, Tennessee, and West Virginia, who came north to work in the factories, that people called it Hillbilly Heaven.

In 1969, a group of young Southern whites from Uptown, called the Young Patriots, joined an alliance with Fred Hampton's Black Panther Party and the Puerto Rican Young Lords, to fight together against poverty, police brutality, and urban renewal.
Hampton called it the Rainbow Coalition.
It didn't last long, but the name did.
Jesse Jackson later borrowed it for his own political movement.
In the early 1970s, a businessman named Jimmy Wong had a big idea for this street.
Wong worked with the Hip Sing Association, one of the old Chinese American fraternal organizations, which moved its Chicago offices here, to Argyle, in 1971.

Across the country, the Hip Sing had long been rivals of the On Leong, the association that dominated the old Chinatown on the South Side, which may help explain the appeal of a Chinatown of their own.
By 1974, Wong and his allies controlled most of the property along these few blocks.
Wong's plan was grand: a new Chinatown, complete with a shopping mall, pagodas, and reflecting ponds, to rival the crowded old one.
It never happened.
An injury forced Wong to retire, and the project stalled.
Then the refugees came, as you heard at the stop, and many of them were exactly the tenants the plan needed.
The ethnic Chinese from Vietnam usually spoke Cantonese or another Chinese language as well as Vietnamese, so they could deal easily with Chinese American landlords.
And many of them already knew how to run a shop, because in Vietnam, the Chinese minority had long been prominent in trade.
The street still needed customers from the rest of the city.
A community booster named Charlie Soo took up the cause in 1979, promoting Argyle to Chicagoans who had never been there, and in 1981 he started an annual food festival on the street.
So a second Chinatown did arrive, in a way, just not the one anyone had planned.
It was built not by developers with a master plan but by families running small businesses, often working long hours, with their children doing homework at the back tables.
Today a younger generation runs many of those businesses, and new restaurants mix with the old.
But the street still feels like what it became in those years, a place where newcomers could find their footing.
If you eat on Argyle Street, there's a good chance you'll end up with a bowl of pho, so here's a little background.
Pho was born in northern Vietnam early in the twentieth century, around Hanoi, and food historians still argue about its ancestors.
Some point to the French, who ruled Vietnam and brought a taste for beef.
Others point to Chinese noodle soups.
The spices in the broth, star anise, cinnamon, cloves, and charred ginger and onion, suggest a bit of both.
When Vietnam was divided in 1954, hundreds of thousands of people fled the communist north for the south, and pho went with them.
In Saigon it became sweeter and more lavish, served with a plate of fresh herbs, bean sprouts, lime, and chilies, and with bottles of hoisin and hot sauce on the table.
That southern style is what refugees brought to America after 1975, and it's what you'll find on most menus here.
To eat it like a regular, taste the broth first, before you add anything.
Then tear in the basil, add sprouts and a squeeze of lime, and work with chopsticks in one hand and the spoon in the other.
Don't be shy about slurping.
Then there's banh mi, the Vietnamese sandwich.
It starts with a light, crackly baguette, another inheritance from the French, stuffed with pâté, cold cuts or grilled meat, pickled carrots and daikon radish, cucumber, cilantro, and sliced chilies.
And look for Vietnamese iced coffee, strong and dark, dripped slowly through a little metal filter over sweetened condensed milk, then poured over ice.
Argyle isn't only Vietnamese.
Look for Chinese barbecue shops with roast ducks and slabs of pork hanging in the window, and for bakeries that sell mooncakes in the fall, around the time of the harvest moon festival.
Few streets in the city let you eat this well for so little.
Why did so many mountain people end up in Uptown?

Back home in Appalachia, machines were replacing coal miners and small farms were failing, and after the Second World War, a steady stream of families headed north to Chicago, Detroit, Cincinnati, and other industrial cities.
Uptown, with its cheap furnished rooms and its day-labor offices, was often their first stop.
Plenty of Chicagoans looked down on them, and landlords, employers, and the police often treated them as a problem to be managed.
In the mid-1960s, a group of college students from Students for a Democratic Society moved into Uptown to organize the poor.
Their project was called Jobs or Income Now.
They organized tenants and people on welfare and protested against slumlords and police abuse.
But some of the young men from the neighborhood felt that middle-class students from elsewhere were running the show.
In 1968, several of them, including Junebug Boykin and Doug Youngblood, founded their own group, the Young Patriots.
They were poor, Southern, and white, and they talked like the neighborhood.
They took on landlords who let buildings rot, police who treated young Southerners as suspects, and city plans to clear blocks of cheap housing.
In 1970 they led a sit-in at a city health clinic in Uptown, demanding that it stay open at hours when working people could actually use it.
Their alliance with the Black Panthers and the Young Lords, the Rainbow Coalition, you heard about at the stop.
By 1973 the Young Patriots had mostly faded away.
In recent years, a few of the surviving members have written and spoken about that time, a surprising chapter in the history of both the New Left and the white working class.
Uptown's habit of organizing didn't fade with them.

In the decades since, tenants' groups, legal aid clinics, and churches here have fought evictions and the loss of cheap housing, often against the same pressures of renewal and rising rents that the Patriots fought.
In the 1950s, the federal government launched a program to move Native Americans off reservations and into cities.
The Bureau of Indian Affairs offered travel money, a little help, and the promise of jobs in places like Denver, Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Chicago.
In Washington, the program was seen as a way to fold Native people into the mainstream and shrink the government's obligations on reservations.
For many who came here, it meant a single check, a month's rent, and directions to Uptown.
By the census count, Chicago's Native population grew from fewer than eight hundred people in 1950 to more than six thousand five hundred in 1970, and Uptown became its center.
In 1953, the American Indian Center opened here, one of the first urban Native community centers in the country.
It became a place for powwows, meals, social services, and simply meeting people from dozens of nations who had landed in the same strange city.
The housing was often terrible.
In May 1970, a Menominee woman named Carol Warrington, who had been withholding rent because her landlord refused to make repairs, was evicted from an apartment near Wrigley Field.
Her neighbors and supporters answered by pitching tents in a parking lot next to the ballpark.
They called the camp the Chicago Indian Village, and they demanded decent housing.

The protests moved from site to site for about two years, and they drew national attention to the lives of Native people in American cities, at the same moment that activists were occupying Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay.
As Uptown gentrified, many Native families moved away, and the American Indian Center eventually moved farther northwest.
But the Chicago area still has one of the largest urban Native communities in the country, with people from well over a hundred tribal nations, and Uptown is where much of that story began.
Walk west on Argyle Street, under the elevated tracks, to number 1345.
Look at the entrance of the long, low brick building, and you'll see a terra cotta portrait of a Native American chief in a feathered headdress.
That was the logo of Essanay Studios, one of the most important movie studios in America in the 1910s.
Essanay was founded in 1907 by George Spoor, a Chicago businessman, and Gilbert Anderson, an actor.
The name comes from their initials, S and A. Anderson became famous as Broncho Billy, one of the first cowboy stars of the movies.
The studio made hundreds of films here, and for a few years, Chicago was one of the capitals of the film industry.
In late 1914, Essanay signed the biggest star in the world, Charlie Chaplin, at a huge salary.
Chaplin came to this studio in the winter and made a film here, called His New Job, released in 1915.
But he hated the cold, gray Chicago winter, and he didn't get along with Spoor.
He soon moved to the company's studio in California.
A young woman named Gloria Swanson also got her start at Essanay as an extra, and went on to become one of the greatest stars of the silent era.
Hollywood's weather, light, and space soon drew the film industry west, and Essanay closed by the end of the 1910s.
Today, the building is part of Saint Augustine College, which has kept the studio's history alive, and you can still see the terra cotta logos over the doors.
Gilbert Anderson, the A in Essanay, was born Max Aronson in Little Rock, Arkansas, in 1880.

He drifted into show business as a young man, and in 1903 he landed several small parts in The Great Train Robbery, the short Western made by Thomas Edison's company that became one of the first big hits of the movies.
Anderson saw the future in it.
After he and George Spoor founded Essanay, Anderson ran the company's Westerns.
He wrote, directed, and starred in a long string of short films as Broncho Billy, a rough but good-hearted outlaw who usually did the right thing by the last reel.

Since you can't shoot the Wild West in a Chicago January, he took his crews on the road, and in 1912 Essanay built a western studio in Niles, California, at the foot of Niles Canyon, east of San Francisco Bay.
Niles is where Chaplin went after his miserable Chicago winter, and where he made several of his Essanay films, including The Tramp, one of the films that defined his famous character.
Anderson sold his share of Essanay in 1916 and gave up acting.

He tried producing, without much luck, though one of the short comedies he produced, The Lucky Dog, is remembered today as the first film in which Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy appeared together, years before anyone thought of them as a team.
For decades afterward, Anderson was mostly forgotten.
Then, in 1958, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences gave him an honorary award for his contributions to the movies.
He died in 1971, at the age of ninety.
The town of Niles, now part of Fremont, California, has kept his memory alive with a museum and a silent film festival named for Broncho Billy.
Chicago, where it all started, has this building, and the chief over the door.
Essanay grew up in a business that was trying hard to become a monopoly.
In 1908, Thomas Edison's company, which held key patents on movie cameras and projectors, joined with its main rivals to form the Motion Picture Patents Company, which critics called the Trust.
Its members included Biograph, Vitagraph, and both of Chicago's big studios, Essanay and Selig.
Only members could make movies with the patented equipment, Eastman Kodak agreed to sell raw film only to them, and theaters had to pay a weekly fee to show their pictures.
Chicago was also home to the Trust's most stubborn enemy.
Carl Laemmle was a German immigrant who had managed a clothing store in Oshkosh, Wisconsin.
In 1906 he put most of his savings into a nickelodeon on Milwaukee Avenue, the White Front, and soon he was renting films to other theaters from Chicago.
When the Trust tried to squeeze him, he refused to pay, and in 1909 he began making pictures of his own.
The Trust took him to court again and again.
Laemmle fought back with publicity.
In 1910, the story goes, a rumor spread that a popular actress known only as the Biograph Girl had been killed in a streetcar accident.
Laemmle announced that she was alive, well, and working for him under her real name, Florence Lawrence.
Historians still argue over whether he started the rumor himself, but the stunt helped create something new: the movie star, known to the public by name.
The independents won.
In 1912 Laemmle and his partners formed Universal, and in 1915 a federal court ruled that the Trust had broken the antitrust laws.
By then the independents were heading for Southern California, for its sunshine, its cheap land, and, by some accounts, its distance from the Trust's lawyers.
Universal opened its own studio city near Los Angeles that same year.
Essanay, a charter member of the Trust, never really adjusted to the new world, and within a few years it was gone.
Charlie Chaplin was the biggest name to pass through this building, but he wasn't the only one.
Essanay's Chicago company was full of people who'd go on to fame.
Francis X. Bushman was the studio's matinee idol, a former sculptor's model who became one of the first romantic leading men of the movies, often paired with the actress Beverly Bayne.
Ben Turpin, the cross-eyed comic, worked here for years and played opposite Chaplin in His New Job.
Wallace Beery, a big, rough-hewn young actor, made a series of comedies here as, of all things, a Swedish maid named Sweedie.
Gloria Swanson, the teenage extra you heard about at the stop, later married him, briefly.
Beery went on to win an Academy Award for The Champ.
Behind the camera, a young writer named Louella Parsons worked on scenarios for the studio, years before she became the most feared gossip columnist in Hollywood.
Essanay also filmed the comic fables of the Chicago humorist George Ade.
Most of what Essanay made is gone.
Silent films were printed on flammable nitrate stock, and once sound arrived, studios saw little reason to keep them.
A Library of Congress study in 2013 estimated that about three quarters of American silent feature films are lost.
But sometimes one comes back.
In 1916, Essanay filmed Sherlock Holmes, starring William Gillette, the actor who had made the detective famous on stage, and whose curved pipe helped fix the image of Holmes for good.
For nearly a century the film was thought lost.
Then, in 2014, a print turned up in the vaults of the Cinémathèque française, in Paris.
After a careful restoration, it was shown again in 2015.
It's the only film Gillette ever made, and the only record of the performance that had defined Sherlock Holmes for a generation of theatergoers.
Walk west on Argyle and then north on Clark Street to Foster Avenue, and continue to the 5200 block of Clark.
This is the heart of Andersonville.
In the late nineteenth century, Swedish immigrants settled here.

The usual explanation is that after the Great Fire of 1871, the city banned wooden buildings within its limits, and this area was then outside the city, so working families could build cheaper wooden houses here.
Andersonville became a village of Swedish shops, churches, and social clubs.
Clark Street had Swedish bakeries, delis, and restaurants, and Swedish was spoken in the stores.
At number 5211, look for the Swedish American Museum, founded in 1976.
It tells the story of Swedish immigration to America, and it has a children's museum about the journey of immigrants.
Look for the Swedish flags along the street, and for the blue and yellow on many of the shops.
Andersonville celebrates its heritage each June with Midsommarfest, a street festival marking the summer solstice, the most important holiday of the Swedish year.
In December, there's a Swedish Christmas festival, with the procession of Saint Lucia, a girl in a white gown with a crown of candles.
Since the 1980s, Andersonville has also been one of the centers of Chicago's gay and lesbian community.
Women and Children First, one of the largest feminist bookstores in the country, has been here since the 1990s.
The neighborhood is known for its independent shops and restaurants, and its business association has campaigned to keep chain stores to a minimum.
As you walk along Clark Street, look for the survivors of Swedish Andersonville.
At number 5210, Simon's Tavern, opened by a Swedish immigrant in the 1930s, still has its old neon sign of a fish holding a martini glass.
You'll also find Swedish pancakes with lingonberries on the menus nearby.
A couple of miles west, along Foster Avenue, the Swedish Covenant church built a hospital and a college, North Park University, which are still there.
Chicago's Swedes were carpenters, builders, machinists, and domestic servants, and some became very successful.
Charles Walgreen, the son of Swedish immigrants, opened his first drugstore on Chicago's South Side in 1901, and built it into one of the largest drugstore chains in the country.
Between the middle of the nineteenth century and 1930, more than a million Swedes left for America, by some estimates about one in five of the people in the country.
The great push came at the end of the 1860s.
Three bad harvests in a row, from 1867 to 1869, brought famine to parts of the Swedish countryside.
Underneath the famine was a deeper problem.
Sweden's population had grown fast, thanks, as one Swedish poet famously put it, to peace, vaccine, and potatoes, and there wasn't enough land to go around.
Farms were divided into ever smaller plots, and many younger sons and daughters had no hope of land of their own.
America offered land, jobs, and, for religious dissenters, freedom of worship.
Letters from relatives who had already made the crossing, and the agents of railroads and steamship lines, did the rest.
Many Swedes went on to the farms of Minnesota and the Dakotas, but a great many stopped in Chicago.
By 1900, it was often said, only Stockholm had more Swedes than Chicago.
The first Swedish neighborhood grew up north of the river, around Chicago Avenue, and people called it Swede Town.
As families saved money and the city grew, they moved north and west, to Lake View, to here, and beyond.
Most of them were young, and many were single.

Swedish women were so much in demand as household help that the Swedish maid became a stock figure in American humor, and Swedish men's skill with wood and tools made them a force in the building trades.

The name Andersonville comes, by the usual account, from John Anderson, a Swedish-born farmer who bought land near what's now Clark Street and Foster Avenue in the 1840s, long before most of the Swedes arrived.
A local school later carried the name.
Decades after that, the business owners on Clark Street revived it for their shopping district, and it sounded perfectly Swedish.
Swedish food follows the Swedish calendar, so what you'll find depends on the season.
At Christmas, the centerpiece is the julbord, the Christmas table, a buffet of pickled herring in several sauces, cured salmon called gravlax, meatballs, ham, sausages, and potatoes.
Then there's lutefisk, the dish Swedish Americans love to argue about: dried cod soaked for days in lye, then rinsed and boiled until it turns translucent and trembling.
In the Swedish tradition, it's served with white sauce, peas, and potatoes.
Wash it down with glögg, hot red wine spiced with cinnamon, cloves, and cardamom, poured over raisins and almonds.
On Saint Lucia's Day, December thirteenth, the Lucia procession comes with saffron buns, curled into the shape of an S and called Lucia cats.
All year round, look for limpa, a dark rye bread sweetened with molasses and flavored with orange peel and anise or fennel.
And look for cardamom in everything.
Swedes put it in buns, cookies, and coffee breads, and the habit of a coffee break with something sweet, called fika, is close to a national institution.
Those Swedish pancakes on the menus nearby are thin, like French crepes, and the lingonberries that come with them are a tart red berry from the northern forests, cooked into a jam.
In Sweden, pancakes are traditionally served on Thursdays, after a bowl of yellow split pea soup, a custom that goes back centuries.
The old Swedish bakeries and delis on Clark Street have mostly closed, as families moved away and the neighborhood changed.
But the traditions hold on, on a few menus, at the museum's holiday programs, and at the festivals that bring Swedish Americans back to Clark Street every year.
The Swedes who built Andersonville didn't all worship the same way.
In Sweden, almost everyone belonged to the state Lutheran church.
But in the nineteenth century, a revival movement swept the countryside.

Its followers, first called readers and later Mission Friends, met in homes to read the Bible and pray together, often without a clergyman, and they stressed a personal experience of faith over the formal rituals of the state church.
For years, such meetings were frowned on by the authorities, and they could even be against the law.
In America, with no state church to answer to, Swedish immigrants sorted themselves out.
Many joined the Augustana Synod, a Swedish Lutheran church founded in 1860.
Others became Methodists or Baptists.
And in 1885, in Chicago, the Mission Friends founded a denomination of their own, the Swedish Evangelical Mission Covenant.
You heard that the Covenant built a hospital and a college a couple of miles west of here.
The college began in Minneapolis and moved to Chicago in 1894, onto land along Foster Avenue, where it became North Park College, now North Park University.
For generations, Swedish American pastors and teachers trained there.
For decades, these churches held their services in Swedish, and they were the heart of immigrant life, with choirs, youth groups, temperance societies, and Sunday schools.
The switch to English came gradually, mostly in the 1920s and 1930s, as the American-born children grew up and the flow of new immigrants slowed.
The Covenant, now called the Evangelical Covenant Church, has long since spread far beyond its Swedish roots, with congregations across the country and around the world.
But it's still headquartered in Chicago, and its story is one reason the Swedish flavor of this part of the city has lasted so long.
Walk north on Clark Street and then east on Bryn Mawr Avenue all the way to Sheridan Road, near the lake.
Here, at number 5555 North Sheridan Road, stands a tall, pink apartment building with a pointed roof.
This is the Edgewater Beach Apartments, completed in 1928.
It's the survivor of a famous resort.
Next to it, on the lake, stood the Edgewater Beach Hotel, a sprawling hotel painted a cheerful yellow, which opened in 1916.
For decades, it was one of the most glamorous resorts in the Midwest.
It had its own private beach, a boardwalk along the lake called the Beach Walk, where big bands played outdoors on summer nights, and guests including presidents and movie stars.
Its broadcasts of dance music went out across the country on the radio.
In June 1949, the hotel was the scene of a famous crime.
Eddie Waitkus, the first baseman for the Philadelphia Phillies, who were in town to play the Cubs, received a note asking him to come to a room in the hotel.
There, a young woman named Ruth Ann Steinhagen, who had become obsessed with him, shot him with a rifle.
He survived.
The incident inspired Bernard Malamud's novel The Natural, about a baseball player who is shot by a mysterious woman.
In the 1950s, Lake Shore Drive was extended north past the hotel, on landfill, cutting it off from the lake, and it went into decline.
It closed in 1967 and was demolished a few years later.
Only the pink apartment building remains, a reminder of the days when Edgewater was a summer resort at the edge of the city.
This is the end of the Uptown and Andersonville tour.
The neighborhood around you was invented, name and all, by one man.
John Lewis Cochran grew up in Philadelphia and came to Chicago as an agent for a tobacco company.
In the mid-1880s he bought land along the lake here, well north of the city, and laid out a subdivision he called Edgewater, for the obvious reason: it ran right to the water.
Cochran sold Edgewater as a thoroughly modern suburb.

It was the first planned development in the area with paved streets, proper drainage, and electric lights, powered by an electric company Cochran set up for the purpose, at a time when most streets in the region were still lit by gas or not at all.
Now look at the street signs: Berwyn, Bryn Mawr, Ardmore, Rosemont, Devon.
Every one of them is also the name of a station on the Main Line, the string of wealthy railroad suburbs west of Philadelphia.

The usual explanation is that Cochran named the streets of his Chicago suburb after the stops he knew from home, to give the new place a little of the old money and polish of the Philadelphia suburbs.
Edgewater became part of Chicago with the rest of Lake View in the great annexation of 1889.
For decades it was a quiet, prosperous neighborhood of big houses, until the 1920s, when the lake views attracted the apartment hotels and high-rise apartment buildings you see along Sheridan Road.
For most of the twentieth century, the city counted Edgewater as part of Uptown.
Residents never liked that, and after years of lobbying, Edgewater became an official community area of its own in 1980, the newest of the city's seventy-seven.
So the name Cochran made up in the 1880s has outlasted his electric company, his suburb, and even the great resort hotel that made it famous.
When the Edgewater Beach Hotel opened, its guests could step out onto the sand.
Today, from here, the lake is a walk away, across a busy highway and a strip of park.
Nearly everything between Sheridan Road and the water is landfill.
Over the course of a century, the city pushed Lincoln Park north by filling in the lake, a stretch at a time.
Stone, sand, and fill were dumped behind new breakwaters and then shaped into lawns, beaches, harbors, and drives.
The last piece, past this point to Hollywood Avenue, came in the 1950s with the extension of the Drive, the change that, as you heard, cut the hotel off from its beach.
Now walk a block or so north, to Hollywood Avenue, where Lake Shore Drive comes to an end and turns into Sheridan Road.
North of there, the pattern breaks.
The parkland stops, and for most of the way to Evanston, apartment towers and houses stand right at the edge of the water, behind their own seawalls.
In Rogers Park, farther north, the ends of many streets become small public beaches, little openings in a wall of private property.
The contrast tells you what the landfill did.
Most of Chicago's lakefront south of this point is public parkland, a front yard that belongs to everyone, which is unusual among the world's great waterfront cities.
North of Hollywood, the shore went to private owners before the park could reach it.
Park advocates have proposed extending the park all the way to the city limits, but so far the idea has stayed on paper.
So when you stand at the end of the Drive, you're standing at the seam between two different ideas of what a lakefront is for.
Ruth Ann Steinhagen's obsession with Eddie Waitkus began when he was a Cub.
She was a teenager who went to Wrigley Field again and again to watch him, and she filled her room with his pictures.
When the Cubs traded him to Philadelphia after the 1948 season, she was devastated.
When the Phillies came to town in June 1949, she took a room at the Edgewater Beach Hotel, where the team was staying, and sent him the note.
After the shooting, she reportedly told the police that she had decided that if she couldn't have him, nobody else would.
Waitkus nearly died.
It took several operations to save him, but he came back, and in 1950 he was playing first base for the Phillies' young team, the Whiz Kids, who won the National League pennant.
Friends said he was never quite the same afterward.
He died in 1972, at fifty-three.
Steinhagen never stood trial.
Less than three weeks after the shooting, a judge declared her insane and sent her to Kankakee State Hospital.
In 1952 she was found sane again, and Waitkus, who had no wish to see her prosecuted, let the charges go.
She lived the rest of her long life quietly in Chicago, and when she died, in December 2012, at eighty-three, the newspapers didn't notice for almost three months.
The writer Bernard Malamud turned the story into a kind of myth.

In The Natural, published in 1952, a young pitcher named Roy Hobbs is shot in a Chicago hotel room by a strange young woman named Harriet Bird, and returns years later, past his prime, as a slugger with a homemade bat called Wonderboy.
Malamud's novel ends in failure and disgrace.
When it became a film in 1984, starring Robert Redford, Roy Hobbs got a happier ending, with a home run that shatters the stadium lights.
This tour explores Wicker Park and Bucktown, two neighborhoods on the Northwest Side, along the diagonal line of Milwaukee Avenue.
Milwaukee Avenue began as a Native American trail running northwest from the river, and it became one of the main roads out of the city toward Wisconsin.
In the second half of the nineteenth century, it was the spine of Polish Chicago.

Poles came to Chicago in huge numbers, many to work in the factories, rail yards, and stockyards, and by the early twentieth century, Chicago had one of the largest Polish populations of any city in the world.
The intersection of Milwaukee, Division, and Ashland was called Polish Downtown, and the neighborhood around it was dense with churches, newspapers, banks, and halls.
Wicker Park itself is named for two brothers, Charles and Joel Wicker, real estate developers who donated a small triangle of land for a park in 1870.
The Great Fire never reached this far, and in the years after it, as families who had lost everything looked for somewhere to rebuild, the Northwest Side filled quickly.
Wealthy German and Scandinavian brewers, merchants, and manufacturers built grand houses around the park, while workers' cottages and two-flats spread out in all directions.
By the mid-twentieth century, the neighborhood had become poor.
Puerto Rican and Mexican families arrived after World War II, and the area faced disinvestment, arson, and neglect.
Then, in the 1980s and 1990s, artists and musicians moved in, drawn by cheap rent.
Wicker Park became the center of Chicago's alternative rock and art scene, and then, as so often happens, one of its most expensive neighborhoods.

We will start at Saint Stanislaus Kostka Church, in the old Polish Downtown, cross the Polish Triangle, walk up Milwaukee Avenue to the mansions of Wicker Park, then to the Six Corners, and finish on the elevated trail called the 606 and in Bucktown.
You are at Saint Stanislaus Kostka Church, on Noble Street just north of Division Street.
The huge brick church with two tall towers was the mother church of Polish Chicago.
The parish was founded in 1867, the first Polish parish in the city, and the present church was completed in 1881, designed by Patrick Keely, the architect of Holy Name Cathedral.
By the end of the nineteenth century, Saint Stanislaus was said to be the largest Catholic parish in the United States, with tens of thousands of parishioners.
Masses were said over and over every Sunday to accommodate the crowds, and the parish ran schools, societies, and a bank.
The priest who built it up, Father Vincent Barzynski, also helped found Polish newspapers and other parishes across the city.
Now look east toward the Kennedy Expressway, which runs just beyond the church.
When the expressway was planned in the 1950s, the route came very close to the church, and there was fear it would be demolished.
Local lore says that the parish's political connections led planners to bend the highway around it.
The church survived, though a lot of the neighborhood didn't.
The writer Nelson Algren set his novel Never Come Morning in this neighborhood, a grim story of a young Polish-American boxer.
It angered many in the Polish community when it was published in 1942.
You'll hear more about Algren at the next two stops.
A short walk south, at Milwaukee and Augusta, is the Polish Museum of America, founded in 1935 and one of the oldest ethnic museums in the country.
The Polish community has since moved further northwest and to the suburbs, but Polish Downtown is where it began.

Saint Stanislaus had a rival, a couple of blocks south on Noble Street: Holy Trinity, a parish founded by Polish nationalists who wanted their church run by a committee of its own members, and not by the religious order that ran Saint Stanislaus.

For about twenty years, the two parishes fought what became known as the Polish church war, with lawsuits, closed doors, and appeals to Rome, until the Pope's representative in America settled it in 1893.
Holy Trinity's grand church, finished in the early 1900s, still stands on Noble Street.
Chicagoans used to say that their city had more Poles than any city in the world except Warsaw.

That was probably never quite true, but by the early twentieth century, several hundred thousand Polish immigrants and their children lived in Chicago, and the city is still the capital of Polish America.
For most of the nineteenth century, there was no Poland on the map.
At the end of the 1700s, Prussia, Russia, and Austria had divided the old Polish kingdom among themselves, and for more than a century, Poles lived as subjects of three foreign empires.
They kept their language, their Catholic faith, and the memory of a lost country, and they rose up more than once, most famously in 1830 and in 1863.
Each time, the rebellion was crushed.
But the great migration to America wasn't mainly about politics.
Polish historians call it the emigration for bread.

Most of the people who came were peasants, from villages where families had too many children and too little land, and where a farmhand earned a small fraction of what a laborer could make in an American factory.
They came in waves, roughly in the order that the three empires let them go.
The first large groups came from the Prussian part of Poland, often as whole families who meant to stay.
Later, in the decades before the First World War, came the Poles of the Russian and Austrian lands, many of them young men who planned to work a few years, save their wages, and go home to buy land.
Some did go home.
Far more stayed.
In America they took the hardest and lowest-paid work there was, and Chicago had plenty of it.

Polish neighborhoods grew up wherever the jobs were: here on the Northwest Side, near the tanneries and factories along the river, behind the stockyards, and beside the steel mills of the far South Side.

Altogether, by one estimate, some two and a half million Poles came to the United States between 1850 and 1920, among them smaller groups with identities of their own, like the Kashubes of the Baltic coast and the highlanders of the Tatra Mountains.
Wherever they settled, the center of their new lives was usually a Polish parish like this one, where the priest, the language, and the saints on the walls were familiar.
The priest who built this parish into a giant was a veteran of a lost revolution.
Vincent Barzynski was born in 1838 in the Russian part of Poland, and he was ordained a priest in 1861.
Two years later, Poland rose against the tsar in what became known as the January Uprising, and Barzynski worked for the rebels' secret national government, getting supplies to the insurgents.
When the uprising was crushed, he fled, first to Austrian territory and then to France.
In Paris, in 1866, he joined the Congregation of the Resurrection, a young religious order founded by Polish exiles, and the order sent him to America, to minister to the Polish settlers of Texas.
After several years there, he came north to Chicago, and in 1874 he was made pastor of Saint Stanislaus Kostka.
He was a builder of almost frightening energy, and he thought big.

In 1873 he was one of the founders of the Polish Roman Catholic Union, a fraternal society that offered its members life insurance and a sense of belonging, and that became one of the pillars of Polish American life.
His order came to run much of Polish Catholic life on the Northwest Side, and in 1898, when it organized an American province, he became its first head.
Barzynski had a clear idea of what Polish America should be: Catholic first, organized around the parish, and obedient to the church.
That put him on a collision course with the nationalists, who wanted Polish life organized around the cause of a free Poland, and with parishioners who wanted a say in running their own churches.
The long war with Holy Trinity, which you heard about at the stop, was one result.
He died in May 1899, at the age of sixty, and his funeral was one of the largest Chicago had ever seen.
The order he served went on running this parish for generations after him.

Nelson Algren wasn't Polish, but he spent a great deal of time in this neighborhood, in its taverns and at its boxing matches, listening to the way people talked, and in 1942 he turned what he heard into Never Come Morning.

Its hero, Bruno Bicek, is a teenage tough who dreams of becoming a prizefighter, caught up in a world of gangs, pimps, and crooked cops, and the book follows him to a killing and an arrest he seems to have expected all along.
The novel came with an introduction by Richard Wright, the author of Native Son, who had become Algren's friend in the radical writers' circles of 1930s Chicago.
Ernest Hemingway praised it in a letter to his editor.
Many Polish Americans saw something else: a slander.
Here was a portrait of their community as a world of thugs and prostitutes, published at the very moment when Poland itself was being crushed under Nazi occupation.
Polish American organizations, among them the Polish Roman Catholic Union, protested, and some critics went so far as to call the book pro-Nazi.
They persuaded Mayor Edward Kelly to have it pulled from the shelves of the Chicago Public Library.
Algren's defenders answered that the book was about poverty, not about Poles, and that the same story could have been told about any people trapped at the bottom of a big city.
Algren himself kept writing about these streets for the rest of his career, and his relationship with Chicago stayed prickly to the end.
The hurt took decades to fade.
But time has a way of settling these arguments, and at the next stop, in the heart of the neighborhood that once wanted his book banned, you'll find his words carved into a fountain.
The Polish Museum of America was started by the Polish Roman Catholic Union, and it still shares a building with the union on Milwaukee Avenue.
It's worth the detour for a few remarkable things.
Start with the Paderewski Room.
Ignacy Jan Paderewski was the most famous pianist of his age, and in 1919 he served as prime minister of a newly independent Poland.

The room holds one of the largest collections of his belongings anywhere, among them his practice piano, the gold pen he used to sign the Treaty of Versailles, and his death mask, made by the American sculptor Malvina Hoffman.
Then look for the great stained glass window called Poland Reborn.
It was made for Poland's pavilion at the New York World's Fair, which opened in the spring of 1939.
That September, Germany invaded Poland, and the pavilion's treasures no longer had a country to go home to.
Some of them found a home here instead.
And find the big painting of Casimir Pulaski at Savannah, by the Polish painter Stanisław Batowski.
Pulaski was the Polish cavalry officer who fought for American independence and died of the wounds he received at the siege of Savannah, in 1779.
The painting won first prize when it was shown at Chicago's Century of Progress fair in 1933, and the Polish Women's Alliance bought it for the museum in 1939.
Illinois still honors Pulaski with a state holiday, on the first Monday of March.

The museum also keeps a library and archives that Polish American families, scholars, and genealogists have used for decades, full of newspapers, letters, and records from the neighborhoods you're walking through.
It keeps limited hours, so check before you go.
Walk west on Division Street to the small triangular plaza where Division Street, Milwaukee Avenue, and Ashland Avenue cross.
This is the Polish Triangle, the heart of what was once called Polish Downtown, and it's where the Division Street station of the Blue Line comes up to the street.
For the first half of the twentieth century, this intersection was the commercial and political center of Polish Chicago.

Around it stood the offices of Polish newspapers, banks, fraternal societies, and the headquarters of the Polish National Alliance, a large fraternal organization that was a power in Polish American life.
One of the Polish-language daily newspapers, Dziennik Związkowy, founded in 1908, is still published.
On Saturdays, the sidewalks were crowded with shoppers speaking Polish, Yiddish, German, and Ukrainian.
In the middle of the plaza is a fountain dedicated to Nelson Algren, with a line from his writing carved into it: "for the masses who do the city's work also keep the city's heart."
Algren knew this intersection well.
His novels were full of the bars, pool halls, and boxing gyms of the Polish Northwest Side, and his most famous book, The Man with the Golden Arm, takes place in the streets around here.
Look west along Division Street.
That stretch was once known as Polish Broadway, lined with taverns and dance halls.
Just west of here is the Chopin Theatre, a 1918 movie house that's now a theater and performance space with a famously eclectic basement café.
In the 1960s and 1970s, the Polish community moved farther northwest, and the neighborhood became largely Puerto Rican and Mexican.
Since the 1990s, it's been gentrifying, and today Division Street is lined with restaurants, bars, and sidewalk cafés.
For half a century, Polish Chicago argued with itself about a basic question: what did it mean to be Polish in America?
Was it, first of all, to be Catholic?
Or was it to work for the rebirth of Poland?
Two great organizations stood for the two answers.
The Polish Roman Catholic Union, which Father Barzynski helped found in 1873, spoke for the church: its members were Catholics, and its leaders were often priests.
The Polish National Alliance, founded in 1880 by Polish exiles in Philadelphia and Chicago, spoke for the nation.
It welcomed people whose roots lay in the lands of the old Polish Commonwealth, whatever their religion, and its great cause was an independent Poland.
Both were fraternal societies, part club and part insurance company, and both grew into some of the largest ethnic organizations in America.
In Chicago, the fight was waged parish by parish.
Saint Stanislaus lined up with the Catholic Union, and its rival, Holy Trinity, with the Alliance.
Each side had its own newspapers, its own heroes, and its own celebrations, and their quarrels filled the pages of the Polish press for years.
Barzynski fought the Alliance with everything he had, and by one account it only began to grow quickly after his death in 1899.
Over time, the two camps learned to work together.
The First World War, and the real chance it offered of a free Poland, gave them a common cause.
And in 1944, they joined with other Polish American groups in the Polish American Congress, to press Washington on Poland's fate as the Second World War came to an end.
Both organizations are still headquartered in Chicago.
Their old argument, between faith and nation, never entirely ended, but it softened into something more like a family disagreement, the kind that gets aired every year at the same dinner table.
When the First World War broke out in 1914, the three empires that had divided Poland went to war with each other, Germany and Austria on one side and Russia on the other.
Poles were drafted into all three armies, and sometimes they fought each other.
For Polish Americans, the war brought terrible news from home, and something they had waited for all their lives: a real chance that Poland might be reborn.
The pianist Ignacy Jan Paderewski became the voice of that hope in America.
He crossed the country giving concerts and speeches to raise money for Polish war relief, and he lobbied President Woodrow Wilson.
In January 1918, when Wilson laid out his Fourteen Points for the peace, one of them called for an independent Poland with access to the sea.
Paderewski also called for a Polish army of volunteers from America.
The Polish Falcons, a network of gymnastic clubs that had long drilled young Polish men, became its recruiting machine, along with the Polish National Alliance.
Many of the volunteers were immigrants who weren't American citizens, and so weren't subject to the American draft.
They trained at a camp in Canada, at Niagara-on-the-Lake in Ontario, and then sailed for France, where a Polish army was taking shape under French command.
Its men wore blue French uniforms, and in the last weeks of the war, General Józef Haller took command of it.
People called it the Blue Army, or Haller's Army.
Some thirty-eight thousand men volunteered, and more than twenty thousand were accepted and shipped overseas.
By one estimate, about three thousand of them came from Chicago.
One photograph from December 1918 shows a couple of hundred volunteers gathered in Humboldt Park, about to leave for the camp.
After the war, the Blue Army went on to Poland and fought in the wars over the new country's borders.

About twelve and a half thousand of the volunteers eventually came back to the United States, and many found that service in a foreign army gave them no claim to the benefits that American veterans received.
Polish Chicago ate well, and it still does.
The old Polish delis and bakeries followed their customers northwest along Milwaukee Avenue long ago, but the food is easy to find, and a few dishes are worth knowing.
Start with pierogi, the half-moon dumplings that every Polish grandmother seems to make better than anyone else's.
The classic filling is potato and farmer's cheese, often with fried onions.
There are also sauerkraut and mushroom, ground meat, sweet cheese, and, in summer, blueberries, served with sour cream and sugar.
Then there's kielbasa, which simply means sausage in Polish.
A good Polish deli might carry a dozen kinds: smoked and fresh, garlicky and mild, thin and dried for snacking.
Along with it come rye bread, dill pickles, and soups, among them a clear red beet broth served at Christmas, and a sour rye soup that's an Easter favorite.
The holidays bring out the best.
On Christmas Eve, Polish families wait for the first star to appear before sitting down to Wigilia, pronounced roughly vee-geel-ya, a meatless feast of many dishes, traditionally twelve.
Before eating, everyone shares a thin wafer, breaking off pieces for one another and exchanging wishes, and an extra place is set for an unexpected guest.
On the Saturday before Easter, families carry baskets of eggs, sausage, bread, and salt to church to be blessed, a custom you'll still see in Chicago's Polish parishes.
And then there are pączki, pronounced roughly poonch-key: rich, yeast-raised doughnuts, filled with jam, often rose or plum, or with custard.
In Poland, the big day for pączki is the last Thursday before Lent.
In Chicago, as in Detroit, it has moved to Fat Tuesday, and lines form outside Polish bakeries before dawn.
Walk northwest up Milwaukee Avenue and then west to Hoyne Avenue, north of Division.
Walk along Hoyne and the side streets around the park, such as Pierce Avenue and Bell Avenue.
These blocks are lined with some of the most elaborate Victorian mansions in Chicago, built in the 1880s and 1890s for brewers, merchants, and manufacturers, many of them German and Scandinavian.
Hoyne Avenue is sometimes called Beer Baron Row.
Look for the towers, turrets, and wraparound porches, the carved stone and pressed metal, and the stained glass.
Look especially for the Hermann Weinhardt House at 2135 West Pierce Avenue, built in 1888, with an almost overwhelming facade of decoration in wood and stone.

Not far from here, on Evergreen Avenue, lived the novelist Nelson Algren, who wrote The Man with the Golden Arm, about a heroin-addicted card dealer, which won the first National Book Award for fiction in 1950.
Algren was the poet of Chicago's down-and-out: drunks, hustlers, boxers, and immigrants.
His book-length prose poem, Chicago: City on the Make, contains a line often quoted about the city: "Like loving a woman with a broken nose, you may well find lovelier lovelies.
But never a lovely so real."
Algren had a long, famous love affair with the French writer Simone de Beauvoir, who visited him in his earlier Chicago apartment in the late 1940s.
Algren lived in this neighborhood for many years.
The block of Evergreen where he lived carries an honorary street sign with his name.
Across the street from the Weinhardt House, at 2138 West Pierce, stands the John Runge House, built in 1884, which is often called the Paderewski House.

According to neighborhood legend, the great Polish pianist Ignacy Paderewski, who later became prime minister of Poland, once played a concert from its balcony for a crowd gathered in the street, because the hall where he was supposed to perform was too small.
No one has ever found a record of the concert, but the name has stuck for a century.
In February 1947, Simone de Beauvoir came to Chicago.
She was already famous in France, as a novelist, as a philosopher, and as the companion of Jean-Paul Sartre, and she was crossing America on a lecture tour.
A friend had given her the phone number of a Chicago writer.
She called Nelson Algren, and he showed her his Chicago: the dives, the flophouses, and, by her own account, a police lineup.
Within a few months, they were lovers.
She came back to stay with him for long stretches in his cramped flat on Wabansia Avenue, a short way from here, and the two of them traveled together as far as Mexico and Central America.
In her letters she called herself his wife.
He gave her an inexpensive ring, which she wore for the rest of her life, and she is said to have been buried wearing it.
But she would not give up Paris, her work, or Sartre, and Algren would not move to France.
The affair went on for years, much of it by mail.
More than three hundred of her letters to him survive, and they were published after both of them had died.
She put him into her novel The Mandarins, as the Chicago writer Lewis Brogan, and dedicated the book to him.
It won France's most famous literary prize, the Goncourt, in 1954.
Later, she wrote about their affair in her memoirs.
Algren, a private man, felt by most accounts that she had exposed him, and he let his anger show in print.
Algren left Chicago in 1975, feeling that the city had never appreciated him, and moved east.
In 1981 he was elected to the American Academy and Institute of Arts and Letters, a late honor, and that May he died at his new home in Sag Harbor, on Long Island.
De Beauvoir died five years later, in Paris.
The Man with the Golden Arm made Algren famous, and Hollywood came calling.
The actor John Garfield bought the film rights first, and after he died in 1952, the director Otto Preminger picked them up.
Algren was brought in to work on the script, but Preminger soon replaced him with a Hollywood screenwriter and changed the story a great deal.
In the novel, Frankie Machine, the card dealer with the golden arm, ends up hanging himself in a flophouse.
In the film, he kicks his habit and walks off into the night with the woman who loves him.
Algren was bitter, and he went to court over the film's credits, though he later dropped the case.
The film, which opened at the end of 1955, starred Frank Sinatra as Frankie, and it earned him an Academy Award nomination.
Its jazz score, by Elmer Bernstein, and its opening titles, by the designer Saul Bass, with a jagged white arm cutting across a black screen, became classics in their own right.
Its biggest impact was on censorship.
Hollywood's Production Code, the industry's rules of decency, banned stories about drug addiction, and the censors refused the film their seal of approval.
Preminger and his distributor, United Artists, released it anyway.
The film was a hit, and in December 1956, the Code was rewritten to allow movies to deal with narcotics, within limits.
The rules that had governed American movies since the 1930s were beginning to crack, and in 1968 they gave way to the ratings system.
For Algren, though, the whole experience confirmed his suspicion of Hollywood.
He had written about real people on real streets, not far from here, and the movie was shot on studio sets, with a happy ending.
He never wrote another book with the success of the one Hollywood had bought.
In the decades after the Great Fire, this was one of the most fashionable addresses on the Northwest Side.
The people who built here wanted everyone to know they had arrived, and they used every style in the book.
With a little practice, you can tell the styles apart.
The oldest are often Italianate: tall, narrow windows topped with heavy hoods, and a deep cornice under the roofline, held up by brackets.
Next, look for a mansard roof, steep and almost vertical, with dormer windows poking out of it.
That's the Second Empire style, borrowed from Paris in the age of Napoleon the Third, and it let builders squeeze a full extra floor under the roof.
Then come the showoffs.

Queen Anne houses love asymmetry: a round or many-sided tower on one corner, a porch wrapping around another, bay windows, and a different texture on every floor, from brick and stone to wooden shingles.
Romanesque houses go the other way, toward weight and power: rough-cut stone, deep round arches over the doors and windows, and walls that look as if they could withstand a siege.
That style was made popular in the 1880s by the Boston architect Henry Hobson Richardson.
Many houses mix several styles at once, which tells you something about the people who built them.
They were self-made men, many of them immigrants, and they wanted a little of everything.
As the neighborhood declined, many of these mansions were carved up into apartments and rooming houses, and some were lost.
Then, from the 1970s on, new owners began buying them and restoring them, often one room at a time.

The neighborhood was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, and in 1991 the city made the heart of it a landmark district, which means that the facades you see can't be torn down or altered without review.
Walk to the small triangular park, the Wicker Park itself, and then to its northeast corner, at the six-way intersection of North Avenue, Damen Avenue, and Milwaukee Avenue.
Look north at the tall Art Deco tower overlooking the intersection.
Built in 1929 as the Northwest Tower, it's nicknamed the Coyote Building, and for years it was a symbol of the neighborhood's art scene.
It's now a hotel.
In the 1990s, this intersection was the center of Chicago's indie rock and art world.
Clubs like the Double Door, just south on Milwaukee, hosted bands on their way up, and in 1997 the Rolling Stones played a surprise show there.
Liz Phair's 1993 album Exile in Guyville was made out of this scene.
The neighborhood got so much attention that it became a backdrop for movies, including High Fidelity, with John Cusack, set in a record store near here.
Along the way, Wicker Park was gentrified so thoroughly that it became a symbol of the process.

In 2001, when MTV's The Real World filmed a season in a loft building on North Avenue, residents and activists protested outside, angry about what they saw as the neighborhood being turned into a brand.
Look for the Flat Iron Building, a wedge-shaped building on the corner of North and Milwaukee, which has housed artist studios for decades.

The neighborhood still has a big art festival each year, and walking down Milwaukee and Division, you'll see plenty of independent shops, bars, and restaurants, along with chain stores that would have been unthinkable thirty years ago.
Long before it was hip, this intersection was a busy shopping district, with stores, banks, and movie theaters, where Polish, German, and Scandinavian families came to shop on Saturdays.
The elevated train, now the Blue Line, stopped right at the intersection, as it still does.
In the early 1990s, the music press took notice.
Bands like Urge Overkill and Veruca Salt, along with Liz Phair, came out of the Chicago scene and became national names, and magazines began asking whether Chicago would be the next Seattle.
It never quite was, but for a few years, this intersection was one of the most exciting places in American music.
The Wicker brothers, Charles and Joel, came to Chicago around 1839 and went into the wholesale grocery business, and Charles also went into politics, serving on the City Council.
The park, as you heard at the start of the tour, was their gift.

In 1870 they had bought about eighty acres along Milwaukee Avenue and divided the land into lots, and the four acres in the middle that they gave the city were probably as shrewd as they were generous, since a park next door made the lots around it easier to sell.
The street that runs past the six corners, Damen Avenue, had a different name until 1927.
It was Robey Street, named for a local politician, James Robey.
That year, over the protests of many residents, the City Council renamed it for Father Arnold Damen, the Jesuit who founded Holy Family Church and the college that became Loyola University.
The old name hasn't quite disappeared: the hotel in the Art Deco tower above the corner is called the Robey.
Hoyne Avenue, where the beer barons built their mansions, carries the name of the man at the center of one of the strangest episodes in Chicago politics.
In April 1876, a lawyer named Thomas Hoyne was elected mayor as a write-in candidate, with about thirty-three thousand of roughly forty thousand votes.
But the sitting mayor, Harvey Colvin, refused to step aside, arguing that the election had been illegal.
For about four weeks, Chicago had two men who each claimed to be its mayor.
That June, a court threw out Hoyne's election, the city ended up paying both men for the weeks in dispute, and a special election that summer chose someone else entirely.
So the three names around you tell three Chicago stories: a real estate deal, a fight over a street sign, and a mayor who never legally was.
In the 1980s, Wicker Park was cheap, a little dangerous, and full of empty space, which is exactly what artists look for.
