Painters, sculptors, and photographers moved into lofts and storefronts around the six corners, and small galleries opened in buildings that landlords could hardly rent.
One of them, the Tower Coyote Gallery, opened in the Northwest Tower.
The usual story is that the artists thought the building looked like a coyote throwing back its head to howl.
Whether or not you can see it, the name stuck, and the tower has been the Coyote Building ever since.
In 1989, the neighborhood's artists launched a festival of their own, called Around the Coyote.
For a few days each fall, studios and galleries opened their doors, and crowds came to look, to buy, and to party.
Its home base was the Flat Iron Building, the one you heard about at the stop.
The festival did what such festivals do.
It showed the rest of Chicago that Wicker Park was interesting, and the rest of Chicago came.
Many of the artists who had given the place its character were soon priced out, and they moved on, to Pilsen, to Logan Square, and beyond.
Around the Coyote itself eventually faded away.
If you look up at the tower today, try squinting at its outline against the sky.
Some people see the coyote right away.
Others never do.
Either way, the name is a small monument to the artists who were here first, and who could no longer afford to stay.
The music you heard about at the stop didn't just happen in clubs.
In the 1990s, Chicago was home to a cluster of small, stubborn record labels that shaped independent music around the world.
The oldest was Touch and Go.
It started in 1979 in East Lansing, Michigan, as a homemade punk fanzine, and became a record label a couple of years later.
Its owner, Corey Rusk, moved it to Chicago in the 1980s.
Touch and Go was known for doing business on a handshake, without long contracts, and for splitting profits evenly with its bands.
Its roster included Big Black, the Jesus Lizard, and Slint, whose 1991 album Spiderland is still treated as a landmark.
Drag City was founded in Chicago at the end of the 1980s by Dan Koretzky and Dan Osborn, and it became known for singular songwriters like Will Oldham, Bill Callahan, and Joanna Newsom.
Thrill Jockey was started in New York in 1992 by Bettina Richards, a former major-label talent scout, and she moved it to Chicago a few years later.
It became the home of Tortoise, the Chicago band that helped define the sound critics called post-rock.
And then there was Steve Albini, who grew up in Montana, came to the Chicago area for college, and led the abrasive band Big Black.
As a recording engineer, he refused to call himself a producer and refused to take royalties, charging bands a flat fee instead.
He recorded a staggering number of albums, among them the Pixies' Surfer Rosa and Nirvana's In Utero, and in the 1990s he built his own studio, Electrical Audio, on the Northwest Side.
When he died in 2024, musicians around the world mourned him.
What tied them together was an attitude: that you could make records your own way, on a small scale, and still reach listeners everywhere.
For a while, that attitude made Chicago one of the capitals of the music world.
Walk north on Damen Avenue to the elevated trail crossing overhead, just south of Cortland Street.
Take the ramp up.
This is the Bloomingdale Trail, more often called the 606, after the first three digits of Chicago's zip codes.
It's an old elevated freight railroad line, the Bloomingdale Line, built at street level in the 1870s along Bloomingdale Avenue.
Around 1915, after pressure from the city to make streets safer, the railroad raised the tracks onto an embankment, with bridges over each cross street.
Freight trains ran along it for decades, serving factories and warehouses.
When the freight traffic stopped, the embankment became an overgrown, unofficial walking path.
The city converted it into a park, which opened in June 2015.
It runs for about two and three quarter miles, connecting several neighborhoods from Bucktown and Wicker Park in the east to Logan Square and Humboldt Park in the west.
Along the way are small parks at street level, public art, and an observatory at its western end.
Like the High Line in New York, the 606 has been a huge success, and like the High Line, it has driven up property values sharply around it.
In the neighborhoods to the west, which were largely Latino and working class, it has raised fears of displacement, and the city has experimented with ways to limit it.
Walk west along the trail, and you'll notice how the neighborhoods change.
As you walk west along the trail from Damen, look back to the east, toward the Kennedy Expressway.
The great dome you see on the skyline belongs to Saint Mary of the Angels, a church built by Polish immigrants and completed in 1920, modeled on Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome.
By the late 1980s, it was crumbling and about to be torn down.
It was saved, restored, and reopened in the 1990s, and its dome is once again one of the landmarks of the Northwest Side.
By the 1890s, Chicago was the railroad capital of America, and it paid a terrible price for it.
Railroads crossed the city's streets at grade in many hundreds of places, and trains ran right through crowded neighborhoods, past schools, stores, and homes.
People were killed and maimed at the crossings with grim regularity.
In May 1892, with the World's Fair coming, the City Council ordered the Illinois Central to raise its tracks on the South Side, near the fairgrounds.
Early the next year, the city set out to get rid of grade crossings everywhere.
Railroad by railroad, ordinance by ordinance, the tracks went up onto embankments of earth held in by walls, with bridges over each street.
By around 1920, by one count, more than five hundred miles of track had been raised, and nearly a thousand street crossings had been eliminated.
The Depression finally brought the program to a halt.
The Bloomingdale Line's turn came in the 1910s, as you heard at the stop, and if you look at the trail's edges, you can still read the engineering.
The path runs along the top of the old earthen fill, held in by the railroad's concrete retaining walls.
And at each cross street, look down from the bridge: for decades, the dark underpasses below were the kind of place people hurried through.
That's the quiet irony of this trail.
All over the city, raised railroad embankments became walls between neighborhoods, splitting them into separate worlds.
Here, one of those walls has been turned into a path that ties them together.
The overgrown embankment didn't turn itself into a park.
It took years of organizing.
In 2003, a group of neighbors formed the Friends of the Bloomingdale Trail.
The next year, the idea of a trail made it into a plan for adding open space to Logan Square, a neighborhood short on parkland.
A national nonprofit, the Trust for Public Land, became the city's lead private partner, bringing together agencies, donors, and designers.
Public design workshops began in 2007, and it took eight more years, and a great deal of money, to get the trail built.
The rising prices you heard about at the stop were steepest along the trail's western half.
By one study, from DePaul University, the value of small buildings near that part of the trail more than quadrupled between 2012 and 2018, far faster than in the city as a whole.
Developers bought old two-flats and small apartment buildings, tore them down, and replaced them with expensive new homes.
The city pushed back.

In 2020 it temporarily froze demolition permits in parts of the area, and in 2021 the City Council passed a special fee on demolitions along the trail and in Pilsen, of at least fifteen thousand dollars per building, and more for larger ones.
The city later reported that demolitions near the trail had dropped sharply.
The argument goes on, here and in cities around the world that have copied the idea: how do you build a beautiful park without pushing out the people it was meant for?
The 606 is a park as well as a path, and it was planted with care.

The landscape architects, Michael Van Valkenburgh Associates, working with the lead artist Frances Whitehead, designed it as a sequence of garden rooms, each with its own mix of trees, shrubs, and grasses, so that the trail changes as you move along it.
Look for serviceberries, small trees with smooth gray bark.
In early spring they're covered with white blossoms, and in early summer they carry dark berries that birds love, and that people can eat too.
These trees are part of an experiment devised with the artist.

They were planted at chosen spots along the trail, in its different microclimates, warmer or cooler, sunnier or shadier, and volunteers have recorded when they leaf out, bloom, and fruit, following the methods of a national network that tracks the timing of the seasons.
Over the years, records like these can show how a changing climate is shifting spring in Chicago.
At the western end of the trail, near Ridgeway Avenue, there's an observatory of a very old kind.
A path climbs a small mound to a steel blade with a notch cut in it, and the notch is aligned to frame the setting sun on the first day of each season, at the solstices and the equinoxes.
On those evenings, people often gather on the mound to watch the sun go down through the slot, the way people have marked the turning of the year for thousands of years.
Between the two ends, the trail does quieter work.

Its trees and flowers give birds, bees, and butterflies a green corridor across a crowded part of the city, high above the traffic, and on a spring morning, it's one of the best places on the Northwest Side to hear birdsong.
Leave the trail at Western Avenue and walk north to Armitage Avenue.
You're now in Bucktown, the neighborhood north of Wicker Park.
The name, the story goes, comes from the goats that Polish immigrants kept in their yards in the nineteenth century.
The area was called Kozie Prery, or goat prairie, in Polish, and a male goat is a buck.
Bucktown was a working-class neighborhood of Polish and German families, with factories along the river and the railroads, until it too was gentrified in the 1990s.
On the corner of Armitage and Western is Margie's Candies, an old-fashioned ice cream parlor and candy shop that has been open since the 1920s.
It's famous for its huge sundaes served in clamshell-shaped dishes, and its walls are covered with memorabilia.
Margie's likes to tell visitors that the Beatles stopped in for sundaes during their tour in the 1960s, and there's even a story that Al Capone was a customer.
Those are stories, not certainties, but the sundaes are real.
This is the end of the Wicker Park and Bucktown tour.
If you keep walking west along the 606, you'll eventually reach Logan Square, where the Logan Square tour begins.
Margie's began in 1921 as the Security Sweet Shop, opened here by a Greek immigrant named Peter George Poulos.
Like many Greeks of his generation in Chicago, he found his way into the candy and ice cream business, and he soon handed the shop to his son, George.
George had met a girl named Margie at the shop when they were both young.
They married, and in 1933 he renamed the business for her.
In the 1940s, while George was away in the military, Margie ran the shop, and from 1954 she ran it on her own.
She was behind the counter for decades, until her death in 1995, at the age of eighty.
Her son Peter, a doctor, kept the shop going after her, the third generation of the family to run it.
Part of the charm is how little seems to have changed.
The booths, the counter, and the candy cases look much as they must have looked to Margie.
The sundaes are the reason to come.
The hot fudge usually comes on the side, in its own little pitcher, so you can pour as much as you dare, and the biggest sundaes are meant to be shared.
Margie's has always been a candy shop, too, and you can still take home a box of chocolates.

It's one of the last of a kind of place that once stood on neighborhood corners all over Chicago, the sweet shop where families came after church, couples came on dates, and kids spent their allowance.
A hundred years on, it has outlasted the factories, the goats, and most of the old Bucktown, and it's still on the same corner, scooping the same kind of sundae.
Every old Chicago institution seems to have a celebrity story, and Margie's has one of the best.
Here's how the family tells it.
On August twentieth, 1965, the Beatles played two shows at Comiskey Park, the White Sox ballpark on the South Side.

After the second show, the story goes, John, Paul, George, and Ringo came up here with a few young women in tow, slid into a booth, and ordered the Atomic Sundae, a towering six-scoop creation, before heading off to their hotel near O'Hare.
The shop has made the most of it.
The Beatles pictures and souvenirs on the walls are there to commemorate the visit, and fans still ask to sit in the booth where the band is said to have sat.
One television report even claimed that Mick Jagger, on a later visit, asked for the same booth.
So what's documented?
The concerts certainly are.
The visit itself rests mostly on the family's memory and on the stories of people who say they were there, and the details shift in the telling.
One account even puts the visit a year earlier, in 1964, when the Beatles played a different Chicago arena.
That's how legends like this usually work.
Nobody kept a record, because nobody thought they needed one, and the story was told and retold until it became part of the place.
Whether or not the Beatles ever sat there, plenty of people have sat in that booth since, hoping they did.
The busy street at the corner is Western Avenue, and its name is a fossil.
From 1851 to 1869, this was the western edge of Chicago.
Everything beyond it was outside the city, and the name stayed long after the city had swallowed the prairie on the other side.

Western is generally called the longest continuous street in Chicago, running about twenty-four miles inside the city limits, from Howard Street on the northern border to 119th Street on the far South Side, and it keeps going into the suburbs beyond.
Driving its whole length is a tour of the city in itself, through dozens of neighborhoods, past car dealers, factories, churches, and restaurants of every kind.
On the far South Side, it's the route of the South Side Irish Parade every March.
About a mile and a half north of here, at Belmont Avenue, Western ran past the most famous amusement park Chicago ever had.
Riverview opened in 1904 on about seventy acres along the river, and for more than sixty years it was where Chicago went to scream.
It had one of the first roller coasters with cars hanging below the track, an early parachute drop, and a beloved wooden coaster called the Bobs.
Not all of it was innocent.
For years, one attraction invited customers to throw balls at a target that dropped a Black man into a tank of water, until protests forced a change in the 1950s.
Riverview closed suddenly after the 1967 season, and the land became a shopping center, a college campus, and a park.
Its grand carousel survived.
It was sold, and it now turns at an amusement park in Georgia, where it's listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
This tour follows Division Street west from Wicker Park, through Ukrainian Village, to Humboldt Park, one of the great parks of the West Side.
In about two miles, you'll walk through the history of half a dozen immigrant communities, each of which made this street its own.

In the late nineteenth century, the blocks where Division Street meets Milwaukee Avenue became the center of Polish Chicago, and Division Street was nicknamed Polish Broadway, lined with Polish shops, banks, bakeries, and taverns.

Germans and Scandinavians settled farther west, around Humboldt Park, and in the early twentieth century, Jewish families moving out of the crowded Maxwell Street district followed them, building synagogues and shops along Division Street.

Around 1900, immigrants from the eastern edge of the Austro-Hungarian and Russian empires, Ukrainians and their neighbors, began building churches south of Division Street, in the neighborhood now called Ukrainian Village.
After the Second World War, a new community arrived.
Puerto Ricans, who had been American citizens since 1917, came to Chicago by the thousands, looking for work.
Many settled first near the lake, in Lincoln Park and Lakeview, but as those neighborhoods were cleared for urban renewal in the 1960s, families moved west.
By the 1970s, Humboldt Park and this stretch of Division Street had become the heart of Puerto Rican Chicago, as they still are.
In 1967, the broadcaster Studs Terkel published his first book of oral history, a collection of interviews with ordinary Chicagoans about their lives and their city.
He called it Division Street: America.
The title was a metaphor.
Most of the people in the book didn't live on Division Street at all, but the name seemed to capture a city divided by race, by class, and by neighborhood.

We'll start at Division Street and Damen Avenue, detour south into Ukrainian Village to see two cathedrals, and then walk west along Paseo Boricua into Humboldt Park, ending at the boathouse on the lagoon.
You're at the corner of Division Street and Damen Avenue.
Wicker Park is just to the north, and the Polish Triangle, where Division Street meets Milwaukee Avenue, is a few blocks to the east.

In the early twentieth century, this stretch of Division Street was the main street of a crowded, working-class neighborhood of Poles, Jews, and Ukrainians, full of bakeries, kosher butchers, saloons, and storefront theaters.
A few doors east of Damen, at number 1916, look for the building that housed the Division Street Russian and Turkish Baths, which opened in 1906.
For generations, men came here to sit in the steam, plunge into ice-cold pools, and get the platza, a scrubbing with brooms of oak leaves soaked in hot, soapy water.
Workingmen, gangsters, politicians, and businessmen all sweated here together.
The novelist Saul Bellow, who grew up a mile west of here, wrote about the baths in his novel Humboldt's Gift.
On June 12th, 1966, this corner was the scene of a turning point in the history of Puerto Rican Chicago.
That day, the city had celebrated its first Puerto Rican parade, downtown.
That evening, near Division and Damen, a police officer shot and wounded a young Puerto Rican man named Arcelis Cruz.
Crowds gathered, angered by years of harassment by the police, and for three nights there was rioting along Division Street, with stores burned and many people injured and arrested.
It was one of the first major riots by Puerto Ricans in an American city.

Afterward, community leaders organized new groups to fight for jobs, housing, schools, and better treatment from the police, and Division Street became the center of Puerto Rican political life in Chicago.
The man who put Division Street into the title of a famous book was born Louis Terkel, in New York City, in 1912, the son of Russian Jewish immigrants.
He came to Chicago as a boy, and his parents ran a rooming house, where he grew up among the workers, drifters, and talkers who passed through it.
He earned a law degree at the University of Chicago, but the law never took.
During the Depression he worked for the New Deal's writers' project and acted in radio soap operas, where he was often cast as a gangster.
A director gave him his nickname, after Studs Lonigan, the hero of James T. Farrell's novels of the Irish South Side, which Terkel happened to be reading at the time.
In the 1950s, his left-wing politics got him blacklisted from television, and he found a home at a small Chicago classical music station, WFMT.
His daily interview program ran there from 1952 to 1997.
He talked with just about everyone, from Bob Dylan to Mahalia Jackson, and with countless people nobody had ever heard of.
Those ordinary people became his life's work.

In 1967 he published Division Street: America, the first of his books of oral history, and he went on to do the same for the Great Depression in Hard Times, for jobs in Working, and for the Second World War in The Good War, which won the Pulitzer Prize in 1985.
His method was simple.
He turned on a tape recorder, asked a question, and listened, for as long as it took.
He believed that people who were never asked about their lives had the most to say about them, and his books proved him right.
He kept at it into his nineties, and he died in Chicago in 2008, at the age of ninety-six.
His recordings, thousands of hours of them, have been preserved, a portrait of an American century in the voices of the people who lived it.
In the early 1900s, few of the crowded flats around Division Street had a bathtub, and a trip to the bathhouse was part of the weekly routine.
For immigrants from Russia, Poland, and Ukraine, it was also a piece of home.
Across Eastern Europe, the steam bath was an old institution, a place to get clean, to sweat out a cold or a hangover, and to talk.
Jewish customers called it the shvitz, from the Yiddish word for sweat, and for observant men, a visit on Friday, before the Sabbath, was an old custom.
A Russian bath works with wet heat.
At its heart is a huge oven packed with rocks and heated for hours.
When an attendant throws water onto the rocks, a blast of steam fills the room, so hot that most people stay on the low benches, and only the brave climb to the top.
Then comes a plunge into ice-cold water, and then you go back in and do it all again.
The Turkish half of the name meant a room of hot, dry air, for those who preferred to bake rather than steam.
These baths had famous regulars.
Saul Bellow was one of them, and Nelson Algren wrote about the place too.

When an Italian American family, the Coluccis, took over the business in the 1970s, the regulars were still mostly Eastern Europeans, and the family ran it for decades, through good times and lean ones, as the old neighborhood around it changed.
The baths closed in 2010, and many people assumed that another piece of old Chicago was gone for good.
But they soon reopened under new owners, first as Red Square, and later as the Chicago Bath House, and more than a century after they opened, the steam is still rising here.
One thing has changed.
The old baths were a world of men.
The bathhouse welcomes women now too, and it has done better for it.
What should you call what happened at this corner in June 1966?
For years, newspapers and official reports called it the Division Street riot.
Many people in the neighborhood call it the Division Street rebellion, or the uprising, and the choice of word is itself an argument.
A riot sounds like senseless destruction.
A rebellion says the anger had causes, and that the people in the street had reasons.
Those reasons got a public airing that summer.

About a month after the riot, the city's Commission on Human Relations held open hearings, and Puerto Rican and other Spanish-speaking residents had an official forum, perhaps for the first time, to describe how they were treated by the police and by the city.
New organizations grew out of those days.
The Spanish Action Committee of Chicago organized Puerto Rican residents to press the city for change.
Before the year was out, Puerto Rican and Mexican activists founded the Latin American Defense Organization, an early effort to bring the two communities together.
Over the next few years came housing groups, education programs, and cultural centers, and in Lincoln Park, the Young Lords, whom you'll hear about later on this tour.
The riot also showed how little had changed for many people, and how easily violence could return.
Eleven years later, after police killed two young men in Humboldt Park, the neighborhood saw a second uprising.

Over the decades, historians and community groups collected the stories of the people who lived through those three nights, and a younger generation came to see them as the moment Puerto Rican Chicago stood up and demanded to be heard.
In June 2026, sixty years on, the community marked the anniversary, and many called it a rebellion.
Walk west on Division Street to Leavitt Street, and south a block to Haddon Avenue.

The small, cream-colored stucco church with the octagonal dome and the square bell tower is Holy Trinity Orthodox Cathedral, and it was designed by Louis Sullivan, the great architect of the early Chicago skyscraper.
Holy Trinity was founded in 1892 by immigrants from the Carpathian Mountains, in what was then the eastern edge of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.
They were Rusyns, a people closely related to the Ukrainians, and many of them joined the Russian Orthodox Church after arriving in America.
They were poor, and they wanted a church that reminded them of home.

Sullivan, whose career was then at its height, gave them a church inspired by the small wooden churches of the Russian countryside, with an eight-sided dome over a square base and a bell tower at the front, but simplified and transformed into his own style.
It was completed in 1903.

Look at the ornament around the door and the windows of the tower, and you'll see Sullivan's delicate swirls and leaves, the same kind of ornament you'll find on his skyscrapers and on the Sullivan Center on State Street.
The little church had powerful friends.
Tsar Nicholas the Second of Russia donated four thousand dollars toward its construction.
Its priest during the building of the church was John Kochurov, who later returned to Russia and, in 1917, became one of the first priests killed in the Russian Revolution.
The bishop who consecrated the church, Tikhon, later became Patriarch of Moscow, and he was persecuted and imprisoned by the Soviet government.
Both men are now saints of the Orthodox Church, and the people of this parish speak of them as their own.
If the church is open, step inside.
It's a single, warm room under the dome, glowing with icons and painted decoration, and it's one of the few places where you can see Sullivan's genius applied to a building so small and so intimate.
Back home in the Carpathian Mountains, most Rusyns weren't Orthodox.
They were Greek Catholics.
Their churches looked Orthodox, with icons, chant, and the old Eastern liturgy, but since the 1600s they had been in union with the Pope in Rome.
One thing set their clergy apart from the Roman Catholic priests most Americans knew.
Their priests could marry.
In America, that became a problem.
Most of the Catholic bishops here were Irish American, and many of them saw the Eastern rite, and above all its married priests, as foreign, confusing, and a scandal to their own flocks.
The breaking point came in Minneapolis.
In late 1889, a Greek Catholic priest named Alexis Toth arrived to serve a small Rusyn parish there.
He was a widower who had taught church law back home.
When he presented his papers to the archbishop, John Ireland, the archbishop asked whether he had been married, and on hearing that he had, refused to recognize him as a priest at all.
In Toth's telling, the meeting was bitter, and it ended without any compromise in sight.
Toth found another way.
In 1891, he and several hundred of his parishioners were received into the Russian Orthodox Church, whose American diocese was then based in San Francisco.
As Toth saw it, he was leading his people home to the faith of their ancestors, before their union with Rome.
He spent the rest of his life traveling to Rusyn communities across the country, and by the time he died, in 1909, many thousands had followed his example.
Holy Trinity, founded in Chicago just a year after his parish made its move, grew out of the same current, and the Russian Church, backed by the tsar's government, sent priests and money to help.
Rome's own policies kept the movement going.
In 1929, a Vatican decree barred married Eastern Catholic priests from serving in America, and another wave of parishes left.
Today Toth is honored as a saint by the Orthodox Church in America, and many American Orthodox parishes trace their roots to his quarrel with the archbishop.
The people who founded this parish went by many names, and the confusion tells you a lot about where they came from.
They called themselves Rusyns.

Their homeland was a string of mountain valleys and villages along the Carpathians, where today's Poland, Slovakia, Ukraine, Hungary, and Romania come together, and they had never had a country of their own.
The Habsburg officials who ruled them called them Ruthenians, an old Latin form of the same name.
Depending on the valley, they might also call themselves Rusnaks, or Lemkos.
In America, the names multiplied.
Many of those who joined the Russian Orthodox Church began calling themselves Russians, which wasn't quite right, but which made a certain sense in a church whose bishops and money came from Russia.
Others came to think of themselves as Slovak Americans, or Ukrainian Americans, and within a generation, cousins from the same village could disagree about what they were.
The twentieth century made it harder still.
After the Second World War, much of the Rusyn homeland was annexed to Soviet Ukraine, and the Soviet authorities simply declared that Rusyns were Ukrainians.

Only after communism fell did a Rusyn revival take hold, with its own schools, newspapers, and festivals, and today Rusyns are recognized as a national minority in several countries of central Europe.
You've almost certainly heard of one American with Rusyn roots.
Andy Warhol's parents, Ondrej and Julia Warhola, came from Miková, a Rusyn village in what is now eastern Slovakia, and Warhol grew up in Pittsburgh going to a Byzantine Catholic church.
He never made much of his background in public.
But a short drive from his parents' village, there's now a museum of his work, and to many Rusyns he's a point of pride: the most famous son of a people much of the world has never heard of.
So if you hear this church called Russian, Rusyn, or simply Orthodox, all of those names are true in their way.
The two saints connected with this church each spent about a decade in America, and both left marks that outlasted them.
John Kochurov came first.
Born in 1871 in a village in central Russia, he finished his studies at the theological academy in Saint Petersburg and volunteered for the church's American mission.
In 1895 he arrived in Chicago, a young priest, to serve a small, poor congregation that didn't yet have a proper church.
For the next twelve years, he was its pastor, organizer, and fundraiser.
He raised money wherever he could, including in Russia, he worked with Louis Sullivan on the design, and he saw the church through to its completion.
Then, in 1907, he was called home.

He taught religion in the schools of Narva, in what is now Estonia, and later served at Tsarskoye Selo, pronounced roughly tsar-skoy-eh seh-lo, the imperial town outside Saint Petersburg, where his life ended in the first days of Bolshevik rule.
Here at Holy Trinity, he's remembered simply as Saint John of Chicago.
His bishop, Tikhon, had come to America in 1898 to lead the Russian Church's North American diocese, then based in San Francisco.
He was a tireless traveler, crossing the continent to visit scattered parishes from Alaska to Pennsylvania, and he saw that the church's future here would be American.
In 1903 he came to Chicago to consecrate this church.
Two years later he moved his headquarters to New York, and that same year he founded a seminary in Minneapolis and a monastery in Pennsylvania.
He encouraged worship in English, and he even proposed that the American church should one day govern itself.
In 1907, Tikhon too was called home, and ten years later, in the turmoil of revolution, he became patriarch, as you heard at the stop.
The idea he had planted here took longer to grow.
In 1970, the church that grew out of his American diocese was granted its independence by the church in Moscow, as the Orthodox Church in America, much as he had imagined.
Walk south on Leavitt Street about a third of a mile, to Rice Street, and turn right toward Oakley Boulevard.
You'll see thirteen copper domes rising above the rooftops.
This is Saint Nicholas Ukrainian Catholic Cathedral, completed in 1915, and modeled on the great Cathedral of Saint Sophia in Kyiv.
The thirteen domes stand for Christ and the twelve apostles.
Ukrainian Catholics follow the Eastern, Byzantine tradition of worship, like the Orthodox, with icons and chanting, but they are in communion with the Pope in Rome.
The first Ukrainian immigrants came to Chicago in the 1890s, mostly from the region of Galicia, then part of Austria-Hungary, to work in the city's factories, rail yards, and stockyards.

Many more came after the Second World War, as refugees who couldn't or wouldn't go home to a Ukraine ruled by the Soviet Union, and many of them settled here, making this the center of Ukrainian life in the Midwest.
If the cathedral is open, step inside to see the walls and domes covered with mosaics and paintings in the Byzantine style.

A block south, at Oakley Boulevard and Superior Street, is a newer church, Saints Volodymyr and Olha, with a huge mosaic over its entrance showing the baptism of the people of Kyiv into Christianity, in the year 988.

It was built in the 1970s by parishioners who left Saint Nicholas after a bitter dispute, partly over whether to switch from the old Julian calendar to the modern Gregorian calendar, which would have changed the date of Christmas.
Just down the block, the Ukrainian National Museum holds folk costumes, embroidery, and pysanky, the intricately decorated Easter eggs for which Ukrainians are famous.
Look around the neighborhood.
Many of the houses are workers' cottages and two-flats from the 1880s and 1890s, and the streets are dotted with Ukrainian churches, credit unions, and social clubs.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, these churches and halls have been centers of fundraising, prayer, and protest, and you'll often see the blue and yellow Ukrainian flag on the porches.
When the Second World War ended, millions of people in Europe found themselves far from home, and a great many Ukrainians were among them.
The war had carried them west: as forced laborers taken to Germany, as prisoners of war, or as refugees fleeing the returning Soviet army.
The Allies had agreed that Soviet citizens should be sent home, and many were, some of them by force.
For Ukrainians who remembered the famine and the purges of the 1930s, going home could mean prison or worse, and many refused.

So they waited, sometimes for years, in camps for displaced persons in Germany and Austria, and they turned those camps into small Ukrainian towns, with schools, churches, choirs, newspapers, and theaters.
In 1948, Congress passed the Displaced Persons Act, and America's doors opened.
Tens of thousands of Ukrainians came, and many of them settled here, around Saint Nicholas and along Chicago Avenue.
They were different from the farmhands and laborers of the first migration.
Among them were engineers, teachers, doctors, and former soldiers, though many at first took whatever work they could find.
Then they built.

In 1951, ten of them gathered in a borrowed room on Chicago Avenue with a few hundred dollars between them, three hundred and fifty-nine, by the institution's own count, and founded a credit union they called Selfreliance.
For its first couple of years, volunteers ran it.
In the 1950s and 1960s, it lent money to more than twelve hundred Ukrainian families to buy homes, helping the neighborhood stay Ukrainian while others around it changed.
Today it's the largest Ukrainian American credit union in the country, and it celebrated its seventy-fifth anniversary in 2026, still headquartered a few blocks from here.
The newcomers founded much more: Saturday schools to teach their children Ukrainian, scouting groups, dance troupes, choirs, and the museum down the street.
Some of the older immigrants found them proud and political, and the two generations didn't always see eye to eye.
Saint Nicholas parish was founded in 1905 or 1906 by a few dozen Ukrainian laborers, and within a decade they had built this.

The architects were Worthmann and Steinbach, a Chicago firm that designed many of the city's Catholic churches, among them Saint Mary of the Angels, the great domed Polish church you may have seen from the 606.
Their model, as you heard, was Saint Sophia in Kyiv, built in the eleventh century, when Kyiv was the capital of the great medieval state called Rus.
Byzantine builders liked to cover a church with domes so that from inside, you look up into a series of heavens.
Here, the domes rise toward the largest one at the center, and their copper was recently restored, work that won a national award from the copper industry in 2025.
Step inside if you can.

Almost every surface is covered with images, and much of what you see dates not from 1915, but from the 1970s, when the parish hired Boris Makarenko, an émigré icon painter, to redo the interior in the Ukrainian Byzantine style.
In that tradition, the main dome is reserved for Christ, ruler of the universe, looking down on the congregation, and the curved wall behind the altar for the Virgin Mary.
The great mosaic over the entrance was the work of three émigré artists, Makarenko among them, along with Sviatoslav Hordynsky, one of the best-known Ukrainian painters in exile.
Cut off from a homeland they couldn't visit, they used the art of medieval Kyiv to build a bridge back to it.
In 1961, Saint Nicholas became the cathedral of a new diocese for Ukrainian Catholics in the western half of the United States.
Not bad for a church built on the wages of factory workers.
As you walk on, compare it with Saints Volodymyr and Olha, down the block, a 1970s take on the same tradition.
The decorated eggs called pysanky, which you heard about at the stop, are made with a technique that's simple to explain and very hard to master.
The artist starts with a raw egg and a small stylus, a tiny funnel on a handle, filled with melted beeswax.
Wherever the wax goes, the color underneath is sealed in.
The egg is dipped in dye, the lightest color first, usually yellow, then darker and darker, orange, red, and finally black, with more wax added at each stage.
At the end, the artist holds the egg beside a candle flame and wipes away the wax, and the whole design appears at once, in brilliant color, for the very first time.
The patterns carry meanings.
Wheat stands for a good harvest, a sun or a star for life and good fortune, and a line that runs around the egg without end stands for eternity.
Many of the symbols are thought to be far older than Christianity, from a time when the egg itself was a sign of spring's return, and the church adopted them for Easter.
And then there's the legend, told in the villages of the Hutsuls, the highlanders of the Carpathian Mountains.
Somewhere, it's said, a monster lies chained to a cliff.
Every year, his servants go out across the world to count how many pysanky have been made.
If there are few, the chains loosen, and evil spreads across the earth.
If there are many, the chains are pulled tight, and love and goodness hold the monster fast for another year.
So as long as people keep making pysanky, the world will be safe.
Other old beliefs held that a pysanka kept in the house protected it from fire and lightning, and some were buried in the fields to bring a good harvest.
Far from home, the tradition became something more: a way of keeping a culture alive.
Every spring, Ukrainian families in Chicago still gather around kitchen tables with candles, beeswax, and jars of dye, and every spring, somebody tells the children about the monster in chains.
Walk north on Oakley Boulevard back to Division Street, and then west to Western Avenue.
Look west down Division Street, and you'll see an enormous steel Puerto Rican flag arching over the road, its stripes and star rippling as if blowing in the wind.
This flag and its twin, about half a mile to the west, were installed in 1995.
Each is nearly sixty feet tall and weighs about forty-five tons.
They mark the two ends of Paseo Boricua, the stretch of Division Street that is the commercial and cultural heart of Puerto Rican Chicago.
The word Boricua comes from Borikén, the name the Taíno people gave to the island of Puerto Rico before the Spanish arrived.
Puerto Ricans first came to Chicago in large numbers in the late 1940s.
Some were recruited by an employment agency to work in steel mills and as domestic workers, and many more followed, settling near the Loop, in Woodlawn, in Lincoln Park, and in Lakeview.
In the 1960s, urban renewal cleared many of those blocks.

In Lincoln Park, a street gang called the Young Lords, led by a young man named José Cha Cha Jiménez, transformed itself into a political organization, occupying buildings and demanding housing for the poor, and it inspired Young Lords chapters in New York and other cities.
But the displacement went on, and families moved west, to West Town and Humboldt Park.
By the 1990s, the community faced a new threat: the gentrification spreading west from Wicker Park, as rising rents began to push families out once again.
Neighborhood leaders and the city created Paseo Boricua, with the flags as its gateways, as a way to plant the community's identity firmly in place.
As you walk west, look for the bakeries, restaurants, and social clubs along the street, and for the murals of Puerto Rican heroes on the walls.

On the corner of Western Avenue, just north of Division Street, is Roberto Clemente Community Academy, a high school named for the great Puerto Rican baseball player, who died in 1972 in a plane crash while flying relief supplies to earthquake victims in Nicaragua.
The flag arching over the street was born in exile, in New York.
On December twenty-second, 1895, a group of Puerto Ricans living in Manhattan met in a hall called Chimney Corner.

They belonged to the Cuban Revolutionary Party, which was plotting to free both Cuba and Puerto Rico from Spain, and they adopted a flag for their island modeled on Cuba's, with the colors reversed: red and white stripes, and a white star on a blue triangle.
Exactly who designed it is still argued about.
Three years later, the United States took Puerto Rico from Spain in the Spanish-American War, and the flag of one revolution became the emblem of another cause: independence from the United States.
To the island's government, that made it dangerous.
In 1948, as the Nationalist Party grew more militant, Puerto Rico's legislature passed what people called the gag law.
It made it a crime to display the Puerto Rican flag, to sing patriotic songs, or to speak or write in favor of independence, with penalties of up to ten years in prison.
Many people were arrested under it, especially after the Nationalist uprisings of 1950.
Then history took a turn.
In 1952, Puerto Rico became a commonwealth, with its own constitution, and the new government adopted that very flag as its official banner.
The gag law was repealed a few years later.
The flag of rebellion had become the flag of the state, and ever since, it has been flown by Puerto Ricans of every political stripe.
Look closely at the blue, though.

Many independence supporters prefer a light, sky blue, which they consider the original color of 1895, while the commonwealth's flag has usually been a darker navy, much like the blue of the American flag.
Which shade you fly can be a statement.
So can no color at all.
In 2016, after Congress put Puerto Rico's finances under a federal oversight board, artists in Old San Juan painted the flag in black and white, as a sign of mourning and resistance.
You may spot that version in this neighborhood too.
Stand under one of the flags and look up.
It's built of steel pipe, bent and welded so that the stripes seem to ripple, and the whole flag looks as if it's snapping in a stiff wind off the lake.

The flags were designed by a Chicago architecture firm, DeStefano and Partners, and put up in 1995, with the backing of the local alderman, Billy Ocasio, Congressman Luis Gutiérrez, and Mayor Richard M. Daley.
Why steel?

The flags' backers have said that it was a tribute to the first generation of Puerto Rican migrants, many of whom came to the Chicago area after the Second World War to work in steel mills and foundries, and as welders.
Some of those first migrants arrived in 1946, recruited on the island by a private employment agency called Castle, Barton and Associates.
The agency brought men to work as laborers in foundries, and women to work as maids in homes in Chicago and its suburbs.
Many found the pay and the conditions far worse than they had been promised.

That November, a group of the women picketed the agency's Chicago office, and with the help of graduate students at the University of Chicago and other reformers, they pressed Puerto Rico's government to protect migrant workers.
The island's government soon set up an office to look after migrants, and it eventually had representatives in Chicago too.
It was one of the first times Puerto Ricans in Chicago organized to defend themselves, and it wouldn't be the last.
In 2022, the city made the two flags official Chicago landmarks, which means they're protected for the future, like the mansions of Wicker Park and the skyscrapers of the Loop.
For a community that had been pushed from one neighborhood to the next, that mattered.
The flags were meant to say that Puerto Rican Chicago wasn't going anywhere, and now the law says so too.
Come back after dark, when the flags are lit, and you'll see why people here call them the gateways to the neighborhood.
Roberto Clemente was born in 1934 in Carolina, Puerto Rico, the son of a foreman on a sugar plantation.
He joined the Pittsburgh Pirates in 1955 and played his whole major league career there, eighteen seasons, as one of the most complete players the game has ever seen.
He won four batting titles and twelve Gold Gloves for his fielding, and he had a right fielder's throwing arm that base runners soon learned not to test.
He was the National League's Most Valuable Player in 1966, and when the Pirates won the World Series in 1971, he was the most valuable player of the Series too.
It wasn't easy.
Clemente was Black and Puerto Rican, and he arrived in an America that was still segregated in many places, in a sport whose writers often mocked his accent by quoting him in phonetic English.
He answered by speaking out, about racism, about the respect owed to Latin American players, and about the poor.
On the last day of September 1972, he got his three thousandth hit, a double.
It was the last regular-season hit of his life.
That December, an earthquake devastated Managua, the capital of Nicaragua, and Clemente organized relief flights from Puerto Rico.
When he heard that supplies were being stolen before they reached the victims, he decided to fly along himself, to make sure they got through.
On New Year's Eve, the overloaded plane crashed into the sea just after takeoff.
His body was never found.
Baseball waived its usual waiting period, and in 1973 he became the first Latin American player elected to the Hall of Fame.
Every year, the major leagues give an award in his name for service to the community.
The high school on the corner took his name the next year.
It had been Tuley High School, where Saul Bellow studied, and when a new building opened across the street in 1974, its students, many of them Puerto Rican, pressed for it to be named for Clemente.
Walk west along Division Street.
At number 2625, on the south side of the street, look for a small wooden house painted in bright colors.
This is La Casita de Don Pedro, a replica of a traditional Puerto Rican country house, the kind that the jíbaros, the farmers of the island's mountains, lived in.
It's used as a community and cultural center, for music and gatherings.
It's named for Pedro Albizu Campos, who led the movement for Puerto Rican independence in the 1930s and 1940s and spent many years in American prisons.

The question of Puerto Rico's status, whether it should remain a territory of the United States, become a state, or become independent, has divided Puerto Ricans for more than a century, and you'll see all of those views expressed along this street.

Paseo Boricua is also the place to try Puerto Rican food: pastelillos, which are fried turnovers; alcapurrias, fritters of green banana and root vegetables stuffed with meat; mofongo, mashed fried plantains with garlic; and the jibarito, a sandwich of thin steak, cheese, lettuce, and tomato served not on bread, but between two slices of flattened, fried green plantain.
The jibarito isn't from Puerto Rico.
It was invented right here in Chicago, in 1996, at a restaurant called Borinquen, less than a mile north of here, and it has since spread around the country.
Every June, the neighborhood holds its Puerto Rican festival and parade, which fill Division Street and Humboldt Park with music, food, and flags.

You'll hear salsa, and also the older Puerto Rican music of bomba and plena, with their hand drums and call-and-response singing, which have their roots in the music of enslaved Africans on the island.
Pedro Albizu Campos was born in 1891 near Ponce, on Puerto Rico's southern coast.
His mother was of African descent, and he grew up poor.
He was also brilliant.
A scholarship took him to the University of Vermont, and then to Harvard.
During the First World War, he served as an officer in the American army, assigned to a segregated unit, and he saw American racism up close, an experience that shaped the rest of his life.
Back at Harvard, he went on to law school, and he's usually counted as the first Puerto Rican to graduate from Harvard Law.
In 1930 he became president of the Nationalist Party, and he turned it into a movement that demanded nothing less than independence.
He was a mesmerizing speaker, and he argued that the American takeover of 1898 had been illegal from the start.

In 1936, after Nationalists killed the island's American police chief, Albizu Campos and other party leaders were convicted of conspiring to overthrow the government, and he was sent to a federal prison in Atlanta.
The next year, on Palm Sunday, police in Ponce opened fire on a Nationalist march held to protest his imprisonment, and about twenty people were killed.
It's remembered as the Ponce Massacre.
He spent most of the rest of his life in prison.
Released in the 1940s, he returned to Puerto Rico and was arrested again after the Nationalist uprisings of 1950.
He was pardoned, then arrested once more in 1954, after four Nationalists opened fire in the United States Capitol, wounding five congressmen.
In prison, he said that he was being bombarded with radiation.
His jailers dismissed it as delusion, and some of his supporters believe it to this day.
He was pardoned again, gravely ill, in 1964, and died the next year.
To his admirers, he's the greatest Puerto Rican patriot of the twentieth century.
To his critics, he led young people into violence and death.
Either way, you'll find his face on murals all over this neighborhood, and the little house in front of you carries his name.
Puerto Rico has belonged to the United States since 1898, but it has never been fully part of it.

In a series of Supreme Court decisions in the early 1900s, the justices described the island as belonging to the United States, but not a part of it, and that strange in-between status has lasted ever since.
Puerto Ricans are American citizens, as you heard at the start of the tour.
Since 1952, the island has governed itself as a commonwealth, with its own constitution and an elected governor.
But people living on the island can't vote for president, and in Congress they have a single delegate without a full vote.
Move to Chicago, though, and a Puerto Rican can vote for president as soon as they register.
That's one reason the island's politics are followed so closely on this street.
On the island, the political parties are organized around the status question.
One favors statehood, one favors the commonwealth, and a smaller party favors independence.
Puerto Ricans have voted on their status again and again, in referendums from 1967 to 2024.
In the most recent ones, statehood came out ahead, but the turnout and the wording were fiercely disputed, the votes weren't binding, and Congress hasn't acted.
In Chicago, the independence cause once took a violent turn.

In the 1970s and early 1980s, a clandestine group called the Armed Forces of National Liberation claimed responsibility for more than a hundred bombings in the name of independence, in New York, Chicago, and elsewhere, and several of its members came from Chicago's Puerto Rican community.
To their supporters, they were political prisoners.
To the families of the people their bombs killed, they were terrorists.
One of them, Oscar López Rivera, a Vietnam veteran who had been a community organizer here, spent about thirty-five years in prison, though he was never tied to a specific bombing.

In 2017, President Obama commuted his sentence, and when he came home that May, motorcycles and crowds waving flags escorted him through this neighborhood, to a hero's welcome here, and to outrage elsewhere.
Bomba and plena are often named together, but they're very different, and once you know what to listen for, you can tell them apart in a few seconds.
Bomba is the older of the two, born on the sugar plantations of colonial Puerto Rico.
Its drums, called barriles, were traditionally made from old rum barrels, with a skin stretched over one end.
One or two drummers keep a steady rhythm on the lower-pitched drums.
The lead drum, called the primo or the subidor, is tuned higher, and it does something unusual.
It doesn't lead.
It follows the dancer.
That's the heart of bomba.

A dancer steps out in front of the drums and challenges the lead drummer with sharp, sudden movements, a flick of the skirt, a stamp of the foot, a turn of the shoulder, and the drummer has to answer each one with a beat, instantly.
It's a conversation and a duel at the same time, and when it's going well, you can't tell who's leading whom.
Meanwhile a singer calls out a verse, and everyone answers in chorus.
Plena is younger.
It took shape around the beginning of the twentieth century, in the working-class neighborhoods of the south coast, and spread to the barrios of San Juan.
It's played on panderos, round hand drums like big tambourines without the jingles, and it has one basic rhythm that almost anyone can learn.
Its songs tell stories: a hurricane, a scandal, a strike, a crime, the latest gossip.
People call plena the newspaper of the people.
For a long time, both were looked down on as the music of poor and Black Puerto Ricans, and by the middle of the twentieth century they seemed to be fading.
A revival late in the century, on the island and in New York and Chicago, brought them back.
Today community groups here teach bomba and plena to children, and you'll hear them at festivals, at protests, and at parties along Paseo Boricua.
If someone hands you a pandero, give it a try.
Continue west on Division Street, past the second steel flag and across California Avenue, into Humboldt Park.
On the south side of Division Street, look for a handsome old building of brick and stone, with steep roofs and a turreted tower, which looks as if it belongs in a German village.
This is the Humboldt Park Receptory and Stables, built in 1896 for the West Park Commission, the agency that ran the West Side parks.
It was designed by two German-born architects, Frommann and Jebsen.
It held the park's offices, a waiting room for visitors, and stables for the horses and wagons that maintained the parks.
Today, it's home to the National Museum of Puerto Rican Arts and Culture.
The park itself was laid out starting in 1869, and named for Alexander von Humboldt, the German explorer and naturalist, who had died ten years earlier.
Its first designer was William Le Baron Jenney, the architect of the Home Insurance Building, often called the world's first skyscraper.
The neighborhood around the park filled with Germans, Scandinavians, Poles, and Jews, and they decorated the park with statues of their heroes.
Look for the bronze of Alexander von Humboldt himself, and a statue of the Viking explorer Leif Erikson, given by the Norwegian community.
Until the 1970s, there was also a monument to Thaddeus Kosciuszko, the Polish general who fought in the American Revolution, given by the Polish community.
Saul Bellow grew up near this park in the 1920s, the son of Jewish immigrants who had come from Russia by way of Montreal.
He went to Tuley High School, near Division and Western, which later became Roberto Clemente Community Academy, and he set the opening of his novel The Adventures of Augie March in these streets.
The book begins, "I am an American, Chicago born."
Bellow himself was born in Canada, but he became the great novelist of Chicago, and in 1976, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
In his own lifetime, Alexander von Humboldt was one of the most famous people in the world.
He was born in Berlin in 1769, into a wealthy Prussian family, and as soon as he had money of his own, he spent it on a voyage.
From 1799 to 1804, with a French botanist named Aimé Bonpland, he explored Spain's colonies in the Americas: the rainforests along the Orinoco River in Venezuela, the Andes, Cuba, and Mexico.

They traveled thousands of miles by canoe, mule, and foot, collected tens of thousands of plant specimens, and measured everything they could: temperature, altitude, air pressure, even the blueness of the sky.
In 1802, Humboldt climbed most of the way up Chimborazo, in Ecuador, then believed to be the highest mountain on earth, higher than anyone on record had climbed before.
Out of those journeys came a new way of seeing nature, not as a collection of separate things, but as a web, in which climate, plants, animals, and people all depend on one another.
He noticed how cutting down forests could change a region's climate, and he wrote against slavery, which he had seen in Cuba.
His last great work, Kosmos, tried to describe the whole universe, and it was a bestseller.
The cold ocean current off the coast of Peru is named for him, along with mountains, rivers, towns, and many plants and animals.
Germans everywhere treated him as a national hero, and when he died, in 1859, he was mourned around the world.
Ten years later, the hundredth anniversary of his birth was celebrated in cities across the United States, especially by German Americans, and that was the year this park was named for him.
There's a fitting twist to the story.

Humboldt's journeys made him a hero in Latin America too, where he's often honored as the scientific discoverer of the continent, and where his name is on everything from schools to a national park in Cuba.
More than a century after Chicago's Germans named this park for him, it became the heart of Puerto Rican Chicago.
The immigrants who settled around this park in the late 1800s filled it with their heroes, and each statue was a statement about who they were.
The Germans came first.
The bronze of Alexander von Humboldt, near the boathouse, was unveiled in 1892, paid for by a German-born brewer named Francis Dewes.
A year later came a statue of Fritz Reuter, a writer most Americans have never heard of.
Reuter wrote in Low German, the everyday speech of northern Germany, and as a young man he had spent years in Prussian prisons for belonging to a student movement for German unity and freedom.
For Chicago's Germans, some of whom had left home for political reasons of their own, he was a hero of the right kind: funny, plain-spoken, and a bit of a rebel.
The Norwegians answered in 1901 with Leif Erikson, the Viking who reached North America around the year 1000.
Notice the day they chose to dedicate him: October twelfth, the anniversary of Columbus's landing.
That was almost certainly no accident.
Scandinavian Americans had argued for decades that Leif, not Columbus, was the first European to reach America, and here they made the point in bronze.
The statue has moved since, though only about two hundred and fifty feet, in 1950.
The Poles followed in 1904 with the grandest monument of all, Thaddeus Kosciuszko on horseback.
Kosciuszko was the engineer who fortified West Point for the Americans during the Revolution, and who later led an uprising for Polish freedom.
You won't find him here today, though.

In the 1970s, the statue was taken down when a ball field next to it was enlarged, and in 1978, Polish American organizations had it restored and moved to the lakefront, where it now stands on Solidarity Drive, near the museums.
So when you walk through the park, you're walking through a kind of argument in bronze: about who discovered America, about who deserves to be remembered, and about whose park this is.
Saul Bellow was nine when his family came to Chicago, in 1924, and settled in a tenement near this park.
His father tried one business after another.

The neighborhood the boy grew up in was poor and crowded, and to him it was endlessly stimulating: full of immigrants arguing politics on street corners, orators on soapboxes, missions, and branch libraries where a bookish kid could read his way into the wider world.
At Tuley High School, he found friends who were just as hungry for books and ideas.
Among them were Isaac Rosenfeld, who became a gifted essayist and critic, and Sydney J. Harris, who became one of Chicago's best-known newspaper columnists.
They read everything they could find, argued about all of it, and dreamed of being writers.
Bellow's mother died when he was seventeen, a loss that echoes through his fiction.
He went on to the University of Chicago and then to Northwestern, and by the 1940s he was publishing novels.
The Adventures of Augie March, which you heard about at the stop, made his name in 1953 and won the first of his three National Book Awards.
Then came Henderson the Rain King, Herzog, and, in 1975, Humboldt's Gift, which won the Pulitzer Prize.
Its title character, the brilliant, self-destroying poet Von Humboldt Fleisher, was modeled on Bellow's friend Delmore Schwartz.

Bellow taught for some three decades at the University of Chicago, and he wrote about this city all his life: its politicians and gangsters, its intellectuals and hustlers, its neighborhoods and their ghosts.
He wrote with a mix of love and exasperation, and with an ear for the way Chicagoans really talk, that few other writers have matched.
He died in 2005, at the age of eighty-nine.

The streets around this park have changed completely since his boyhood, but in his books, the Humboldt Park of the 1920s is still alive, with its peddlers, its schemers, its scholars, and its strivers, all of them talking at once.

Walk north through the park, past the formal rose garden with its circular beds, to the lagoon and the long, low boathouse on its shore, with its wide, overhanging roof and its open arches facing the water.
The boathouse was built in 1907, in the Prairie style, as part of the remaking of the park by one of the great landscape designers in American history, Jens Jensen.
Jensen was a Danish immigrant who came to Chicago in 1886 and got a job as a laborer in the West Side parks.
He worked his way up to superintendent of Humboldt Park, but in 1900, he was fired for refusing to go along with the political corruption that ran the park system.
When reformers took over in 1905, they brought him back to run all of the West Side parks.
Jensen loved the native landscape of the Midwest: the prairies, the woods, and the rivers he found when he went exploring outside the city.
He believed that people who lived in crowded city neighborhoods needed to experience that landscape, and he brought it into the parks.

Here, he created what he called a prairie river, a waterway that winds through the park like a natural stream, its banks lined with flat, layered limestone, like the rock ledges along the rivers of Illinois, and planted with native wildflowers and grasses.
He's considered the father of the Prairie style in landscape design, the counterpart of Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie style in architecture.
A couple of miles south, in Garfield Park, Jensen designed one of the largest greenhouses in the world, the Garfield Park Conservatory, which opened in 1908.
He called it landscape art under glass, and it's still one of the hidden treasures of the city.
This is the end of the Division Street tour.
Humboldt Boulevard leads north from the park about a mile, to Palmer Square, where the Logan Square tour begins.
Jens Jensen ran the West Side parks for about fifteen years after the reformers brought him back, and he used them as a laboratory.
His masterpiece was Columbus Park, on the far West Side, which he designed in the years around the First World War.

There he created a whole prairie landscape in miniature: a broad meadow, a winding prairie river, a swimming hole edged with stone, and something you won't find in any other Chicago park he designed, a council ring.
That's a low circle of stone benches around a fire pit, where people could sit facing one another as equals, to tell stories, sing, or talk things over.
For Jensen, it was democracy in the shape of a landscape, and he built council rings wherever he could.
He was also a crusader.
In 1913, he founded a group called the Friends of Our Native Landscape, to save wild places across the Midwest, and its members would include the great conservationist Aldo Leopold.
Jensen campaigned to protect places like the Indiana Dunes, and he argued that every city child deserved to know the prairie, the woods, and the river.
Around 1920, after more battles with the politicians who ran the parks, he left the park system for good.
He designed estates for wealthy clients, among them Henry Ford and Julius Rosenwald, but his heart was always in public landscapes.
After his wife died in the 1930s, he moved to the family's summer place at Ellison Bay, on the Door County peninsula in Wisconsin.
There, in 1935, he founded The Clearing, a school in the woods where people could come to learn from the land itself, and from each other, in the spirit of the folk schools of his native Denmark.
It's still running, on the bluffs above Green Bay.
Jensen died there in 1951, at the age of ninety-one.
His ideas have outlived him.
Today's movement to plant native gardens, and to bring prairie back into cities, follows the path he cut a century ago.
Eleven years after the riot on Division Street, it happened again, here in the park.
On June fourth, 1977, Puerto Rican families filled Humboldt Park after that year's Puerto Rican parade.
In the course of the day, there was gunfire, and two young Puerto Rican men, Julio Osorio, who was twenty-six, and Rafael Cruz, who was twenty-five, were shot and killed by Chicago police.
What happened, and why, has been disputed ever since.
The police said they had moved in after a gang shooting in the park that had already wounded several people.
Many in the crowd said the police had provoked the trouble and fired recklessly.
Either way, the killings set off about a day and a half of rioting.
Crowds, mostly of young Puerto Ricans, fought with the police, and many people were hurt and arrested.
There was little or no accountability for the two deaths, and for many in the community, the lesson was bitter.
Eleven years and many promises after 1966, it seemed that not enough had changed.
But the neighborhood answered in its own way.
By some accounts, the riot helped spur a new Puerto Rican parade along Division Street, first held in 1978, through the heart of the community instead of downtown.
And the generation that came of age in those years went on to build the institutions you've seen on this tour, from cultural centers and schools to Paseo Boricua and its steel flags.
The families of the two men kept their names alive for almost half a century.
In June 2026, honorary street signs went up for them at California and Evergreen Avenues, at the edge of the park, near where they died.
The dedication called the signs a permanent marker of the community's truth, its grief, and its resilience.
Jensen's other great West Side creation, the Garfield Park Conservatory, a couple of miles south of here, is worth the trip, above all for one room.
When it opened in 1908, most greenhouses displayed plants like specimens in a museum, in pots and neat rows.
Jensen wanted something else: whole landscapes under glass.

Working with the Prairie School architects Schmidt, Garden and Martin, and with a New York firm of greenhouse engineers, he designed a series of huge glass houses whose low, rounded profile, it's often said, was meant to recall a haystack on a Midwestern farm.
The Fern Room is the heart of it.

Jensen built a still, dark lagoon, edged with layered stone like the ledges along the prairie river in front of you, and planted its banks with ferns, mosses, and lichens, so that you seem to step into a swamp forest from the age before flowers.
That's the idea.
About three hundred million years ago, the land that's now Illinois was covered with steamy swamps full of giant ferns and their relatives, and their remains became the coal beds under the state.
Jensen's room is a glimpse of that lost world, in the middle of the West Side, and some of its oldest plants have been growing there for generations.
On June thirtieth, 2011, a violent hailstorm hit the conservatory, and roughly half of the glass in several of its houses was shattered, including much of the Fern Room's roof.
Rare plants were suddenly open to the sky.
It took years to repair all the damage.
The new panes are laminated, so that in the next big storm they may crack, but they shouldn't shatter.
The Fern Room reopened with Jensen's lagoon at its center, just as he laid it out.
On a winter day, when the park outside is frozen, it's one of the most peaceful places in Chicago: warm, green, quiet, and smelling of wet earth and stone.
This tour explores Logan Square, on the Northwest Side, about five miles from the Loop.
It's built around one of the great features of Chicago that many visitors never see: the boulevard system.

In 1869, the Illinois legislature created park districts for the city's North, West, and South Sides, and they planned a ring of large parks around the edge of the city, linked by broad, landscaped boulevards.

When it was finished, the system ran for more than twenty-five miles in a great arc, from Lincoln Park on the north through the West Side parks, Humboldt, Garfield, and Douglas, to Washington and Jackson Parks on the South Side.
The West Side parks were designed by William Le Baron Jenney, the engineer of the Home Insurance Building, and later reshaped by the landscape architect Jens Jensen.
The boulevards were meant to be pleasure drives for carriages, lined with elms and mansions.
Logan Square sits at a corner of that ring, where Logan Boulevard turns south and becomes Kedzie Boulevard.
The neighborhood is named for General John A. Logan, a Civil War general and senator from Illinois, who helped establish Memorial Day.
His statue stands in Grant Park.
The area was annexed to Chicago in 1889, and when the elevated railroad reached it in the 1890s, it filled with Scandinavian, German, and Polish families.
Along the boulevards, wealthier families built mansions and handsome two- and three-flat buildings faced with gray Indiana limestone, which Chicagoans call greystones.
In the second half of the twentieth century, Logan Square became a largely Latino neighborhood, with Puerto Rican, Mexican, and Cuban families.
In the last twenty years, it's become one of the most popular neighborhoods for young Chicagoans, with the restaurants, bars, and rising rents that come with that.
We'll start at Palmer Square, walk north up Kedzie Boulevard to the square itself, and then east along Logan Boulevard.
You're at Palmer Square, a long, oval park along the boulevard where Kedzie Boulevard and Humboldt Boulevard meet.
It's named for John M. Palmer, who was governor of Illinois when the park districts were created in 1869.
Many people assume it honors Potter Palmer, the merchant who built the Gold Coast, but it doesn't.
Look at the houses and apartment buildings around the square.
You'll see a remarkable mix: big Victorian mansions, Prairie School houses, and courtyard apartment buildings.
These were built from the 1890s to the 1920s, when the boulevard was a prestigious address for the middle class and the newly prosperous.
Now look at the boulevard itself.
Kedzie Boulevard runs north from here, with a wide grassy median in the middle and service drives on either side.
The boulevards were designed to be parks in themselves, places to stroll and ride, and to give the neighborhoods along them a sense of grandeur.
Notice the greystones along the boulevard: two- and three-story buildings with flat fronts of rough or carved Indiana limestone.
A greystone usually has one apartment on each floor.
Families would often own the building, live on one floor, and rent out the others.
The two-flat and three-flat were the backbone of Chicago's neighborhoods, a way for immigrant and working families to own property, and they're still everywhere in the city.
Most greystones are faced with Bedford limestone, quarried in southern Indiana, the same stone used for the Empire State Building and the Pentagon.

After the Great Fire of 1871, Chicago required fireproof materials in much of the city, and the stone, which was easy to carve and relatively cheap to ship by rail, became the city's signature building material for middle-class homes.
There are tens of thousands of greystones still standing in Chicago, and there's nothing quite like them in any other American city.
South of the square, Humboldt Boulevard runs about a mile to Humboldt Park, where the Division Street tour ends.
Together, these boulevards are part of a single system, more than twenty-five miles long, and in 2018, the whole system was listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
When the legislature drew up the park plan in 1869, Chicago was a city of about three hundred thousand people with only a few parks, most of them small.
Its motto, adopted in 1837, was Urbs in Horto, Latin for city in a garden, but the garden was mostly a hope.
Doctors believed that crowded streets bred disease and that open air could cure it, and real estate men noticed that land beside a park sold for more than land beside a railroad yard.
Instead of one park board, the state created three, one for each of the sides of the city that the river divides, and each with its own commissioners and its own taxes.
That's why the system was never quite a single design.
On the West Side, the commissioners hired William Le Baron Jenney, and his plan of 1871 started right about here.
A boulevard would run south from this corner of the city past three new parks, Humboldt, Central, and Douglas, and then turn east toward the South Side.
Central Park was renamed Garfield Park in 1881, after President Garfield was assassinated.
Then the city burned, in October 1871, and the financial panic of 1873 followed two years later.
Money dried up, and the boulevards were built in pieces over the next two decades, many of them across open prairie where almost no one lived yet.
That was partly the point.
The commissioners were betting that if they built the boulevards, the houses would follow, and around Palmer Square, eventually, they did.
The separate boards lasted for more than sixty years, joined over time by nineteen smaller park districts formed in outlying neighborhoods.
Park jobs were political plums, as you heard on the Division Street tour, and by one account the West Park Commission alone was some twenty million dollars in debt by the depths of the Depression.
In 1934, all twenty-two districts were merged into the single Chicago Park District that runs the parks today.
So who was the Palmer this square honors?
John McAuley Palmer was born in Kentucky in 1817 and came to Illinois with his family as a teenager.
He became a lawyer, and in the Civil War he rose to major general.
In 1865, the army put him in command in Kentucky.
It was a slave state that had stayed in the Union, so the Emancipation Proclamation had never applied there, and slavery was still legal.
Palmer set out to end it anyway.
He issued passes that let enslaved people leave their owners and travel to find paid work, and white Kentuckians called them Palmer passes.
Slaveholders were furious, and a Kentucky grand jury indicted the general for helping an enslaved woman escape.
As governor, he was a fierce defender of the rights of the states, even against his own party.
After the Great Fire, when Chicago's mayor called in federal troops under General Philip Sheridan to keep order, Palmer protested that the city had no right to do it.
He drifted from the Republicans to the Democrats, and the legislature sent him to the United States Senate in 1891.
Then, in 1896, came the strangest race of his life.

When the Democrats nominated William Jennings Bryan, who wanted to back the dollar with silver as well as gold, the party's gold men bolted and nominated Palmer for president, with a former Confederate general, Simon Bolivar Buckner, as his running mate: two old soldiers from opposite sides of the war, on one ticket.
They won about one percent of the vote, and many of their backers quietly hoped the Republican, William McKinley, would win.
When it was laid out, this whole route, from here north past Logan Square and east along Logan Boulevard, was called Humboldt Boulevard.
The stretch north of here now carries the name of John Kedzie, a real estate developer and outspoken critic of slavery who helped organize the Republican Party in Illinois.
Potter Palmer, by the way, has a park of his own, far to the south, at 111th Street.
Put your hand on the front of a greystone, and you're touching the floor of an ancient sea.
About three hundred and forty million years ago, a warm, shallow sea covered what's now southern Indiana, which then lay in the tropics.

Its floor was alive with small creatures that built skeletons of lime: moss animals called bryozoans, which grew in lacy colonies; sea lilies called crinoids, starfish relatives that waved on long, jointed stalks; and single-celled creatures no bigger than a grain of sand.
Their broken remains piled up in sandy shoals and were cemented, over time, into the rock that geologists call the Salem Limestone, and that everyone else calls Indiana limestone.
Because the grains are small and even, the stone has no direction to it, the way wood does.
Stonecutters call that a freestone: you can saw or carve it any way you like, and it won't split along hidden layers.

By the 1880s, quarries around Bedford and Bloomington were cutting it from the hills in enormous blocks with steam-powered machines and sending it north by rail, about two hundred and fifty miles to Chicago.
Look closely at a weathered stone front, and you may see what it's made of: tiny specks and ovals, and now and then a little ring or a short stack of disks, which are pieces of crinoid stalk.
Notice the color, too.
Some fronts are a warm buff, and others a cool gray.
The difference is iron.
Stone that lay above the water table, where the iron in it slowly rusted, turned buff, and stone from deeper down stayed gray.
And step around to the side of a greystone if you can.
