The stone is usually only on the front, with plain brick on the sides and back, because the builders spent their money where the street could see it.
Quarry families cut stone for generations.
If you've seen the 1979 movie Breaking Away, set in Bloomington, you've met their descendants: the local kids the college students look down on are called cutters, after the stonecutters.
Walk north along Kedzie Boulevard toward Logan Square.
On the west side of the boulevard, near the square, is a red brick church with a tall steeple.
This is the Norwegian Lutheran Memorial Church, known as Minnekirken, which means memorial church in Norwegian.
It was built in 1912, when Logan Square had a large Scandinavian population.
Norwegian immigrants came to Chicago in great numbers in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and for a while, Chicago had one of the largest Norwegian communities outside Norway.
As Norwegian Americans moved to the suburbs and assimilated, most of the Norwegian churches switched to English, merged, or closed.
But Minnekirken has kept holding services in Norwegian, making it one of the last churches of its kind in the United States.
Look along the boulevard for other signs of the old Scandinavian and German neighborhood: churches, lodges, and halls, many of them now used by Latino congregations or turned into apartments.
Walk to the center of Logan Square itself, the round plaza where Logan Boulevard, Kedzie Boulevard, and Milwaukee Avenue meet.
In the middle stands a tall white marble column, topped with a marble eagle.
This is the Illinois Centennial Monument, built in 1918 to mark the hundredth anniversary of Illinois becoming a state.
It was designed by Henry Bacon, the architect of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, and the sculptor Evelyn Longman.
The column is about seventy feet tall.
Look at the carved reliefs around the base.
They show figures representing the history of Illinois, including Native Americans, explorers, farmers, and laborers, symbols of the forces that built the state.
The square is the heart of the neighborhood.
On Sundays, the Logan Square Farmers Market fills the streets around it, and in summer, there are concerts and festivals.

Look around at the buildings facing the square, and you'll see some fine old commercial buildings and banks, from the time when Logan Square was a busy shopping district at the end of the elevated line.
The monument was paid for by the Ferguson Fund, a bequest left to the Art Institute by Benjamin Ferguson, a lumber merchant who wanted to fill Chicago with public sculpture.
The same fund paid for many of the city's best-known monuments, including Lorado Taft's Fountain of Time, on the Midway in Hyde Park.
On the southeast side of the square, near Milwaukee Avenue, look for a small cottage-like building with a steep roof.
It's an old comfort station, built in the 1920s as a public restroom and a shelter for people waiting for streetcars, and it's now a tiny arts space.
Down below the square is the Logan Square station of the Blue Line.
For decades, Logan Square was the end of the elevated line from downtown, and the busy terminal made the square a shopping center for the whole Northwest Side.
In 1970, the line was extended northwest in a subway beneath Milwaukee Avenue, and later all the way to O'Hare Airport.
Norwegians reached Chicago in the 1830s, when it was still a muddy little town, and for most of the next century, the city was the capital of Norwegian America.
Many newcomers passed through on their way to farms in Illinois, Wisconsin, and Minnesota, but many stayed, working as sailors on the lake boats, as carpenters, and as builders.
They settled first near the river, close to downtown, and then moved steadily northwest, up Milwaukee Avenue, to Wicker Park and Humboldt Park, and finally here.
By 1900, there were more than forty-one thousand Norwegians in Chicago.
By a common reckoning, only two cities in the world had more: Kristiania, which is now called Oslo, and Bergen.
They also had one of the most remarkable newspapers in America.
Skandinaven was founded in Chicago in 1866 by John Anderson, a Norwegian-born printer, and a few partners.
It grew into the largest Norwegian-language newspaper in the world, and no paper in Norway itself came close.
It was read in Norwegian homes all over the Midwest.
One of Norwegian Chicago's proudest moments came in 1893.
For the World's Fair, a Norwegian sea captain named Magnus Andersen had a copy built of the Gokstad ship, a real Viking vessel that had been dug out of a burial mound in southern Norway in 1880.

To prove that such a ship could really cross an ocean, Andersen and a crew of eleven sailed it from Bergen across the Atlantic and on through the Great Lakes, reaching Chicago in July, to cheering crowds.
The ship still survives, at Good Templar Park in Geneva, Illinois, west of the city, where volunteers are working to preserve it.
The church in front of you has a quieter history.
It was built as Christ Norwegian Lutheran Church, and its first congregation lost the building in the Depression.
In 1934, a new congregation bought it, reopened it, and gave it the name it carries now.
The most famous boy to grow up in Norwegian Logan Square was Knute Rockne, who became the most celebrated football coach in America.
He was born in 1888 in Voss, in western Norway.
His father, Lars, a blacksmith and carriage maker, came to Chicago in 1891 to show a carriage he had built at the coming World's Fair, and the family followed.
Knute was about five.
He grew up around here, went to Brentano School and then to North West Division High School, later renamed Tuley, played football and ran track, and left without a diploma.
For about four years he worked as a mail dispatcher at the Chicago post office, and in 1910, at twenty-two, he went to Notre Dame, where two friends had urged him to join them.
He was older than his classmates, and he studied pharmacy.
On November first, 1913, Notre Dame played Army at West Point.
Rockne, an end, and his quarterback stunned the Army team with a barrage of forward passes, and Notre Dame won, thirty-five to thirteen.
The forward pass had been legal for years, but that game made it famous.
Rockne stayed on to teach chemistry and help coach, and from 1918 until his death, he was the head coach.
His teams won one hundred and five games, lost twelve, and tied five, one of the best records in the history of college football.
Then there's the Gipper.
George Gipp, his greatest player, died of an infection in December 1920.
Eight years later, at halftime against Army, Rockne told his team that Gipp, on his deathbed, had asked that some day the boys win one for him.
Notre Dame won.
The only source for that request was Rockne himself.
He died on March thirty-first, 1931, when a passenger plane carrying him crashed in Kansas after a wooden wing came apart, and the outcry helped push airlines toward all-metal planes.
In 1940, Hollywood made his life into a movie, Knute Rockne, All American, with a young Ronald Reagan as the Gipper.
Reagan carried the nickname the rest of his life.
Three people made the column in front of you: a lumber dealer who never saw it, the architect of the Lincoln Memorial, and a sculptor who had learned her trade in Chicago.
The lumber dealer was Benjamin Ferguson.

When he died in 1905, he left about a million dollars to the trustees of the Art Institute, to pay for lasting statues and monuments in Chicago's parks and boulevards, honoring worthy Americans and important events in the nation's history.
The first work it paid for was Lorado Taft's Fountain of the Great Lakes, beside the Art Institute, in 1913, and the fund still looks after this column today.
For the state's hundredth birthday in 1918, the fund helped pay for two monuments.
One was a smaller, gilded copy of the Republic, the giant statue from the World's Fair of 1893, by Daniel Chester French, which still stands in Jackson Park.
The other was this column.
Henry Bacon designed the Republic's pedestal and this column while he was building the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, where French made the great seated Lincoln.
The sculptor was Evelyn Longman.
Born in Ohio in 1874, she paid for her training at the Art Institute in Chicago with money she had saved working in an office.
In 1901 she went to New York, where French took her on as an assistant.
Her first task was the lettering on a set of bronze doors he was making for the Boston Public Library, a job he disliked.
She soon outgrew it.
In 1906 she beat more than thirty other sculptors in a competition to design bronze doors for the chapel of the Naval Academy at Annapolis.
Later she made a gilded winged giant called the Genius of Telegraphy, which stood for decades on top of the headquarters of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company in Manhattan.
New Yorkers called it Golden Boy, and it now stands in Dallas.
In 1919, the year after this column was finished, she was elected a full member of the National Academy of Design, often described as the first woman sculptor so honored.
Start at the top.
The eagle is about ten feet tall and weighs something like eight tons, and it's carved from marble, like the column, though the first plan called for bronze.
It perches on a rock, looking out over the Northwest Side.
Now look at the column itself.
It's in the Doric style, the plainest and sturdiest of the classical orders, with a simple, cushion-like capital at the top and shallow vertical grooves, called flutes, running up the shaft.
It's the same order Henry Bacon chose for the ring of columns around the Lincoln Memorial, which he was building at the same time.
This column is made of marble from Tennessee, and it's said to be built of thirteen solid drums, stacked one on another.
Then walk around the base, which is carved with Evelyn Longman's reliefs.
The story starts on the south side, with a woman seated on a throne, who stands for Illinois.
Around her, in procession, come the figures who made the state, as the artists of 1918 saw it.

Descriptions of the carvings name a Native American figure called Hiawatha, after the hero of Longfellow's poem, a frontiersman in the mold of Daniel Boone, and Ceres and Mercury, the Roman gods of the harvest and of trade.
That's a very 1918 way to tell the story, and it has drawn criticism.
After the protests of 2020, Chicago set up a committee to review its public monuments, and in 2021 it published a list of forty-one works to reconsider.
This column was on it.
The committee said it was one of many works that use images of Native Americans to illustrate the pageant of the region's history without recognizing their violent removal from it.
The committee leaned toward adding to monuments rather than taking them down, with new public art and new lessons for schools.
The column stands where it always has, and it's still the neighborhood's gathering point, where people meet under the eagle for markets, festivals, celebrations, and protests.
Walk northwest a short way up Milwaukee Avenue to the Logan Theatre, with its old vertical sign and its marquee.
It opened in 1915, and it's one of the oldest movie theaters in the city still showing films.
Milwaukee Avenue was the main commercial street of the neighborhood.
In the early twentieth century, it was lined with stores, banks, and movie theaters, and the elevated line brought shoppers from all over the Northwest Side.
Below you, the Blue Line now runs in a subway, connecting Logan Square to downtown in one direction and O'Hare Airport in the other.
Like much of Logan Square, the theater went through hard times and was restored in 2012, with its original Art Deco details and stained glass.
It's a good example of how the neighborhood has been revived.
Walk along Milwaukee Avenue, and you'll find everything from old Mexican taquerias and Puerto Rican bakeries to some of the most acclaimed new restaurants and bars in the city.

The neighborhood has become a destination for food and drink, but the change has also pushed out many longtime residents, and many murals and community groups in the area speak about the fight against displacement.
Milwaukee Avenue is one of Chicago's diagonal streets.
Most of the city is laid out on a strict grid, but a few streets run at an angle, because they follow old Native American trails that were later used as roads by settlers and wagons.
Milwaukee Avenue follows the old trail northwest toward the city of Milwaukee, which is how it got its name.

Follow it about a mile farther northwest, and you'll come to Avondale, and the neighborhood that Polish Chicagoans call Jackowo, named for Saint Hyacinth Basilica, a huge church with a dome and towers that was completed in 1921.
In the late twentieth century, Jackowo was the heart of Polish Chicago, with Polish delis, bakeries, travel agencies, and bookstores lining Milwaukee Avenue.
And about two miles west of here, in a neighborhood called Hermosa, Walt Disney was born, in 1901, in a modest wooden house on Tripp Avenue that his father, Elias, a carpenter, built himself.
His mother, Flora, is said to have drawn up the plans.
The family moved to a farm in Missouri when Walt was four, and later returned to Chicago, where he went to high school and took art classes before heading west.
Walt Disney's father, Elias, was a carpenter and contractor who built houses in this part of the city, and he also built a church.
Saint Paul Congregational Church was dedicated on October fourteenth, 1900.
Elias sometimes preached when the minister was away, and Flora served as treasurer.
The minister was Walter Parr, a close friend, and when the Disneys' fourth son was born the next year, they named him Walter.
The church still stands, on Keeler Avenue, a block or so from the house where Walt was born, and it still serves the neighborhood, now as a Spanish-speaking Baptist congregation.
Why did they leave?
The family story is that Elias was frightened by crime.
Two teenage boys from a family nearby were caught up in a robbery at a streetcar barn, and he decided the city was no place to raise his children.
He sold the house on Tripp Avenue in February 1906, and that spring, the Disneys were farming near Marceline, where his brother already owned land.
They came back in 1917, after Elias invested in O-Zell, a Chicago company that made jelly and fruit juice.
Walt enrolled at McKinley High School, on the Near West Side, and drew cartoons for its paper, the Voice.
In the evenings he studied drawing at the Chicago Academy of Fine Arts, a school often confused with the Art Institute.
He also worked at the jelly plant.
In September 1918, after the Army turned him away as too young, he joined the Red Cross ambulance corps by claiming to be older than he was.
By the time he reached France, the war was over.
He drove ambulances, decorated their canvas sides with cartoons, and kept sending drawings home to the Voice.
He came home in 1919 but soon left for Kansas City to make his way as an artist, and O-Zell failed, leaving his father's stock worthless.
Two Los Angeles designers, Brent Young and Dina Benadon, bought the birthplace on Tripp Avenue in 2013 and restored it, and in October 2023 it opened for public tours for the first time.
Logan Square's fame as a place to eat began, many people would say, with a small café on the boulevard.
Lula Café opened in 1999, on Kedzie Boulevard just south of the square, when this was still a mostly Latino, working-class neighborhood.

Its cooks built the menu around what they could get from Midwestern farms and changed it with the seasons, and it became a pioneer of Chicago's farm-to-table movement, and a magnet for the artists and young people who were beginning to move here.
A quarter century later, it's still going.
Eleven years after Lula, Longman and Eagle opened on Kedzie Avenue, just north of the square.
It's a tavern, with a long whiskey list and a menu of rich, inventive food, and upstairs there are six small rooms for overnight guests.
Its name is said to come from the monument in the square: the eagle on top, and Evelyn Longman, the sculptor who carved the reliefs.

When the Michelin guide arrived in Chicago, it gave this neighborhood tavern a star, and Longman and Eagle kept it for seven years, before moving to the guide's list of restaurants that offer good food at moderate prices.
On Logan Boulevard, the chef Diana Dávila runs Mi Tocaya, which serves antojos, the snacks and small plates of Mexican markets and street stalls, and it, too, has been recognized by Michelin.
Its signature cocktail is called the Chicana, with hibiscus and mezcal.
Those restaurants put Logan Square on the city's food map, and they brought in visitors from all over Chicago and beyond.
But the neighborhood's older food is worth seeking out, too.

Along Milwaukee Avenue and the side streets, you can still find Mexican taquerias and bakeries with trays of sweet bread, Puerto Rican and Cuban counters, and a few reminders of the Polish neighborhood farther up the avenue.
Some have been here for decades, and rising rents have made each of them a little harder to keep open.
If you're hungry, the best way to help keep the old places alive is simple: eat there.
In 2000, about two of every three people in Logan Square were Latino.
By 2020, it was closer to one in three.
Over the same years, the white population grew by more than two thirds, household incomes rose sharply, and white residents came to outnumber Latinos.
For a neighborhood that had been a center of Latino Chicago for a generation, it was a startling change, and it happened within twenty years.
Why?
Rents and prices climbed as the neighborhood became fashionable, and many longtime renters couldn't keep up.

Landlords sold, new owners renovated, and some two-flats and three-flats, the buildings that once let working families buy a home and pay the mortgage with the rent from upstairs, were turned into single-family houses.
Researchers still argue about how much each of these mattered.
One analysis found that smaller households, with more singles and couples and fewer children, explain more of the neighborhood's falling population than conversions do.
You could see it in the schools, as neighborhood elementary schools lost students and fought to stay open.
The most visible fight was over a city-owned parking lot on Emmett Street, across from the Logan Square Blue Line station.
Neighborhood groups and the local alderman, Carlos Ramirez-Rosa, pushed for an apartment building there that would be entirely affordable, so that people of modest means could live next to the train.
Some nearby property owners fought it, and in 2020 a group of them sued.
The city sold the lot to a nonprofit developer for one dollar and put in ten million dollars of public financing.
In May 2022, after eight years of planning, argument, and litigation, the building opened: seven stories, one hundred apartments, half of them for public housing tenants.
Almost seven hundred people applied for the other fifty.
It has since been named for Lucy Gonzalez Parsons, the labor radical, and it carries a mural honoring the neighborhood's Latino community.
One building can't reverse a trend.
But it was a statement about what this neighborhood should be, and who it should be for.
Walk back to the square and then east along Logan Boulevard.
This stretch, running east toward the Kennedy Expressway, is one of the grandest residential streets on the Northwest Side.
Look at the mansions on the north side of the boulevard.
Many were built in the early twentieth century by the neighborhood's prosperous families: Scandinavian and German businessmen, contractors, and professionals.
You'll see Prairie School houses, Classical Revival homes with columns, and Romanesque mansions in stone.
Look also at the big apartment buildings, with their courtyards and limestone fronts.
These courtyard buildings were a Chicago innovation of the early twentieth century, bringing light and air to every apartment, with a garden in front.
At the eastern end of the boulevard, the elevated tracks of the Blue Line and the Kennedy Expressway cut across the landscape.
The construction of the expressway in the 1950s sliced through the neighborhood, and the boulevards and the expressway meet awkwardly here.
The expressway was the Northwest Expressway when it opened in 1960.

A few days after President Kennedy was assassinated in November 1963, it was renamed the Kennedy Expressway, and it's now one of the busiest highways in the country, carrying traffic between downtown and O'Hare.
The boulevard system once continued from here toward the lake.
From the end of Logan Boulevard at Western Avenue, carriages could turn onto Diversey Parkway and ride east all the way to Lincoln Park.

On a Sunday afternoon in 1900, you could have driven a horse and buggy along an unbroken chain of parks and boulevards for miles around the edge of the city, from the lakefront on the North Side to the lakefront on the South Side.
That was the dream of the men who planned the system in 1869, and much of it still survives, though most of the people who travel it today are in cars.
This is the end of the Logan Square tour.
The Logan Square station on the Blue Line, back at the square, will take you downtown.
Or, if you walk about a mile south along California Avenue, you'll reach the 606 trail, which you can follow east toward Bucktown and Wicker Park.
John Alexander Logan, the general this neighborhood honors, was one of the most complicated men in Illinois history.
He was born in 1826 in southern Illinois, the region called Little Egypt.
He served in the Mexican War, became a lawyer, and went into politics as a Democrat.
In 1853, as a young state legislator, he pushed through one of the harshest laws in the North, barring free Black people from settling in Illinois.
A Black newcomer who stayed more than ten days could be fined fifty dollars, and one who couldn't pay could be auctioned off to work for whoever paid it.
When the Civil War came, his district was full of Southern sympathizers, and for a while his loyalty was in doubt.
He chose the Union.
He is said to have fought as a volunteer at Bull Run while still a congressman, and then he went home and raised a regiment.
His dark hair and complexion earned him the nickname Black Jack, and he's often called the best of the political generals, who rose through politics, not West Point.
On July twenty-second, 1864, outside Atlanta, the commander of the Army of the Tennessee was killed, and Logan took over in the middle of the battle.
But General Sherman gave the permanent command to a West Point man, and Logan never quite forgave it.
He finally got the army in May 1865, in time to lead it through Washington in the Grand Review.

After the war, he returned to Congress as a Radical Republican, of the wing that fought hardest for the freed slaves, and in 1868 he helped prosecute President Andrew Johnson at his impeachment trial.
He went on to the Senate, and in 1884 he ran for vice president with James G. Blaine.
They lost narrowly.
Logan died the day after Christmas in 1886, and his coffin lay in the Capitol, on the bier that had held Abraham Lincoln's.
The man behind the Black Law ended his career on the side of the people it was written to keep out.
Conscience or politics?
You can decide.
The big U-shaped apartment buildings along the boulevard, wrapped around a garden, are worth a closer look, because they solved a very Chicago problem.
Most Chicago lots are long and narrow, typically twenty-five feet wide and a hundred and twenty-five feet deep, with an alley behind.
That shape suits a two-flat.
But crowd a big apartment building onto a row of those lots, and the apartments in the middle are left dark and stuffy.
The courtyard building, which first appeared in the late 1880s and came into its own in the 1910s and 1920s, bends the building into a horseshoe around a garden that opens to the street.
Notice the doors.

Instead of a single lobby and long, dark hallways, there are several entrances around the court, each opening onto its own stairway, and each stairway usually serves just two apartments on each floor.
So nearly every apartment has windows on at least two sides, and in the days before air conditioning, a breeze could pass straight through.

At the back, open wooden porches and stairs climbed to every kitchen door, for deliveries of ice and coal and for carrying out the trash, and those back porches became a Chicago institution of their own.
The builders were competing with the single-family house, which in Chicago was cheap enough that many families could buy one.
So the courtyard building was designed to feel like a home, not a tenement.
The garden served as a shared front yard.
Many apartments had a sunroom across the front and a dining room with a built-in china cabinet.
Builders gave the buildings names, carved over the doors, and often put them near parks, boulevards, and elevated stations, so tenants had greenery outside and a quick ride downtown.
The courtyard building's heyday ended with the Depression, when building stopped, and Chicago's zoning code of 1957 effectively ruled out new ones.
So nearly every courtyard building you see in the city comes from a window of about forty years.
Look for the name over the entrance, and the year, if the builder carved one.
Picture this boulevard a century ago, and you have to imagine a different kind of tree.
The pleasure drives were lined with American elms, and when the trees were grown, their high, arching branches met overhead, so a carriage rolled down a green tunnel, like the nave of a cathedral.
Towns all over America planted elms that way, because they grew fast, tolerated soot and poor soil, and left room for traffic underneath.
Then came Dutch elm disease.
It's named for the Dutch scientists who identified it, not for where it came from.
It's a fungus, carried by bark beetles, that clogs the vessels carrying water up the trunk until the crown wilts and dies.
It reached America around 1930, probably in logs from Europe, and spread across the Midwest after the Second World War.
In the 1970s and 1980s, as it swept through Chicago, the city cut down elm after elm along streets like this one.
The tree most often planted in their place was ash, which grew fast and seemed indestructible.
Chicago ended up with tens of thousands of ash trees on its parkways.
Then, in 2006, a small, shiny green beetle from Asia called the emerald ash borer turned up in Illinois.
Its larvae tunnel under the bark, and an infested ash usually dies within a few years.
The city fought back with the largest treatment program of its kind in the country, injecting about sixty-six thousand parkway ash trees with insecticide in 2013 and 2014.
But in 2018 it stopped, and many of those trees have since come down.
The lesson foresters took is variety.
A boulevard of a single kind of tree is beautiful, and it's also a feast for a single pest.
Today the city mixes species, so the next disease can't take a whole street at once.
Among them you may spot young elms again, of varieties that resist the disease, some developed at the Morton Arboretum, in the western suburbs.
As you walk, look up and count how many kinds of trees you can find on one block.
This tour explores the Near West Side, just across the South Branch of the river from the Loop.
It's a part of the city where some of the most important chapters of American labor and social history took place, and where an old industrial district has been remade in the last twenty years.
In the late nineteenth century, the Near West Side was one of the most crowded immigrant neighborhoods in the country.

Irish, Germans, Bohemians, Italians, Greeks, Russian and Polish Jews, and many others lived packed into small wooden houses and tenements, working in the factories, rail yards, and garment shops nearby.
The streets were unpaved, the garbage was rarely collected, and disease was common.

It was here, in 1889, that Jane Addams opened Hull House, which became the most famous settlement house in America and a laboratory for reforms that changed the country, from child labor laws to playgrounds to juvenile courts.
It was here too, in 1886, that the Haymarket bombing took place, an event that shook the labor movement and is remembered around the world each year on May first.

The area north of Randolph Street was for a century the city's wholesale market district: produce on Randolph Street, and meat along Fulton Market, with cold storage warehouses, packing houses, and loading docks.
Since the 2000s, that district has been transformed.
Restaurants moved into old warehouses on Randolph, and then technology and corporate headquarters arrived, including Google and McDonald's.

We'll start where the Great Fire of 1871 began, walk west to Hull House at the University of Illinois Chicago, then north up Halsted Street through Greektown, past Old Saint Patrick's Church and Union Station, to the Haymarket, and finish in Fulton Market.
You're on DeKoven Street, just west of Jefferson Street, in front of the Chicago Fire Academy, where the city trains its firefighters.
Look for the tall bronze sculpture of twisting flames in front of the building, called the Pillar of Fire.
It marks the spot where, on the night of October eighth, 1871, the Great Chicago Fire began, in a barn behind the cottage of Patrick and Catherine O'Leary.
The summer and fall of 1871 had been extremely dry.
Chicago was a city of wood: wooden houses, wooden sidewalks, wooden barns full of hay, lumber yards, and even some streets paved with wooden blocks.
The night before, a big fire had burned several blocks just north of here, and the exhausted firefighters were slow to respond.
A strong wind from the southwest drove the flames north and east, into the heart of the city.
The fire jumped the South Branch of the river, burned through the downtown, leapt the main river, and burned through the North Side for more than a day.
About three hundred people died, around seventeen thousand buildings were destroyed, and about a hundred thousand people, a third of the city, were left homeless.
The story that Mrs. O'Leary's cow kicked over a lantern was made up by a newspaper reporter named Michael Ahern, who admitted it many years later.
Catherine O'Leary, an Irish immigrant, was blamed for the rest of her life and hounded by reporters.
Other theories have pointed to a neighbor nicknamed Peg Leg Sullivan, who first raised the alarm, or to men gambling in the barn.
No one really knows.
In 1997, the city council formally exonerated Mrs. O'Leary and her cow.
Oddly enough, the O'Leary cottage itself survived.
The wind carried the flames away from it.
It's fitting that the Fire Academy stands here.
The disaster led Chicago to rebuild in brick, stone, and iron, and to rethink how it fought fires.
When the fire broke out in the O'Leary barn, Chicago had a fire alarm system that other cities envied.
Since the 1860s, alarm boxes on street corners had been wired by telegraph to a central office in the courthouse downtown.
To prevent false alarms, the boxes were kept locked, and the keys were held by trusted people nearby, often shopkeepers.
High in the courthouse tower, a watchman scanned the skyline every night for the glow of a fire.
On paper, help should have come quickly.
It didn't.
Near the barn, a neighbor ran to a drugstore that had one of the alarm boxes.
What happened there is still disputed.
The druggist said later that he turned in the alarm, but if he did, the signal never reached the central office.
Up in the tower, the watchman, Mathias Schaffer, did see the glow to the southwest.
But in the dark he misjudged the distance, and he had the operator below send out the alarm for box three forty-two, about a mile beyond the real fire.
When Schaffer realized his mistake, he asked the operator to correct it.
The operator, William Brown, refused, by most accounts because he feared that a new signal would only confuse the engine companies already on their way.
So some of the engines headed for the wrong neighborhood, and lost precious minutes.
The department was also small for the job it faced: fewer than two hundred firefighters, with about seventeen horse-drawn steam engines, for a city of some three hundred thousand people.
Each engine could throw a strong stream of water, but only as far as its hoses could reach.

By the time enough engines were in place, the fire had spread through the sheds, fences, and cottages around the barn, and the wind was lifting burning embers over the firefighters' heads to start new fires a block or more ahead.
Many historians believe that from then on, no fire department of the time could have stopped it.
On the same night that Chicago burned, a far deadlier fire was racing through the forests of northeastern Wisconsin, a little over two hundred miles north of here.
It's remembered by the name of the lumber town at its center, Peshtigo.
The whole upper Midwest was parched that fall.
Chicago had seen only a fraction of its normal rain since early summer, and in the north woods, small fires had been smoldering for weeks in the forests and the peat bogs.
Logging made things worse.
The lumber companies left behind great piles of branches and treetops, called slash, and crews building a new railroad cleared land by burning it.
Then, on the evening of October eighth, 1871, a powerful storm system swept across the region, with strong, gusty winds out of the southwest.
The same winds that carried the flames from the O'Leary barn toward downtown Chicago whipped the scattered fires of Wisconsin into a single wall of flame.
Survivors described a roar like a train, and whirlwinds of fire that tossed houses and wagons.
In Peshtigo, people threw themselves into the river and stayed there for hours, while their town burned around them.
No one knows exactly how many people died.
Estimates run from about twelve hundred to well over two thousand, which makes it the deadliest wildfire in American history.
It burned more than a million acres.
That same night, fires also tore through towns in Michigan, including Holland and Manistee.
Over the years, some writers have suggested that all these fires started at once, set off by fragments of a comet.
Scientists reject the idea.
Meteorites are cold by the time they reach the ground, and the drought and the wind explain the fires well enough.
The telegraph lines around Peshtigo had burned, so news of the disaster was slow to get out, and by then the world's attention was fixed on Chicago.
To this day, far more people know the story of the cow and the lantern than the name of Peshtigo.
The cow story was a newspaper invention, but people have never stopped looking for the real culprit, and two suspects have drawn the most attention.
The first is the O'Learys' neighbor, Daniel Sullivan, known as Peg Leg because he had a wooden leg.
He told the official inquiry that he was sitting across the street that night, saw flames in the barn, and hobbled inside to save the animals.
In the 1990s, a Chicago lawyer and amateur historian named Richard Bales went back to the old property records and maps of the block.
He argued that from where Sullivan said he was sitting, other buildings would have blocked his view of the barn.
Bales suggested that Sullivan may already have been in the barn when the fire started, perhaps by accident, and then told a story to protect himself.
It's a careful argument, but it's still a theory.
Bales's research did help persuade the city council to clear Catherine O'Leary's name.
The second suspect is a man named Louis Cohn.

According to a story published after his death in 1942, Cohn, who had grown wealthy, admitted that as a teenager he'd been shooting dice in the barn that night with some other boys, and that a lantern was knocked over as they scrambled away.
Cohn left money to Northwestern University's journalism school, and the story is often told along with his gift.
But no one has produced his confession in his own words, so it can't be checked.
The O'Learys' own story took an unexpected turn.
Their son James, a child at the time of the fire, grew up to be Big Jim O'Leary, the gambling king of the stockyards district.
For decades he ran a saloon and gambling house on South Halsted Street, near the yards.
When he died, in 1925, the newspapers remembered him as a man who would bet on anything, and as the son of the woman Chicago had blamed for the fire.
You are at the corner of Halsted Street and Polk Street, in front of a red brick Italianate mansion with a wide porch.
This is Hull House, built in 1856 as the country home of a real estate developer named Charles Hull, when this was the edge of the city.
By 1889, the neighborhood around it had become a crowded immigrant slum.
That year, two young women, Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr, rented the house and moved in.

Their idea, borrowed from a settlement house in London called Toynbee Hall, was that educated people should live among the poor as neighbors, learning about their needs and working with them on solutions.

Hull House grew into a complex of thirteen buildings covering most of a city block, with a kindergarten, a day nursery, a gymnasium, a theater, a music school, an art gallery, a public kitchen, and classes in English and citizenship.
The women who lived and worked here, including Florence Kelley, Julia Lathrop, and the physician Alice Hamilton, became some of the most influential reformers in the country.
They investigated child labor, sweatshops, and industrial disease, and they pushed for laws to address them.
Hull House residents helped create the country's first juvenile court, here in Chicago in 1899.
Jane Addams became one of the most famous women in the world.
She was also a committed pacifist, which made her deeply unpopular during the First World War.
In 1931, she became the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
In the 1960s, most of the Hull House complex was demolished to build the University of Illinois campus, over the protests of the neighborhood.
Only the original mansion and the residents' dining hall survive, and they're now a museum.
Walk a block west and you'll be on Taylor Street, the heart of Little Italy, the remnant of the Italian neighborhood that once surrounded Hull House.
Italian immigrants arrived in large numbers from the 1880s, and Hull House offered them English classes, kindergartens, and help with work.

Much of the neighborhood was cleared for the university and the expressway, but Taylor Street still has old Italian restaurants, bakeries, the Shrine of Our Lady of Pompeii, and a lemonade stand, Mario's, that has been selling Italian ice from a sidewalk window every summer since the 1950s.
Jane Addams didn't come to Hull House by a straight road.
She was born in 1860 in Cedarville, a small town in northern Illinois.
Her father, John Addams, owned mills, served in the state senate, and had been a friend of Abraham Lincoln.
Her mother died when she was two.
Jane had a curved spine, probably from a form of tuberculosis, and as a girl she worried that her looks embarrassed her handsome father.
She adored him, and took in his sense of duty.
In 1881 she graduated at the top of her class from Rockford Female Seminary, at a time when few women went to college at all.
That summer her father died suddenly.
She started medical school in Philadelphia, then left it, ill and depressed.
For most of the 1880s she drifted, traveling in Europe and living with family, a well-educated woman with no clear purpose, as many women of her class were.
She later called those years the snare of preparation: a life spent getting ready for something that never began.
Two scenes in Europe shook her.
In London's East End, she watched a late-night auction of spoiled fruit and vegetables, and never forgot the hands of the hungry crowd, reaching up for food.
Then, in the spring of 1888, she went to a bullfight in Madrid.
Her companions, including her friend Ellen Gates Starr, left in disgust, but Addams stayed and watched for hours as bulls and horses were killed.
That evening she felt ashamed, and she wrote later that it made her see all her preparation as a kind of moral failure.
Soon afterward she told Starr about the plan she'd been turning over for months, to rent a house in a poor neighborhood and live there.
Starr was eager to join her.
The next year, back in Chicago, they found the old Hull mansion on Halsted Street, and on September eighteenth, 1889, they moved in.
Hull House didn't just serve its neighbors.
It studied them, and then it went into politics on their behalf.
One of its residents, Florence Kelley, was hired by the state in 1892 to investigate the sweatshops of Chicago, where whole families, children included, sewed garments for pennies in crowded rooms.

The next year, Hull House women and their allies pushed a bill through the Illinois legislature that barred factories from hiring children under fourteen and limited women's work in factories to eight hours a day.
Governor John Peter Altgeld made Kelley the state's chief factory inspector, to enforce it.
Manufacturers fought back, and in 1895, the Illinois Supreme Court struck down the eight-hour limit, as a violation of the freedom of contract.
Two years later, a new governor removed Kelley from her post.
She moved to New York, and spent the rest of her life campaigning for labor laws across the country.
Also in 1895, the residents published a book called Hull-House Maps and Papers.
Its centerpiece was a set of colored maps of the blocks around Hull House, showing, house by house, where people had come from and how much they earned.
It was modeled on a famous survey of poverty in London, and it was one of the first studies of its kind in America.
That same year, Jane Addams took on the garbage.
The streets of the ward were heaped with refuse, and complaints about the contractor who was supposed to collect it had gone nowhere.
So Addams put in a bid for the contract herself.
The bid wasn't accepted, but the mayor appointed her garbage inspector for the ward, a paid city job and the only one she ever held.
For a time, she was up before dawn to follow the garbage wagons on their rounds, and the streets got cleaner.
It was politics at street level, and it put Hull House at odds with the ward's powerful alderman, Johnny Powers.
More than once, Hull House backed candidates to unseat him, and lost.
Jane Addams believed that her neighbors needed beauty as much as bread, and Hull House was full of art.
The first new building on the property, opened in 1891, was the Butler Art Gallery, paid for by a Chicago businessman, Edward Butler.
Its ground floor held a reading room that became a branch of the public library.
Upstairs, Hull House hung paintings borrowed from wealthy collectors, so that people who'd never set foot in a museum could see them, free, a few doors from home.
In 1900 came something stranger, which Hull House called the Labor Museum.
Addams had noticed that many immigrant children were ashamed of their parents, who seemed old-fashioned and foreign.

So the museum invited older women from the neighborhood to demonstrate the skills they'd brought from the old country, spinning wool by hand, weaving at looms, and other crafts, arranged to show how each one had developed over the centuries.
Children who had shrugged at their mothers' skills watched them with new respect.
Hull House was a theater, too.
A company of neighborhood amateurs, the Hull-House Players, was led from about 1900 by a former professional actress, Laura Dainty Pelham.

They staged serious modern plays, by Ibsen, Shaw, and Galsworthy, when Chicago's commercial theaters seldom did, and they're often counted among the founders of the little theater movement, the small, serious playhouses that spread across the country in the 1910s.
There was a music school, founded in 1893 by Eleanor Smith, where neighborhood children studied for years.
And from the late 1920s, the Hull-House Kilns turned out pottery, shaped and painted by neighborhood artists, among them Mexican immigrants, which collectors prize today.
None of it was meant as charity.
Addams thought of art as something that belonged to everyone, and she wanted the people of Halsted Street to make it as well as look at it.
Walk north on Halsted Street, under the Eisenhower Expressway, into Greektown, the stretch of Halsted between Van Buren and Madison lined with Greek restaurants.
Greek immigrants settled on the Near West Side in large numbers in the early twentieth century, and many of them ran restaurants, candy shops, and produce stands.
When the expressway and the university displaced much of the old Greek neighborhood, the restaurants on this strip remained.
Greektown is said to be the birthplace of flaming saganaki, the cheese that's set alight at the table to cries of Opa.
A restaurant here called the Parthenon claimed to have started the practice in the late 1960s.
Now turn east on Adams Street to Des Plaines Street.
The church on the corner, with two towers of different designs, is Old Saint Patrick's Church.
It was dedicated in 1856, and it survived the Great Fire, which burned to the north and east of here.
That makes it the oldest public building in Chicago.
It was built by Irish immigrants, many of whom had fled the famine.
Look at the two towers.
One has a pointed spire, the other an onion dome.
They're often said to represent the Western and Eastern traditions of the church.

If you can go inside, the interior is a masterpiece of Celtic Revival art: stained glass windows and painted walls designed by the artist Thomas O'Shaughnessy in the early twentieth century, with intricate designs based on the illuminated Book of Kells.
Old Saint Pat's is known today for a hugely popular summer street party, which it has held since the 1980s, and for being one of the liveliest parishes downtown.
A few Greeks lived in Chicago by the middle of the nineteenth century, but the great wave came between about 1890 and 1920.
Most were young men from the villages of the Peloponnese, the mountainous peninsula of southern Greece, many of them from around Sparta and from the region of Arcadia.
Hard times pushed them out, including a collapse in the price of currants, the small dried grapes that many villages lived on.
Many meant to make some money and go home.
Many stayed.
They settled a little south of here, in a triangle of streets formed by Halsted Street, Harrison Street, and Blue Island Avenue.
Its shape gave it a name, the Delta, after the triangular Greek letter.
There were coffeehouses where men played cards and argued about politics back home, grocery stores selling olives and cheese from barrels, and Greek newspapers.

In 1897, Greeks here founded Holy Trinity, the city's first permanent Greek Orthodox church, and in 1908 the parish opened the Socrates School, said to be the first full-time Greek school in the United States.
By some counts, Chicago's Greek community was the largest in America until after the Second World War, when New York's overtook it.
Many young Greeks started out as street peddlers, selling fruit and flowers from pushcarts, close to the city's big produce markets.
When the city tightened its rules on street vendors, they moved indoors, and opened fruit stores, florists, confectioneries, and lunchrooms.

By the 1920s, Greeks ran a large share of the cheap restaurants in Chicago, the coffee shops and lunch counters where working people ate, and for generations after that, a Chicago diner was very often a Greek diner.
Later, many Greek families moved to the North Side and the suburbs, and the Delta was cleared for highways and the university.
But Halsted Street stayed the symbolic heart of Greek Chicago.
The National Hellenic Museum, which tells the story of Greek immigrants in America, stands at Halsted and Van Buren, and each spring a Greek Independence Day parade marches up the street.

The gyro as most Americans know it, a big cone of seasoned ground beef and lamb turning slowly in front of an upright broiler, sliced thin into a warm pita with onion, tomato, and a cucumber and yogurt sauce, is very largely a Chicago creation.
In Greece, the dish called gyros, pronounced roughly yee-ros, from the Greek word for turn, is usually made of slices of pork or chicken stacked on a spit.
It's a cousin of the Turkish doner kebab, and Greek refugees from Asia Minor are usually credited with bringing the method to Greece in the 1920s.
In America, Greek cooks in Chicago remade it.
Several men claim a share of the story.
George Apostolou, a Greek immigrant, said that he started selling gyros at his restaurant here in 1965, building the cones by hand.
Hand-built cones took skill and hours of work, and not every lunch counter could manage them.
In the early 1970s, a few Chicago companies worked out how to make cones in factories, from ground meat pressed into shape, and to ship them frozen.
Now any diner with an upright broiler could sell gyros.
One of those companies, Kronos, started in the 1970s by Chris Tomaras, grew into what was, by some accounts, the biggest maker of gyro cones in the world.
From Chicago, the frozen cone spread across the country, to diners, food courts, and hot dog stands.
Here at home, the gyro took its place on the menus of countless fast food stands, right next to the hot dogs and the Italian beef.
So if you order a gyro almost anywhere in America, there's a good chance that the cone it was sliced from, or at least the idea of it, came out of a factory in the Chicago area.
The one thing Chicago never settled is how to say it.
Greeks say yee-ros.
Many Americans say it like the first part of gyroscope.
And plenty of people just point at the picture on the menu.
If Old Saint Patrick's is open, step inside and let your eyes adjust.
Much of what glows around you is the work of one man, the Chicago artist Thomas O'Shaughnessy.
O'Shaughnessy was swept up in the Celtic Revival, the movement around 1900 that set out to recover Ireland's ancient art, language, and literature.

He's said to have been inspired by an exhibit of Irish art at the 1893 World's Fair, and he studied the illuminated manuscripts of medieval Ireland, above all the Book of Kells, with its endlessly interlaced knots, spirals, and fantastic beasts.
Between about 1912 and 1922, he designed fifteen stained glass windows for this church.
Look closely at the borders and the backgrounds, where the patterns weave over and under one another as they do on the pages of the old manuscripts.
As the sun moves around the building during the day, the colors change.
The most famous of them is a set of three panels, representing Faith, Hope, and Charity.
It's a memorial to Terence MacSwiney, the Lord Mayor of Cork, who died in a London prison in 1920, after a hunger strike of seventy-four days, during Ireland's war of independence.
His death made headlines around the world, and in Chicago's Irish parishes he was a martyr.
One historian of stained glass has called it arguably the finest window of its kind in the Midwest.
O'Shaughnessy also covered the walls and ceiling with painted Celtic stencils.
Over the decades they were lost, and the church declined along with its neighborhood.
By the early 1980s, the parish had only a handful of registered members.
A new pastor, Father Jack Wall, arrived in 1983 and set out to make it a home for the young people who worked downtown.
The parish grew into the thousands.
In the 1990s, in time for the parish's hundred and fiftieth anniversary, it restored the windows and recreated the stencils, and the church glows again much as O'Shaughnessy meant it to.
Walk east on Adams Street to Canal Street.
On your right is Union Station, the great railroad terminal of Chicago.
Chicago is the railroad capital of North America.
In the age of the passenger train, almost every rail trip across the country involved changing trains in Chicago, because lines from the East ended here and lines to the West began here.
Travelers had to cross the city, often by taxi or transfer coach, from one station to another.
Union Station opened in 1925, designed by the firm of Graham, Anderson, Probst and White, the successors of Daniel Burnham.
Walk inside to the Great Hall, a vast waiting room with a barrel-vaulted skylight soaring about a hundred feet above the floor, Corinthian columns, and wooden benches.
It's one of the grandest rooms in the city.
The station has appeared in many films.
The most famous scene is in The Untouchables, from 1987, when a baby carriage bounces down the grand staircase during a shootout, a homage to a famous scene in the Russian film Battleship Potemkin.
Today, Union Station is Amtrak's hub for the Midwest and the busiest station for the Metra commuter trains.
Long-distance trains still leave from here for New York, New Orleans, Seattle, Los Angeles, and San Francisco.
The first railroad out of Chicago, the Galena and Chicago Union, ran its first train in 1848 on a few miles of track heading west.
Within a decade, Chicago was the hub of the American railroad network, and it still is.
More freight lines meet here than anywhere else in North America, and about a quarter of all freight rail traffic in the country passes through the Chicago area.
Union Station once had a matching concourse building on the east side of Canal Street, with a vast glass and steel roof.
It was demolished in 1969 and replaced by an office tower, a loss that helped spur the preservation movement in Chicago.
Before 1883, there was no such thing as standard time.
Every town set its clocks by the sun, so that noon came when the sun stood highest in the sky.
Because the sun moves from east to west, noon in Chicago came about eighteen minutes later than noon in Detroit, and about ten minutes earlier than noon in Saint Louis.
For people who walked or rode horses, that hardly mattered.
For the railroads, it was chaos.
Each railroad ran on its own time, often the local time of its headquarters city, and a junction like Chicago could have several different times showing on the clocks of its stations.
Timetables had to be converted from one time to another, and travelers missed their connections.
The railroads fixed the problem themselves.
In October 1883, their managers met at the General Time Convention, at the Grand Pacific Hotel in the Loop, and adopted a plan worked out by a railroad official named William F. Allen.
The country would be divided into four zones, Eastern, Central, Mountain, and Pacific, each an hour apart, and every railroad would run on the time of its zone.
The change took effect on Sunday, November eighteenth, 1883, which became known as the day of two noons.
In places that had to turn their clocks back, the clocks struck noon, and then, a few minutes later, struck it again.
Chicago sits a little east of the middle of the Central zone, so here the railroad clocks went back about nine and a half minutes, and most of the city soon followed.
Not everyone liked it.
Some people objected to what they called railroad time, and a few insisted that the only true time was God's time, the time of the sun.
For years, some towns kept their own local time.
It wasn't until 1918 that Congress wrote the time zones into law.
Stand under a departures board here and you can see what those railroad managers achieved: every train, from every direction, runs on the same clock.
Union Station gets its name from the railroads that built it together.

Its owners were the Pennsylvania Railroad, the great Eastern line whose trains ran to New York and Washington, and two Western lines: the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy, known as the Burlington, and the Chicago, Milwaukee, Saint Paul and Pacific, known as the Milwaukee Road.
The Pennsylvania owned half, and the other two a quarter each.
A fourth railroad, the Chicago and Alton, rented space as a tenant.
The same railroads had shared an older and smaller station on this site since the 1880s, and by the early 1900s it was hopelessly crowded.

Daniel Burnham's firm planned the new one, but Burnham died in 1912, before construction began, and the partners who carried on his practice, soon renamed Graham, Anderson, Probst and White, saw it through.
The work took about twelve years, slowed by the First World War, shortages of materials, and labor troubles, and much of it had to be done while trains kept running.
The site was a hard one.
The station is squeezed between Canal Street and the river, and its tracks run below street level, so that the streets above, like Adams and Jackson, cross over them.
Most of the tracks don't pass through.
They come in from the north and from the south and end at platforms on either side of the middle, an arrangement railroad people call a double stub-end terminal.
Milwaukee Road trains used the north side, and the Pennsylvania and the Burlington the south.

In its prime, the station was home to some of the most famous named trains in America: the Pennsylvania's Broadway Limited to New York, the Burlington's sleek, stainless steel Zephyrs to Denver and the West, and the Milwaukee Road's Hiawathas, among the fastest steam-powered trains in the world, racing to Milwaukee and the Twin Cities.
None of those railroads exists anymore.
All of them disappeared into mergers.
But their station is still here, and still one of the busiest in the country.
Step into the Great Hall, and before you look up, find the two statues on the east wall.
They're by the sculptor Henry Hering, and they've been here since the station opened.
One figure holds a rooster, the bird of morning, and stands for Day.
The other holds an owl, and stands for Night.
Together they make a simple point: a great railroad station never sleeps.
Now look up at the skylight.

During the Second World War, when the station was handling close to a hundred thousand passengers a day, many of them soldiers and sailors, the glass was blacked out, so that the station would make a less visible target for enemy bombers.
The bombers never came, but the blackout coating stayed on for years, and for a long time the Great Hall was a dim, gray place.
The old skylight also leaked, and water stained and damaged the plaster.
In 2018, Amtrak finished a restoration that cost about twenty-two million dollars.
It built a new skylight of clear glass a few feet above the old one, and the Great Hall now gets about half again as much daylight as before.
The plaster was repaired, and the statues of Day and Night were restored and lit.
As you look around, think about what this room was for.
In the 1920s, a railroad station was a city's front door, the first thing many visitors saw, and the railroads wanted that first impression to be overwhelming.
A traveler who stepped off a train after a night in a sleeping car walked up from the platforms into this room, all marble and light, and knew they had arrived somewhere important.
Over the years there have been many plans for the station's future, from towers above it to a rebuilt concourse.
Whatever comes next, the station is protected as a city landmark, and the Great Hall is likely to look much as it does now for a long time to come.
Walk north on Des Plaines Street, across Washington and Randolph.
Just north of Randolph, on the east side of the street, is a bronze sculpture of a wagon with figures standing on it.
This marks the site of the Haymarket affair.
In the 1880s, a nationwide movement was campaigning for an eight-hour workday.
On May first, 1886, tens of thousands of workers struck in Chicago.
On May third, police fired on strikers at the McCormick Reaper Works, killing at least two.
Anarchist leaders called a protest meeting here, at the Haymarket, for the evening of May fourth.
The meeting was peaceful and smaller than expected.
The mayor, Carter Harrison, attended for a while and then went home.
But as the last speaker was finishing, around a hundred and eighty police officers marched in to break up the crowd.
Someone threw a bomb into their ranks.
It killed one officer instantly, and in the chaos that followed, police opened fire.
Seven officers died, most of them from the bomb or from police bullets fired in confusion, and at least four civilians were killed.
The bomb thrower was never identified.
Eight anarchists were tried and convicted, largely for their speeches and writings rather than for any proof that they were involved in the bombing.
Four were hanged in November 1887, including Albert Parsons, the husband of Lucy Parsons.
Another took his own life in jail.
In 1893, Governor John Peter Altgeld pardoned the three survivors, calling the trial unjust, an act that ended his political career.
The Haymarket affair became a symbol for labor movements around the world, and it's one reason that International Workers' Day is celebrated on May first in many countries.
This sculpture, by Mary Brogger, was dedicated in 2004.
A statue of a police officer that used to stand here was blown up twice by radicals in 1969 and 1970, and it now stands at police headquarters.
The trial of the Haymarket defendants opened on June twenty-first, 1886, before Judge Joseph Gary, and from the start it was less a search for the bomb thrower than a trial of anarchism itself.
Choosing the jury took three weeks, and nearly a thousand potential jurors were questioned.
Instead of drawing names at random, the court sent a special bailiff out to round up candidates, and the defense charged that he picked men hostile to the accused.
Several jurors admitted that they were prejudiced against anarchists, or had already formed an opinion, and the judge seated them anyway, once they said they could be fair.
One defendant, Albert Parsons, had slipped out of Chicago after the bombing and was hiding in Wisconsin.
On the first day of the trial, he walked into the courtroom and surrendered, to stand with his comrades.
It was a brave gesture, and it cost him his life.
The prosecution didn't need to show who had thrown the bomb.

It argued that the defendants had conspired to encourage violence, through their newspapers and their speeches, and so they were all guilty of murdering Officer Mathias Degan, whoever had actually thrown it.
In his closing, the state's attorney, Julius Grinnell, told the jurors that the law itself was on trial, and urged them to make examples of these men, hang them, and save the nation's institutions.
On August twentieth, the jury found all eight guilty.
Seven were sentenced to death, and the eighth, Oscar Neebe, to fifteen years.
The appeals failed.

On the day before the executions, the governor commuted the sentences of Samuel Fielden and Michael Schwab to life in prison, and the youngest of the condemned, Louis Lingg, killed himself in his cell with a small explosive that had been smuggled in to him.
On November eleventh, 1887, the remaining four were hanged at the Cook County jail.
Today, most historians see the trial as one of the great miscarriages of justice in American history.
John Peter Altgeld, the governor who pardoned the surviving Haymarket defendants, was an immigrant himself.
He was born in 1847 in a village in western Germany, and his parents brought him to a farm in Ohio as a baby.
His father, a stern man, saw little use for schooling.
Young Altgeld served in the Union army as a teenager, near the end of the Civil War, and came home with a fever that weakened him for the rest of his life.
He taught school, studied law, and worked his way west, and in 1875 he arrived in Chicago with little money.
He became a lawyer, a judge, and a very successful real estate investor, and by the end of the 1880s he was a rich man.
In 1892, he was elected governor of Illinois, the first Democrat to win the office in decades, and the first governor of the state born abroad.
He came into office believing the Haymarket trial had been a travesty, and he studied the record closely.
On June twenty-sixth, 1893, he pardoned Fielden, Neebe, and Schwab.
He didn't simply grant mercy.
In a long written statement, he argued that the jury had been packed, that the judge had been biased, and that nothing in the evidence connected the men to the bomb.
He also blamed the police, whose brutality toward strikers, he suggested, had fueled the anger behind the violence.
The reaction was ferocious.
Newspapers across the country called him a friend of anarchy and an alien, and he was burned in effigy.
He had expected the backlash, and it cost him.
In 1896 he lost his bid for a second term.
Altgeld died in 1902, at fifty-four, after collapsing at the end of a speech in Joliet.
A decade later, the poet Vachel Lindsay wrote a tribute to him called The Eagle That Is Forgotten.
Chicago didn't forget him entirely.
In Lincoln Park stands a statue of him by Gutzon Borglum, the sculptor who went on to carve Mount Rushmore, with a family of working people beside him.
Two very different monuments have stood for the Haymarket, and both have had eventful lives.
The first was a bronze statue of a Chicago policeman, put up in 1889 in the middle of the square with money raised from the city's business leaders.
The sculptor, Johannes Gelert, showed the officer with one hand raised, as if ordering the crowd to disperse.
In 1900, the statue was judged a traffic hazard and moved to Union Park, about a mile west.
In 1927, on the anniversary of the bombing, a streetcar jumped its track and knocked it off its pedestal.
The motorman supposedly said he was tired of seeing that policeman with his arm raised all the time.
It's a good story, and it may even be true.
Later the statue came back to Randolph Street, near its old spot.
On an October night in 1969, a bomb blew off its legs and scattered pieces onto the expressway below, and the radical Weathermen claimed the attack.
The city rebuilt it, and in October 1970 it was blown up again.
After that, police guarded it around the clock, until it was moved indoors in 1972.
It has stood inside police buildings ever since.
The second monument is in Forest Park, just west of the city, in what was then Waldheim Cemetery, where the five dead defendants were buried.
It was dedicated on June twenty-fifth, 1893, the day before the governor pardoned the three survivors.
The sculptor, Albert Weinert, made a figure of Justice placing a laurel wreath on the head of a fallen worker.
Carved on its base are the last words that August Spies called out from the scaffold: The day will come when our silence will be more powerful than the voices you are strangling today.
Over the years, many radicals asked to be buried close to it, among them the anarchist Emma Goldman.
The ground around it is still a place of pilgrimage, and in 1997, the monument was named a National Historic Landmark.
Walk west on Randolph Street.
This is Restaurant Row, one of the city's busiest dining strips.
For a century, this stretch was the Randolph Street Market, Chicago's wholesale produce market, where farmers and wholesalers sold fruit and vegetables from wagons and then from trucks.
Starting in the late 1990s, chefs began opening restaurants in the old market buildings, and the street became one of the most celebrated restaurant districts in the country.
This is a good place to think about how much of what America eats came out of Chicago.
Kraft cheese started in 1903, when James L. Kraft began selling cheese to Chicago grocers from a horse-drawn wagon.
Cracker Jack was popularized by the Rueckheim brothers, German immigrants who sold popcorn on Chicago's streets.
The Twinkie was invented in the Chicago area in 1930.
The Baby Ruth candy bar and Lemonheads are Chicago products.
For decades, when the wind blew right, the Loop smelled of chocolate from the Blommer Chocolate factory, on the river just north of here.
Then there's the food Chicago is famous for.

The Chicago-style hot dog is an all-beef frankfurter on a poppy seed bun, dragged through the garden, as people say: yellow mustard, bright green relish, chopped onion, tomato slices, a pickle spear, sport peppers, and celery salt, but never ketchup.
The Italian beef sandwich, thin-sliced roast beef soaked in its juices on a long roll, topped with sweet or hot peppers, was born in the Italian neighborhoods of the Near West Side.
And deep-dish pizza was created in the 1940s, by most accounts at Pizzeria Uno, near Michigan Avenue, though there are rival claims.

In the last few decades, Chicago has also become one of the world's great cities for fine dining, from Charlie Trotter's, which opened in 1987, to Alinea, in Lincoln Park, and the restaurants of this street.
For much of the twentieth century, Chicago was the candy capital of America.
At its peak, the city had well over a hundred candy companies, with some twenty-five thousand workers, and by some estimates it made about a third of all the candy in the country.
The reasons were practical.
Chicago sat at the center of the railroad network, so sugar, corn syrup, milk, and nuts could come in cheaply from every direction, and finished candy could go out to every town in the country.
The city had plenty of workers, many of them immigrant women, and room for big factories.
Some of the best-known names in American candy grew up here.
Emil Brach opened a small candy shop in 1904, and Brach's grew into a giant, with an enormous factory on the West Side.

Salvatore Ferrara started in 1908 on Taylor Street, in Little Italy, making sugar-coated almonds, the kind handed out at Italian weddings, and his company went on to make Red Hots and Atomic Fireballs.
Otto Schnering founded the Curtiss Candy Company in 1916, naming it, by most accounts, after his mother's family, because Schnering sounded too German during the First World War.
Curtiss made Butterfinger.
Frank Mars moved his company here from Minneapolis around 1929, and it was in Chicago that Snickers and Three Musketeers were born.
Tootsie Roll moved its headquarters and its factory here in the 1960s.
From the 1970s on, many of the factories closed or left.
The reasons were complicated, but candy makers often pointed to the price of sugar in the United States, which federal import quotas kept far above the world price.
Some production moved to Canada and Mexico, where sugar was cheaper, and Brach's left the city in the 2000s.
Still, Chicago never stopped making candy.
Tootsie Rolls still come from a plant on the Southwest Side, and Ferrara, now a much larger company, still makes candy in the Chicago area.
Chicago has a habit of inventing famous foods and then arguing about who did it.
Two stories show how slippery the history can be.
The first is the Baby Ruth.
The Curtiss Candy Company brought out the bar in 1921, just as Babe Ruth was becoming the most famous athlete in America.

But the company always insisted that it was named not for the slugger but for Ruth Cleveland, the daughter of President Grover Cleveland, who had been the nation's darling as a baby in the White House.
The trouble is that Ruth Cleveland had died of diphtheria in 1904, seventeen years earlier.
Many people suspect the story was a way to cash in on the ballplayer's fame without paying him.
When Babe Ruth later tried to sell a candy bar under his own name, Curtiss fought it, and won, arguing that buyers would confuse the two.
The second is deep-dish pizza.
The usual story says it was invented in 1943 at Pizzeria Uno by its owners, Ike Sewell, a Texan, and Ric Riccardo, a restaurateur.
But both were businessmen, not cooks, and others have claimed the credit.
Some give it to Rudy Malnati, who managed the restaurant for years, and whose son Lou later started his own pizza chain.
Others credit a cook named Alice Mae Redmond, who worked in Uno's kitchen and later at Gino's East.
No recipe or record from 1943 survives to settle it.
There's a further twist.
Most Chicagoans don't eat deep dish very often.
The everyday pizza of the city's neighborhoods is thin and crisp, and cut into small squares instead of wedges, a style known as tavern cut.
The story goes that bars served it to keep their customers drinking.
And stuffed pizza, a deep dish with a second layer of crust on top, has its own rival origin stories, from Chicago restaurants that opened in the 1970s.
In this city, a good argument about food is part of the meal.
Notice how wide Randolph Street is here.
There's a reason.
In 1850, the city built a market hall right in the middle of the street at Des Plaines, and the roadway was laid out broad enough for farmers to pull up their wagons and sell from them.
A bird's-eye view of Chicago from 1857 shows the widened street and the market hall, with a bell tower on top.
The produce wholesalers stayed long after the farmers were gone, and a few food distributors still work in the district today.
The first restaurants that changed the street came in the early 1990s, when the area was still dark and empty at night.
Vivo, an Italian restaurant, opened in 1991, and others followed.
In 1997 came Blackbird, a small and sleek restaurant led by the chef Paul Kahan, which drew national attention.

Kahan and his partners later opened Avec next door, with long communal tables and small plates meant for sharing, and then the Publican, a couple of blocks north on Fulton Market, a beer hall devoted to pork and oysters.

In 2010, Stephanie Izard, who had won the television cooking competition Top Chef two years before, opened Girl and the Goat on this street, and the lines out the door made Randolph Street a destination for diners from all over the country.
Dozens of restaurants opened in the blocks around it over the next decade.

When the Michelin guide began rating Chicago restaurants, at the end of 2010, the West Loop quickly became one of the places where its stars clustered, and some of the city's most ambitious tasting-menu restaurants are within a short walk of here.
Not everything has lasted.
Rents climbed with the neighborhood's fame, and several of the restaurants that made the street famous have since closed.
Restaurant Row keeps changing, which is nothing new for a street that started out as a market, where every morning brought different crates and different buyers.
Continue west on Randolph Street to Morgan Street, then turn right and walk north, under the elevated tracks on Lake Street, to Fulton Market, the street of the old meatpacking district.
Look at the low brick buildings with their steel canopies over the sidewalks, built to shelter loading docks where carcasses were moved into cold storage.
A few meat and food wholesalers are still here.
But in the last fifteen years, the district has transformed into one of the most expensive parts of the city.
At 1000 West Fulton Market, on the corner of Morgan Street, look for the tall brick building that was once the Fulton Market Cold Storage warehouse.
Since 2015, it's been Google's headquarters in Chicago.
Google's arrival is widely credited with setting off the transformation of the neighborhood, as other companies followed.
The area also became a center for hotels, galleries, and restaurants.
Chicago's famous chefs opened restaurants in the old warehouses, and the neighborhood is now one of the most important dining destinations in the country.
Look at the street signs here.
They don't say Fulton Street.
They say Fulton Market, a name that has stuck to this stretch for more than a century.
The meat trade on Fulton grew up in the 1880s, as an offshoot of the Union Stock Yards, a few miles to the south.
At the stockyards, the big packers slaughtered animals by the millions.

But someone had to cut the carcasses into the pieces that butchers, hotels, and restaurants wanted, and get them where they were going, and much of that work came to be done here, close to downtown and the railroads.

In 1887, a group of small meat dealers joined together to build a shared market on Fulton Street, and over the next four decades the street filled with low brick buildings for meat dealers, poultry houses, and produce merchants.
The big packers, like Armour and Swift, opened branch houses here too.
Most of the buildings you see went up between the 1880s and the late 1920s.

For most of the twentieth century, this was a working district, busiest in the hours before dawn, when trucks lined the curbs and workers in white coats hauled sides of beef and pork across the loading docks.
The street smelled of meat and diesel, and hardly anyone lived nearby.
The trade shrank after the Second World War.
The big packers moved their slaughterhouses west, closer to the cattle, and the stockyards closed in 1971.
Supermarket chains began buying meat already cut and boxed, so they no longer needed middlemen in the city.
Still, some meat and food businesses held on, and a handful are still here, sharing the street with restaurants, offices, and shops.
If you come by early on a weekday morning, you may still see a refrigerated truck backed up to one of the old docks, its driver wheeling boxes inside while the restaurants next door are still dark.
It's a small reminder that for most of its life, this street fed the city.
The big brick building at the corner of Fulton Market and Morgan Street was built in the 1920s as the Fulton Market Cold Storage warehouse.
It was essentially a giant refrigerator, ten stories tall, where meat and other food could be kept frozen until it was sold.
Cold storage buildings like this one were built to keep heat out, which is why the original walls had very few windows.
The walls were thick and heavily insulated, and the concrete floors were built to carry enormous loads of frozen goods.
For almost ninety years, the building did just what it was built to do, and from the street it looked like what it was, a huge, nearly blank brick box.
In 2012, the Chicago developer Sterling Bay bought it, with a plan to turn it into offices.
The first problem was the cold itself.
After decades of refrigeration, the building was frozen to its core, and it had to be thawed out slowly, over months, so that the structure wouldn't be damaged as it warmed.
Then the builders stripped the inside back to its concrete frame, opened large new windows in the brick walls, and added a new six-story wing alongside.
Inside, they left the heavy concrete columns and floors exposed, the kind of industrial look that technology companies like.
Google signed on as the main tenant, and in late 2015 it moved its Chicago offices here, bringing hundreds of employees to a street of meat dealers and warehouses.
The building took a new name from its address, 1000 West Fulton Market: One K Fulton.
Look at the walls and you can still read the change.
The rows of large windows are cut into what was once nearly solid brick.
Google is now moving many of its Chicago workers to the old Thompson Center in the Loop, but it has said it will keep its offices on Fulton Market too.
The change in Fulton Market didn't just happen.
It was helped along, step by step, by decisions at City Hall.
For decades, the city protected this area as an industrial zone, where new offices and homes weren't allowed, so that factories and food businesses wouldn't be priced out by developers.
In the 2010s, those protections came apart.
In 2012, a new station opened at Morgan Street on the elevated line along Lake Street, a block south of here, which made the district an easy ride from downtown.

In 2014, the city's Plan Commission adopted a plan that named this area the Fulton Market Innovation District, and opened the door to offices for technology and creative companies, while promising to look after the food businesses that were still here.
