In 2015, the city council made the old market blocks a landmark district, protecting the faces of the historic buildings, while still allowing new construction behind and around them.
And in 2017, the city lifted the industrial protections from part of the wider manufacturing corridor around Fulton Market.
The result was one of the fastest real estate booms in the city's history.
Office towers and apartment buildings rose on old parking lots and around the warehouses.
Companies moved their headquarters here from the Loop and the suburbs, chasing young workers who wanted to be near good restaurants and the train.
Hotels and private clubs opened in old factories.
Not everyone was pleased.

Many of the remaining meat and produce businesses, facing rising taxes and rents, or simply offered a good price, sold out and moved away, and people who had worked here for decades watched the district they knew disappear.
Others argued that those businesses would have left anyway, and that the boom brought jobs and tax money the city needed.
Look along the street and you can often see both sides of the argument at once: an old loading dock across from a glass office lobby.
Walk one block west to Carpenter Street, then south to Washington Boulevard.
The glass building at 110 North Carpenter Street is the global headquarters of McDonald's, which moved here from its suburban campus in Oak Brook in 2018.
McDonald's has deep roots in the Chicago area.

Ray Kroc, a milkshake mixer salesman from the Chicago suburb of Oak Park, met the McDonald brothers in California and in 1955 opened his first franchise restaurant in Des Plaines, Illinois, just northwest of Chicago.
From there he built it into the biggest restaurant chain in the world.
On the ground floor here, there's a McDonald's restaurant that serves a rotating menu of items from McDonald's around the world.
This site has an even more famous past.
It was the home of Harpo Studios, owned by Oprah Winfrey.
Harpo is Oprah spelled backwards.
From 1990 to 2011, The Oprah Winfrey Show was taped here, in a converted old armory, and it was the most watched talk show in American television history.
Oprah came to Chicago in 1984 to host a struggling morning show, AM Chicago, and within a year it had become her show.
She was one of the most influential people in American media, and she made Chicago the home of her empire.
The building Harpo used had a grim earlier history.

It was originally the Second Regiment Armory, and in July 1915, after the Eastland capsized in the Chicago River, it served as the city's temporary morgue, where families came to identify hundreds of bodies laid out on the floor.
Some of the people who worked for Harpo said the building was haunted, and the story was told for years.
Harpo's arrival in 1990 was a sign of the West Loop's future.
When Oprah moved here, the area was full of warehouses and empty lots, and few people lived here.
Harpo Studios closed in 2015, and its buildings were torn down to make way for the McDonald's headquarters.
Today, the West Loop is one of the fastest-growing neighborhoods in the city.
This is the end of the West Loop tour.
The Morgan station on the Green and Pink Lines, a couple of blocks north on Lake Street, will take you back to the Loop.
Ray Kroc was fifty-two, and had been a salesman for most of his working life, when he first saw the McDonald brothers' restaurant.
He left school young.
In 1918, still a teenager, he lied about his age to join the Red Cross as an ambulance driver, and he trained in the same company as another teenager who would become famous, Walt Disney.
According to Kroc, Disney was considered an odd one, because when the others went out to chase girls, he stayed behind and drew pictures.
The war ended before Kroc got overseas.
In the 1920s he played piano in bands and at a radio station, and sold land in Florida during the real estate boom there.
Then, for most of the next two decades, he sold paper cups for the Lily-Tulip company, and became one of its best salesmen in the Midwest.
One of his customers had invented a machine that could mix five milkshakes at once, the Multimixer, and Kroc went into business selling it across the country.
In 1954, he noticed that one small restaurant in San Bernardino, California, had ordered eight of his machines.
He went out to see why.
He found a stand selling just a few things, hamburgers, fries, shakes, and soft drinks, cheaply and very fast, to long lines of customers.
He talked the brothers, Richard and Maurice McDonald, into letting him sell franchises.
The partnership was never easy.
The brothers were cautious, and Kroc wanted to grow fast.
In 1961 he bought them out for two point seven million dollars.
They kept their original restaurant but lost the right to their own name, and renamed it the Big M. A new McDonald's soon opened nearby, and before long, the Big M was out of business.
Kroc's real genius may have been in what came next.
His financial man, Harry Sonneborn, persuaded him that the company should own or lease the land under each restaurant and rent it to the franchisee.
McDonald's became, in part, a real estate company, and the steady rent made it rich.

Somewhere in this building is one of the most unusual schools in the world: Hamburger University, McDonald's training center for restaurant managers and owners, which moved here with the headquarters in 2018.
It began in 1961, in the basement of a McDonald's restaurant in Elk Grove Village, northwest of the city, with a small class of students.
The idea is usually credited to Fred Turner, who had started out a few years earlier as a grill man at one of Ray Kroc's first restaurants, and who would one day run the whole company.
Turner was obsessed with doing everything the same way, every time.
He helped write the company's first operations manual, which spelled out exactly how to cook a hamburger, how to make the fries, and how long food could sit before it had to be thrown away.
Hamburger University's job was to teach that system to everyone who ran a McDonald's, so that a burger in Ohio would taste just like a burger in Oregon.
Graduates receive a degree in what the company calls, with a wink, Hamburgerology.
Over the decades, hundreds of thousands of people have earned one, and the school now teaches in many languages, with campuses in other countries as well.
For decades, Hamburger University was part of the company's wooded campus in Oak Brook, in the western suburbs, where McDonald's had moved its headquarters in 1971.
Before that, the company had been based in downtown Chicago.

When McDonald's decided to come back to the city, it said it wanted to be closer to its customers and to the young workers it hoped to hire, and the West Loop, with its restaurants and trains, was the place.
The move was part of a larger shift.
For decades, big companies had left Chicago for office parks in the suburbs.
In the 2010s, many of them started coming back, and few moves sent that message more loudly than McDonald's leaving its suburban campus for this block.
When Oprah Winfrey took over AM Chicago in January 1984, she was twenty-nine, and she'd been co-hosting a talk show in Baltimore.
Chicago was then the home base of the king of daytime talk, Phil Donahue, whose show had been made here for a decade.
Within about a month, the newcomer was beating him in the local ratings.
Her style was different.
Donahue was an earnest, intelligent interviewer.
Winfrey talked about her own life, her weight, her childhood, her mistakes, and she treated her audience as friends.
In 1985 she also became a movie star, with an Academy Award nomination for her role in Steven Spielberg's film The Color Purple.
Then came the question of how to take the show national.
According to the film critic Roger Ebert, the two of them went out to dinner, and Winfrey told him she was weighing offers to syndicate it.
Ebert said he took a napkin and worked out how much she might make, using the numbers from his own syndicated show with Gene Siskel.
Whether or not the napkin made the difference, The Oprah Winfrey Show went national on September eighth, 1986, and within a year it was the top talk show in the country.
In 1988, her own company took ownership of the show, and bought the old armory on this block to make into her studios.
From here, she shaped the country's tastes.
Her book club, begun in 1996, could turn a novel into a bestseller almost overnight.
The products she praised on her favorite things shows sold out.
In 2004, she gave every member of her studio audience a new car.
She taped her final episodes here in May 2011.
That same month, the city gave the block of Carpenter Street beside the studio an honorary name, Oprah Winfrey Way.
Three years later, Harpo sold the property, and by the end of 2015, the company had moved its work to California.
This tour explores the Near West Side, just southwest of the Loop, around Halsted Street, Roosevelt Road, and Taylor Street.
Few places in America have seen so many immigrant communities come and go, and few have been so completely remade, again and again.

In the late nineteenth century, the Near West Side filled with the poorest newcomers to the city: Irish and Germans first, then Bohemians, and then, in the 1880s and 1890s, Italians, Greeks, and Jews from Eastern Europe.
They crowded into wooden cottages and tenements, often several families to a house, with outhouses in the yards and the smells of the river and the factories in the air.
In 1889, Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened Hull House, on Halsted Street, to serve them.
The Jewish community centered on Maxwell Street and its famous open-air market.
The Italians centered on Taylor Street, which is still called Little Italy.
The Greeks settled to the north, along Halsted Street, in what became Greektown.
In the twentieth century, Mexican families and Black migrants from the South moved in, as the earlier groups moved on to other neighborhoods.
Then, starting in the 1930s, government planners began to clear the neighborhood.

First came public housing, then the expressways, and then, in the 1960s, the new Chicago campus of the University of Illinois, which wiped out much of the old Italian neighborhood and most of Hull House.
In the 1990s, the university expanded again, south over Maxwell Street.
Yet pieces of the old Near West Side survive: churches, a police station, an Italian lemonade stand, and a sausage stand that never closes.
We'll start at Maxwell Street, walk north to Holy Family Church and Taylor Street, and then west to the old Cook County Hospital.
You're on Halsted Street at Maxwell Street, about a mile southwest of the Loop.
Look around: you'll see university dormitories, shops, and parking garages.
But for about a century, this was the site of the Maxwell Street Market, the most famous open-air market in America, and one of the birthplaces of the Chicago blues.
The market grew up in the 1880s, when Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe settled here and began selling goods from pushcarts and stands along the street.

By the early twentieth century, Maxwell Street was a crowded bazaar where you could buy almost anything, new, used, or stolen: clothes, shoes, tools, pots and pans, live chickens, and hardware, from peddlers shouting and haggling in Yiddish, English, and a dozen other languages.
People used to say that you could have your hubcaps stolen at one end of the street and buy them back at the other.
Sunday mornings were the busiest, and the crowds were enormous.
As the Jewish families prospered and moved west, Black migrants from the South moved in, and in the 1940s and 1950s, musicians from the Mississippi Delta came to play on the street for tips.
To be heard over the noise of the crowds, they plugged electric guitars and amplifiers into outlets in the storefronts, with long extension cords.
Some historians say that's one reason the Chicago blues became so loud and so electric.
Little Walter, Bo Diddley, and many other musicians played here when they were starting out.
In the 1980 movie The Blues Brothers, John Lee Hooker plays on Maxwell Street, and Aretha Franklin sings in a diner nearby.
Maxwell Street also gave Chicago one of its signature foods: the Maxwell Street Polish, a grilled Polish sausage on a bun, piled with grilled onions, yellow mustard, and hot sport peppers.
It's credited to a Macedonian immigrant named Jimmy Stefanovic, who took over a hot dog stand at the corner of Maxwell and Halsted in 1939.
His stand, Jim's Original, has moved a block east, to Union Avenue, but it still serves Polish sausages and pork chop sandwiches, around the clock.
In 1994, the city closed the old market and moved it east, toward the river, to make way for the expansion of the University of Illinois at Chicago.
Blues fans, historians, and preservationists fought to save the street, but almost all of its buildings were torn down.
Since 2024, though, the market has come back to this stretch of Maxwell Street on a handful of Sundays each year, from spring to fall.
Look for the few old facades that were saved along Halsted Street, and for the plaques that tell the market's story.
Why was Sunday the big day here?
Because the first merchants on Maxwell Street were observant Jews.
From sundown on Friday to sundown on Saturday, the Jewish Sabbath, they kept their stalls and shops closed.
So the market came roaring back to life on Sunday morning, the one day when most working people in the city had time to shop, and when most of the big stores downtown were closed.
The shopkeepers didn't wait for customers to find them.
Many hired pullers, men who stood out on the sidewalk, sized up everyone who passed, and talked them into the store, or tugged them in by the sleeve.
Inside, nothing had a fixed price.
The merchant named a figure, the customer acted shocked, and the bargaining began.
Regulars liked to say that only a stranger paid the first price.
By the 1930s, the crowds on a busy Sunday were estimated at fifty thousand people or more.
A young sociologist at the University of Chicago, Louis Wirth, who had come to America as a Jewish boy from a village in Germany, walked these streets while he was writing his 1928 book, The Ghetto.
In the market, he saw something very old: a bazaar that the immigrants had carried with them from the towns of Eastern Europe and set down, almost unchanged, in the middle of an American city.
After 1994, the market kept its name but lost its street.
It moved first to Canal Street, near the river, and then, in 2008, to Des Plaines Street, a little farther north.

By then, many of the vendors and their customers were Mexican and Mexican American, and the smells drifting over the stalls were of grilled meat, tacos, churros, and champurrado, a thick, hot chocolate drink made with corn.
The bargaining, though, never stopped.
In 1964, a photographer named Mike Shea, who had worked for Life magazine, brought a movie camera down to Maxwell Street, and he kept coming back, Sunday after Sunday, sixteen times in all.
What he made from that footage is a short documentary, in black and white, called And This Is Free.
It has no narrator.
The camera simply drifts through the crowd, among the shoppers and the hustlers, the preachers and the families out for the day, and lets you watch and listen.
Nearly everywhere the camera goes, there's music.
Robert Nighthawk, one of the great slide guitarists to come up from the Delta, plays on a corner with a small band behind him.
Johnny Young plays the mandolin, a rare sound in the blues.

A young harmonica player named Carey Bell is there, and so is Big John Wrencher, a fixture of the market, who had lost his left arm in a car crash a few years before and played the harmonica with the hand he had left.
Shea had help from a young guitarist from the North Side, Mike Bloomfield, who knew many of the musicians and came along on those Sundays to win their trust.
A year later, Bloomfield was standing beside Bob Dylan on the night Dylan went electric at the Newport Folk Festival.

The sound was recorded by Gordon Quinn, who went on to help found Kartemquin Films, the Chicago documentary studio behind Hoop Dreams, and the editing was done with help from Howard Alk, one of the founders of The Second City.
Nighthawk died in 1967, and the film holds some of the only footage of him playing.
For years it was hard to see, but it has since been released on disc, along with more music from the street.
If you want to know what this corner looked and sounded like on a Sunday morning in its prime, the film is the closest you can come.
The Maxwell Street Polish has a rival for the title of this corner's greatest gift to Chicago.
In 1929, a man named Abe Drexler, whom everyone called Fluky, opened a hot dog stand at Maxwell and Halsted.
That same year, the stock market crashed, and as hard times settled over the city, Drexler came up with a bargain.
For a nickel, he'd sell you a hot frankfurter on a bun, loaded with mustard, relish, onion, pickle, peppers, lettuce, and tomato.
People called it the Depression sandwich, because it was practically a meal, and it cost next to nothing.
Fluky's, which later left Maxwell Street for other parts of the city and the suburbs, has long claimed that this was the birth of the Chicago-style hot dog, with everything on it.
Food historians are more careful.
Bruce Kraig, who has written widely about the hot dog, has pointed out that there's no record from the time to prove the story.
By one account, a newspaper used the same name, Depression sandwich, in 1931, for something else entirely: ham and cheese.
What nobody disputes is where the frankfurter itself came from.
In 1893, two brothers-in-law from Austria-Hungary, Emil Reichel and Sam Ladany, sold their all-beef sausages to the crowds at the World's Columbian Exposition.
The next year, by the company's account, they opened a shop on Halsted Street, and their business, Vienna Beef, went on to supply hot dog stands all over the city.
At first they delivered by horse and wagon, and their fleet didn't switch to trucks until 1928.
Today, look for the company's name on the signs of hot dog stands across Chicago.
For many Chicagoans, it's a promise that what's inside is the real thing.
Walk west along Maxwell Street to number 943, a sturdy old building of brick and stone with a big arched doorway.
This is the old Maxwell Street police station, built in 1888.
For decades, it was the headquarters of one of the busiest police districts in Chicago, in what was then one of its poorest and most crowded neighborhoods.
The newspapers called the district Bloody Maxwell.
If the building looks familiar, you may have seen it on television.
In the 1980s, it appeared in the opening credits of the police drama Hill Street Blues, as the outside of the show's fictional station house.
Today, it's the headquarters of the university's police department.
The streets around here produced an extraordinary number of famous people, many of them the children of poor Jewish immigrants.
Benny Goodman, the King of Swing, grew up nearby and learned to play the clarinet in the boys' band at Hull House.
Arthur Goldberg, the son of a peddler, grew up here and became a justice of the Supreme Court.
And so did Jacob Rubenstein, who changed his name to Jack Ruby, ran nightclubs in Dallas, and in 1963 shot Lee Harvey Oswald, the assassin of President Kennedy.

By the 1920s, most of the Jewish families had moved west, to Lawndale and beyond, but the market stayed, and so did many of the Jewish merchants, who kept their shops on the street and drove in every morning.
For decades, Maxwell Street was a place where Black and white, rich and poor, immigrant and native-born Chicagoans rubbed shoulders, in a city that was otherwise sharply divided.
In 1906, the Chicago Tribune called the Maxwell Street district the wickedest police district in the world.
That may have been newspaper exaggeration, but not by much.

The officers who worked out of this station patrolled some of the most crowded blocks in America, where tens of thousands of immigrants, Jewish, Italian, Irish, Greek, and Bohemian, lived packed into wooden cottages and rear tenements, many of them desperately poor.
Most of the district's crimes were the crimes of poverty and crowding: theft, fights, gambling, and the robbing of workingmen on payday.
But it had its own particular terrors, too.
In the Italian blocks to the north, extortionists sent letters signed with the mark of a black hand, demanding money from shopkeepers and families.
Those who refused risked having their homes or shops bombed.
The victims rarely came to the police, because they didn't trust them, or because they feared what would happen if they did.
Nearby was the territory of the Valley Gang, an Irish gang of thieves and brawlers.
During Prohibition, its leaders, Terry Druggan and Frankie Lake, went into beer, running breweries in partnership with Johnny Torrio and Al Capone.
They're remembered for one of the strangest stories of the era.
Jailed in 1924 for defying a court order against their brewing, they are said to have come and gone from the county jail almost as they pleased, after spreading money among the jailers.
When the newspapers found out, the story goes, the sheriff himself was sentenced to jail.
The station was built to stand for order in the middle of all that disorder, and it did, for a long time.
Chicago police officers worked out of it for one hundred and ten years, until 1998, when the district moved to a new building.
Hill Street Blues first went on the air in January 1981, and it didn't look like any police show before it.

Its creators, Steven Bochco and Michael Kozoll, wanted it to feel real, and the director of its first episode, Robert Butler, borrowed the look of a real documentary: The Police Tapes, a 1977 film about a police precinct in the South Bronx, with its handheld cameras and its morning roll call.
On Hill Street, the camera jostled through crowded rooms, and several conversations overlapped at once.
Stories ran on from one week to the next, and some never quite ended.

Most episodes opened at roll call, where Sergeant Phil Esterhaus ran through the day's business and sent the officers out with the words that became a national catchphrase: let's be careful out there.
The show never said which city it was in.
Most of it was filmed in Los Angeles, but its opening credits and some of its street scenes were shot here, in Chicago, and the gritty, wintry, nameless city on the screen looked a lot like this one.
At first, almost nobody watched.
By one count, the show finished eighty-seventh out of ninety-six shows in its first season, which made it one of the lowest-rated dramas ever brought back for a second.
But the critics loved it, and that fall it won eight Emmy Awards, a record for a drama series in a single year that stood until The West Wing won nine in 2000.
It ran for seven seasons and changed the way television told stories.
Then the building found a second career.
When another police drama, Chicago P.D., began in 2014, its producers chose this doorway as the entrance to their own fictional station, the Twenty-first District.
The rooms you see inside are a set on a soundstage on the West Side.
So the officers you see walking through this door on screen are actors, while the real ones, the university's, work inside.
Of all the boys who grew up in this police district, the most famous in his own day was a prizefighter.
He was born Dov-Ber Rasofsky in New York in 1909, and his family moved to Chicago when he was small.
His father, a devout scholar of the Talmud, ran a little grocery near Maxwell Street and hoped his son would follow him into a life of study.
Then, when the boy was in his early teens, robbers came into the store and shot his father dead.
The family fell apart.
His mother suffered a breakdown, and the younger children were sent to an orphanage.
The boy ran wild in the streets, and by his own account, he ran errands for gangsters, among them Al Capone.
Then he found boxing.
He fought under a new name, Barney Ross, so his mother wouldn't find out, and he saved his purses to bring his family back together.
In 1933, he beat Tony Canzoneri for the lightweight championship of the world, and the next year, he took the welterweight title from Jimmy McLarnin.
He went on to hold world titles in three weight classes, and in a decade of rising hatred of Jews, at home and abroad, Jewish fans across the country cheered him as their own.
When the United States entered the Second World War, Ross, by then past thirty, joined the Marines.
On Guadalcanal, late in 1942, he and several wounded comrades were cut off overnight under enemy fire, and Ross, wounded himself, held off the enemy until morning.
He was awarded the Silver Star.
But the morphine he was given for his wounds and for malaria left him addicted, and the habit nearly destroyed him.
In 1946, he checked himself into a federal hospital, and he came out clean.
He told his story in a book, and Hollywood turned it into a film, Monkey on My Back.
He spent his last years in Chicago, and he died here in 1967.
Walk north to Roosevelt Road and west to May Street.
The tall Gothic church with the slender spire is Holy Family Church, and next door, the elaborate building with the mansard roof is Saint Ignatius College Prep.
They're two of the very few buildings in Chicago older than the Great Fire of 1871.

Holy Family was founded in 1857 by Father Arnold Damen, a Dutch Jesuit priest, to serve the Irish immigrants who were then pouring into this part of the city, many of them fleeing the famine in Ireland.
When the church was built, between 1857 and 1860, this was still thinly settled land at the edge of the city, and people asked Damen why he was building such a big church out here.
Within a couple of decades, Holy Family was one of the largest English-speaking parishes in the country.
It's the second-oldest church building in Chicago, after Old Saint Patrick's.
On the night of October 8th, 1871, the Great Fire started at the O'Leary barn on DeKoven Street, less than a mile to the east.
The O'Learys were members of this parish.
A strong wind from the southwest drove the fire north and east, toward the downtown, and away from Holy Family, and the church survived.

According to parish tradition, Father Damen, who was away preaching in New York, prayed all night before an image of Our Lady of Perpetual Help, promising that if his church was spared, lights would burn before her image forever.
It's a legend, but the parish has kept the promise, and lights still burn before her image in the church today.
Next door, Saint Ignatius College opened in 1870, the year before the fire.
It was the beginning of what became Loyola University Chicago, which later moved to the North Side, while the high school stayed here.
In the late twentieth century, Holy Family was in such bad shape that it was nearly torn down.
Parishioners, former parishioners, and preservationists raised millions of dollars to save it, and it has been restored.
Arnold Damen was born in 1815 in a village in the south of the Netherlands.
As a young man, he heard a Belgian Jesuit, Pierre-Jean De Smet, who had come back to Europe from the American frontier to recruit young men for the missions among the Native nations of the West.
In 1837, Damen sailed with him to America.
He never made it to the frontier.
The Jesuits trained him in Missouri, ordained him a priest, and put him to work in Saint Louis, where he became a popular pastor and preacher.
In 1857, the bishop of Chicago invited the Jesuits to open a parish in his city, and Damen was the one they sent.
His new parish covered something like fifty square miles, most of it prairie.
But Damen's real fame came from the road.

With a small band of fellow Jesuits, he traveled from city to city giving parish missions, a kind of Catholic revival that could last a week or more, with sermons every day, crowds that packed the churches to the doors, and long lines outside the confessionals.
His voice, people said, could fill the largest church without strain, and his sermons on sin, death, and judgment brought whole congregations to tears.
By one count, made in 1879, he had personally led more than two hundred missions in his twenty-two years in Chicago.
At home, he built.
Besides the church and the college next door, he opened schools for thousands of the parish's children, taught largely by religious sisters.
And when the Great Fire left about a hundred thousand people homeless, his parish, untouched by the flames, helped feed and shelter the victims.
In his last years, he left the running of the parish to others and kept on preaching.
He was in Omaha, at the Jesuit college there, when he died, on New Year's Day, 1890, at the age of seventy-four.
Holy Family was dedicated on August twenty-sixth, 1860, with thirteen bishops in attendance, a sign of how much the young Catholic Church in America expected of it.
Its style is Victorian Gothic, and it's the only Gothic church left in Chicago from before the Civil War.
The plans came from an architectural firm called Dillenburg and Zucker, and the interior was completed by John Van Osdel, who is often called the city's first professional architect.
If the church is open, step inside and look up.
High along the walls of the nave, above the arches, run the clerestory windows, which let light pour down into the church from above.
They were made in 1860 by a stained glass maker named W. H. Carse, and they're believed to be the oldest stained glass in Chicago.
They have survived the fire, a century and a half of coal smoke and city grime, and the decades when the church nearly fell apart.
Then look toward the front of the church, at the tall high altar, with its forest of Gothic spires, and at the carved figures of saints and angels.
Many of the church's statues were carved by Anthony Buscher, a Chicago woodcarver who worked on the church in its early years.
Next door, the school's building, designed by Toussaint Menard, went up in 1869, with a western addition five years later.

Its style is French Second Empire, which was the height of fashion in the years after the Civil War, and you can see it in the steep roofline, the dormer windows, and the stacked rows of tall windows.
It's a Chicago Landmark.

Inside, the school still keeps some of its grand nineteenth-century rooms, including a great gallery on the fourth floor, where a marble plaque honors the school's graduates who served in the nation's wars.
Step back to the sidewalk, and look at the two buildings side by side, the church and the school, a pair of survivors from the city that burned.
Look high above the sanctuary, to either side, and you'll find two small statues of boys dressed as altar servers.
They come with one of the best-loved stories in Catholic Chicago.
One stormy night, the story goes, two boys knocked at the door of the priests' house and asked for Father Damen.
Their mother was dying, they said, and she needed a priest.
Damen took his holy oils and followed them out into the dark, across the muddy prairie, to a poor cottage at the edge of the parish.
Inside, he found a woman close to death, and he heard her confession and gave her the last rites.
When he told her that her sons had brought him, she stared at him.
Her only two sons, she said, had drowned some time before.
Damen, the story continues, had statues carved in memory of the boys and set them up in the church, where you see them now.
And people say that their eyes follow the priest as he moves around the altar.
Is any of it true?
There's no account of the story from Damen's own lifetime, and historians treat it as folklore.
Similar tales, of a priest led through the night by a mysterious messenger to someone who is dying, are told in other places too.
The statues, though, are real, and they're old.
They're attributed to Anthony Buscher, the woodcarver who made many of the church's figures in its early years.
And the story has lasted for generations, passed down by parishioners to their children, and retold in books of Chicago ghost stories.
When you look up at the two boys, notice how they seem to be watching the altar.
Then see whether you can catch them watching you.
Walk north on May Street to Taylor Street, and turn right.
You're in Little Italy.
At number 1068, look for a tiny red, white, and green stand.
This is Mario's Italian Lemonade, which has been serving Italian ice, made with bits of real lemon, every summer since 1954.
On hot nights, the line stretches down the block.
Italians began settling on the Near West Side in the 1880s and 1890s, many of them from the villages of southern Italy and Sicily, and others from Tuscany and the north.

They worked as laborers, peddlers, and railroad workers, and by the early twentieth century, this was one of the largest Italian communities in Chicago, with its own churches, bakeries, social clubs, and bocce courts.
Taylor Street was its main street.
The neighborhood had a darker side, too.

In the late 1920s, a gang of teenagers from these streets, called the 42 Gang, became a training ground for the Chicago mob, and several of its members rose high in the Outfit, among them Sam Giancana, who became the boss of the Chicago mob in the 1950s.
Then, in 1961, Mayor Richard J. Daley announced that the new Chicago campus of the University of Illinois would be built here, on the north side of the neighborhood.
To make room, the city would clear dozens of blocks, home to thousands of Italian, Greek, Mexican, and Black families, and almost all of Hull House.
The residents fought back.
Their leader was Florence Scala, the daughter of an Italian tailor, who had grown up going to classes at Hull House.
She organized protests and sit-ins at City Hall, and the fight went all the way to the United States Supreme Court, which refused to hear the case.
Scala lost.
The campus opened in 1965, a complex of concrete buildings designed by Walter Netsch, of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill.
Studs Terkel interviewed Florence Scala for his book Division Street: America, and her account of a neighborhood destroyed in the name of progress is one of the most moving in the book.

Some of Little Italy survived south of the campus, and you'll still find Italian groceries, bakeries, and restaurants along Taylor Street, including Al's, which claims to have been making Italian beef sandwiches since 1938.
Of all the people who worked among the Italians of Chicago, one became a saint.
Frances Xavier Cabrini was born in 1850 in Lombardy, in northern Italy, the youngest of thirteen children, so small and frail that few expected her to live long.
As a girl, she dreamed of being a missionary in China.
In 1880, she founded her own order, the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart, and she asked the pope to send her to the East.
Pope Leo the Thirteenth, the story goes, told her instead: not to the East, but to the West.

So in 1889, she sailed for New York, to serve the Italian immigrants who were arriving by the hundreds of thousands, many of them to lives of grinding poverty, in an American Church run mostly by Irish and German clergy.
For the next twenty-eight years, she hardly stopped moving.
She crossed the Atlantic again and again, and her sisters opened schools, orphanages, and hospitals from New York to Buenos Aires.
She came to Chicago more than once.
In 1905, she opened Columbus Hospital, on the North Side, facing Lincoln Park.
A few years later, she bought land a few blocks from here, at the corner of Lytle Street and Gilpin Place, and opened a second hospital, for the Italians of the Near West Side.
It was later renamed for her, and so was the little street beside it, today's Cabrini Street.
She died in Chicago, at Columbus Hospital, on December twenty-second, 1917, at the age of sixty-seven.
She had become an American citizen in 1909, and so, when the Church canonized her in 1946, she became the first citizen of the United States to be made a saint.
A few years later, she was named the patron saint of immigrants.

And when the housing authority built a project on the Near North Side in 1942, in what was then an Italian neighborhood, it was named for her: the Frances Cabrini Homes, the beginning of what became Cabrini-Green.
Ask who invented the Italian beef sandwich, and you may start an argument on Taylor Street.
Everyone agrees on the outline.
In the early twentieth century, Italian families on the Near West Side celebrated weddings on very little money.
Some were called peanut weddings, because the guests were treated to peanuts, beer, and sandwiches.
To feed a big crowd from one roast, the cooks sliced the beef as thin as they could, simmered it in a seasoned broth, and piled it onto Italian bread, so a little meat went a long way.
After that, the stories part ways.
The family behind Al's traces the sandwich to Anthony Ferreri, who, they say, was making it for weddings and feasts in the 1920s, before his son Al and other family members opened their stand.
Another family, the Scalas, says that its founder, Pasquale Scala, a butcher and sausage maker, was making it in the 1920s too, and the Scala company now supplies beef to many stands around the city.
Nobody wrote it down at the time, and the truth, like the gravy, is hard to pin down.
Ordering one takes a little vocabulary.
A beef can be dry, with the meat lifted out of the juice and drained; wet, with extra juice spooned on top; or dipped, with the whole sandwich plunged into the gravy until it's soaked through.
Then come the toppings: sweet, for roasted green peppers, or hot, for giardiniera, a spicy relish of chopped vegetables, pickled and packed in oil.
Ask for a combo, and you'll get a grilled Italian sausage tucked into the same bun.
Regulars eat it standing up, leaning over the counter with their elbows out, so the juice drips on the counter and not on their shoes, a posture some Chicagoans call the Italian stance.
In 2022, a television series, The Bear, carried the Italian beef far beyond Chicago.
Its story is set in a fictional family sandwich shop, and a real one, Mr. Beef, on Orleans Street in River North, stands in for it on screen.
A few blocks west of here, and a little to the north, on Loomis Street, is a small park called Arrigo Park, with a tall pedestal that has stood empty since 2020.
For more than half a century, it held a bronze statue of Christopher Columbus, by Moses Ezekiel, an American sculptor who lived and worked in Rome.
He finished it in 1892, and it was shown in the Italian pavilion at the World's Columbian Exposition the next year.
Then, for decades, it stood in a niche above the entrance of the Columbus Memorial Building, on State Street.
After that building was torn down in 1959, a state legislator from this neighborhood, Victor Arrigo, led a campaign to bring the statue here.
It was dedicated on Columbus Day, October twelfth, 1966, and after Arrigo died, in 1973, the park was renamed for him.
For many Italian Americans, the statue stood for pride, in a neighborhood that had lost so much.
For others, Columbus stood for conquest, and for the suffering of the Native peoples of the Americas.
In July 2020, during a summer of protests across the country, demonstrators tried to pull down the Columbus statue in Grant Park, and there were clashes with the police.
A week later, before dawn, crews acting on Mayor Lori Lightfoot's orders took this statue down too.
The Joint Civic Committee of Italian Americans went to court, arguing that a 1973 agreement bound the Park District to keep the statue on display.
In 2025, the two sides settled.
The statue is to be lent to the committee and shown indoors, in a museum of Italian American history that, by one report, will be named for Florence Scala.
And the park is to get a new monument.

In February 2026, after a public call that drew more than one hundred and fifty nominations, the Park District announced its choice: Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini, the nun who spent her life serving Italian immigrants.
Until the new monument is built, the pedestal waits.
Walk west on Taylor Street, past Racine Avenue, to Ada Street.

On the north side of the street stands a three-story building of red brick, the last surviving piece of the Jane Addams Homes, which opened in 1938 as one of the first public housing projects in Chicago.
The Jane Addams Homes were built by the federal government during the New Deal, and named for the founder of Hull House, which stood a short walk to the northeast.

They were low-rise apartment buildings arranged around grassy courtyards, with modern kitchens and bathrooms, and for the working families who moved in, they were a huge improvement over the tenements and shacks they replaced.
The courtyard was decorated with stone sculptures of animals, by the Chicago artist Edgar Miller, made under a New Deal art program, and some of them have been preserved.
Like nearly all public housing at the time, the project was segregated.

In the decades that followed, the Chicago Housing Authority built much bigger projects, including the high-rise towers of Cabrini-Green and the Robert Taylor Homes, almost all of them in Black neighborhoods, because white aldermen blocked public housing in their wards.
The projects concentrated poverty, the buildings were poorly maintained, and by the 1990s, many had become dangerous places to live.
In 2000, the city began tearing them down, under what it called the Plan for Transformation, and replacing many of them with mixed-income housing.
The Jane Addams Homes were demolished too, except for this one building, saved by former residents and historians.
It's now home to the National Public Housing Museum, which tells the story of public housing in America through the lives of the people who lived in it.
As you continue west along Taylor Street, look for a small plaza with a bronze statue of a baseball player in mid-swing.

It's Joe DiMaggio, the Yankee Clipper, the son of Italian immigrants, standing outside the National Italian American Sports Hall of Fame, a reminder of how much this neighborhood once meant to Italian Americans across the Midwest.
When the Chicago Housing Authority was created in 1937, it chose as its first executive secretary a thirty-eight-year-old woman named Elizabeth Wood.
She had been born in Japan, the daughter of American missionaries, and for seventeen years, she ran the authority.
She believed, against much of the city, that public housing should be built wherever there was land for it, including in white neighborhoods, and that its tenants should not be sorted by race.
In 1949, after Congress passed a major new housing act, Wood's staff proposed sites for thousands of new apartments, many of them on vacant land in white parts of the city.
The aldermen, who under a new state law had to approve every site, threw most of them out and substituted their own, in neighborhoods that were already Black and poor.
Then came Trumbull Park.

In 1953, a Black family, Betty and Donald Howard, moved into the Trumbull Park Homes, an all-white project on the Far South Side, apparently because an official took Betty Howard, who was light-skinned, to be white.
For months, mobs surrounded the project, throwing stones and setting off firecrackers and small bombs, and the family had to be escorted in and out by the police.
Wood refused to back down, and more Black families moved in.
In 1954, the authority's board pushed her out.
Civil rights groups asked whether she had been punished for her stand on integration, and many historians believe she was.
Her fight was taken up in court.
In 1966, tenants led by Dorothy Gautreaux sued the authority, with Alexander Polikoff, a lawyer working with the American Civil Liberties Union.
In 1969, a federal judge, Richard Austin, ruled that the authority had chosen its sites and its tenants by race, and ordered that new public housing be small and scattered across the city.
From 1987 on, for more than twenty years, a court-appointed receiver ran that program.
The animals were meant to be played on.

Edgar Miller designed them for a courtyard with a fountain at the heart of the project, and he gave them simple, rounded, heavy forms, in the streamlined style of the 1930s, the kind of shapes that seem made for small hands and feet.
There were seven pieces in all, carved from blocks of limestone, among them a bear, a bull, a buffalo, a lion, and sheep.
And children did play on them.
For more than sixty years, kids who grew up in the Jane Addams Homes rode the bull and climbed on the bear, and many former residents remember the animals as one of the best parts of growing up here.
Over the years, residents painted them, again and again, in bright colors.
When the rest of the project came down, the animals were taken away, in 2007, and they spent years in storage.
For a long time there was no money to repair them, and at one point, only one of the seven had been restored.
Then a sculpture conservator, Andrzej Dajnowski, took on the job of cleaning and repairing them, and after more than fifteen years away, Animal Court came home.
Today, the animals stand on the museum grounds, and you can see them free whenever the museum is open.
When you look at them, notice how much life Miller got out of so few lines.
He wasn't trying to make the animals look real.
He was carving the idea of a bear or a bull, the way a child might draw one: solid, friendly, and strong.
And think of the thousands of children who climbed on them, long before anyone thought of them as art.
The National Public Housing Museum opened its doors here on April fourth, 2025, and the idea for it came from people who had lived in public housing themselves.

When the rest of the Jane Addams Homes were being torn down, a longtime tenant leader, Deverra Beverly, rallied residents and their allies to save this one building, and to make it a place where the story of public housing would be told by the people who knew it from the inside.

The Jane Addams Homes were one of four neighboring projects on the Near West Side, which came to be known together as Abla, a name made from their initials: the Jane Addams Homes, the Robert Brooks Homes, Loomis Courts, and the Grace Abbott Homes.
Together, they were home to thousands of families.
The heart of the museum is three apartments, re-created room by room, each one the home of a real family that lived here.
The first belonged to the Turovitz family, a Jewish family who moved in when the project opened, in 1938.
The second recalls an Italian American family in the 1950s.
The third belonged to the Hatch family, a Black family who lived here in the 1960s and early 1970s.
The rooms were furnished with the help of the families' own memories.
Walk through them in order, and you can watch the story of public housing change.
For the families who moved in early on, an apartment here often meant the first home they'd ever had with heat, hot water, and a bathroom of their own.
The museum doesn't hide what went wrong in the decades that followed, but it insists on something the usual story leaves out: that for millions of Americans, the projects were, first of all, home.
Walk west on Taylor Street to Ashland Avenue, north to Harrison Street, and west past Wood Street.
You're now in the Illinois Medical District, one of the largest concentrations of hospitals and medical schools in the country.
The long, grand building with the ornate facade of stone and terra cotta is the old Cook County Hospital, completed in 1914.
For most of the twentieth century, County, as everyone called it, was the hospital for the poor of Chicago, open to anyone, whether they could pay or not.

It was enormous, with thousands of beds, and it was famous for training young doctors, who saw more patients, and more kinds of illness and injury, in a few months than many doctors elsewhere saw in years.
Many medical firsts happened here.
In 1937, a doctor named Bernard Fantus set up a way to collect, store, and preserve donated blood, so it would be ready when patients needed it.
He called it a blood bank, and it was the first of its kind in an American hospital.
In 1966, County opened one of the first trauma units in the country, dedicated to treating the victims of shootings, stabbings, and accidents.
The hospital also inspired the long-running television drama ER, set in the emergency room of a Chicago hospital called County General.
In 2002, a new county hospital opened next door, and the old building stood empty for almost twenty years.
Preservationists fought off plans to demolish it, and in 2020, it reopened as two hotels and medical offices, with its facade restored.
This is the end of the Little Italy and Maxwell Street tour.
The Illinois Medical District station on the Blue Line is nearby, and it will take you back downtown.

Bernard Fantus was born in Budapest in 1874 and went to school in Vienna before he came to Chicago, where he trained as a doctor and became a professor of therapeutics, the study of medicines and treatments.
He was a practical man with a soft spot for his youngest patients.
Years before the blood bank, he wrote a book on how to hide bitter medicines in candy, so that sick children would take them.
Before the 1930s, a blood transfusion was an emergency all its own.
A donor had to be found, tested, and brought to the patient's bedside, often in the middle of the night, and the blood went from one person to the other almost at once.
Fantus had read reports from the Soviet Union of blood being collected and stored for later use, and he set out to do the same here.
Mixed with a chemical to keep it from clotting, and kept cold, donated blood, he found, could be saved for up to ten days.
He opened his laboratory on March fifteenth, 1937.
At first he called it a blood preservation laboratory, but he soon gave it a plainer name, and the name explained how it worked.
Like a bank, it took deposits and made withdrawals.
A patient who received blood was expected to have family or friends give blood to replace it, so that the bank would never run dry.
In its first year, it supplied more than thirteen hundred transfusions.

Fantus described the bank in the Journal of the American Medical Association that same year, and within a few years, hospitals across the country and around the world were opening blood banks of their own.
He didn't live long enough to see much of it.
He died in 1940, and the county named the hospital's outpatient clinic, the Fantus Clinic, in his honor.

The building was designed by Paul Gerhardt, the county's architect, and when it opened in 1914, it was meant to say something: that the sick poor of Cook County deserved a hospital as dignified as any bank or courthouse in the city.
Its style is Beaux-Arts, the formal classical manner taught at the great architecture school in Paris, and its eight stories are dressed in columns, carved ornament, and a grand central entrance.
In 1993, while it was still a working hospital, the building had a starring role in a movie.
In The Fugitive, Harrison Ford plays a doctor on the run, who sneaks in disguised as a janitor to search the records of the prosthetics department for the one-armed man who killed his wife.
After the county moved its patients out, it planned to tear the old building down.
Preservationists fought back, and Preservation Chicago put it on its list of the most endangered buildings in the city in 2003, and again in 2004.
Eventually, the building was named a Chicago Landmark and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the county chose a private team to restore it.
The restoration took five years, from 2015 to 2020, and cost about one hundred and forty million dollars, with the help of historic tax credits.
About eighteen million dollars of it went to the facade alone, which was cleaned and repaired piece by piece.
Inside, the old hospital wards became two hotels, with more than two hundred rooms between them, along with a food hall on the ground floor and offices for doctors of the county health system.

Look up at the facade as you pass, and imagine it as it was for most of the twentieth century: dark with soot, with ambulances pulling up at the doors, and patients waiting inside on long wooden benches, sometimes for hours, to see a doctor.
The old county hospital was the center of a whole neighborhood of medicine, and its oldest neighbor is Rush Medical College.
Rush was chartered on March second, 1837, two days before the city of Chicago itself, by a young doctor from New York named Daniel Brainard.
He named it for Benjamin Rush, the Philadelphia physician who signed the Declaration of Independence.
Its building on the North Side burned in the Great Fire, and a few years later, the college moved here, beside the county hospital, where its students could learn at the bedsides of the city's poor.
Next door to Rush stood Presbyterian Hospital, and it was there that one of Rush's professors, James Herrick, made a famous discovery.
In 1904, a young dental student from the Caribbean island of Grenada, Walter Clement Noel, came to the hospital with anemia.
When Herrick's intern, Ernest Irons, looked at the young man's blood under a microscope, he saw red blood cells stretched into thin, curved shapes, like sickles.
Herrick's paper about the case, published in 1910, was the first description in Western medicine of what we now call sickle cell disease.
Two years later, Herrick published another landmark paper, one of the first to describe a heart attack in a living patient and tie it to a blocked coronary artery.
Rush and Presbyterian eventually joined forces, along with Saint Luke's Hospital, and today the medical center's campus is crowned by a tower that, seen from above, is shaped like a butterfly.
It opened in 2012, a few blocks east of here, near Ashland Avenue.
And the modern county hospital that replaced this one bears the name of John H. Stroger Junior, who in 1994 became the first Black president of the Cook County Board.
This tour explores Pilsen, on the Lower West Side, about two miles southwest of the Loop.
It's one of the most vibrant neighborhoods in Chicago, famous for its murals, its Mexican bakeries and restaurants, and its long history as a home for immigrants.
The neighborhood was settled in the second half of the nineteenth century by Czech immigrants, who called themselves Bohemians, along with Germans, Irish, Poles, Slovaks, and others.
They came to work in the lumber yards and factories along the South Branch of the Chicago River and in the rail yards around it.
In the 1870s and 1880s, Chicago was the largest lumber market in the world, and huge stacks of white pine from Michigan and Wisconsin lined the river just south of here.
The name Pilsen comes from the Czech city of Plzeň.
The story goes that one of the early restaurants in the neighborhood was named At the City of Pilsen, and the name spread to the whole area.
Pilsen was a working-class neighborhood with a strong tradition of labor activism.
Workers here were involved in the great railroad strike of 1877 and in the eight-hour movement of the 1880s.

In the 1950s and 1960s, the Czech and Polish families began moving to the suburbs, and Mexican families arrived, many of them displaced from the Near West Side by the construction of expressways and the University of Illinois campus.
By 1970, Pilsen was majority Mexican, and it became the heart of Mexican Chicago.
Activists, artists, and community groups transformed it, painting murals on walls all over the neighborhood and building institutions, from a high school to a national museum.
Today, Pilsen is facing the pressures of gentrification, and you may see signs and murals protesting it.
We'll start at the eastern end of 18th Street, near Halsted Street, and walk west, ending at the National Museum of Mexican Art.
You're on Halsted Street, near 16th Street, at the northeastern edge of Pilsen.
Look north, where Halsted rises over the railroad tracks.
In July 1877, this was the site of what's known as the Battle of the Viaduct.
That summer, a nationwide railroad strike broke out after the railroads cut wages.
In Chicago, workers from many industries joined the strike.
Here on Halsted, crowds of workers clashed with police and militia over several days.
Around thirty people were killed in Chicago during the strike, many of them young workers, and many of them from this neighborhood.
The strike was crushed, but it shocked the country, and it helped launch decades of labor struggle in Chicago.
Walk south to 18th Street.
The blocks around Halsted and 18th Street are known as the Chicago Arts District, with galleries and studios in old industrial buildings, many of them opened since the 1990s.
As you walk west on 18th Street, look up at the facades.
You'll see brick buildings with stores on the ground floor and apartments above, many built in the late nineteenth century by Czech immigrants.
Some still have names and dates carved over their doorways, and some have the projecting bay windows of Czech and German design.
Today, the storefronts are mostly Mexican bakeries, restaurants, and shops.
Pilsen was also part of the story of Haymarket.

Many of the workers who joined the eight-hour strikes of May 1886 lived here, and the McCormick Reaper Works, where police killed strikers on May third, the day before the Haymarket bombing, stood just southwest of the neighborhood, at Blue Island and Western Avenues.

Cyrus McCormick had invented a mechanical reaper that let one farmer harvest as much grain as several men with scythes, and his Chicago factory made the city the center of the farm machinery industry.
The company later became International Harvester.
The strike reached Chicago on July twenty-third, 1877.

That evening, a young typesetter named Albert Parsons climbed onto a platform downtown and spoke to an enormous crowd of workers, by some estimates tens of thousands, about wages, hours, and the power of the railroads.
The next day, he was fired from his job at the Chicago Times, and two plainclothes police officers came for him.
By his own account, he was brought before the chief of police and a roomful of angry businessmen, who told him to get out of town.
For about two years afterward, he later wrote, no print shop in Chicago would hire him.
Across the city, workers walked out of the rail yards, the lumber yards, the packinghouses, and the factories, and crowds moved from shop to shop, calling on others to join them.
The city answered with its police, with businessmen and veterans sworn in as special patrols, with the state militia, and finally with regular army troops sent by the federal government.
The worst fighting came here, on July twenty-sixth, when the police estimated the crowd around the Halsted Street viaduct at about ten thousand people.
The strikers had stones and bricks; the police and soldiers had clubs and guns.
The battle surged back and forth across the viaduct and along Halsted Street for hours.

That same day, a few blocks to the north, police forced their way into a hall on 12th Street, where the furniture workers' union had met with employers to talk about wages and the eight-hour day, and drove the men out with their clubs.
Both sides drew lessons from that week.

Chicago's business leaders helped pay for new armories for the militia, and after the Haymarket bombing nine years later, a group of them bought land on the lakeshore north of the city and gave it to the army for a post, Fort Sheridan, so that troops would be close at hand.
And many of the workers who struck that week went on to join unions and the eight-hour movement, while some, like Parsons, turned to far more radical ideas.
The story of the reaper begins on a farm in the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia.
Cyrus McCormick's father, Robert, had spent years trying to build a machine that could cut grain, and he never got it to work.
In 1831, the son tried again, with the help of Jo Anderson, a man enslaved by the McCormick family, and that summer, their horse-drawn machine cut grain in a field near the farm.
McCormick wasn't the only one at work.
Obed Hussey patented a reaper in 1833, a year before McCormick did, and the two men fought for decades, in demonstration fields and in the courts.
What made McCormick rich was not only the machine, but where and how he sold it.

He saw that the future of grain farming lay on the flat prairies of the Midwest, and in 1847 he moved to Chicago and built a factory on the north bank of the river, with backing from the city's first mayor, William Ogden.

He's often credited with selling his reapers in ways that were new at the time: at a fixed price, with a written guarantee, often on credit, to be paid off after the harvest, and through traveling agents who showed farmers the machine at work in their own fields.
The Great Fire destroyed the factory in 1871, and two years later, the company opened a much larger works, out on the South Branch of the river.
By the 1880s, it was one of the biggest factories in Chicago.
Cyrus died in 1884, and his son, Cyrus Junior, took over.
In 1902, with the help of the banking house of J. P. Morgan, the company merged with its fiercest rival, the Deering company, and several others, to form International Harvester.
The new company built the Farmall tractor in the 1920s, one of the machines that ended the age of the horse on American farms.
In 1985, it sold its farm equipment business, and the next year, what was left took a new name: Navistar.
Many of the old houses you're walking past were built from one tree: the eastern white pine.
It once grew in vast forests across northern Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota, in stands of trees that could be centuries old and well over a hundred feet tall.
Its wood was light, soft, and straight-grained, easy to saw and to nail, and it kept its shape as it dried.
It was ideal for the cheap, quick balloon-frame houses and barns that went up all over the prairie.
The logging was done in winter.

Crews of lumberjacks felled the trees and hauled the logs on sleds over iced roads to the riverbanks, and when the ice broke up in spring, the logs were floated downstream to the sawmills at the river mouths, in towns like Muskegon and Menominee.
There the logs were sawn into boards, stacked onto schooners, and sailed across Lake Michigan to Chicago.
Along the South Branch, the lumbermen dug slips into the land, narrow channels where the schooners could tie up and unload.
Gangs of lumber shovers, many of them Czech and German immigrants from this neighborhood, carried the boards off the boats by hand and stacked them in towering piles to dry.
In 1880, Chicago handled more than a billion board feet of lumber, graded, dried, and shipped by rail to the treeless farm towns of the prairies and the plains.
By the end of the century, the great pine forests were nearly gone.
The loggers left behind a wasteland of stumps and dry branches, called the cutover, which burned again and again.
Chicago's lumber trade moved on, to the pines of the South and the firs of the Pacific Northwest.
The northern forests have grown back, but only scraps of the old white pine woods survive, and today the white pine is Michigan's state tree.
So when you look at an old Pilsen cottage, with its narrow front and its steep roof, you may be looking at a piece of a forest that vanished more than a century ago.
Walk west on 18th Street to Allport Street.
On the corner, the big brick and stone building with a tower is Thalia Hall.
It was built in 1892 by a Czech immigrant named John Dusek, and it was said to be modeled on an opera house in Prague.
It held a theater, a hall, shops, and apartments, and for decades it was the center of Czech cultural life in the neighborhood: plays, concerts, political meetings, and social clubs.
It sat largely unused for many years, and it was restored and reopened in 2013 as a music venue.
A block north, on Allport Street, is Saint Procopius Church, built in the 1880s for the Czech Catholic community, one of the first Czech parishes in Chicago.
Benedictine monks from the parish founded a college here, which later moved to the suburbs and became Benedictine University.
Today, Saint Procopius serves a largely Mexican congregation, and its masses are in Spanish.
Just to the east, at 1831 South Racine Avenue, is a building that was once Casa Aztlán, a community center that was the heart of the Chicano movement in Pilsen.
In the 1970s, the artist Ray Patlán and others covered its walls with murals of Mexican history, workers, and revolutionaries.
In 2017, after the building was sold and converted to apartments, the murals were painted over, to the anger of many in the neighborhood, and it became a symbol of the fight over gentrification.
Czech Pilsen was famous for its societies.

There were gymnastic clubs called Sokols, which promoted physical fitness and Czech national pride, savings and loan associations that helped immigrants buy houses, freethinkers' clubs, and theater groups.
Many Czechs here were skeptical of the church, and the neighborhood had both devout Catholic parishes and halls for those who'd rather debate politics on a Sunday.
One of the most famous Czech Chicagoans, Anton Cermak, began his career in this part of the city, as a teenager working in the rail yards and then driving a wagon hauling kindling.

He became mayor in 1931, built a coalition of immigrant groups that became the foundation of the Democratic machine, and was killed in 1933 in Miami by a bullet that may have been meant for President-elect Franklin Roosevelt.
Twenty-second Street was renamed Cermak Road in his honor.
Chicago's Czechs played a part in the creation of their homeland.
During the First World War, Czech Americans raised money and recruited volunteers for the cause of Czech independence from Austria-Hungary.
In 1918, Tomáš Masaryk, the leader of the independence movement, came to Chicago, and huge crowds turned out to greet him.
Later that year, Czechoslovakia declared its independence, and Masaryk became its first president.
Many of the Czechs who came to Chicago had little love for the Catholic Church.
At home, it was bound up with the Habsburg emperors who ruled the Czech lands from Vienna, and with the memory of the 1600s, when the Habsburgs had stamped out Czech Protestantism by force.
In America, for the first time, people could say so out loud.
In 1870, they founded the Congregation of Bohemian Freethinkers of Chicago.
It wasn't a church, but it did much of what a church did.
It set up building and benevolent societies, kept a school and a library, ran programs for children and lectures for adults, and sponsored concerts and plays.

In 1875, a publisher named August Geringer began printing Svornost, which means Concord, the first Czech daily newspaper in the United States, and for many years its editor was the freethinker František Zdrůbek.
Two years later, the freethinkers opened a Czech school that met on Sundays, and Geringer himself taught there on Sunday afternoons.
The freethinkers' greatest monument is on the city's Northwest Side.

Early in 1877, after a priest, as the story goes, had refused to bury a Czech woman in a Catholic cemetery, more than twenty Czech societies met and agreed to build a cemetery of their own, where any Czech could be buried, whatever he or she believed.
The Bohemian National Cemetery was chartered that April, and its first burial took place on July first.
Today it holds well over a hundred thousand graves, and it's listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
For decades, Czech Chicago was really two communities, side by side.
Catholics sent their children to parish schools like the one at Saint Procopius, read their own daily paper, Národ, and were buried in Catholic ground.
Freethinkers sent theirs to the free schools, read Svornost, and, when the time came, were buried among their own, in the Bohemian National Cemetery.
Tomáš Masaryk was born in 1850 in Moravia, the son of a coachman, and he became a professor of philosophy in Prague.
But the person who shaped his life most was an American.
Charlotte Garrigue came from a wealthy family in Brooklyn, and she was studying music in Leipzig, in Germany, when she met the young Czech scholar.

They married in New York in 1878, and Masaryk did something almost unheard of for a man of his time: he took her family name as his own middle name, and he signed himself Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk for the rest of his life.
Charlotte, a passionate believer in women's rights, helped translate John Stuart Mill's The Subjection of Women into Czech.
Masaryk's ties to Chicago began long before 1918.

In 1902, at the invitation of Charles Crane, the heir to a Chicago manufacturing fortune and a man fascinated by the Slavic world, he gave a series of lectures at the University of Chicago and met the Czech community here.
It was the beginning of a long friendship, and Crane became one of the most important American friends of the Czech cause.
After Czechoslovakia won its independence, the two families grew even closer.
Crane's son, Richard, became the first American minister to the new country, in 1919, and in 1924, Masaryk's son, Jan, married Crane's daughter Frances.
Tomáš Masaryk served as president until 1935, and he died two years later.
Jan Masaryk became a diplomat himself.
During the Second World War, he spoke to his occupied country by radio from London, and after the war, he returned home as foreign minister.
In March 1948, two weeks after the Communists seized power in Prague, he was found dead in the courtyard beneath a window of the foreign ministry.
The new government called it suicide.
Many Czechs never believed it, and later investigations have suggested that he may have been murdered, but the question has never been settled.
The Czechs didn't stay in Pilsen forever, and the path they took out of it is one of the clearest in Chicago's history.
Many of the first Czech settlers, in the 1850s and 1860s, lived closer to downtown, on the Near West Side.

After the Great Fire, as the lumber yards and factories along the South Branch grew, more and more of them settled here, and by the end of the nineteenth century, Chicago had become the third-largest Czech city in the world, after Prague and Vienna.
Then, as families saved money, they moved west along 22nd Street, the street that's now Cermak Road.
Around 26th Street and California Avenue, they built a new neighborhood, known as Czech California.
By 1910, Czechs owned about four out of five of the houses there.
After the First World War, they kept going, across the city line into the suburbs of Cicero and Berwyn.
Many found work at Western Electric's giant Hawthorne Works in Cicero.
In Cicero and Berwyn, Cermak Road was lined with so many savings and loan associations that people called it the Bohemian Wall Street.
With their help, thousands of Czech families bought brick bungalows on quiet, tree-lined streets, the dream that had started in a frame cottage in Pilsen.
And for decades, Cicero has held a fall festival called Houby Day, after the Czech word for mushrooms, which Czech families have long gathered in the woods.
Each time the Czechs moved on, new arrivals took their places.
In Pilsen, and in Czech California, which is now Little Village, the newcomers were Mexican, and the old Czech halls, churches, and storefronts gradually became theirs.
If you look closely at the cornerstones and the names carved over the doorways, you can still read the story of one community in buildings now used by another.
Walk south on Racine Avenue to Cermak Road, and look south, toward the river, at the massive brick power plant with its tall smokestack.
This is the Fisk Generating Station, which opened in 1903, and it's one of the most important buildings in the history of electricity.
In 1892, a young Englishman named Samuel Insull, who had been Thomas Edison's private secretary, came to Chicago to run a small electric company.
Insull believed that electricity could be cheap enough for everyone, if it were made in huge central plants and sold to as many customers as possible, around the clock.

Here, at Fisk Street, he installed what was then the largest steam turbine generator in the world, a new kind of machine that was smaller, cheaper, and more powerful than the old piston steam engines.
It worked, and it set the pattern for how electricity has been generated ever since.

Insull's company, Commonwealth Edison, came to supply the whole city, and he built an empire of utilities across the Midwest, along with elevated railways and electric interurban lines that ran on his power.
For a time, Insull was one of the most powerful men in America.
He built the Civic Opera House on Wacker Drive, a huge office tower with an opera house inside, which opened in 1929.
Because from the river it looks like an enormous armchair, people called it Insull's Throne.

His wife had been an actress, and he spent lavishly to return her to the stage, and Orson Welles later acknowledged that Insull was one of the models for Citizen Kane, who builds an opera house for his wife, a singer.
Then came the Depression.
In 1932, Insull's holding companies collapsed, and hundreds of thousands of small investors lost their savings.
Insull fled to Europe.
He was brought back, tried for fraud, and acquitted, but he died nearly penniless in Paris in 1938.
The Fisk plant burned coal for more than a century.

By the 2000s, it was one of the oldest coal plants in the country, and Pilsen residents, together with their neighbors in Little Village, where another old coal plant stood, organized a long campaign against the pollution, which they blamed for asthma and other illnesses.
In 2012, both plants shut down.
It was one of the great victories of the environmental justice movement in Chicago.
When Samuel Insull went looking for a steam turbine big enough for Fisk Street, the company best able to build it was reluctant to try.
The turbines General Electric had made until then were much smaller, and the company's head, Charles Coffin, balked at the size Insull wanted: five thousand kilowatts.
Insull pressed, and the two men struck a deal.
General Electric would take the risk of building the machine, and Insull's company, Chicago Edison, would pay to install it.
The turbine stood upright, unlike the turbines of later years, and when it was first tested, in March 1903, Insull was there to watch.
It worked, and on October second, 1903, the station went into service.
The plant was designed by a young Chicago engineering firm, Sargent and Lundy, founded a dozen years earlier by Frederick Sargent and a partner with a memorable first name, Illinois Lundy.
The firm is still based in Chicago, and it still designs power plants around the world.
Progress came so fast that by 1909, the first Fisk turbine had been replaced by bigger machines, and General Electric took it back to its works in Schenectady, New York.
It's still on display there, and the American Society of Mechanical Engineers has named it a landmark of engineering history.
In 1907, Chicago Edison merged with its sister company, Commonwealth Electric, to form Commonwealth Edison, and the name survives today, on the electric bills of northern Illinois.
Insull's other great idea was about prices.

On a trip home to England in the 1890s, he saw a new kind of meter in the seaside town of Brighton, which recorded not only how much power a customer used, but the most that customer drew at any one moment.
With meters like it, Chicago Edison could charge each customer a share of what it cost to build the plants, and then very little for each hour of use beyond that.
The more steadily a customer used power, the less each unit cost, and the more steadily the turbines ran.
That was the secret of cheap electricity, and versions of it are still built into electric rates today.
When Insull's empire collapsed in 1932, he resigned from his companies and sailed for Europe.
At home, he became a symbol of everything that had gone wrong in the 1920s.
Franklin Roosevelt, campaigning for president that fall, attacked him by name, and prosecutors in Chicago charged him with embezzlement, and later with mail fraud.
Insull went to Greece, and the Greek courts refused American requests to send him back.
Then, early in 1934, under heavy pressure from Washington, the Greek government ordered him to leave the country.
What followed made headlines around the world.
Insull, then seventy-four years old, boarded a small Greek freighter, the Maiotis, and put to sea, bound, it was said, for Egypt.
For about two weeks, the papers followed the old man's voyage across the eastern Mediterranean, guessing where he might try to land.
When the ship anchored at Istanbul, Turkish police came aboard and took him off, and he was handed over to the Americans and brought home to face trial.
The federal trial opened in Chicago in October 1934.
The government's case was led by the United States attorney in Chicago, Dwight Green, who later became governor of Illinois.
Insull took the stand and told the story of his life, from office boy in London to master of a utility empire, and the jury found him not guilty.
He was acquitted in the state courts too.
Insull went back to Europe.
In July 1938, he collapsed and died of a heart attack in a station of the Paris subway, at the age of seventy-eight.
Historians still argue about him.
To some, he was a swindler who built a house of cards and left small investors holding the losses.
To others, he was a visionary who made electricity cheap and plentiful, whose holding companies were no worse than many others, and who was made a scapegoat for the Depression.
The laws that followed his fall, which broke up utility holding companies and put them under federal regulation, shaped the power industry for the rest of the century.
By the early 2000s, Fisk and its sister plant, the Crawford station in Little Village, stood in the middle of crowded neighborhoods, surrounded by homes, schools, and playgrounds.
In 2002, a study from the Harvard School of Public Health estimated that pollution from the two plants was causing forty-one premature deaths and twenty-eight hundred asthma attacks every year.
Two neighborhood groups were at the heart of the fight to close them.
One was the Pilsen Environmental Rights and Reform Organization, whose initials spell perro, Spanish for dog.
The other was the Little Village Environmental Justice Organization.
They knocked on doors, held marches and vigils, and packed hearings at City Hall.
In 2010, aldermen introduced a Clean Power Ordinance that would have forced the plants to cut their soot drastically, or shut down.
It never made it out of committee, but it kept up the pressure.
On February twenty-ninth, 2012, the plants' owner, Midwest Generation, announced that it would close them both, in a deal brokered with help from Mayor Rahm Emanuel.
By that fall, both had stopped burning coal.
The next year, Kimberly Wasserman, a leader of the Little Village group, won the Goldman Environmental Prize, one of the world's top honors for grassroots activists, for her part in the campaign.
The story didn't end there.

In April 2020, during the first weeks of the pandemic, a developer demolished the Crawford plant's smokestack, and a huge cloud of dust rolled over the homes of Little Village, at a time when people were being told to stay inside to protect their lungs.
The anger that followed pushed the city to tighten its rules for demolitions and to look harder at where it allows polluting industries to operate.
