For Pilsen, the closing of Fisk was a turning point, and it raised a new question that the neighborhood is still answering: when the smokestacks go dark, and the air gets cleaner, who gets to stay and breathe it?
Walk west along Cermak Road toward Ashland Avenue.
The large school building here is Benito Juárez Community Academy, a public high school.
It exists because of a fight.
In the early 1970s, Pilsen had no high school of its own, and students had to go to an overcrowded school far away, where many of them dropped out.
In 1973, students and parents organized protests, staged walkouts, and demanded a high school for the neighborhood.
After years of pressure, the city agreed.
Benito Juárez High School opened in 1977, named for the nineteenth-century Mexican president who was a hero of reform.
Look at the building, with its open plaza and the murals around the campus.
The school became a symbol of what Pilsen's community organizing could achieve, and many of the activists who fought for it went on to careers in politics and public service.
The neighborhood's activists also fought successfully for a health clinic, a library, and community housing.
Mexican Chicago is far older than many people realize.
Mexican workers arrived in the 1910s and 1920s, recruited by the railroads, the steel mills of South Chicago, and the meatpackers, and settled near the yards and the mills.
During the Depression, many were pressured or forced to leave, in deportation and so-called repatriation drives that also swept up American citizens.

After the Second World War, Mexican immigrants came back in growing numbers, and today Chicago has one of the largest Mexican American communities in the United States, centered here in Pilsen and in Little Village, just to the southwest, whose main street, 26th Street, is one of the busiest shopping streets in the city.

Benito Juárez, for whom the school is named, was a Zapotec Indian from the mountains of Oaxaca who became president of Mexico in 1858 and led the country's resistance to a French invasion in the 1860s.
He's remembered for a line that's inscribed on monuments across Mexico: "Among individuals, as among nations, respect for the rights of others is peace."

In the early 1970s, Pilsen's teenagers started high school in a small building in the neighborhood, the Froebel branch of Harrison High School, where ninth graders took classes before moving on to the main school.
The main school was a long way to the west, and getting there, many families said, meant crossing the turf of rival gangs.
Parents petitioned for a full high school in Pilsen, and the Board of Education turned them down.
Then the board moved to close the Froebel branch itself.
That was the last straw.
On June fifth, 1973, students and parents set off on a long march from Froebel to the offices of the Board of Education downtown.
There were more demonstrations, a boycott, and a takeover of the Froebel building, and at last the board agreed to spend almost nine million dollars on a new school.
Much of the organizing came from Pilsen Neighbors, the community council, and from three women who are remembered as the school's founding mothers: Mary Gonzales, Teresa Fraga, and Raquel Guerrero.
They and the students who marched with them had learned that in Chicago, a neighborhood got what it was organized enough to demand.

The school was designed by one of the most celebrated architects in Mexico, Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, who had designed the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City and Aztec Stadium, the great soccer stadium there.
It was dedicated on September sixteenth, 1977, Mexican Independence Day.

For the families who had fought for it, the building was a declaration of its own: that the Mexican children of Pilsen deserved a school as good as any in the city, in their own neighborhood, named for a hero of their own history.
Over the decades since, its graduates have included teachers, artists, union organizers, doctors, and elected officials, many of them the first in their families to finish high school.
Rudy Lozano was born in Texas in 1951 and came to Chicago as a boy.
By his twenties, he was an organizer for the International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union, signing up workers in the garment shops and factories of the city, many of them immigrants.
He rose to become the union's chief organizer in the Midwest.
He believed that Mexican and Black Chicagoans, working side by side, could change the city, and he worked hard to bring them together.
In 1983, he ran for alderman in the 22nd Ward, on the Southwest Side, and came within seventeen votes of forcing the machine's incumbent into a runoff.
His supporters charged that many Latino voters had been wrongly purged from the rolls.

That same spring, Harold Washington was elected Chicago's first Black mayor, with the help of a coalition that Lozano had worked to build, and Washington enlisted him as his liaison to the city's Latino communities.
Then, on June eighth, 1983, he was shot and killed in his home in Little Village.
He was thirty-one.
A young gang member was convicted of the murder, but many of Lozano's friends never believed he acted alone, and questions about the killing have never gone away.
His work went on without him.
His campaign manager, Jesús García, known as Chuy, won the 22nd Ward seat in 1986, and decades later, he was elected to Congress.
Others who had worked beside Lozano went on to lead unions, community groups, and city departments.
The neighborhood remembers him.
In 1989, the Chicago Public Library opened its Rudy Lozano branch in Pilsen, a school bears his name, and July twenty-ninth is honored as Rudy Lozano Day.
Benito Juárez was born in 1806 in a small village in the mountains of Oaxaca, and by the age of three, he had lost both his parents.
He grew up herding sheep for an uncle, speaking only his people's language, Zapotec.
At twelve, he walked to the city of Oaxaca, where his sister worked as a cook for a merchant family, the Mazas, whose daughter Margarita he would one day marry.
A bookbinder who was a devout Franciscan lay brother took him in and saw to his schooling.
He learned Spanish, studied law, and rose to become governor of his state.
In 1853, the dictator Antonio López de Santa Anna sent him into exile, and he spent a hard year and a half in New Orleans, where, it's said, he rolled cigars to make a living.

He came back to help overthrow Santa Anna, and then to help write the Reform laws, which separated church and state, ended the special courts of the clergy and the army, and put much of the Church's land up for sale.
When the French army invaded, the Mexicans won a famous victory at Puebla on May fifth, 1862, the Cinco de Mayo, which is still celebrated far more in the United States than in Mexico.
But the French took the capital the next year and made an Austrian archduke, Maximilian, emperor of Mexico.
Juárez never gave up.
He carried his government north in a black carriage, all the way to the town of Paso del Norte, on the Rio Grande, which is now called Ciudad Juárez in his honor.
When the French withdrew, Maximilian was captured, tried, and executed by a firing squad in 1867, despite pleas for mercy from around the world, among them one from the French novelist Victor Hugo.
Juárez died in office five years later.
His birthday, March twenty-first, is a national holiday in Mexico, and his face is on Mexican money.
For the students who walk through these doors, he's a reminder that a shepherd boy who didn't speak Spanish until he was twelve could become the president who saved his country.
Walk north on Paulina Street back to 18th Street, to the elevated Pink Line station at 18th Street.
Walk up into the station if you can.
The station's walls are covered with brightly colored murals, painted by local artists, beginning in the 1990s.
You'll see images of Mexican history, Aztec gods, the Virgin of Guadalupe, and portraits of Pilsen's people.
Pilsen is one of the great outdoor mural galleries of the United States.

The mural movement here began in the 1970s, inspired by the great Mexican muralists of the early twentieth century, Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco, and David Alfaro Siqueiros, who painted murals as public art meant for working people.
Chicago artists like Ray Patlán, Marcos Raya, and many others followed their example, painting walls that told the stories of the community.
Look for murals on the sides of buildings along 18th Street, 16th Street, and the railroad embankment along 16th Street, which is covered for blocks with murals.
As you walk, look for newer murals too.
Some of them address gentrification and displacement, a sign that Pilsen's artists still use walls to speak out.

Look north along Paulina Street toward 17th Street, and you'll see the two tall towers of Saint Adalbert Church, built in 1914 for a Polish congregation, in the grand Renaissance style of the Polish cathedral churches built across Chicago in those years.
For a century, it was one of the landmarks of the Lower West Side, with towers about a hundred and eighty-five feet tall.
The archdiocese closed it in 2019, despite years of protests by parishioners, and its future has been uncertain.
Like the Czechs, the Poles of Pilsen have mostly moved away, and their churches tell the story of the neighborhood's changes.
For the artists of the 1970s, the murals were a way to turn the neighborhood's walls into its history books, telling the stories of people who rarely saw themselves in the official ones.

Walk the side streets, and you'll see that tradition alive: murals of Aztec warriors, farmworkers, immigrants crossing the border, famous Mexican artists like Frida Kahlo, and neighborhood heroes whose names you won't find in any textbook.
Trains have stopped here since the 1890s, on a line that riders long called the Douglas branch, and that became the Pink Line in 2006.
The station itself was rebuilt in the early 1990s.
The murals came soon after.

In the mid-1990s, an artist and teacher named Francisco Mendoza began leading young people in painting the station's stairways, corridors, and platforms, with support from the National Museum of Mexican Art, and the work went on for several years.
Some of the young painters came through Gallery 37, a city program that paid teenagers to make art.
As you climb, look for a great stone disk.
It's the Aztec Sun Stone, often called the Aztec calendar, although most scholars see it less as a working calendar than as a monument to the sun and to the ages of the world.
The original is a slab of basalt nearly twelve feet across, carved not long before the Spanish conquest, and buried after it.
It was rediscovered in 1790, when workers were repaving the main square of Mexico City.

At its center is a face, usually identified as the sun god, with a tongue shaped like a stone knife, surrounded by the signs of the twenty days and of the four worlds that, the Aztecs believed, had been created and destroyed before this one.
Look for the Virgin of Guadalupe too, in her blue-green mantle scattered with gold stars, standing on a crescent moon held up by an angel.
According to tradition, in December 1531, she appeared to an Indigenous man named Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac, just outside Mexico City, and spoke to him in his own language, Nahuatl.
When the bishop asked for a sign, the story goes, Juan Diego opened his cloak, roses tumbled out, and her image was found on the cloth.
That cloak hangs today in the basilica at Tepeyac, one of the most visited shrines in the world.
In 1810, the priest Miguel Hidalgo carried her image on the banner of Mexico's war for independence, and her feast day, December twelfth, is one of the great days of the year in Mexican Chicago.
The great Mexican muralists were children of the Mexican Revolution.

When the fighting ended, around 1920, the new government's minister of education, José Vasconcelos, set out to teach a nation where most people couldn't read, and he handed artists the walls of public buildings in Mexico City, to paint the country's history where everyone could see it.
Three of them, Rivera, Orozco, and Siqueiros, became known as the big three, and in the 1930s, all three painted in the United States.
Orozco painted a burning Prometheus in a college dining hall in California, and an epic of the Americas in the library at Dartmouth College.

Rivera covered the walls of the Detroit Institute of Arts with the assembly lines of the Ford plant, and in New York, he painted a mural at Rockefeller Center that was destroyed because it included a portrait of Lenin.
In Los Angeles, Siqueiros painted a crucified Indian beneath an American eagle, and it was soon painted over.
Of the three, Siqueiros was the great experimenter.

He painted with industrial lacquers and spray guns, and in 1936, one of the young artists in his workshop in New York was Jackson Pollock, who, it's often said, first saw paint poured and dripped there, the technique he later made famous.
Decades later, young Mexican American artists in Chicago took up the tradition.

In 1970, a young painter named Ray Patlán became the first artist in residence at Casa Aztlán, the community center on Racine Avenue, and began painting with neighborhood teenagers, on walls they passed every day.
When the first murals faded, other artists, among them Marcos Raya, painted new ones over them, and the walls became a conversation between generations.
Patlán later moved to California, where he went on painting murals for decades.
He died in 2024, at seventy-seven.
Outdoor murals don't last forever.
Sun, rain, and Chicago winters fade and crack them, and so the walls of Pilsen keep changing, as old murals are restored, painted over, or replaced.
The wall in front of you may look quite different twenty years from now.
The church whose towers rise over Paulina Street was built by Poles, but it's named for a Czech.
Saint Adalbert, in Czech, Vojtěch, was born around 956 into a noble family in Bohemia, and he became the bishop of Prague.
He clashed with the powerful men of his diocese, left Prague more than once, and finally set out as a missionary to the pagan Prussians on the shores of the Baltic Sea.
In 997, they killed him.

The Polish duke Bolesław the Brave, the story goes, bought back his body for its weight in gold and laid it in the cathedral at Gniezno, and Adalbert became one of the patron saints of Poland, as well as of Bohemia.

So it was natural for Polish immigrants to name a parish for him, and the church you see, finished in 1914, was built to recall the great churches of Rome; some have compared it to the basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls.
Inside, it held a copy of Michelangelo's Pietà.
The fight over its closing lasted for years, and some parishioners carried their appeals all the way to Rome.
In 2017, the archdiocese agreed to sell the building to a music school, but that sale was never completed, and in 2019, a developer agreed to buy the church for about four million dollars.
In 2022, the Pietà was moved to the nearby church of Saint Paul, where the parish now worships.
And in 2025, the city moved to make the church an official Chicago Landmark, which means that, whatever becomes of it inside, its towers are likely to stay.

When you look up at them, you're looking at a building that tells two stories at once: of the Polish families who saved their pennies to build it, and of a Czech bishop, dead for a thousand years, whose name followed his admirers across an ocean.
Walk west to Wood Street and south to 19th Street, to Harrison Park.
Here, in a building that was once a park boathouse, is the National Museum of Mexican Art.
The museum was founded in 1982 by a group of teachers, led by Carlos Tortolero, who wanted a place to show Mexican art and culture in the neighborhood.
It opened in 1987.

Its collection now numbers in the thousands of objects, covering ancient Mexican art, colonial art, the great twentieth-century painters and printmakers, folk art, and contemporary Mexican and Mexican-American art.
It's one of the largest Latino arts institutions in the country, and admission is free.
The museum is especially famous for its Day of the Dead exhibition each fall, which fills the galleries with altars, or ofrendas, built by artists and community members to honor the dead.
The museum began in a time when Mexican art was rarely shown in American museums, and its founders were determined that it would be in the neighborhood, free, and open to everyone.

Its galleries tell the story of what its founders call Mexican culture without borders, the idea that the culture of Mexico doesn't stop at the border, but continues in Chicago, in Texas, in California, and wherever Mexican people live.
It's a fitting idea for a neighborhood that has been home to so many people from somewhere else.
This is the end of the Pilsen tour.
If you're hungry, 18th Street is lined with taquerias, Mexican bakeries selling sweet breads called pan dulce, and other restaurants.
The Day of the Dead isn't a Mexican Halloween.

It falls on the first two days of November, the Catholic feasts of All Saints and All Souls, but its roots reach back to the ancient peoples of Mexico, who honored their dead with festivals of their own.
On the first of November, families remember the children they've lost, and on the second, the adults.
At the heart of the holiday is the ofrenda, the altar of offerings.

A family builds it at home, or at the grave, often in tiers, and covers it with the things the dead loved in life: photographs, their favorite foods and drinks, cigarettes or a bottle of tequila, toys for a child, candles to light the way, and copal incense.
Bright orange marigolds, called cempasúchil, are scattered over the altar and sometimes laid in a path to the door, because their color and scent are said to guide the spirits home.
There's pan de muerto, a sweet bread decorated with strips of dough shaped like bones, and skulls made of sugar, with a name written across the forehead.
The grinning skeletons of so much Day of the Dead art owe a great deal to one artist.
José Guadalupe Posada was a printmaker in Mexico City around 1900, who drew calaveras, skeletons acting out the follies of the living, for cheap broadsheets sold on the street.
His most famous figure is a skeleton lady in a grand hat piled with feathers and flowers, mocking Mexicans who put on European airs.
Decades later, Diego Rivera painted her into a great mural in Mexico City, strolling through a park beside Posada himself, and he gave her the name she's known by today: La Catrina.
In 2008, the United Nations cultural agency added the Day of the Dead to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.
But in Pilsen, it was never a museum piece.
In the weeks before November, look in the windows of homes and shops along 18th Street, and you may see altars of all sizes, built by families who are simply keeping their dead close.
The park around the museum was created in 1912 and named for Carter Harrison, the elder, five times mayor of Chicago.
Harrison was a Kentuckian, born in 1825, who came to Chicago in the 1850s and made a fortune in real estate.
He was a showman.
He rode around the city on a white Kentucky mare, in a broad slouch hat, and he courted the city's immigrant voters, German, Irish, Czech, and Polish alike.

He was mayor from 1879 to 1887, four terms in a row, and he ran what his enemies called a wide-open town, easygoing about saloons and gambling, and beloved in the working-class immigrant neighborhoods like this one.
In 1893, he won a fifth term, to be the mayor of the World's Columbian Exposition.
On October twenty-eighth, 1893, two days before the fair was to close, a young man named Patrick Prendergast rang the bell at Harrison's house on Ashland Avenue.
Prendergast had backed Harrison's campaign, and he had convinced himself that the mayor owed him a job as the city's chief lawyer, the corporation counsel.
When Harrison came into the hall, Prendergast shot him, and the mayor died within the hour.
The fair's grand closing ceremony was canceled, and a memorial service took its place.
Prendergast was convicted of murder.
Clarence Darrow, then a young lawyer, tried to save him from the gallows by arguing that he was insane, but he failed, and Prendergast was hanged in 1894.
He's often said to be the only one of Darrow's clients ever to be executed.
The mayor's son, Carter Harrison Junior, was later elected mayor five times too, so between them, father and son ran the city for about twenty years.
The park keeps the family name, and its old park building has held the museum since it opened, with a new wing added in 2001.
If you walk back along 18th Street, follow your nose.
In a Mexican bakery, you serve yourself.
Pick up a metal tray and a pair of tongs near the door, walk along the cases, choose what you like, and bring it to the counter.
The best known of the sweet breads is the concha, a soft, round roll with a crackly sugar topping scored to look like a seashell.
There are orejas, ears of flaky pastry; cuernos, horns; and marranitos, little pigs of soft gingerbread, darkened with piloncillo, an unrefined brown sugar.
In early January, for the feast of the Three Kings, bakeries sell the rosca de reyes, a ring of sweet bread with a tiny figure of the baby Jesus baked inside.
Whoever finds it in their slice is supposed to host a tamale party on the second of February.
Mexican bakeries have been part of 18th Street since the 1970s.
Then there are carnitas.

In 1975, Inocencio Carbajal, from the city of Uruapan, in the Mexican state of Michoacán, opened a shop on 18th Street, making carnitas the way he'd learned from his father and uncle: pork simmered slowly in big pots of lard, until it's tender inside and crisp at the edges.
Carnitas Uruapan, at 1725 West 18th Street, still sells it by the pound, with tortillas and salsa, and when the day's batch is gone, it's gone.
The family, now in its third generation, has opened more places, in Gage Park and in Little Village.
And on a hot day, look for a paletería, selling paletas, Mexican ice pops made with real fruit, in flavors like mango with chile, tamarind, cucumber, and rice pudding.
Order one, find a bench in the park, and you'll be doing exactly what Pilsen families have done on summer afternoons for half a century.
This tour explores Chicago's Chinatown, centered on Wentworth Avenue and Cermak Road, about two miles south of the Loop.
Chinese immigrants began arriving in Chicago in the 1870s, many of them moving east from California, where anti-Chinese violence and discrimination had grown fierce.
In 1882, Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act, which banned almost all immigration from China and barred Chinese immigrants from becoming citizens.
It was the first major American law to bar immigrants by nationality, and it stayed in force until 1943.
The Chinese community in America remained small, largely male, and isolated, and it relied on its own institutions for support.
Chicago's first Chinatown grew up downtown, around Clark Street and Van Buren Street, with laundries, groceries, and restaurants.
In the early 1900s, rising rents and pressure from landlords pushed the community to look elsewhere.
Around 1912, the On Leong Merchants Association, one of the most powerful organizations in Chinese Chicago, began leasing buildings here, around Wentworth and 22nd Street, which is now Cermak Road.
Much of the community followed, and this became Chicago's Chinatown.
For decades, Chinatown was hemmed in by railroads, the river, expressways, and other neighborhoods, and it could barely grow.
After immigration laws were reformed in 1965, new waves of immigrants arrived, from Hong Kong, Taiwan, mainland China, and Southeast Asia.
Chinatown expanded north onto old railroad land, with a shopping plaza and a riverside park, and its residents spread into neighboring Bridgeport and beyond.
Today, Chinatown is one of the few Chinatowns in America whose population is still growing.
We'll start at the Chinatown Gate on Wentworth Avenue, walk south along Wentworth, and then north to the river and Ping Tom Memorial Park.
You're at the Chinatown Gate, which spans Wentworth Avenue just south of Cermak Road.
It was built in 1975 and designed by a local architect, Peter Fung.
Look at the green tiles of its roof, its red columns, and the golden characters in the center.
Those four characters read Tian Xia Wei Gong, a phrase from classical Chinese philosophy, made famous by Sun Yat-sen, the founder of the Republic of China.
It's often translated as "the world belongs to all," or "what is under heaven is for all."

Sun Yat-sen visited Chicago while organizing support for the revolution that overthrew China's last emperor in 1911, and Chinese communities in America were an important source of money for his movement.
Look south down Wentworth Avenue.
This is the old main street of Chinatown, lined with restaurants, bakeries, tea shops, herbal medicine stores, and gift shops.
Look for the street signs, which are in both English and Chinese.
As you walk, notice the many family associations and benevolent associations, often in second-floor offices with their names in Chinese characters over the doors.
For generations, these associations were the backbone of Chinese immigrant life, helping new arrivals find work and housing, settling disputes, and caring for the elderly and the dead.
Walk a few steps south on Wentworth to number 2216, the largest and most striking building on the street.
It's covered in ornate terra cotta, with green and red tiles and two pagoda-like towers on the corners.
This is the On Leong Merchants Association Building, completed in 1928.
It was designed by two Norwegian-American architects, Christian Michaelsen and Sigurd Rognstad, who drew on Chinese motifs to give it its distinctive look.
Look for the dragons, lions, and floral patterns in the terra cotta.
For decades, it was nicknamed Chinatown City Hall.
It housed the On Leong association's offices, a school, a meeting hall, and a temple.
The association acted as a kind of local government, resolving disputes, collecting dues, and representing the community.
Like some other Chinese associations of the era, the On Leong was also involved in gambling, and in the late 1980s, after a federal investigation, the association lost the building.
Today, the building is called the Pui Tak Center, and it's owned by a Chinese Christian church.
It offers English classes, programs for immigrants, and community events.
It's one of the most important buildings in Chinatown, a city landmark, and a reminder of how the community took care of itself in the years of exclusion.
Chinatown's biggest celebration is the Lunar New Year, in late January or February, when a parade with lion and dragon dancers, drums, and firecrackers winds down Wentworth Avenue.
The lion dancers stop at shops and restaurants, where owners hang lettuce and red envelopes of money above their doors for the lion to eat, for good luck in the new year.
In summer, Chinatown holds a street fair along Wentworth, and in the fall there's the Moon Festival.
The man whose motto crowns the gate went by several names, and each one tells part of his story.
He was born in 1866 as Sun Wen, in a farming village in southern China, not far from Macau.
At thirteen, he sailed to Hawaii, where an older brother had prospered, and he studied at a missionary school in Honolulu.
Later he trained as a doctor in Hong Kong, where he was baptized a Christian.
In the West, he's known as Sun Yat-sen, the Cantonese way of saying a name he took as a young man.
In China, he's best known as Sun Zhongshan.
During years of exile in Japan, he lived under a Japanese alias, Nakayama, meaning middle mountain, and in Chinese those same characters are read Zhongshan.

Today, many Chinese cities have a Zhongshan Road, his home county was renamed Zhongshan in his honor, and the high-collared jacket he made popular is called the Zhongshan suit, although in the West it's better known as the Mao suit.
He spent years as a fugitive, raising money among Chinese communities around the world for the cause of overthrowing the Qing dynasty.
In 1896, Chinese officials seized him in London and held him prisoner inside their legation, and he was freed only after his old teacher from medical school went to the newspapers.
In 1904, to travel freely in the United States, where the exclusion laws would have kept him out, he obtained papers claiming that he'd been born in Hawaii.
In October 1911, he was in Denver, on a fundraising tour, when he read in a newspaper that a revolt had broken out in the city of Wuchang.
Province after province broke away from the empire, and on the first day of 1912, he was sworn in as the provisional president of the new republic.
In return for the young emperor's abdication, he soon agreed to hand the presidency to a powerful general, Yuan Shikai.
He died in Beijing in 1925, his work unfinished.
Taiwan honors him today as the father of the nation, and mainland China as a forerunner of its revolution.
Long ago, the story goes, a monster called the Nian lived in the mountains, or in some tellings beneath the sea.
On the last night of every year, it came down to the villages to devour the crops, the animals, and sometimes the people, and every year, the villagers fled into the hills.
Then one year, an old beggar stayed behind.
When the beast arrived, he was waiting, with red paper pasted on the doors, candles burning, and stalks of bamboo bursting with loud cracks in a fire.
The Nian, terrified of the color red, the light, and the noise, ran away.
The old man, some say, was an immortal in disguise.
That's why, as the story is told, the new year is red and loud.
The Chinese phrase for celebrating the new year, guo nian, can be read as getting past the Nian.
Families paste red banners on either side of the door, written with lucky verses, and set off firecrackers, whose ancestors were those bursting stalks of bamboo.
The old Chinese word for firecracker means exploding bamboo.
Some say the lion dance began the same way, as a way to scare off evil with a creature fiercer than the evil itself.
Before a new lion dances for the first time, a dot of red is painted on its eyes, to wake it and bring it to life.
And when the lion reaches for the lettuce a shopkeeper has hung over the door, it's playing on words: in Cantonese, the word for lettuce sounds almost exactly like the words for growing wealth.
The lion eats the greens and then spits them out, scattering good fortune over the shop and the crowd.
Look in shop windows for the character fu, meaning good fortune, hung upside down.
That's another pun.
The word for upside down sounds like the word for arrived, so an upside-down fu announces that good fortune has come.
And about a week before the new year, many families send off the Kitchen God, who's said to report on the household to the Jade Emperor in heaven.
They offer him sweets, so that he'll have only sweet things to say.
Why do so many American Chinatowns look alike?
Part of the answer lies in San Francisco.
In April 1906, an earthquake and the fires that followed left its Chinatown in ashes, and some city leaders saw their chance to move the Chinese out of the heart of the city for good.
The neighborhood's merchants fought back, and one of them, Look Tin Eli, had an idea.
Chinatown would be rebuilt in a style so exotic, so unmistakably Chinese, that it would become one of the sights of San Francisco, and too valuable to move.
Two of the first new buildings went up at the corner of Grant Avenue and California Street in 1907 and 1908.
Their designers were Americans who had never been to China.
Working largely from old drawings of Chinese temples, they put pagoda towers, upturned eaves, and colored tiles on top of ordinary Western commercial buildings.
The look was a hit with visitors, and it spread to Chinatowns across the country.
It's a style you'd hardly find in China itself, a kind of architecture invented in America.
The On Leong Building, finished two decades later, is one of the grandest examples, and like the buildings in San Francisco, it was designed by architects who weren't Chinese.
Its towers, glazed tiles, and terra cotta show an American idea of China, commissioned by Chinese Americans to tell the city who they were.
The colors carry meaning.
Red stands for luck and joy, and it's the color of weddings and the new year.
In imperial China, yellow was reserved for the emperor, and gold suggests wealth.
Green tiles, like the ones on the gate, were used on temples and on buildings a step below the emperor's, like the palaces of princes.
The gate itself follows an old Chinese form called a paifang, a ceremonial archway.
In Chinese cities and villages, archways like this marked the entrances to neighborhoods, or honored local worthies: a famous scholar, a devoted son, or a widow known for her virtue.
Here, it marks the front door of Chinatown.
Walk south on Wentworth to 23rd Street, and then west to number 238 West 23rd Street.
This old brick warehouse is the Chinese American Museum of Chicago.
The museum opened in 2005, in a building that was once a warehouse for a Chinese grocery business.
In 2008, a fire badly damaged the building and destroyed part of the collection.
The community raised money to restore it, and it reopened in 2010.
The museum tells the story of Chinese immigrants in the Midwest.

You'll learn about the laundries and restaurants that were among the few businesses open to Chinese immigrants during the exclusion era, about the paper sons, immigrants who entered the country using false identities as the sons of Chinese American citizens, and about the community's long fight against discrimination.
The museum also has exhibits about the Chinese immigrants who worked on the transcontinental railroad, and about the people of Chinatown, past and present.
It's small, but it's well worth a visit.
When the Chinese community moved here a century ago, it moved into an Italian neighborhood.
The streets around Wentworth were home to Italian immigrants, and some of the churches were theirs.
Just south of here, on Alexander Street, Saint Therese Chinese Catholic Church occupies a building that was once an Italian parish.
Over the decades, as Italian families moved away, the parish was taken over by Chinese Catholics, and today it serves Chinatown, with masses in Cantonese, Mandarin, and English.
Chinatown's population has changed too.
For most of its history it was overwhelmingly Cantonese, from the area around Guangzhou and Hong Kong.
Since the 1980s, more immigrants have come from mainland China, and you'll hear Mandarin and other dialects on the street as often as Cantonese.
Chinatown's history was shaped by the law.
Under the Chinese Exclusion Act, most Chinese men in America couldn't bring their wives and children from China, and the community remained overwhelmingly male for decades.
Many men spent their whole working lives in laundries and restaurants, sending money home to families they rarely saw.
Only after the act was repealed in 1943, and especially after immigration reform in 1965, did Chinatown become a neighborhood of families, which is what you see today.
Most of the Chinese who came to America in the first great wave came from one small corner of China: a handful of rural counties in the delta of the Pearl River, southwest of Guangzhou.
The most important of them was Taishan, also spelled Toisan, a county of rocky hills and thin soil, where many families couldn't live on what their land produced.
When word reached the delta that gold had been found in California, young men began leaving for what they called Gold Mountain.
Over the following decades, Taishan sent so many of its sons overseas that it became known as the home of the overseas Chinese.
For generations, the Chinese most often heard in American Chinatowns, Chicago's included, was the Taishan dialect, which can be hard to follow even for speakers of standard Cantonese.
Many of Chicago's early merchants, among them members of the Moy family, came from Taishan.
The money the emigrants sent home transformed the place.
Families with a man on Gold Mountain built new houses, schools, and ancestral halls.
One emigrant who had made his fortune in Seattle, Chin Gee Hee, came home and built a railroad through the county, early in the twentieth century, with money raised from Chinese overseas.

In the neighboring county of Kaiping, returning emigrants built well over a thousand fortified towers, called diaolou, to protect their families from bandits, who knew which households received money from abroad.
Many of the towers mix Chinese roofs with columns, domes, and balconies copied from buildings the emigrants had seen in America and Europe, and in 2007, they were named a World Heritage Site.
For many of the men who worked in Chicago's laundries and restaurants, home meant one of those villages, and the family they'd left there.
Some came back to Chicago after visits home with new wives or sons, and some went home for good.
Today, many Chinese American families can still name the village their great-grandparents left, and some travel back to see the halls and houses that Gold Mountain money built.
The paper son system began with a disaster.
On April eighteenth, 1906, an earthquake struck San Francisco, and in the fires that followed, the city's birth records burned.
Chinese men who'd been in America for years could now say they had been born in San Francisco, and no one could prove otherwise.
As citizens, they could visit China and report the birth of a son there, and every son on paper was a right of entry to the United States.
Those rights, called slots, could be sold to young men who weren't related at all, and each paper son took the name of the family whose slot he'd bought.
The government knew what was going on, and it fought back with questions.
From 1910 to 1940, most Chinese arriving in San Francisco were held at the immigration station on Angel Island, in San Francisco Bay, while inspectors questioned them, sometimes for days.
How many windows did your house in the village have?
Who lived in the third house in your row?
Then the inspectors asked the paper father the same questions, and compared the answers.
A few mistakes could mean being sent back to China.
So paper sons studied.
They bought coaching books, full of details about the families and villages they were claiming, and memorized them, and many are said to have thrown the books overboard as their ship came into port.
Some waited on the island for weeks, and some for months.
Some of them poured their fear and anger into poems, which they carved into the wooden walls of the barracks.
After the station closed, the poems were forgotten, until 1970, when a park ranger noticed the writing on the walls of a building that was due to be torn down.
Well over a hundred poems have since been recorded, and the barracks are now a museum.
In the 1950s, the government offered paper sons a chance to confess, and many were allowed to keep their status.
Tens of thousands came forward, although some were deported.
Even so, many Chinese American families still carry paper names, and some only learned their true family names decades later.
Chicago's first Chinese laundry opened in 1872, on Madison Street, and by 1883, there were nearly two hundred of them across the city.
Why laundries?
In China, washing clothes was mostly women's work, and few of the men who came to America had ever done it.
But in the American West, where women were scarce, there was plenty of demand, and few white men wanted the job.
A laundry took little money to start: a rented storefront, some tubs, and a stove to heat the irons.
It didn't require much English, and it didn't compete head-on with white workers, which mattered at a time when Chinese workers were being driven out of mines, factories, and whole towns.
The work was grueling.
Laundrymen often worked from early morning until late at night, scrubbing by hand and pressing shirts with heavy irons, and many of them slept in the back of the shop.
Customers usually got a ticket marked with Chinese characters, and its matching half was tied to the bundle.
The laundries also produced one of the great cases in American law.

In the 1880s, San Francisco required a permit to run a laundry in a wooden building, and the city granted permits to all but one of the white applicants while turning down every Chinese applicant, about two hundred in all.

A laundryman named Yick Wo took his case to the Supreme Court, and in 1886, the justices ruled unanimously that a law enforced so unequally violated the Constitution's promise of equal protection, even for people who weren't citizens.
Lawyers still cite the case today.
In the 1930s and 1940s, a University of Chicago student named Paul Siu, himself a Chinese immigrant, spent years getting to know Chicago's laundrymen for his doctoral research.
He described men he called sojourners, who lived in America, sometimes for decades, while their hearts and plans stayed in China.
His study, The Chinese Laundryman, is still read as a classic portrait of Chinese Chicago in the years of exclusion.
Walk back north to Cermak Road.
Near the Cermak-Chinatown station on the Red Line, look for a long wall covered in colorful glazed tiles, with dragons twisting across it.
This is the Nine Dragon Wall, built in 2003.
It's modeled on a famous wall in Beihai Park in Beijing, built in the eighteenth century, during the Qing dynasty.
Nine dragon walls are a traditional feature of imperial Chinese architecture.
In Chinese tradition, the dragon is a symbol of power, strength, and good fortune, and the number nine is associated with the emperor.
Screen walls like this one were traditionally placed in front of gates, and folk belief held that evil spirits can only travel in straight lines, so a wall in the way keeps them out.
Look closely at the nine large dragons, each in a different color, and at the many smaller dragons hidden throughout the wall.
Now cross Cermak Road to the north.
On the corner of Wentworth and Archer Avenue stands the Chinatown branch of the Chicago Public Library, which opened in 2015.
It was designed by the architecture firm Skidmore, Owings and Merrill as a rounded triangle of glass, wrapped in vertical fins, so that it has no front or back.
Inside, a two-story atrium lets in daylight from above.
The old library was in a cramped storefront, and the new one became one of the busiest branches in the city, full of students, retirees reading Chinese newspapers, and families.
It's a good place to see everyday Chinatown.
Just west of the library is Chinatown Square, a two-level outdoor shopping plaza that opened in 1993, on land that was once a railroad yard.
Look for the twelve bronze statues of the animals of the Chinese zodiac: the rat, ox, tiger, rabbit, dragon, snake, horse, goat, monkey, rooster, dog, and pig.
See if you can find the animal for your birth year.
The restaurants and bakeries here, and along Archer Avenue, are where many Chicagoans come for dim sum.
As you walk, look up at the elevated tracks of the Red Line and the expressways at the edges of the neighborhood.
In the 1950s and 1960s, the Dan Ryan and Stevenson expressways were built along Chinatown's edges, taking homes and businesses and walling the neighborhood in even more tightly.
That's part of why the purchase of the railroad land to the north, in the 1980s, mattered so much: it was the first room the neighborhood had found to grow in decades.
Only a handful of old nine dragon walls survive in China, and the three most famous each have their own story.
The oldest and biggest stands in the city of Datong, in the north.
It was built in 1392, in front of the palace of a Ming dynasty prince, a son of the dynasty's founder.
It's about a hundred and fifty feet long and more than twenty-five feet high, and although the palace is long gone, the wall survived.
The wall that Chicago's is modeled on, in Beihai Park in Beijing, was built in 1756, in the reign of the Qianlong emperor.
Unlike most screen walls, it's decorated on both sides, with nine great dragons on each face, and by one count, more than six hundred dragons in all, large and small.
The third, inside the Forbidden City, was built in the 1770s for the same emperor, in front of the palace where he planned to spend his retirement.
It comes with a legend.
As the story goes, when the wall was nearly finished, a worker broke one of the glazed tiles on the belly of a white dragon.
There was no time to fire a new one before the inspection, and the punishment for the mistake would have been death.
So a craftsman carved a replacement out of wood overnight and painted it to match, and no one noticed.
Look closely at that dragon today, and you can see the piece of wood among the tiles, where its paint has worn away.
The wall here is a smaller, partial copy of the one in Beihai Park, made of glazed tiles from China.
The Chinatown Chamber of Commerce dedicated it on September ninth, 2003, a date full of nines, and a plaque calls it one of only three such walls outside China.
Look at the colors of the nine great dragons, and then try counting the small ones.
There are said to be more than five hundred.
Why these twelve animals, and why in this order?
The best-known answer is a story.
Long ago, the Jade Emperor, the ruler of heaven, announced a race.
The first twelve animals to cross a great river and reach him would each have a year named after them.
The rat was small and couldn't swim well, so it asked the ox for a ride, and the good-natured ox agreed.
Just as the ox reached the far bank, the rat leaped off its head and scurried ahead to finish first.
That's why the rat leads the zodiac and the ox comes second.
The tiger fought the current to come in third, and the rabbit hopped across on stones and floating logs.
The dragon, who could have flown across and won easily, stopped to bring rain to a village that needed it, and came in fifth.
And so on, down to the pig, who stopped for a meal and a nap, and came in last.
And the cat?
In one version, the cat and the rat were friends, and they planned to ride across together on the ox.
But the rat didn't wake the cat on the morning of the race, or in other tellings pushed it into the river, and the cat was left out of the zodiac altogether.
Cats have chased rats ever since.
In Vietnam, though, the cat got its revenge: the Vietnamese zodiac has a year of the cat in place of the rabbit.
The animals are only half of the system.
Each year is also linked to one of five elements, wood, fire, earth, metal, and water, so it takes sixty years for every animal to meet every element.
Some combinations carry superstitions of their own.

In Japan, an old belief held that girls born in a year of the Fire Horse would bring misfortune to their husbands, and in 1966, a Fire Horse year, the number of births in Japan fell by about a quarter.
The next Fire Horse year arrived in 2026.
In Cantonese, going out for dim sum is called yum cha, which simply means drinking tea, and the tea comes first.
The custom grew up in the teahouses of Guangzhou, where travelers and merchants stopped to rest, and over time, the snacks served with the tea became the main attraction.
Dim sum is usually translated as touching the heart: little things to eat that hit the spot.
An old phrase for a proper morning out is one cup, two pieces, a pot of tea and a couple of dumplings.
In the old style of service, servers push carts through the dining room, you point at what you want, and they mark a card on your table.
Many places now hand you a paper menu to check off instead.
Either way, a few dishes are classics.
Har gow are shrimp dumplings in a wrapper so thin it's nearly clear, and a skilled chef, it's said, should pleat each one at least seven times.
Siu mai are open-topped dumplings of pork and shrimp.
Char siu bao are fluffy steamed buns filled with sweet barbecued pork.
There are rice noodle rolls, slippery and soft, and phoenix claws, which is the elegant name for chicken feet, braised until they're tender.
For dessert, try an egg tart, a cousin of the British custard tart and the Portuguese pastel de nata, which came to Cantonese bakeries by way of Hong Kong and Macau.
There's etiquette too.
When someone pours tea for you, tap two fingers on the table to say thank you.
The story goes that the Qianlong emperor, traveling in disguise, once poured tea for one of his servants.
The servant couldn't kneel and bow to the emperor without giving away his secret, so he bent two fingers and tapped them on the table, like a tiny pair of kneeling legs.
And when your teapot is empty, leave the lid open or tilted to one side, and someone will come by to refill it.
Walk north along Wentworth Avenue or through the residential streets, past the townhouses built on more former railroad land, to Ping Tom Memorial Park, along the South Branch of the Chicago River.
This park opened in 1999, on another old railroad yard.

It's named for Ping Tom, a Chinatown businessman and civic leader, who led the effort to buy the railroad land that allowed Chinatown to expand north, to build Chinatown Square, and to create this park.
He died in 1995, before it opened.
The park has a Chinese-style pavilion, a boathouse where you can rent kayaks, and a dock for the water taxi, which runs downtown in the warmer months.
Look north, and you'll see a dramatic view of the skyline, one of the best views of the city.
Then look south, at the old railroad lift bridge that crosses the river just beyond the park.
The whole span of that bridge rises straight up between its two towers to let boats pass.
Every June, the river in front of the park fills with long, narrow dragon boats, paddled by teams of twenty and steered to the beat of a drummer in the bow, for the Chicago Dragon Boat Race.
Dragon boat racing comes from a two-thousand-year-old Chinese festival, and the race here draws teams from all over the region.
Look at the park's boathouse, a low building whose roof rises and falls in a series of peaks, like waves.
It was designed by the Chicago architect Jeanne Gang, whose firm also designed the rippling Aqua tower downtown, and it opened in 2013.
Chinatown has also found its political voice.
For decades, the neighborhood was split among several city council wards, and its residents had little say at City Hall.

When the ward map was redrawn in 2022, Chinatown and its neighbors were united in a single ward, the eleventh, the old political home of the Daleys in Bridgeport, which became the first ward in the city's history with an Asian American majority.
In 2023, Nicole Lee became the first Chinese American ever to serve on the Chicago City Council.
For Chinatown, the park is a symbol of how a neighborhood that was once squeezed in on all sides found room to grow.
This is the end of the Chinatown tour.
If you want, you can take the water taxi back downtown.
Ping Tom was born in Chicago in 1935, into one of Chinatown's best-known families.
His father, Tom Y. Chan, had been born in 1881 in a village in southern China, in the same county as Sun Yat-sen.
He learned to make noodles in New York, came to Chicago, and founded the Chinese Noodle Company, which made egg noodles and the skins for wontons and egg rolls.
He became a civic leader too, raising money for Chinese war orphans and for American war bonds during the Second World War.
When he died, in 1944, he couldn't be buried beside his wife in the cemetery where she lay, for reasons that some believe were racist.
Ping went to the Haines School in Chinatown, and then won a scholarship to the Francis W. Parker School on the North Side.
In time, he ran the family businesses, which came to include the noodle company and a company that made chop suey pails, the folded paper cartons Americans still carry home full of Chinese food.
That carton is a Chicago invention too.
A Chicago inventor named Frederick Weeks Wilcox patented a version of it in 1894, as a pail for oysters.
But Ping Tom is remembered for the land.
He believed Chinatown, boxed in by railroads and expressways, couldn't survive as a neighborhood of families unless it found room to grow.
In 1984, he founded a company, the Chinese American Development Corporation, that bought the old Santa Fe railroad land north of Cermak Road and began building on it.
He also pressed the city to turn more of the old railroad land along the river into a park for the people of Chinatown.
He didn't live to see it.
Ping Tom died of cancer in July 1995, at the age of sixty.
On October second, 1999, the Chicago Park District dedicated this park in his name, and it has since grown north along the river, with a field house and the boathouse.
Many of the homes you passed on the way here stand on the old railroad land he fought to open up.
The dragon boat races remember a poet.
More than two thousand years ago, in the age of the Warring States, Qu Yuan served as a minister to the king of Chu, a great kingdom along the Yangtze.
He was a loyal adviser, the story goes, but rivals at court slandered him, and he was sent into exile.
There he wrote some of the most celebrated poems in the Chinese language, among them a long lament called Encountering Sorrow.
When he heard that the capital of Chu had fallen to a rival kingdom, he walked into the Miluo River, holding a heavy stone, and drowned.
The people who loved him rowed out in their boats to search for him, beating drums and splashing with their paddles to frighten away the fish, so that they wouldn't eat his body.
They threw rice into the water for the fish to eat instead.
Later, as the story goes, Qu Yuan's ghost appeared and told them that a river dragon was stealing the rice, so they began wrapping it in leaves tied with colored thread.
That's the origin, as it's told, of the Dragon Boat Festival, held on the fifth day of the fifth month of the Chinese calendar, which usually falls in late May or June.
Families eat zongzi, sticky rice wrapped in bamboo or reed leaves, filled with pork, egg yolk, beans, or dates, depending on the region.
They hang bundles of mugwort and calamus on their doors to keep away illness, because the fifth month was traditionally a season of sickness.
Historians suspect that the festival is older than Qu Yuan, and that it began with rituals honoring dragons, the bringers of rain, and with boat races meant to drive off disease in the hot months.
In 2009, the United Nations cultural agency added the Dragon Boat Festival to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.
The boats keep the dragon alive: watch for the carved head at the bow, the tail at the stern, and the scales painted along the sides.
Look south along the river at the railroad bridge with two tall towers.
It's the Canal Street railroad bridge, finished around 1914 for the Pennsylvania Railroad, and today it's the only lift bridge on the Chicago River.
It was designed by the engineering firm of Waddell and Harrington, and its senior partner, John Alexander Low Waddell, was the great champion of this kind of bridge.
In the early 1890s, he designed one of the first modern lift bridges, which carried Halsted Street over this same South Branch.
A lift bridge has one big advantage over the bascule bridges downtown, whose leaves tilt up into the air: its span stays level, so it can be very long and very heavy, which suited a railroad.
The trick is in the towers.
The span hangs from steel cables that run up and over giant wheels at the top of each tower, called sheaves, and down to counterweights that weigh about as much as the span itself.
Because the span and the counterweights balance each other, the motors don't have to lift the full weight, only to get it moving.
As the span rises, the counterweights sink, and if you're watching when the bridge moves, you may see them sliding down inside the towers.
The span is about two hundred seventy feet long, and it weighs about fifteen hundred tons, by most accounts.
It replaced an old swing bridge on the same spot, and the new bridge, it's said, was built right above the old one, so that the trains could keep running while the work went on.
The bridge now belongs to Amtrak, and since 2007, it's been an official Chicago Landmark.
It's one of the last reminders of the railroad empire that once covered this side of the river, including the yards where you're standing.
When it rises, you're watching a machine more than a century old do exactly what it was built to do.
This tour explores Bridgeport and the old Union Stock Yards, on the Southwest Side, about three miles south of the Loop.
If you want to understand how Chicago really worked in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, its industry, its immigrants, and its politics, this is the place.
Bridgeport began with the Illinois and Michigan Canal.
Digging started in 1836, at the South Branch of the Chicago River, and the workers were mostly Irish immigrants, who settled in shanties near the canal's starting point.
The area was first nicknamed Hardscrabble.
The name Bridgeport is said to come from a low bridge over the river that forced boats to unload their cargo here.
When the canal opened in 1848, Bridgeport became an industrial district of lumber yards, brickyards, packinghouses, and rolling mills.

In 1865, just south of here, a group of railroads and meatpackers opened the Union Stock Yards, a vast complex of pens, chutes, and slaughterhouses where cattle, hogs, and sheep shipped in by rail from across the West were bought, sold, and killed.
Companies like Armour, Swift, and Morris built enormous packing plants beside the yards.
They turned the slaughter of animals into a moving assembly line, or more precisely, a disassembly line, where carcasses moved along overhead rails past workers who each made one cut.
Henry Ford later said that the packinghouses' overhead trolleys helped inspire his assembly line.
Swift and others used refrigerated railroad cars to ship fresh meat across the country.
For decades, Chicago was the meatpacking capital of the world.
Carl Sandburg, in his 1914 poem Chicago, called the city "Hog Butcher for the World."
The work was brutal and dangerous, the pay was low, and the smell hung over the whole South Side.
The neighborhoods around the yards, Bridgeport, Canaryville, and Back of the Yards, filled with Irish, German, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Croatian, and Mexican workers.
Bridgeport also gave Chicago its politics.
From 1933 to 1979, and again from 1989 to 2011, almost every mayor of Chicago came from this one neighborhood: Edward Kelly, Martin Kennelly, Richard J. Daley, Michael Bilandic, and Richard M. Daley.
We'll start at the White Sox ballpark, walk west through Bridgeport to Halsted Street, and then south to the gate of the old stockyards, ending at a church in Canaryville.
You're near the Sox-35th Street station on the Red Line, in front of the home of the Chicago White Sox, at 35th Street and the Dan Ryan Expressway.
The ballpark opened in 1991, and it has had several names since, most recently Rate Field.
Look across 35th Street, to the north, at the parking lot.
That was the site of old Comiskey Park, which opened in 1910 and was the Sox's home for eighty years.
Look for a marble plaque in the pavement, which marks the location of its home plate.
Old Comiskey saw some of the most famous moments in baseball.
In 1919, the White Sox lost the World Series to the Cincinnati Reds, and it came out that eight Sox players had been paid by gamblers to throw it.
The players were acquitted in court, but the new commissioner of baseball, Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis, banned all eight for life, including the great hitter Shoeless Joe Jackson.
A famous story has a boy outside the courthouse pleading, "Say it ain't so, Joe."
That line is probably a reporter's invention, but the scandal was real, and the team became known as the Black Sox.
In 1933, during the Century of Progress fair, Comiskey Park hosted the first Major League Baseball All-Star Game.
That same year, it also hosted the first East-West All-Star Game of the Negro Leagues, which was played here for most of the next three decades and drew huge crowds.
And in 1979, between games of a doubleheader, a radio host blew up a crate of disco records in center field, during a promotion called Disco Demolition Night.
The crowd stormed the field, and the White Sox had to forfeit the second game.
The Sox finally won the World Series again in 2005, their first championship since 1917.
Bridgeport is White Sox territory.
The North Side has the Cubs.
That divide is still one of the most reliable ways to start an argument in Chicago.
Why were they called the Black Sox?
The obvious answer is the scandal.

But there's an older story, that the team's owner, Charles Comiskey, was so stingy that he made his players pay to have their own uniforms washed, and when they refused, the uniforms got dirtier and dirtier.
Comiskey's stinginess is often given as a reason why his players were tempted by the gamblers' money.
The laundry story is probably part legend, but Chicagoans have been telling it for a century.
The South Side was also the capital of Black baseball.

A few blocks south of here, at 39th Street, stood the White Sox's earlier ballpark, which later became the home of the Chicago American Giants, owned and managed by Andrew Rube Foster, a former star pitcher.
In 1920, Foster organized the Negro National League, the first successful professional league for Black players, and he's often called the father of Black baseball.
Charles Comiskey, whose name was on the old ballpark across the street, was a Chicago boy.
He was born here in 1859, the son of an Irish immigrant known as Honest John Comiskey, who sat on the city council.
Charles chose baseball over politics, and by twenty-three he was managing the Saint Louis Browns while playing first base.
His Browns won four pennants in a row, from 1885 to 1888, and in 1886 they beat Chicago's National League champions, the White Stockings, in a series for the championship of the world.
In 1894, he bought a minor league team in Sioux City, Iowa, in a league run by his friend Ban Johnson, and soon moved it to Saint Paul, Minnesota.
Then he set his sights on his hometown.

In October 1899, James Hart, who ran Chicago's National League club, agreed to let him in on conditions: Comiskey's team had to play south of 35th Street, far from Hart's ballpark on the West Side, and it couldn't use the city's name.
Hart is said to have assumed that few fans would put up with the smell of the stockyards.
Comiskey borrowed the old name of Hart's own team, the White Stockings, which it no longer used, and the newspapers soon shortened it to White Sox.
Johnson's league renamed itself the American League, declared itself a major league in 1901, and went to war with the National League for players and fans.
Comiskey's team won the new league's first pennant.
His greatest triumph came in 1906.
That season, the Cubs won a hundred and sixteen games, still the best winning percentage in modern baseball history.
The White Sox had a team batting average of two thirty, the worst in their league, and they were nicknamed the Hitless Wonders.
They won with pitching and defense, and when the two Chicago teams met in the World Series, the Hitless Wonders beat the Cubs four games to two.
It's still the only World Series the two teams have ever played against each other.
Sportswriters called Comiskey the Old Roman.
He died in 1931, at his retreat in Eagle River, Wisconsin, and his family kept the team until 1959.
The most inventive owner the White Sox ever had grew up in the game.
Bill Veeck was born in Chicago in 1914, and his father, a sportswriter, became president of the Cubs, so young Bill spent his boyhood around the ballpark on the North Side.
He told the world how to say his name in the title of his autobiography: Veeck, as in wreck.
In the Second World War, he served with the Marines in the South Pacific, and on the island of Bougainville, the recoil of an anti-aircraft gun smashed his leg.
It was eventually amputated, and for the rest of his life he wore wooden legs, with holes cut in them to use as ashtrays.
As owner of the Cleveland Indians, he signed Larry Doby in July 1947, making him the first Black player in the American League, eleven weeks after Jackie Robinson's debut with the Brooklyn Dodgers.
The next year, he signed the great Negro Leagues pitcher Satchel Paige, then in his forties, and Cleveland won the World Series.
Later, with the lowly Saint Louis Browns, he sent a man three feet seven inches tall up to bat.
Eddie Gaedel walked on four pitches, and the league quickly voided his contract.
Veeck bought the White Sox in 1959, and that fall they won their first pennant in forty years.
The next season, he unveiled the first exploding scoreboard in the major leagues, which set off fireworks and spun pinwheels after every White Sox home run.
Illness forced him to sell in 1961.
He came back in 1975, gathering investors to buy the team when it looked likely to move to Seattle.
In 1976, he put his players in shorts for a game.
In 1978, he hired Larry Doby again, this time as manager, only the second Black manager in major league history.
And the anti-disco promotion that ended in a riot in 1979 was cooked up by his son Mike, the team's promotions director, together with a local disc jockey.
Veeck sold the team for good in 1981, and he died in Chicago in 1986.
Five years later, he was elected to the Hall of Fame, the owner who never stopped believing that a ball game should be fun.
The East-West game began as a promoter's idea in the depths of the Depression.
In 1933, Gus Greenlee, a Pittsburgh nightclub owner who had grown rich in the numbers racket, was reviving the Negro National League, and he wanted a showcase.
Some historians give the credit for the idea to two Pittsburgh sportswriters, Roy Sparrow and Bill Nunn.
Greenlee joined forces with Robert Cole, the owner of the Chicago American Giants, and they booked Comiskey Park.
The first game, on September tenth, 1933, drew a crowd of perhaps twenty thousand.
What set it apart from the major league All-Star Game was who picked the players.
The fans did.
Black newspapers across the country, above all the Chicago Defender and the Pittsburgh Courier, printed ballots, and readers voted for the starting lineups.
For Black America, it was a national election, held every summer.
The game grew into the biggest event in Black sports.
Fans came from all over the country, many dressed in their best clothes, and the hotels, clubs, and theaters of Bronzeville filled up for a weekend of parties.
In 1936, the East-West game outdrew the major leagues' own All-Star Game.
On August first, 1943, a crowd of fifty-one thousand seven hundred and twenty-three packed Comiskey Park, the largest in the game's history.

The players included many of the greatest in baseball history: Satchel Paige, the slugging catcher Josh Gibson, and the outfielder Cool Papa Bell, who was said to be so fast that he could switch off the light and be in bed before the room got dark.
Anyone who doubted that Black players belonged in the major leagues only had to come and watch.
After 1947, when the major leagues began signing the best Black players, the Negro Leagues slowly faded, and the East-West game faded with them.
But for a generation, the biggest yearly gathering of Black baseball fans in America happened right here, on the South Side.
Walk west on 35th Street, across the expressway and into the residential streets of Bridgeport, to Lowe Avenue, and turn south.
At number 3536 South Lowe, there's a modest brick bungalow.
A police booth often stood nearby.
This was the home of Richard J. Daley, mayor of Chicago from 1955 until his death in 1976.
Daley was born in Bridgeport in 1902, the only child of Irish American parents, and he lived in this neighborhood all his life.
He worked in the stockyards as a young man, studied law at night, and rose through the Democratic Party organization of the eleventh ward, the most powerful political base in the city.
As mayor and as chairman of the Cook County Democratic Party, Daley ran what was probably the most powerful urban political machine in America.
Patronage jobs were handed out in exchange for votes and loyalty, and the precinct captains knew every voter on their block.
Under Daley, the city built expressways, O'Hare Airport, McCormick Place, and much of the modern Loop, and it was called "the city that works."
It also built huge public housing projects that concentrated poverty, and it resisted the civil rights movement's campaign against segregation.
The police violence during the 1968 Democratic convention happened on his watch.
The newspaper columnist Mike Royko called him simply "Boss."
Just south of here, at 37th and Lowe, is the Nativity of Our Lord church, where the Daley family worshipped, and where his funeral was held.
In his youth, Daley was president of the Hamburg Athletic Club, one of the neighborhood social clubs that were partly gangs.
Members of such clubs were accused of attacking Black Chicagoans during the 1919 race riot.
What role, if any, Daley played has never been established, and he never spoke about it.
His son, Richard M. Daley, was mayor from 1989 to 2011, even longer than his father.
Daley was famous for his loyalty, his temper, and his tangled sentences.
During the turmoil of 1968, he told reporters, "The policeman isn't there to create disorder.
The policeman is there to preserve disorder."
Everyone knew what he meant.
His machine was also famous for getting out the vote, sometimes too well.

In the presidential election of 1960, John F. Kennedy won Illinois by fewer than nine thousand votes, and Republicans charged that the Daley machine had stolen the election for him in Chicago, with votes cast in the names of the dead.
Whether the fraud was enough to change the result has been argued ever since, and it's become one of the great legends of Chicago politics.

In 1948, a University of Chicago law student named Abner Mikva walked into his local Democratic ward office, eager to volunteer for two reform candidates, Adlai Stevenson for governor and Paul Douglas for the Senate.
The ward committeeman, Timothy O'Sullivan, looked him over and asked who had sent him.
Mikva said nobody had.
As Mikva told the story for the rest of his life, the answer came back: We don't want nobody nobody sent.
We ain't got no jobs.
Those two sentences sum up how the machine worked.
It ran on jobs.
The party controlled tens of thousands of positions in city and county government, from street sweepers to building inspectors, and each one went to someone sent by a ward boss.
In return, the job holder worked his precinct at every election, or lost the job.
When Daley first won the mayor's office, in April 1955, a North Side alderman and saloonkeeper named Paddy Bauler is said to have danced a jig and declared that Chicago ain't ready for reform.
For decades, it seemed he was right.
Mikva found his own way in.
He won a seat in the state legislature as an independent Democrat, and later a seat in Congress, and he went on to be a federal appeals judge and White House counsel to President Clinton.
What finally broke the jobs system was a lawsuit.

In 1969, a young lawyer named Michael Shakman ran as an independent for a convention to rewrite the state constitution, and he sued, arguing that armies of patronage workers gave the machine's candidates an unfair advantage.
The case produced a series of federal court orders known as the Shakman decrees.
The first, in 1972, banned firing government workers for political reasons.
A second, in 1983, banned political hiring.
Enforcing them took decades.
In 2006, a top aide to Mayor Richard M. Daley was convicted of rigging city hiring to reward political workers, and the city wasn't released from federal oversight until 2014.
When Richard J. Daley died in December 1976, the city council chose a quiet lawyer from his own neighborhood to take his place.
Michael Bilandic, the son of Croatian immigrants, had been the eleventh ward's alderman, and he was the machine's man.
He won a special election the next year, and in 1979 he seemed certain to win a full term.
His challenger was Jane Byrne, who had served under Daley as the head of the city's consumer sales department.
Bilandic had fired her in 1977, after she publicly attacked a taxi fare increase his administration had approved.
Few people gave her a chance.
Then came the snow.
On January thirteenth and fourteenth, 1979, about twenty inches fell, on top of snow left by earlier storms.
Side streets stayed buried for weeks.
Cars disappeared under drifts, garbage piled up in the alleys, and the trains of the Chicago Transit Authority broke down or ran far behind.
To speed up service, the transit authority had some trains skip stations in Black neighborhoods on the South and West Sides, leaving riders standing on frozen platforms as the trains rolled past.
Byrne made the snow her campaign.
Her message, in effect, was that the city that works had stopped working.

Jesse Jackson endorsed her, and on February twenty-seventh, 1979, she won the Democratic primary by about seventeen thousand votes, with strong support in the Black wards that had felt abandoned on those platforms.
In April, she won the general election with eighty-two percent of the vote, and she became the first woman to serve as mayor of Chicago.
Politicians took note, in Chicago and far beyond.
For years afterward, the mayors of snowy cities were said to think of Michael Bilandic whenever a big storm rolled in, and to make very sure the plows reached the side streets.
The Daley house is a Chicago bungalow, and once you learn to recognize the type, you'll see it all over the city.
Between about 1910 and 1940, Chicagoans built some eighty thousand of them, and they still make up about a third of the city's single-family houses.
Most stand in a great crescent, four to seven miles from downtown, that sweeps around the city's outer neighborhoods.
Chicagoans call it the Bungalow Belt.
The Chicago bungalow was shaped by the Chicago lot, which is typically twenty-five feet wide and a hundred and twenty-five feet deep.
So the house turns its narrow end to the street.
It's usually a story and a half tall, built of brick, with a low roof and deep, overhanging eaves.
In front, look for a bay of windows, often with panes of colored art glass.
Inside, you'd typically find oak trim, built-in cabinets, and a basement raised a few feet above the ground, so that its windows catch some light.
What made the bungalow remarkable was who could buy one.
It was modern, with central heat, indoor plumbing, and electric light, but it was small enough to be affordable, and developers put them up by the dozen, block after block, for working families.
Many buyers borrowed from neighborhood savings and loan associations, often run by and for a single ethnic group.
For the children of immigrants who had grown up in crowded cottages and flats near the stockyards, a bungalow a few miles farther out was proof that the family had made it.
The Bungalow Belt became a political term, too.
Its homeowners, many of them city workers, were long seen as the backbone of the machine's vote, and later as the voters every candidate for mayor had to win.
Around 2000, the city began a program to help owners restore their bungalows' original details, and a nonprofit, the Historic Chicago Bungalow Association, still runs it.
Walk west to Halsted Street and north to number 3518.
The small Spanish-style movie theater with the vertical sign is the Ramova Theatre, opened in 1929.
The Ramova was an atmospheric theater.
Its auditorium was designed to look like a Spanish courtyard under an open night sky, with twinkling stars and drifting clouds on the ceiling, and it seated about fifteen hundred people.
For decades, it was the neighborhood movie house, and the diner next door, the Ramova Grill, was famous for its chili.
The theater closed in 1985 and stood empty for decades.
It was restored and reopened in 2023 as a concert venue, with a brewery, and the Grill was revived.
Halsted Street was Bridgeport's main shopping street, lined with taverns, bakeries, and shops serving the Irish, Lithuanian, Polish, Italian, and Croatian families who lived on the side streets.
Today, the neighborhood is changing again.
Many Mexican American families live here now, and Chinatown has spread into Bridgeport's northeastern corner, so you'll see Chinese restaurants and signs alongside the old Irish taverns.

A few blocks west of here, on 35th Street, the huge concrete building known as the Bridgeport Art Center was once a warehouse for Spiegel, one of the big Chicago mail-order companies, which, like Sears and Montgomery Ward, shipped catalogs and goods to homes across the country.
Today, it's full of artists' studios.
Look at the houses on the side streets as you walk.
Many are small wooden cottages, some sitting below the level of the street, because the city raised the streets for sewers long after they were built.
A couple of blocks south, at 37th and Halsted, is Schaller's Pump, which has been serving drinks since 1881, making it one of the oldest taverns in Chicago.

For decades, it stood across the street from the headquarters of the eleventh ward Democratic organization, Daley's political home, and it's said that more city business was settled at its bar than at City Hall.
During Prohibition, it was a speakeasy, and legend says it never actually stopped selling beer.
The Ramova's name is Lithuanian, and it's a clue to who lived on these streets when the theater opened.
The story goes that in the summer of 1929, a naming contest was held through the Lithuanian newspaper Draugas, whose name means friend.
The winner was Ramova, which was said to mean a peaceful place.
Before that, the new theater had been advertised under a far less poetic name, the Roxee.
Lithuanians began arriving in Chicago in large numbers in the 1880s and 1890s.
Their homeland was then part of the Russian Empire, and many were escaping poverty and service in the Russian army.
Many found work in the stockyards, and Bridgeport became the first center of Lithuanian Chicago.
In 1892, they founded the city's first Lithuanian parish, Saint George, and its big church rose a few blocks northwest of here.
Halsted Street filled with Lithuanian taverns, bakeries, shops, and halls, and Chicago came to be called the largest Lithuanian city outside Lithuania.
There's a reason so much Lithuanian was printed here.

From 1864 to 1904, the Russian authorities banned books and newspapers in the Lithuanian language printed in its own alphabet, so Lithuanian publishing flourished abroad, and Chicago became one of its capitals.
Walk one block west of Halsted, and you'll find Lituanica Avenue.
It used to be Auburn Avenue, and in the 1930s it was renamed for the Lituanica, the plane that two Chicago Lithuanian pilots flew across the Atlantic in 1933.
Saint George's church stood on that street.
It closed in 1990, and it has since been torn down.

Over the twentieth century, Lithuanian Chicago moved south and west, to the neighborhood around Marquette Park, where a stretch of 69th Street is called Lithuanian Plaza Court, and later to the suburbs.
But the name on the marquee here still speaks the old language.
