On July fifteenth, 1933, two Chicago Lithuanians took off from Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn, bound for Kaunas, then the capital of Lithuania, without a stop.
Steponas Darius was born in Lithuania in 1896 and came to America with his family as a boy.
In the First World War, he fought in France with the American army, and he was gassed and wounded.
Afterward, he went back to Lithuania, where he became a military pilot and helped introduce basketball, publishing the country's first rules for the game in 1926.
Stasys Girėnas, three years older, had come to America as a young man and served in the American army at home.
In Chicago, he started a taxi company.
The two men met in 1927, and they soon began to dream of flying nonstop from America to Lithuania.
In 1932, they bought a Bellanca, a sturdy six-seat airplane, and rebuilt it for the long crossing.
Lithuanian American groups helped raise the money, and in the spring of 1933, the plane was christened the Lituanica.
Before they left, the two men wrote a short testament addressed to Young Lithuania, dedicating the flight to the nation's young.
They crossed the ocean.

But in the early hours of July seventeenth, after more than thirty-seven hours in the air and nearly four thousand miles, the Lituanica crashed in a forest near the town of Soldin, then in Germany and now in Poland, about four hundred miles short of Kaunas.
Both men were killed.
Investigators concluded that it was an accident, most likely a failed emergency landing in bad weather and fog.
But many Lithuanians suspected the new Nazi government.
Rumors said searchlights at a camp near Soldin had caught the plane in their beams, and the Germans had moved the bodies before Lithuanian officials arrived.
Autopsies found no bullets, and the doubts have never entirely gone away.
In Lithuania, Darius and Girėnas became national heroes.
Their faces appeared on the ten litas banknote, Kaunas named its stadium for them, and the wreck of their plane is kept in a museum there.
In Chicago, a monument to the two fliers stands in Marquette Park, on the Southwest Side.
About a mile north of here, Archer Avenue slants along the northern edge of Bridgeport.
It follows the route of the old Illinois and Michigan Canal, and it's named for William Beatty Archer, a canal commissioner who handed out jobs to the Irish diggers.
Follow it southwest for about a dozen miles, and you reach Resurrection Cemetery, in the suburb of Justice.
That stretch of road belongs to Chicago's most famous ghost.
As the story is usually told, she was a young woman with light hair and a white dress who went dancing one night at a ballroom out on Archer Avenue.
She quarreled with her date, set off walking home, and was struck and killed by a driver who never stopped.
She was buried at Resurrection in her white dress.
Since the 1930s, drivers on Archer Avenue have told of picking up a quiet young woman who asks for a ride.
She says little, and as the car passes the cemetery gates, she's gone.
In one early account, from 1939, a young man named Jerry Palus said a girl he'd met at a dance directed him down Archer Avenue, asked to get out at the cemetery, and vanished.
Later drivers reported hitting a young woman in white outside the cemetery, only to find no one there.
The most famous night came in August 1976, when a man called the police in Justice to report a girl locked inside the cemetery after dark.
An officer found no one, but two bars of the gate were bent apart, with what looked like the marks of small hands seared into the metal.
Crowds came to see them.
The cemetery said a truck had damaged the bars.
Who was she?
Researchers have proposed several real young women.
One was Mary Bregovy, who died in a car crash downtown in 1934.

Another was Anna Norkus, a twelve-year-old from a Lithuanian family, killed in 1927 on her way home from the Oh Henry Ballroom on Archer Avenue, though she's buried at Saint Casimir, the Lithuanian cemetery, not Resurrection.
None of them fits perfectly.
Resurrection Mary belongs to a very old kind of tale, the vanishing hitchhiker, told around the world.
But on Archer Avenue, people still keep an eye out for her.
Walk south on Halsted Street, past the old railroad tracks, to Exchange Avenue, and turn west to Peoria Street.
Here stands a triple-arched limestone gate.
It's almost all that remains of the Union Stock Yards.
The gate was built in 1879, and its design is attributed to the young firm of Burnham and Root, who also designed buildings inside the yards.
Look at the carved head of a steer over the central arch.
It's said to represent Sherman, a prize steer named after John B. Sherman, the yards' longtime manager.
Through this gate passed buyers, sellers, workers, and visitors.
Touring the stockyards was one of the most popular attractions in Chicago, and visitors came from around the world to watch the killing floors.
The yards covered hundreds of acres, with miles of pens, and at their peak, tens of thousands of people worked here and in the packing plants.
In 1906, Upton Sinclair published The Jungle, a novel about a Lithuanian immigrant family working in the yards, based on weeks of reporting here.
Sinclair wanted to expose how workers were treated, but readers were more horrified by his descriptions of rotten meat, rats, and filth.
"I aimed at the public's heart," he said, "and by accident I hit it in the stomach."
Within months, Congress passed the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act.
In December 1910, a fire in a meatpacking warehouse here killed twenty-one firefighters, including the city's fire chief, James Horan.

Nearby stood the International Amphitheatre, a huge arena built next to the yards in 1934, which hosted political conventions, including the 1968 Democratic National Convention, and concerts by Elvis Presley and the Beatles.
As the meat industry decentralized, moving closer to the ranches, the packers left Chicago.
The Union Stock Yards closed in 1971.
Today, the land is an industrial park.
Just north and west of here, a fork of the river was so polluted with packinghouse waste that it bubbled with gas.
It's still called Bubbly Creek.
The packers liked to say that they used every part of the pig except the squeal.
Nothing was wasted.
Blood, bones, hooves, hides, and fat were turned into fertilizer, glue, soap, gelatin, brushes, buttons, and even strings for musical instruments and tennis rackets.
The waste that couldn't be used went into the river, and into Bubbly Creek.
The neighborhoods around the yards, especially Back of the Yards, just to the west, were among the most crowded and polluted in the city.
Families lived in wooden houses beside the pens and the smokestacks, the air smelled of animals and rendering vats, and children worked in the plants.
The packers fought unions for decades, and the great strikes of 1904 and 1921 were both broken.
It wasn't until the late 1930s and 1940s that the packinghouse workers finally won union contracts, with Black, white, and Mexican workers organizing together.
Before 1865, Chicago's livestock trade was scattered among several competing yards along different railroad lines, and moving animals between them meant driving herds through the city streets.
The Civil War changed the scale of everything.
The Union army needed meat, and during the war, Chicago passed Cincinnati as the nation's biggest pork packer.
So a group of meatpackers and railroad men organized one central market.
The state legislature granted a charter, the new company raised a million dollars, and it bought three hundred and twenty acres of swampy prairie south of the city.
To lay it out, it hired a railroad engineer named Octave Chanute.

He designed a grid of streets and alleys lined with pens, with room for about twenty-one thousand cattle, seventy-five thousand hogs, and twenty-two thousand sheep, and with railroad tracks running right up to the chutes.
The Union Stock Yards opened on Christmas Day, 1865.
Chanute went on to build the first bridge across the Missouri River, at Kansas City.
In his sixties, he became a pioneer of flight.
In 1896, he tested gliders on the sand dunes of Indiana, and he later advised and encouraged the Wright brothers.
The yards grew into a city of their own, with hotels, a bank, and a daily newspaper for the livestock trade.
Every morning, buyers rode through the alleys on horseback, sizing up the animals in the pens and bidding for them.
Fire was a constant danger.
On May nineteenth, 1934, during a drought and a fierce heat wave, a fire broke out in the hay of a cattle pen, perhaps from a cigarette tossed by a passing driver.

It swept across several blocks, destroying pens, buildings, and the great show pavilion, and it did about eight million dollars in damage, the most destructive fire in the city's history after the fire of 1871.
The company rebuilt quickly.
By the end of that year, a new arena, the International Amphitheatre, stood where the pavilion had burned.
In the 1870s, beef traveled east on the hoof.
Cattle were crowded into stock cars in Chicago and shipped alive to slaughterhouses in the East.
It was cruel and wasteful.
Animals lost weight on the way, some died, and the railroads charged as much to haul the parts of a steer nobody would eat as the parts that became steak.
Gustavus Swift saw a better way.
He was a Yankee from Cape Cod, born in 1839, who had gone to work for a butcher as a boy, and he came to Chicago in 1875 as a cattle buyer.
His idea was to slaughter the cattle here and ship only the dressed meat, kept cold so that it would arrive fresh.
He's said to have started by shipping meat in winter, in ordinary boxcars with the doors left open.
In 1878, he hired an engineer named Andrew Chase to design a true refrigerator car.
Chase's car was insulated and ventilated, with ice in a compartment near the roof, so that cold air sank naturally over the meat.
The big railroads wanted nothing to do with it.
They had invested heavily in stock cars, pens, and feedlots for live cattle, and they feared losing that business.
So Swift paid for the cars himself, and he found one line willing to haul them, the Grand Trunk, a Canadian railroad that made little money from live cattle.
His cars rolled east through Michigan and Canada.
He contracted for ice cut in Wisconsin and built icing stations along the way to refill the cars.
Next, he had to win over the customers.
Eastern butchers, whose living depended on slaughtering animals locally, fought the Chicago meat, and many shoppers distrusted beef killed a thousand miles away.
Swift teamed up with local dealers, opened his own branch houses, and undersold the competition.
It worked.
Within a few years, the other big packers had refrigerator cars of their own, and Chicago beef was on tables across the country.
When Swift died in 1903, his company was one of the largest businesses in America, and the refrigerator car was changing the way the whole country ate.
Philip Danforth Armour was born in 1832, on a farm in Stockbridge, in upstate New York.
At nineteen, he left home for the California gold rush.
He didn't strike it rich in the diggings.

Instead, he started a business hiring miners who'd run out of luck to build sluices, the wooden channels that carried water through the gold fields, and by the age of twenty-four, he had saved about eight thousand dollars, a small fortune at the time.
He settled in Milwaukee, went into the grain trade, and then into pork packing, as a partner of John Plankinton.
Near the end of the Civil War, he made the bet that made his name.
The army's demand had driven pork prices sky high, and Armour was convinced they would collapse once the Union won.
So he sold pork short, promising to deliver it months later at the high wartime price.
When the war ended and prices fell, as he'd predicted, he made a fortune, while many of his competitors in Cincinnati were ruined.
In 1875, he moved to Chicago, where the family firm already had a packing plant, and he built Armour and Company into one of the biggest businesses in the world.
He added beef and lamb to pork, built his own refrigerator cars, and found a use for nearly everything his plants produced.
He was famous for his hours.
He's said to have been at his desk by seven in the morning, and he expected his managers to keep up.
He was hard on rivals, and he fought hard against unions.
The park beside the White Sox ballpark, Armour Square, was named in his honor in 1904.
Armour died of pneumonia at his Chicago home in January 1901.
His son, J. Ogden Armour, expanded the company further, but he's said to have lost most of the family fortune in the 1920s.
Today, the Armour name lives on mostly as a brand of canned meats on supermarket shelves.
Finish by walking southeast to 45th Street and Lowe Avenue, in the neighborhood called Canaryville.
The name may have come from the flocks of sparrows that fed on the grain spilled around the stockyards, or from the rowdy young men of the neighborhood, who were called canaries.
No one knows for sure.
The big brick church with the tall, square tower is Saint Gabriel Church, built in 1887 and 1888, and designed by John Wellborn Root, of Burnham and Root.
Root designed few churches, and this is a fine one, with massive brick walls and Romanesque arches, and a tower that rises in simple stages, with almost no ornament.
It's the same spirit you saw in his Monadnock Building downtown.
The church was built for an Irish parish led by Father Maurice Dorney, who was one of the most powerful men in the stockyards district.
He was known as the King of the Yards.
He helped settle strikes between workers and packers, found jobs for his parishioners, and fought the saloons.
It's said that he persuaded the packers to donate money for the church, and that the bricks were laid by men from the yards.

Canaryville and Back of the Yards were tough, working-class neighborhoods, and in 1939, a young organizer named Saul Alinsky worked with churches, unions, and local groups here to create the Back of the Yards Neighborhood Council.
It became a model for community organizing across the country, and its methods later influenced, among many others, a young organizer named Barack Obama.
This is the end of the Bridgeport and Stockyards tour.
Saul Alinsky was born in Chicago in 1909, to Russian Jewish immigrant parents.
He studied at the University of Chicago, and as a graduate student in criminology, he got to know members of the Capone gang, an unusual education for a future organizer.
He went on to work with young offenders and in a state prison.
In the late 1930s, his work brought him here, and he came to believe that what the neighborhood needed most was power.
His partners were a local man, Joseph Meegan, who ran Davis Square Park, and Bernard Sheil, an auxiliary bishop of Chicago who had founded the Catholic Youth Organization.
The neighborhood was divided by old hatreds.
Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Irish, Mexican, and other families had their own parishes, and many barely spoke to one another.
Alinsky's idea was a council made not of individuals but of organizations, like parishes, unions, clubs, and businesses.
On July fourteenth, 1939, about three hundred and fifty people from seventy-six groups came to the first meeting of the new Back of the Yards Neighborhood Council.

Two days later, the packinghouse workers' union held a mass rally at the Chicago Coliseum, and Bishop Sheil spoke from the same platform as John L. Lewis, the fiery leader of the new industrial unions.
For Catholic workers, the sight of a bishop beside the union's leader sent a powerful message.
Alinsky later wrote a biography of Lewis.
Alinsky took the council's methods across the country.
In 1940, with money from the department store heir Marshall Field the Third, he founded the Industrial Areas Foundation to train organizers.
His books, Reveille for Radicals, in 1946, and Rules for Radicals, in 1971, became handbooks for activists.
One of his rules was that ridicule is the most potent weapon there is.
He died in 1972, in Carmel, California.
People on the left and the right still argue about his ideas, which may be the truest measure of his influence.
Around 1900, the neighborhoods around the stockyards were among the most crowded in America, and they had almost no open space.
Children played in the streets, in the alleys, and beside the railroad tracks.
Chicago's great parks, like Washington Park and Jackson Park, were miles away, and few working families had the time or the carfare to get there.
Reformers, including Jane Addams of Hull House, had long argued for playgrounds in the poorest neighborhoods.
In 1903, the South Park Commission set out to build a whole system of small parks.
It hired the Olmsted Brothers, the firm run by the sons of Frederick Law Olmsted, to design the grounds, and Daniel Burnham's firm to design the buildings.
In 1905, ten of the new parks opened on the South Side.
Among them were Davis Square, a mile or so west of here, Sherman Park, named for John B. Sherman, the longtime chief of the stockyards, and Armour Square, beside the White Sox ballpark.
They had playgrounds, ball fields, and swimming pools, and something no American park had had before, a field house.
Inside were gymnasiums, branch libraries, meeting halls, lunchrooms, and locker rooms with showers, a luxury at a time when many homes nearby had no bathtub.
They were the first park field houses in the country.
Theodore Roosevelt called the new parks the most notable civic achievement in any American city, and cities across the country copied them.
Davis Square was named for Nathan Smith Davis, a Chicago doctor who helped found the American Medical Association, and it became the heart of Back of the Yards.
In the 1930s, its director, Joseph Meegan, was one of the founders of the neighborhood council that made this corner of Chicago famous among organizers.
Many of the original field houses still stand, and they're still busy.
They set the pattern for the park buildings that anchor neighborhoods all over Chicago today.
At 42nd and Halsted, a few blocks northwest of here, stood a building that once fed the whole livestock world, the Stock Yard Inn.
It went up in 1912, right after fire destroyed the hotel that had stood on the site, and it was built to look like an old English inn, with half-timbered walls and steep gables.
The inn had rooms for the cattlemen, buyers, and salesmen who came to the yards, and several dining rooms.
The most famous was the Sirloin Room.

There, as diners remembered it, you walked up to a case of raw steaks, chose the one you wanted, and watched as it was branded with a red-hot iron, so you'd know the steak on your plate was the one you picked.
The beef came from the yards across the street, and for decades a steak dinner here was part of any business trip to the stockyards.
The building was also home to the Saddle and Sirloin Club, the private club of the livestock business, whose name is said to come from the sirloin steaks and saddles of lamb its members dined on.
Starting in 1903, the club collected oil portraits of the leading figures of the livestock world, breeders, packers, and stockmen.

Most of the early portraits were lost in the great stockyards fire of 1934, but the club kept collecting, and after the yards closed, the collection moved to Louisville, Kentucky, home of a big national livestock show.
As the packers left Chicago, so did the inn's customers.
The Stock Yard Inn closed in 1976 and was torn down the next year.
But Chicago's reputation for steak outlived it.
The city's great steakhouses, with their aged beef and dark wood, still trade on the idea that Chicago is the place to eat a steak, an idea that grew up right here, beside the pens.
This tour explores Bronzeville, on the South Side, a few miles south of the Loop.
In the first half of the twentieth century, it was one of the most important Black communities in America, a city within a city that newspapers and sociologists called the Black Metropolis.
Its story is the story of the Great Migration.
Between the First World War and 1970, about six million Black Southerners moved north and west, fleeing segregation, lynching, and poverty, and looking for jobs in the industrial cities.
Chicago was one of the main destinations.

The Illinois Central Railroad ran straight up from Mississippi and Louisiana to Chicago, and the Chicago Defender, a Black newspaper smuggled into the South by Pullman porters, urged readers to come north.
Chicago's Black population grew from about forty-four thousand in 1910 to more than two hundred thousand by 1930.
But the newcomers faced discrimination in Chicago too.

White property owners used restrictive covenants, real estate practices, and violence to confine Black residents to a narrow strip on the South Side, called the Black Belt, running along State Street.
In July 1919, tensions exploded in a race riot, set off when a Black teenager, Eugene Williams, drowned after being stoned by white men at a segregated beach.
Thirty-eight people died.
Confined to a small area, Black Chicagoans built their own world.
There were Black-owned banks, insurance companies, newspapers, cosmetics makers, churches, theaters, nightclubs, and hospitals.
Jazz and blues flourished here.

Writers, artists, and intellectuals made it a center of what's sometimes called the Chicago Black Renaissance, including the novelist Richard Wright, the poet Gwendolyn Brooks, and the dancer and choreographer Katherine Dunham.
The name Bronzeville was coined in the 1930s by an editor at the Chicago Bee newspaper, who held a contest to elect a Mayor of Bronzeville.
After the Second World War, much of the neighborhood was cleared for public housing and institutions, and it declined, but in recent decades it's been rediscovered and restored.
We'll start at the Illinois Institute of Technology, walk east and south through the old heart of the community, past the home of Ida B. Wells, and end at the tomb of Stephen Douglas, near the lake.
You're on the campus of the Illinois Institute of Technology, near State Street and 34th Street.
In front of you, set back on a lawn, is a long, low glass building with a steel frame.
This is S. R. Crown Hall, completed in 1956, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and home to the university's architecture school.
Mies designed the whole campus, starting in the 1940s, as a grid of simple steel, glass, and brick buildings.
Crown Hall is his masterpiece.
Look at the roof.
It's hung from four enormous steel plate girders that sit on top of the building, so the inside can be one vast, open room, with no columns at all.
Mies called it universal space, a room that could be used for anything.
Now consider what stood here before.
On this very site stood the Mecca Flats, a huge apartment building built in 1892 with interior courtyards and skylit atriums.
By the 1910s, it had become home to Black families, and it was famous across the South Side, celebrated in a song called the Mecca Flat Blues.
Over the years, it became badly overcrowded, and the institute, which owned it, demolished it in 1952 to expand the campus, despite protests from the tenants.
The poet Gwendolyn Brooks later wrote a long poem about it, called In the Mecca.
Look east to the station at State Street, where the elevated Green Line passes through a stainless steel tube over a student center designed by the Dutch architect Rem Koolhaas, opened in 2003.
The university itself has a storied Chicago origin.

In 1890, a young minister named Frank Gunsaulus preached a sermon on what he would do if he had a million dollars: build a school where young people of any background could learn practical skills for the new industrial age.
In the congregation was Philip Armour, the meatpacker, who reportedly came up to him afterward and offered to fund it.

The Armour Institute opened in 1893 and later merged with another school to become the Illinois Institute of Technology, which hired Mies van der Rohe in 1938 to lead its architecture program and design its new campus.

When Mies took over the architecture school here in 1938, the Armour Institute was a cluster of old buildings in a crowded, run-down part of the South Side, and its leaders wanted to rebuild on a far larger site, to a plan by their new director.
By 1941 Mies had laid out the entire campus on one grid.
Everything follows a single measure: a module twenty-four feet square and twelve feet high.

The spacing of the columns, the heights of the walls, and the placement of the buildings and the walks between them are all multiples of it, so that buildings put up decades apart would still line up with one another.
Mies kept the materials just as strict: a frame of steel painted black, panels of buff brick, and big sheets of glass.
Look at a corner of one of the older brick buildings nearby.
Fire codes required the steel columns to be wrapped in concrete, which hid the very frame Mies wanted you to see.
So he wrapped the concrete in steel plate and fastened steel beams to the outside, to show what was holding the building up.
The steel you see does no structural work at all.
It's there to tell the truth about the steel inside, a kind of honest ornament, and architects still argue about whether that's a contradiction.
The smallest building on the campus may be the most surprising.
A short walk north is the Carr Memorial Chapel, finished in 1952, the only religious building Mies ever designed.
It's a plain brick box with a glass front, and generations of students have called it the God Box.
Crown Hall was the climax.

Its main floor is a single room about a hundred and twenty feet wide and two hundred and twenty feet long, raised a few feet above the lawn, with workshops and classrooms tucked into a half-sunken level below.
Mies reportedly called it the clearest structure he had ever built.
In 2001 it was named a National Historic Landmark.

The Mecca was designed by the architects Willoughby Edbrooke and Franklin Burnham, no relation to the famous Daniel, and it was meant at first as a hotel for the crowds coming to the world's fair of 1893.
After the fair, it became an apartment house for prosperous white families, with nearly a hundred apartments.

Their doors opened onto long balconies with ornate iron railings, stacked one above another around the inside of the building, so that the whole place faced inward, like a village built around its own indoor street.
The Depression hit it hard.
Apartments were cut up, repairs stopped, and by the 1940s well over a thousand people were crowded into the building.
Around 1940, the institute bought it, planning to tear it down for the new campus.
The tenants fought back.
They organized, went to court, and pressed the politicians, and for more than a decade they held off the wreckers.
In December 1950, Harper's Magazine published a long article about the building by the journalist John Bartlow Martin, under the title The Strangest Place in Chicago.
Martin walked the balconies and talked with the people who lived there.
He found a crumbling, dangerously overcrowded building that was also a real community, full of working people, many of them from the South, who didn't want to lose their homes.

A Life magazine photographer, Wallace Kirkland, took pictures there too, and his photographs of tenants leaning on the iron railings, looking down into the courts, are still the best-known images of the building.
Martin went on to write speeches for the presidential candidate Adlai Stevenson and to serve as ambassador to the Dominican Republic.
None of it saved the Mecca.
The tenants were moved out, and the wreckers finally came.

On the ground where all those families had lived, Mies built his great glass room, a building that opens itself to the street on every side, where once there had been a building that turned its whole life inward.
Gwendolyn Brooks was born in Topeka, Kansas, in 1917, and her family brought her to Chicago when she was a baby.
She grew up in a small house on the South Side, filling notebooks with poems.
By the family's account, her mother predicted she would be a lady Paul Laurence Dunbar, a woman to rival the celebrated Black poet.
She published her first poem in a children's magazine at thirteen, and as a teenager she sent verses to the Defender, which printed dozens of them.
She knew the Mecca from the inside.

By her own account, after college she worked there for a few months as the assistant to a self-styled spiritual adviser who sold charms and potions, and part of her job was delivering them to his customers in the building.
Decades later, that memory became her long poem In the Mecca, published in 1968.
It follows a mother searching the building for her missing little girl, meeting the neighbors one by one along the way.
It was a finalist for the National Book Award.

In between came her first book, A Street in Bronzeville, in 1945, and in 1960 the poem most people know, We Real Cool, about seven pool players at a place called the Golden Shovel, with lines that end, again and again, on the word we.
Then, in 1967, she went to a writers' conference at Fisk University in Nashville and met a new generation of young Black poets, who wanted to write for Black readers first.
By her own account, she came home transformed.

She began leading poetry workshops for young people in Chicago, including members of a South Side gang called the Blackstone Rangers, and she moved her work from a big New York publisher to small Black presses.
In 1968, she succeeded Carl Sandburg as poet laureate of Illinois, and she held the title until her death in 2000.
In 1985, she became the first Black woman appointed poetry consultant to the Library of Congress, the post now called poet laureate of the United States.
Walk east on 33rd Street to Indiana Avenue.
On the corner stands what remains of Pilgrim Baptist Church, a stone building with a massive, solid base.
It was built in 1890 and 1891 as a synagogue for Kehilath Anshe Ma'ariv, one of Chicago's oldest Jewish congregations, and it was designed by Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan.
Adler's father had been the congregation's rabbi.
The building was known for its superb acoustics and for Sullivan's ornament.
As the Jewish community moved south and the neighborhood became Black, the building was sold in 1922 to Pilgrim Baptist Church.
It was here that gospel music was born.
In the 1930s, the church's music director was Thomas A. Dorsey, a former blues pianist who had played under the name Georgia Tom.
After the death of his wife and newborn son, he wrote Take My Hand, Precious Lord, one of the most famous gospel songs ever written.
Dorsey fused the rhythms of blues and jazz with religious lyrics, and his music, at first controversial in more traditional churches, swept the country.
Mahalia Jackson, who came to Chicago from New Orleans as a teenager, sang here and worked with Dorsey.
She became the greatest gospel singer of her time.
In January 2006, a fire destroyed the church's roof and interior.
Only the stone walls survive.
There have been plans to build a museum of gospel music on the site.

Thomas Dorsey was born in Georgia in 1899, the son of a preacher and a mother who played the church organ, and he learned both kinds of music early, the hymns of Sunday morning and the blues of Saturday night.
Around the end of the First World War, he came north to Chicago, where he played piano at rent parties and in speakeasies and studied composing and arranging.
In the mid-1920s, he led the band behind Ma Rainey, the Mother of the Blues, on her tours.
Then, in 1928, he teamed up with the guitarist Tampa Red, and as Tampa Red and Georgia Tom they recorded a sly, bawdy blues called It's Tight Like That, which became a huge hit.
But Dorsey was torn between the clubs and the church, and he suffered at least one long breakdown.
He began writing religious songs with the bounce and the blue notes of the music he played in the clubs.
Many ministers and church musicians were horrified at first, and some kept his songs out of their churches.
In 1931, at Ebenezer Baptist Church, farther south in Bronzeville, he and the singer Theodore Frye organized what's often called the first gospel chorus.
Soon afterward, with the singer Sallie Martin, he helped found the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses, which carried the new music to churches across the country.
He also set up his own company to publish and sell his sheet music, one of the first of its kind, and for a while, it's said, people called any gospel song a Dorsey.
He wrote hundreds of songs.
One of them, Peace in the Valley, was later sung by Elvis Presley on national television.
But none was loved like Precious Lord.
On the evening of April fourth, 1968, in Memphis, Martin Luther King Junior leaned over a motel balcony and asked the musician Ben Branch to play it at a rally that night, and to play it real pretty.
Moments later, King was shot.
Dorsey died in 1993, at ninety-three.
Mahalia Jackson grew up in New Orleans, singing in a Baptist church and soaking up the records of the blues singer Bessie Smith.
In 1927, at sixteen, she came to Chicago, where she worked as a laundress and a maid and sang with a group called the Johnson Singers and in the choir at Greater Salem Baptist Church.
Later, to support herself, she trained as a beautician and ran a beauty shop and a flower shop.
She turned down offers to sing the blues in nightclubs.
Blues are the songs of despair, she liked to say, but gospel songs are the songs of hope.
In 1947, she recorded Move On Up a Little Higher, a song by the Reverend William Herbert Brewster, for a small label called Apollo.
It sold in the millions, perhaps more than any gospel record before it.

On October fourth, 1950, she sang at Carnegie Hall in New York, in one of the first gospel concerts ever held there, and in the 1950s she signed with Columbia Records and became a star of radio and television.
She was a friend and supporter of Martin Luther King Junior from the days of the Montgomery bus boycott.
At the March on Washington, in August 1963, she sang an old spiritual, I Been 'Buked and I Been Scorned, shortly before King spoke.
By several accounts, as he worked through his prepared text, she called out to him: Tell them about the dream, Martin.
He set his notes aside, and the speech that followed is the one the world remembers.
When King was killed in 1968, she sang Precious Lord at his funeral in Atlanta.
She died in 1972, and by most accounts tens of thousands of people filed past her coffin in Chicago.
You heard that this building began as a synagogue.
It wasn't the only one.

In the late nineteenth century, the avenues south of downtown, from Michigan and Indiana over to Grand Boulevard, now King Drive, were home to many of Chicago's prosperous Jewish families, most of them from Germany, while poorer Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe crowded the West Side.
Their congregations built some of the city's finest temples.
Then, around the time of the First World War, the Black Belt pushed south and east, and the Jewish families moved on, toward Hyde Park, Kenwood, and South Shore.
Their congregations followed them and sold the old temples, one by one, to Black churches, many of them founded by migrants from the South.
About a mile and a half south of here, at 45th Street and Vincennes Avenue, stands Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church.
It was built in 1899 as Isaiah Temple, one of the last buildings by Dankmar Adler, who had designed this one with Louis Sullivan.
Ebenezer bought it in 1921, and the gospel chorus it started in 1931 was among the first anywhere.
It's now on the National Register.
A little farther south, at 46th Street and King Drive, is the former Sinai Temple, built in 1912 for Chicago's first Reform congregation and designed by Alfred Alschuler.
Sinai stayed until 1944.
The building then housed a Catholic high school, Corpus Christi, and in the early 1960s it became Mount Pisgah Missionary Baptist Church.
In 2020, the city made it a landmark.
These buildings suited their new owners well.
Reform temples of that era were laid out much like big Protestant churches inside, with pews facing a raised platform, a pipe organ, and a choir loft.
A Baptist congregation could move in and start singing.
And the sound that Adler designed for organ and choir served gospel just as well.
Look at the old stone walls in front of you.
They were raised by one community of newcomers, and filled with the music of another.
Walk west and south to State Street near 36th Street.
In the 1910s and 1920s, the stretch of State Street between roughly 26th and 39th Streets was called the Stroll.
It was the main street of Black Chicago, crowded day and night with people going to theaters, cabarets, dance halls, and saloons.
Jazz musicians from New Orleans came here, including King Oliver, Jelly Roll Morton, and a young Louis Armstrong.
On the east side of State Street, at number 3619, is the Overton Hygienic Building, completed in the early 1920s.
It was built by Anthony Overton, a businessman who made a fortune with a line of cosmetics for Black women, including a face powder called High-Brown.
The building also housed the Douglass National Bank, one of the first nationally chartered banks owned by Black Americans, and other Black-owned businesses.
Next door, at 3647 South State, is the Chicago Bee Building, an Art Deco gem with green and cream terra cotta, completed around 1931.
It housed the Chicago Bee, a newspaper Overton founded.
Today, it's a branch of the Chicago Public Library.
Overton's businesses were hit hard by the Depression, and his bank failed in 1932.
But his buildings show what Black entrepreneurs built in Bronzeville in a time when they were shut out of most of the economy.

Louis Armstrong arrived in Chicago by train from New Orleans in 1922, at twenty-one, to play second cornet in King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band at a dance hall called Lincoln Gardens, on 31st Street, a short distance northeast of here.
The records they made in 1923 are among the first great jazz recordings.

Later, the center of nightlife moved south, to 47th Street, where the Regal Theater, a grand movie palace and stage, presented Duke Ellington, Nat King Cole, Ella Fitzgerald, and later James Brown and the Jackson Five.
A few blocks south, at 39th Street, is Wendell Phillips High School, which in the 1920s became the first predominantly Black high school in Chicago.
Its students included the singer and pianist Nat King Cole, the soul singer Sam Cooke, and the jazz singer Dinah Washington.
And in the 1920s, a group of its former basketball players formed a team that played at the Savoy Ballroom on 47th Street.
They became the Harlem Globetrotters.
They had never been to Harlem; the name was chosen to tell audiences that the players were Black.
A block north of here, at the corner of 35th and State, stood the bank of Jesse Binga, for a time the most celebrated Black businessman in Chicago.
Binga was born in Detroit in 1865, and after years of odd jobs out West, he reached Chicago in the early 1890s with very little money.
He started out peddling fruit and then went into real estate.
His method made him rich.
He leased run-down buildings on the edge of the Black Belt, fixed them up, and rented them to Black families who couldn't find housing anywhere else.
In 1908, he opened a private bank in a storefront on State Street.
He married Eudora Johnson, an heiress to a South Side gambling fortune, and in 1921 his bank won a state charter as the Binga State Bank.
In 1929, he opened the Binga Arcade, a five-story office building at 35th and State.
Not everyone welcomed his success.
He bought a house on what is now King Drive, at 59th Street, in a white neighborhood, and in 1919 and 1920 it was bombed again and again, at least five times.
He refused to move.
The end came with the Depression.
In the summer of 1930, state examiners closed the Binga State Bank, and thousands of depositors lost their savings.
It was one of the first in a wave of failures that wiped out most of Bronzeville's banks, including, two years later, the Overton bank you heard about.
Binga was convicted of embezzlement and sentenced to ten years in prison.
He was released after about five.
He spent his last years working as a handyman and usher at Saint Anselm, a Catholic church on the South Side, and he died in 1950.
His bank had been built on the savings of people shut out of white banks, and it fell when the whole economy collapsed around them.
In 1915, a young woman named Bessie Coleman came up from Texas to join her brothers in Chicago.
She was one of thirteen children in a family that picked cotton, and she had managed one term of college in Oklahoma before the money ran out.
In Chicago, she went to beauty school and found work as a manicurist in a South Side barbershop.
Her brothers came home from the First World War full of stories about France, and one of them teased her that French women could fly airplanes and she never would.
She decided she would.
No flight school in America would take a Black woman, so Robert Abbott, the publisher of the Defender, advised her to go to France, and Abbott and the banker Jesse Binga helped pay for her training.
She studied French at night, sailed for France in November 1920, and learned to fly in a fragile biplane at a flying school on the French coast.
On June fifteenth, 1921, she earned her license from the international aviation federation, the first Black woman to earn a pilot's license.
Back in America, she became a stunt flier, thrilling crowds at air shows with loops and figure eights, and the press called her Queen Bess.
She dreamed of opening a flying school for Black students, and she is said to have refused to perform where Black spectators had to come in through a separate gate.
On April thirtieth, 1926, in Jacksonville, Florida, she was rehearsing for an air show, with her mechanic at the controls, when the plane went into a dive and then a spin.
She wasn't wearing a seat belt, it's said, because she had been leaning out to study the field below, and she fell to her death.
She was thirty-four.
The mechanic died in the crash, and investigators reportedly found that a loose wrench had jammed the controls.
Some ten thousand people came to her funeral in Chicago, and she's buried at Lincoln Cemetery, just southwest of the city.
Every year since 1931, Black pilots have flown over her grave in salute.
Black Southerners who came to Chicago gained something they had been denied at home: the right to vote.
And because segregation packed them into a few wards on the South Side, their votes added up to real power.
The first to wield it was Oscar De Priest, a house painter turned real estate man, born in Alabama.
In 1915, voters in the Second Ward, which took in much of the Black Belt, made him the first Black member of the Chicago City Council.
Two years later, he was indicted, accused of taking money to protect gambling houses.
The famous lawyer Clarence Darrow won his acquittal, but under pressure from his own Republican Party, De Priest had already given up his seat.
His great ally was the Republican mayor, Big Bill Thompson, who won the Black wards by enormous margins and rewarded them with jobs.
In 1928, when the district's longtime congressman, Martin Madden, died, Thompson's organization picked De Priest to take his place on the ballot.
He won, becoming the first Black member of Congress in twenty-eight years, and the first ever elected from a Northern state.
When the First Lady, Lou Hoover, invited his wife, Jessie, to a White House tea in 1929, Southern newspapers and politicians were outraged.
Then the Depression changed everything.
Black voters had been loyal to the party of Lincoln since emancipation, but the New Deal drew them to the Democrats.
In 1934, a Democrat named Arthur Mitchell beat De Priest by about three thousand votes and became the first Black Democrat ever elected to Congress.
The man who built the Democrats' Black organization here was William Dawson, a lawyer from Georgia and a veteran of the First World War.
He started out as a Republican alderman, switched parties in 1939, and in 1942 won a seat in Congress, which he held until his death in 1970.
In 1949, he became the first Black chairman of a standing committee of the House.
To his critics, Dawson was a boss who put the party ahead of civil rights.
To his admirers, he made sure Black Chicago got its share of the jobs and favors.
Walk east on 35th Street to Calumet Avenue.
On the north side of the street, at 315 East 35th Street, stood the Sunset Café, one of the most famous jazz clubs of the 1920s.
The Sunset was a black and tan club, a place where Black and white audiences mixed, which was unusual and sometimes illegal at the time.
Louis Armstrong played here in the 1920s, with Carroll Dickerson's orchestra and the pianist Earl Hines.
The club was managed by Joe Glaser, who became Armstrong's manager for the rest of his career.
Young white musicians, like Benny Goodman, Gene Krupa, and Bix Beiderbecke, came to listen and learn.
Chicago in the 1920s was the jazz capital of the world.

Musicians had come up from New Orleans, many on the Illinois Central, and the music changed here, from collective improvisation to the age of great soloists, and Armstrong's recordings with his Hot Five and Hot Seven bands, made in Chicago, defined it.
The building that housed the Sunset survives, and it later became a hardware store.
Those who have been inside say that some of the original murals from the club are still on the walls behind the store's shelves.
When Louis Armstrong came up from New Orleans in 1922 to join King Oliver's band, the piano player was a young woman from Memphis named Lillian Hardin.

She had studied music at Fisk University, moved to Chicago with her mother around the end of the First World War, and found a job demonstrating sheet music in a music store on State Street, playing whatever song a customer wanted to hear.
From there she moved into the bands, where she was billed as Hot Miss Lil.
By her own account, she wasn't impressed at first by the young man from New Orleans, with his country clothes and his old-fashioned bangs.
But she soon heard what he could do.
They married on February fifth, 1924, and she set about changing his career.
As she told it later, she warned him that as long as he played second cornet to Oliver, he would never be a star.
That fall, he left Oliver's band and went to New York to play with Fletcher Henderson's orchestra.
When he came back to Chicago at the end of 1925, she had him booked with her own band at the Dreamland Café, and, as the story goes, she had the club bill him as the world's greatest trumpet player.
She also played piano on his Hot Five records, and she wrote or co-wrote several of the tunes they recorded.
The marriage didn't last.
They separated in the early 1930s and divorced in 1938, but she kept his name, and they stayed on friendly terms.
She went on working as a pianist, bandleader, and songwriter for the rest of her life.
Louis Armstrong died in July 1971.
A few weeks later, on August twenty-seventh, Lil was playing at a memorial concert for him in Chicago when she collapsed at the piano, in the middle of the Saint Louis Blues.
She died soon afterward.
The woman who had pushed Louis Armstrong toward stardom went out playing in his honor.
On February twenty-sixth, 1926, Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five went into a recording studio in Chicago to cut a novelty song called Heebie Jeebies.
Partway through, Armstrong stopped singing the words and broke into a stream of nonsense syllables, bouncing and swinging like a horn solo.
It became one of the most famous scat vocals ever put on a record.
Armstrong told the story of how it happened for years afterward.
He had the lyrics on a sheet of paper, he said, and in the middle of the take, he dropped it.
There was no time to stop and start over, so he kept going, making up sounds to fill the space until he could pick up the words again.
In his telling, the record company liked what it heard and released the take just as it was.
Many jazz historians doubt it.
The scat passage fits a little too neatly into the arrangement, and singers had been scatting on records since the days of ragtime.
But whatever happened in that studio, the record was a national hit.
According to musicians who were young in Chicago at the time, friends took to greeting each other in Armstrong's nonsense syllables.
The title was brand new slang.
The cartoonist Billy DeBeck had coined the phrase heebie-jeebies in his comic strip Barney Google in 1923, for a bad case of the jitters, and within a few years the whole country was using it.
Armstrong didn't invent scat, but he made it famous, and he made it an art.
After him came Cab Calloway's hi-de-ho, Ella Fitzgerald's dazzling flights of invention, and generations of singers who used their voices like instruments.
And in the story Armstrong chose to tell, it all began with a sheet of paper fluttering to the floor of a Chicago studio.
The pianist who played beside Armstrong here at the Sunset went on to rule the South Side's nightlife for a decade.
Earl Hines grew up near Pittsburgh and came to Chicago in the mid-1920s.
He played with a bright, hard attack, punching out melodies in octaves with his right hand so that they cut through a big band like a trumpet.
People called it trumpet-style piano.
In December 1928, he opened at a new club called the Grand Terrace, at 39th Street and what is now King Drive, about half a mile south of here, leading his own big band.
He stayed for about twelve years.
The club belonged, in part, to the mob.
Al Capone's organization reportedly held a quarter share.
What made the Grand Terrace famous was radio.
Its late-night shows went out live over a national network, and by the mid-1930s Hines's band was said to be on the air more than any other band in the country.
A radio announcer gave Hines his nickname, as the story goes, when he introduced him one night as Fatha Hines, and it stuck.
Later on, the club moved here, into the Sunset's old space on 35th Street.
Hines's bands were also a school.

The singer Billy Eckstine joined him in the late 1930s, and in the early 1940s his band included the young Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, and Sarah Vaughan, the musicians who would soon invent bebop.
Because the musicians' union had banned recording in those years, almost none of that band's music was ever recorded, and it's remembered as one of the great lost bands of jazz.
Hines kept playing into his seventies, and he died in 1983.
Walk east on 35th Street to Martin Luther King Drive.

In the middle of the boulevard stands the Victory Monument, unveiled in 1928, to honor the soldiers of the Eighth Illinois Infantry, a Black National Guard regiment that fought in France in the First World War as the 370th Infantry.
Look at the bronze panels showing a soldier, a mother, and a figure of Columbia.
The statue of a soldier on top was added in 1936.
Each August, a few blocks south on King Drive, the Bud Billiken Parade, one of the largest African American parades in the country, celebrates the start of the school year.
On the northeast corner of the intersection, look at the building at 3501 South King Drive.
This was the headquarters of the Supreme Liberty Life Insurance Company, one of the largest Black-owned businesses in the North.
In the 1930s, a young man named John H. Johnson worked as an office boy here.
In 1942, using the company's mailing list and a five-hundred-dollar loan secured by his mother's furniture, he launched a magazine called Negro Digest.
In 1945, he started Ebony, which became the most widely read Black magazine in the world, and later Jet.
Johnson Publishing became one of the most important Black businesses in America, and it was based in Chicago.
A few blocks north, at 3435 South Indiana Avenue, was the longtime headquarters of the Chicago Defender.
Founded in 1905 by Robert S. Abbott, it campaigned against lynching and segregation and urged Southern Black families to come north, playing a major role in the Great Migration.
In 1956, it became a daily paper.
The regiment this monument honors is older than the First World War.

It grew out of a Black militia battalion of the 1890s, and when war with Spain broke out in 1898, it became the Eighth Illinois Volunteer Infantry, with Black officers from its commander, Colonel John R. Marshall, on down, at a time when nearly all Black troops were led by white officers.
It was sent to Cuba that summer, to relieve white troops who had been struck down by tropical fevers, and it stayed into the next year as part of the occupying force.
Back home, the regiment got something no Black unit in the country had: an armory built for it.
The Eighth Regiment Armory went up in 1914 and 1915, a few blocks west of here, at 35th Street and Giles Avenue.
It was the first armory in the United States built for a Black regiment.
In 1917, the Eighth went to war again, under Colonel Franklin Denison, a Chicago lawyer.

In France, it became the 370th Infantry, and like the other Black regiments of its division, it was lent to the French army, largely because American commanders didn't want Black combat troops fighting beside white ones.
The men fought in French helmets, with French rifles.
In July 1918, Denison was relieved of command, officially because of illness, and a white colonel took his place.
That fall, the regiment fought its way across northern France as the German army fell back, and its men won many French and American medals for bravery.
According to regimental lore, the Germans called them the Black Devils.
The street where the armory stands is named for one of the regiment's dead.
In 1922, the city renamed Forest Avenue for Lieutenant George Giles, the regiment's highest-ranking officer killed in the war.
Since 1999, the old armory has housed a public high school, the Chicago Military Academy.
You heard that each August the Bud Billiken Parade comes down King Drive.
The name behind it began as a fad and a newspaper gimmick.
In 1908, a Kansas City art teacher named Florence Pretz patented a little figure she called the Billiken, a grinning, pointy-headed elf with a round belly, sitting with its feet stuck out in front.
She billed it as the god of things as they ought to be.
For a few years, Billikens were everywhere, as dolls, charms, banks, and postcards.
The fad faded, but the sports teams at Saint Louis University are still called the Billikens.
In 1923, the Chicago Defender started a page for children, and it needed a mascot.
The paper's founder, Robert Abbott, and his editor Lucius Harper are usually credited with the idea of Bud Billiken.
By one account, Abbott had seen a Billiken figure in a Chinese restaurant, and the paper presented the Billiken as a Chinese guardian of children, though it was really an American invention.
Bud Billiken became the make-believe editor of the children's page, and young readers all over the country joined Bud Billiken clubs.
For Black children far from Chicago, the page was a window onto a bigger world, and a place to see their own names in print.
The parade began in 1929, as a thank-you to the newsboys who sold the Defender on street corners.
It grew into one of the biggest days of the year on the South Side, with marching bands, drill teams, floats, and dancers.
Politicians of every kind have marched in it, because there are few better places in Chicago to be seen.
These days it heads south on King Drive toward Washington Park, where the day ends with family picnics on the grass.
More than a century after the fad, the little god of things as they ought to be still has his day on the South Side.
In August 1955, a fourteen-year-old Chicago boy named Emmett Till went to visit relatives in the Mississippi Delta.
In a country store in the small town of Money, he was accused of whistling at or flirting with the white woman behind the counter.
A few nights later, her husband and his half-brother came for him at his great-uncle's house.
They beat him, shot him, and threw his body into the Tallahatchie River, weighted down with a heavy metal fan from a cotton gin.
When the body was sent home to Chicago, his mother, Mamie Till Bradley, made a decision that changed American history.
She insisted on an open casket.
Let the world see what I've seen, she said.
The funeral was held on September third, 1955, at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ, at 4021 South State Street, about a mile southwest of here.
Over four days, the lines stretched around the block, and estimates of how many people filed past the casket run from fifty thousand to more than a hundred thousand.

Then Jet, the pocket-sized weekly published by John Johnson's company, printed photographs of Emmett's face in the casket, taken by its photographer David Jackson, in its issue of September fifteenth.
Most white newspapers wouldn't run them.
The issue sold out, and copies were passed from hand to hand across the country.
That same month, an all-white jury in Mississippi acquitted the two men after deliberating for about an hour.
A few months later, safe from being tried again, they admitted the killing to a magazine writer, who paid them for their story.
For a generation of Black Americans, those pictures were a turning point.
Rosa Parks is reported to have said that Emmett Till was on her mind that December, when she refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery.
In 2023, Roberts Temple became part of a new national monument named for Emmett Till and for his mother, who spent the rest of her life telling his story.
Walk south on Martin Luther King Drive to number 3624, a large stone house with a turret on the west side of the boulevard.
This was the home of Ida B. Wells from 1919 to 1929.
Ida B. Wells was born into slavery in Mississippi in 1862.
She became a teacher and then a journalist in Memphis, and in 1892, after three of her friends were lynched, she began investigating lynchings across the South.
Her reporting showed that the usual justifications given for lynching were usually false, and that lynching was a tool of terror to keep Black Americans down.
A mob destroyed the offices of her newspaper, and she was forced to leave Memphis.
She settled in Chicago, married a lawyer and newspaper publisher named Ferdinand Barnett, and raised a family while continuing her crusade.
She was a founding member of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, and in 1913 she founded the Alpha Suffrage Club, one of the first suffrage clubs for Black women.
When the national suffrage parade in Washington tried to make Black women march at the back, she stepped out of the crowd and joined the Illinois delegation in the front.
In 2020, she was awarded a posthumous Pulitzer Prize.

A short walk south and east, at 37th Street and Langley Avenue, on the site of the Ida B. Wells Homes public housing project, stands a monument to her by the Chicago sculptor Richard Hunt, called the Light of Truth, dedicated in 2021.
Bronzeville's writers made the neighborhood famous.
Richard Wright, who came from Mississippi, set his novel Native Son, published in 1940, in these streets.

The poet Gwendolyn Brooks, who grew up here, wrote about the kitchenette apartments and street corners of what she called Bronzeville, and in 1950 she became the first Black writer to win a Pulitzer Prize.
A few blocks southwest, at 3831 South Michigan Avenue, is the South Side Community Art Center, opened in 1940 as part of a New Deal arts program, and dedicated the next year by Eleanor Roosevelt.
It's still a working art center, the last of its kind from that program.
The fight against housing segregation was waged here too.
In 1937, a real estate broker named Carl Hansberry bought a house in a white neighborhood just south of Bronzeville, defying a covenant that banned Black residents.
His family was met with a hostile mob, and the case went all the way to the Supreme Court, which ruled in the family's favor in 1940.
His daughter, Lorraine Hansberry, drew on those memories for her play A Raisin in the Sun, which opened on Broadway in 1959, the first play by a Black woman ever produced there.
Ida B. Wells first came to Chicago for the world's fair of 1893, and she came to protest it.
The fair's organizers had shut Black Americans out of almost any real part in planning it, and out of most of its exhibits.
So Wells joined forces with Frederick Douglass, then in his seventies, to put out a pamphlet called The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition.
Douglass wrote the introduction.
Wells wrote about lynching and about the convict lease system, under which Southern states rented out prisoners, most of them Black, as forced laborers.
The lawyer Ferdinand Barnett, her future husband, and the educator Irvine Garland Penn wrote the rest.
They handed out copies at the fair's Haitian pavilion, where Douglass, a former American minister to Haiti, served as Haiti's representative.
The fair did make one gesture.
It set aside August twenty-fifth as Colored American Day.
Wells called for a boycott, dismissing the day as meaningless.
Douglass went anyway and gave a powerful speech, and Wells is said to have told him afterward that she had been too hasty.
She stayed in Chicago, and over the next four decades she built a life of activism here.
She helped found one of the first clubs for Black women in the city, which was later named for her.
In 1910, she and Barnett opened the Negro Fellowship League on State Street, a reading room, social center, and employment office for young men arriving from the South.
To keep it open, she took a job as an adult probation officer from 1913 to 1916, and she put her salary into the league.
It closed in 1920.
She never left politics.
In 1930, she ran for the Illinois Senate as an independent, and lost.
She died the next spring, in March 1931.
Her autobiography, Crusade for Justice, edited by her daughter Alfreda Duster, wasn't published until 1970, and it brought her story to a new generation.
Richard Wright came to Chicago in 1927, at nineteen, after growing up poor in Mississippi and Memphis.
He found the South Side crowded and hard.
He washed dishes, worked as a porter and a busboy, swept streets, and sorted mail as a clerk at the main post office, and when the Depression came, he lost that job and went on relief.
He also found his first readers.
Around 1933, he joined the John Reed Club, a writers' group sponsored by the Communist Party, and soon the party itself, whose magazines published his early poems.
He helped start the South Side Writers Group, a circle that included the poet Margaret Walker, and he worked for the Federal Writers' Project, helping to write a guide to Illinois.
He also worked at a boys' club on the South Side, and he wrote later that the restless, angry young men he met there were part of the model for his most famous character, Bigger Thomas.
Wright moved to New York in 1937, but Chicago stayed in his book.
In 1938, while he was writing Native Son, Chicago police arrested a young Black man named Robert Nixon for the killing of a white woman, who had been beaten with a brick during a burglary.
The Chicago Tribune covered the case in openly racist language.
Friends in Chicago sent Wright the clippings, and in his essay How Bigger Was Born, he admitted borrowing details from the coverage.
Nixon was executed in 1939.
Native Son came out in March 1940.
It was the first novel by a Black author chosen as a main selection of the Book-of-the-Month Club, and it became a best seller.
The next year, Wright won the Spingarn Medal, the highest honor of the civil rights organization that Wells had helped to found.
In 1951, a film of the novel, shot in Argentina, was released, with Wright himself, then in his early forties, playing Bigger.
By then he had moved to Paris, where he died in 1960, at fifty-two.
You heard that Carl Hansberry's fight ended at the Supreme Court.
The case, Hansberry versus Lee, is still taught in law schools, though not for the reason you might expect.
The house is at 6140 South Rhodes Avenue, about three miles south of here.
In the late 1920s, white property owners in the surrounding neighborhood had signed a restrictive covenant, a private agreement never to sell or rent to Black people.
It was to take effect only if the owners of ninety-five percent of the frontage signed it.
In an earlier lawsuit, in 1934, both sides simply agreed that enough owners had signed, and the court enforced the covenant.
In 1937, Hansberry, a successful real estate broker, bought the house and moved in with his family.
His daughter Lorraine was seven.
She later recalled the mob outside and a brick that came crashing through a window, and she wrote that her mother patrolled the house at night with a loaded pistol while her father fought in court.
A neighbor named Anna Lee sued to undo the sale.
In court, Hansberry's lawyers, led by Earl Dickerson, showed that only about fifty-four percent of the owners had actually signed.
The Illinois courts ruled against the family anyway.
The question, they said, had already been settled by the earlier case, for everyone in the neighborhood.
In November 1940, the Supreme Court unanimously reversed.
The justices didn't strike down racial covenants.
They ruled that the Hansberrys couldn't be bound by a lawsuit in which nobody had stood up for their interests, as a matter of due process.
That's why law students still study it, as a landmark in the law of class actions.
Courts kept enforcing covenants until 1948, when the Supreme Court ruled in Shelley versus Kraemer that they could no longer do so.
The fight took its toll.
Carl Hansberry began planning to move his family to Mexico, and he died there in 1946.
His daughter came to believe that American racism had helped kill him.
In 2010, the city made the house a landmark.
Walk east on 35th Street, across Cottage Grove Avenue, to the small park near the lakefront.
Here, on top of a tall granite column, stands a bronze statue of Stephen A. Douglas, one of the most powerful politicians in America before the Civil War.
He's buried in the tomb at its base.
Douglas was a senator from Illinois, nicknamed the Little Giant for his short stature and enormous energy.
He's remembered today mostly as Abraham Lincoln's great rival.

In 1858, they ran against each other for the Senate, and their seven debates across Illinois, about whether slavery should be allowed to spread into the western territories, drew huge crowds and national attention.
Douglas won the Senate seat.
Two years later, they ran for president, and Lincoln won.
When the Civil War began, Douglas rallied his supporters behind the Union.
He died in Chicago in June 1861, at forty-eight.
Douglas had an estate here, on the lake, and he gave land nearby for the first University of Chicago, founded in 1857, which went bankrupt in the 1880s.
The current university, in Hyde Park, was founded separately a few years later.
After his death, the land just west of here became Camp Douglas, a Union army training camp, and then a prison camp for captured Confederate soldiers.
Conditions were terrible, with overcrowding, cold, and disease, and thousands of prisoners died here, by some estimates more than four thousand.
Many of them are buried in a mass grave at Oak Woods Cemetery, a few miles south.
The statue on top of the column is by Leonard Volk, a sculptor who was related to Douglas by marriage.
In 1860, Volk also made a plaster life mask of Douglas's rival, Abraham Lincoln, which is one of the most accurate records we have of Lincoln's face.
Saint-Gaudens used a cast of it for the Standing Lincoln in Lincoln Park.
This is the end of the Bronzeville tour.
The law that made Douglas famous, and nearly ruined him, was the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854.

As chairman of the Senate's committee on the territories, he wanted to organize the vast prairie west of Missouri and Iowa, partly, many historians think, to clear the way for a Pacific railroad running west from Chicago.
To win Southern votes, the bill repealed the Missouri Compromise of 1820, which had banned slavery in those lands, and left the question to the settlers.
Douglas called it popular sovereignty.
The North erupted.
He was burned in effigy so often, he is supposed to have said, that he could have traveled from Boston to Chicago by the light of his own effigies.
That September, he came home to defend the law.
A huge crowd jeered and shouted him down for hours.
By one account, sometime after midnight he lost his temper and told the crowd that it was now Sunday morning, that he was going to church, and that they could go to hell.
The fury gave birth to the Republican Party, and it drew a Springfield lawyer named Abraham Lincoln back into politics.
Douglas famously said that he didn't care whether slavery was voted up or voted down.
What fewer voters knew was how much of his own family's income came from it.
In 1847, he married Martha Martin, the daughter of a North Carolina planter.
When her father died the next year, he left her a cotton plantation on the Pearl River in Mississippi, with about a hundred enslaved people, and Douglas managed it, for a share of the profits.
After Martha died in 1853, he kept drawing income from it as guardian of their two young sons, while insisting that he had never owned a slave, which was true only on paper.
Chicago is still reckoning with that legacy.

In 2020, after a campaign started by Chicago schoolchildren, the Park District took his name off Douglas Park, on the West Side, and renamed it for the abolitionists Frederick and Anna Murray Douglass.
The sound of the name stayed.
Its meaning changed completely.
By 1864, Camp Douglas, just west of here, held thousands of Confederate prisoners, and Confederate agents working out of Canada saw an opportunity.
Freed and armed, those men might set the Midwest on fire.
The plan depended on the Sons of Liberty, a secret society of Northern Democrats who opposed the war.

In August 1864, when the Democratic National Convention brought huge crowds to Chicago, a young Kentucky cavalry captain named Thomas Hines slipped into the city with a few dozen Confederate soldiers in civilian clothes, expecting the Sons of Liberty to supply hundreds of armed men.
Too few came, and the attack was called off.
They tried again in November, with the rising set for election day, when Lincoln was running for a second term.
This time the camp's commander, Colonel Benjamin Sweet, was ready.
He had informers, among them a Confederate prisoner named John Shanks, who escaped with Sweet's blessing and kept him posted on the plotters' plans.

In the early hours of November seventh, the day before the election, Sweet's soldiers swept through the city, arresting suspected conspirators and seizing hidden weapons, including dozens of double-barreled shotguns.
Among those arrested was an English soldier of fortune, George Grenfell, who had ridden with Confederate cavalry.
Sentenced to hang, he was sent instead to a remote island prison off Florida, and he vanished in 1868 trying to escape in a small boat.
Hines got away, and here the story turns into legend.
As he and his friends told it later, soldiers surrounded the house where he was hiding in the middle of the night.
He crawled inside a mattress, and the woman of the house, pretending to be gravely ill, lay on top of it while the soldiers searched.
They never found him.
Later, the story goes, he slipped out among visitors carrying umbrellas in the rain.
How dangerous was the plot, really?
Historians still argue.
Some think Sweet and the Republican newspapers inflated it, to make the Democrats look treasonous just before the vote.
Hines went home to Kentucky after the war and ended up as chief justice of the state's highest court.
Look up at the monument.
It took fifteen years to finish.
The cornerstone was laid on September sixth, 1866, by President Andrew Johnson, who had come west on a speaking tour with General Ulysses Grant in his party.
The tour, which the newspapers called the Swing Around the Circle, turned into a disaster for Johnson, who traded insults with hecklers from town to town.
Less than two years later, the House impeached him.
Douglas's body was moved into the tomb in 1868, but the monument above it rose slowly, and it wasn't finished until 1881, at a cost of about ninety thousand dollars.
The whole monument stands about ninety-six feet high.
Douglas looks out from the top of the granite column, in a statue nearly ten feet tall.
Around the base sit four figures of women, who stand for Illinois, History, Justice, and Eloquence.
Eloquence is a fitting choice.
Douglas was one of the great stump speakers of his day, a short man with a deep, booming voice that seemed far too big for his body.
Inside the base is the crypt, where Douglas lies in a sarcophagus of Vermont marble, from the state where he was born.
It's carved with what are said to be his last words, a message for his sons: Tell my children to obey the laws and uphold the Constitution.
They suit a man who spent his career trying to hold the Union together by compromise, and who spent his last weeks rallying the country to save it.
Walk around the base and look up at the figure on top once more.

The man who argued that each territory should decide the question of slavery for itself has stood here through everything that came after: the war, emancipation, the Great Migration, and the rise of the Black Metropolis all around him.
The tomb is now a state historic site and a Chicago landmark.
This tour explores Hyde Park, on the lakefront about seven miles south of the Loop.
It's home to the University of Chicago, two great parks, and some of the most important sites in American history and science.
Hyde Park began as a separate suburb in the 1850s, founded by a lawyer named Paul Cornell, who bought land here and persuaded the Illinois Central Railroad to build a station.
It was a quiet, leafy place, with summer homes and hotels along the lake.
Chicago annexed it in 1889.
Then two events transformed it.
In 1890, the University of Chicago was founded here, with money from the oil magnate John D. Rockefeller.
And in 1893, Chicago hosted the World's Columbian Exposition in Jackson Park, along the lake.
The fair celebrated the four hundredth anniversary of Columbus's voyage, a year late.
It was Chicago's announcement to the world that it had recovered from the Great Fire and become a great city.
Daniel Burnham was in charge of construction, and Frederick Law Olmsted, the designer of Central Park in New York, laid out the grounds.
At its center was the White City, a group of enormous neoclassical buildings arranged around lagoons, painted white and lit up at night with electric lights.
More than twenty-five million visits were recorded over six months.
The fair introduced visitors to the Ferris wheel, to electric lighting on a grand scale, and, according to company legend, to products like Cracker Jack and Juicy Fruit gum.
It also had a dark side.
Black Americans were largely excluded from its exhibits, and Ida B. Wells and Frederick Douglass published a pamphlet in protest.
And in Englewood, to the west, a con man named H. H. Holmes was committing murders in a building he owned.
How many people he killed, and how many of them were fairgoers, is still argued over, and the legends have grown with time.
In the twentieth century, Hyde Park became one of the most racially integrated neighborhoods in Chicago, through determined efforts by residents.
It's also the neighborhood where Barack Obama lived, taught, and began his political career.
We'll start on the lakefront at Promontory Point, walk south to the Museum of Science and Industry and through Jackson Park, and then west along the Midway to the University of Chicago.
You're on Promontory Point, a small peninsula sticking out into Lake Michigan at 55th Street, reached by a tunnel under Lake Shore Drive.
It's one of the most beloved places on the South Side.
The Point is man-made.
It was built on landfill in the 1930s, as part of a long project to extend the lakefront parks south from downtown.
The landscape was designed by Alfred Caldwell, the same landscape architect who created the Lily Pool in Lincoln Park.

Look at how he shaped it: a gentle meadow, rising toward the center, ringed with trees, with a stone field house and a small tower that looks like a lighthouse, and a council ring, a circle of stone benches meant for gathering around a fire.
And around the edge, the shoreline is armored with huge limestone blocks laid in steps down to the water.
Those steps are what Hyde Parkers love most.
On a summer day, people sit on them to sunbathe, read, picnic, and jump into the lake.
In the early 2000s, the city planned to replace the old limestone with concrete, as it had along much of the lakefront.

Neighbors fought the plan for years, arguing that the stone steps were part of the park's design and history, and the battle over the Point became a symbol of the neighborhood's stubborn independence.
Look north from the tip of the Point.
You'll see one of the best views of the Chicago skyline, rising out of the lake about seven miles away, across the curve of the shoreline.
Look south, and you'll see the dome of the Museum of Science and Industry, our next stop.
For almost twenty years, this peaceful meadow was part of the nation's defense against nuclear attack.
In the early 1950s, as the Cold War deepened, the Army began ringing American cities with Nike missile batteries, meant to shoot down Soviet bombers before they could reach their targets.
Chicago and its industrial suburbs were surrounded by them, and one of them was right here.
Each battery came in two parts: a launch area, where the missiles were kept and fired, and a control area, with radar to find the bombers and steer the missiles to them.
In Hyde Park, the launchers went into a meadow in Jackson Park, south of here near the 63rd Street beach, and the radar went onto the Point.
Picture it: behind fences and barbed wire, south of the field house, a cluster of radar towers, the tallest about a hundred and fifty feet high, sweeping the sky over the lake.
In time, the first Nike Ajax missiles gave way to the bigger Nike Hercules, which could carry nuclear warheads.
Hyde Park did not take it quietly.
In 1955, members of the Hyde Park-Kenwood Community Conference protested the radar center on the Point.
In 1961, a local branch of the Committee for a Sane Nuclear Policy protested plans to enlarge it.
During the Vietnam War the protests grew louder, and the neighborhood never stopped treating the base as an intruder in its favorite park.
By then, long-range rockets had replaced bombers as the real danger, and the batteries were growing obsolete.
The Army gave up its lease, and in 1971 the towers came down.
Hyde Parkers celebrated with a victory rally.
A few traces may linger underground.
In recent years, Army engineers have dug at the Point, searching for fuel tanks the base might have left behind.
Listen for loud, raucous chatter in the trees, and look for a flash of bright green.
Those are monk parakeets, small parrots from South America, and they've been living wild in Hyde Park for about half a century.
They come from the temperate south of that continent, from Argentina and its neighbors, where winters can turn cold.
